title: Mourinho reveals he agreed to succeed Ferguson at Manchester United in 2013 - then changed his mind
dek: In a new Netflix documentary, José Mourinho and Sir Alex Ferguson describe a secret 2013 deal for Mourinho to take over at Old Trafford, undone by a tearful phone call and a promise to Chelsea
body: José Mourinho has revealed one of the best-kept secrets of his career: in 2013, he agreed to succeed Sir Alex Ferguson as Manchester United manager, only to tear up the plan within hours and return to Chelsea instead.

The confession, first reported in Hebrew by ONE, comes from a new three-part Netflix documentary titled 'MOURINHO', which premieres globally on August 11. Ferguson himself sat for an interview and confirmed the episode from his side.
"I go to Chelsea in 2013, but in that period, there is something nobody knows," Mourinho says in the documentary, opening up about a chapter of his career he had never publicly discussed before.

According to Ferguson's account, United had lined up Mourinho as his successor after announcing his own retirement, with the Portuguese coach having just left Real Madrid. "He got the offer, yes... then, within hours, it changed," Ferguson recalled.

The Scot described receiving an emotional phone call that same evening that upended the succession plan. "Early evening, he phoned me, and he was crying," Ferguson said, describing how Mourinho backed out of the arrangement almost as soon as it was struck.

Mourinho told Ferguson directly that he could not go through with it. "Alex, I can't take it - I've given my word to Chelsea and I'm not going to break my word," he said, according to the documentary.

Mourinho explained his thinking was driven by emotion rather than ambition, after a difficult final season at the Bernabéu. "After Real Madrid, I needed to feel loved... I made a decision with my heart," he said.
United instead turned to David Moyes, who was appointed as Ferguson's successor in the summer of 2013 and lasted less than a year in the job before being dismissed.

Mourinho's second spell at Chelsea brought the Premier League title in 2014-15, but he was sacked the following season. He eventually did take charge at Old Trafford, arriving in May 2016 to replace Louis van Gaal.

His two and a half years at Manchester United yielded the Europa League and League Cup, but ended in his dismissal in December 2018 - the job he had once agreed to take, and walked away from, three years earlier.

The Netflix documentary also features interviews with John Terry, Frank Lampard, Iker Casillas, Zlatan Ibrahimović, Didier Drogba, Samuel Eto'o, Javier Zanetti and Petr Čech, charting Mourinho's career from Porto to Roma.

body: Ben Saraf's rookie summer has not silenced the skeptics. In a review of the Brooklyn Nets' crowded 2025 draft class, The Athletic's John Hollinger singled out the Israeli guard as one of the picks still searching for answers, well over a year after Brooklyn used five first-round selections in a single draft.

"Saraf's unconventional left-handed game showed some flashes, but he still isn't a threat from outside and only rarely manages to get all the way to the rim," Hollinger wrote, in Hebrew translation carried by ONE, as part of a wider verdict that the Nets "whiffed" on most of that draft class outside of Egor Demin.

The 20-year-old Saraf, taken 26th overall in 2025 out of Ratiopharm Ulm in Germany, spent this summer trying to build on a rookie season in Brooklyn. Across Summer League, split between the California Classic and Las Vegas, he averaged 10 points, 2.5 rebounds, 3.3 assists and 1.2 steals a game, shooting 37.3 percent from the field and 33.3 percent from three.

He came off the bench in four of his six Summer League outings, a sign the Nets are still working out where he fits in a backcourt that has grown suddenly congested. Hollinger's larger complaint was about efficiency: Saraf shot 14 of 36 from three-point range in that stretch, numbers that read better in isolation than they felt on the floor, where defenses rarely bent to respect his jumper.

Hollinger's critique lands at an awkward moment for Saraf, who now has to fight for minutes in Brooklyn's training camp against Mikell Brown Jr., Egor Demin and Nolan Traore — all part of the same 2025 draft haul, and all seen as needing a bigger role to justify their positions. Coach Jordi Fernández will use camp to sort out a rotation that, on paper, has more ball-handlers than playing time to go around.

None of it is fatal for Saraf, who was drafted as much for his size, vision and passing instincts as for his shot. But Hollinger's framing — flashes without a finished product — captures where the Israeli guard sits heading into his second NBA season: promising enough to matter, unproven enough to still be judged.

title: Sparta Prague ultras accused of attacking Prague Pride marchers and burning flags
dek: ONE reports that hardcore fans of the Czech champions clashed with participants at the 16th Prague Pride parade, seizing rainbow flags and setting them alight — though Czech police described the day as passing without major incident.
body: Ultras from Sparta Prague, the reigning Czech champions, attacked participants at this year's Prague Pride parade, seized flags associated with the LGBTQ+ community and burned them in public, ONE reported on Monday.

According to the Israeli outlet, the club's hardcore support group also unfurled a banner along the march route condemning the event, in what it described as the latest flashpoint in a long-running standoff between sections of the Czech capital's football fan scene and the pride community.

Saturday's march was the 16th edition of Prague Pride, staged under the slogan "Times Are Changing" and drawing an estimated 45,000 participants through the city center to Štvanice island — matching last year's turnout, according to local reporting.
ONE said Sparta's ultras have waged a years-long campaign against the LGBTQ+ community, with supporters of other Czech clubs sometimes joining the protest actions around Pride events.

Organizers and police had braced for a tense atmosphere. Security was built around hundreds of officers, including anti-riot units and dedicated conflict-prevention teams, with the heightened presence coming weeks after a car-ramming attack at Berlin's Christopher Street Day Pride festival on July 26 killed one woman and injured around 29 people. Marchers in Prague observed a minute of silence for the victims.

Notably, other coverage of Saturday's parade struck a different tone. A Prague police spokeswoman told local media that officers "did not encounter any significant complications" during the more than two-hour event, and reporting from Czech and English-language outlets on the day described scattered religious protesters and a pro-Palestinian demonstration along the route, without mentioning an organized confrontation involving Sparta supporters. That discrepancy could not be resolved by the time of publication, and readers should treat the specifics of ONE's account with appropriate caution pending further confirmation.

Whatever the scale of Saturday's incident, it fits a pattern for Sparta's support base, which has repeatedly drawn disciplinary and public attention this year. In May, a Prague derby against city rivals Slavia was abandoned in stoppage time after fans invaded the pitch and threw pyrotechnics, with several Sparta players targeted, prompting the Czech league's disciplinary body to warn that "such behavior will not be tolerated in professional football."

Sparta have also previously been fined by UEFA over supporter misconduct, and the club has had to publicly push back on accusations of fan behavior toward opposing players in recent European campaigns.

Prague Pride organizers have framed this year's march as carrying extra weight given the Berlin attack, casting the event as a statement of visibility and resilience rather than retreat — a backdrop against which any confrontation with football ultras lands with particular force.

title: CSKA Sofia beat Septemvri Sofia 3-0 as Yanev manages squad before Maccabi Tel Aviv return leg
dek: The Bulgarian champions rotated heavily in Sunday's league win, but a first-half injury to defender Angelo Martino leaves a fitness doubt three days before Thursday's Europa League second leg against Maccabi Tel Aviv.

body: CSKA Sofia already hold a commanding grip on their Europa League tie with Maccabi Tel Aviv, and it showed in how lightly Hristo Yanev treated Sunday's domestic fixture. The Bulgarian champions rotated heavily against Septemvri Sofia in the Parva Liga and still won comfortably, 3-0, with an eye squarely on Thursday's return leg.

ONE reports that Yanev mixed regulars with fringe players throughout, deliberately managing minutes rather than chasing a statement performance three days before Maccabi arrive in Sofia. It worked: CSKA never looked troubled and closed the game out with room to spare.

The one blemish was an injury scare. Left-back Angelo Martino, who started the first leg against Maccabi in Batumi, was withdrawn in the 19th minute as a precaution, and his fitness for Thursday is now in question.
"We took Martino off as a precaution," Yanev said, according to ONE. "I hope we'll be able to use him in Thursday's important match against Maccabi Tel Aviv."

The coach also addressed the club's packed fixture list, with a European tie sandwiched between league rounds. "Right now we're not thinking about postponing matches," he said. "We're finding our rhythm, and I hope we continue that way."

CSKA go into the second leg with a significant cushion. The Bulgarians won the first leg 3-0 on August 6 in Batumi, Georgia — Maccabi's adopted home ground for European fixtures — in the Europa League's third qualifying round, putting the tie almost out of reach for the Israeli champions.
Thursday's return leg kicks off at 21:00 in Sofia, with CSKA needing only to avoid a heavy defeat to progress to the play-off round and keep their own European ambitions alive.

For Maccabi, already facing long odds after the first-leg mauling, the sight of their opponents rotating freely in domestic action — and still winning at a canter — is hardly the news they wanted three days out.

title: Health Ministry calls on public to donate blood amid shortage
dek: Director-General Moshe Bar Siman Tov urges Israelis to give blood as Magen David Adom reports a decline in national reserves, especially type O.
body: Israel's Health Ministry and Magen David Adom have issued a public appeal for blood donations after reporting a decline in national blood-supply reserves, with a particular shortage of type O blood, the universal donor type.

Health Ministry Director-General Moshe Bar Siman Tov said blood is needed daily for surgeries, births, routine medical treatment and emergency care, as well as for treating soldiers wounded in the ongoing conflict.

"Blood donation is a simple act that saves lives, and is part of our mutual responsibility in routine and emergency situations," Bar Siman Tov said, calling on the public to visit Magen David Adom donation centers.
Those who last donated more than three months ago were specifically encouraged to return, with the ministry saying reserves need to be replenished on an ongoing basis to keep pace with demand.

title: Colorado Rapids' $6 million bid for Maccabi Tel Aviv's Abu Farhi still unresolved
dek: The MLS side are pushing for a breakthrough in talks for the 20-year-old forward, but personal terms and a family stake in his economic rights remain unsettled.

verificationSources.label: Yahoo Sports — Herrington to Hull City fee

body: Colorado Rapids have opened talks for Sayed Abu Farhi, but the Maccabi Tel Aviv forward's move to MLS is far from done. ONE reported on Monday that the American club are hoping to force a breakthrough during the day, with an offer of roughly $6 million already on the table.

Maccabi's board has so far rejected that opening bid and is continuing to push for a higher fee, according to the report, unwilling to sanction the sale of one of the more promising products of its youth system without a fight over the price.

Abu Farhi himself has yet to agree personal terms with the Rapids, ONE added. There is a further complication too: 17.5 percent of the player's economic rights are held by his family, a stake that will also need to be settled before any transfer can be finalized.

Time is not unlimited. Should the deal not come together by Wednesday, the report said, Abu Farhi will instead travel with Maccabi Tel Aviv's squad for their Europa League qualifying assignment against CSKA Sofia rather than push ahead with a move.

Maccabi reached this stage of the competition in emphatic fashion, beating Moldova's Sheriff Tiraspol 6-0 on aggregate in the previous round. The first leg against CSKA Sofia was played in Batumi, Georgia, on August 6, with Israeli clubs currently barred from hosting European fixtures at home under UEFA's restrictions.

Colorado's aggression in the market is underpinned by fresh funds elsewhere. The Rapids recently agreed to sell teenage defender Lucas Herrington to Hull City in a deal that could be worth up to $23 million with add-ons — among the largest sales in MLS history — giving the club's front office room to spend on reinforcements this summer.

Abu Farhi, 20, has established himself this season as a regular in Maccabi Tel Aviv's attack, scoring seven goals and adding three assists in Ligat ha'Al. Primarily a central striker who can also play off the left, he has represented Israel at U17, U19 and U21 level.

For now, nothing is signed. Monday's deadline for a breakthrough belongs to Colorado, not Maccabi — and the Israeli club could yet send Abu Farhi to Sofia with the rest of the squad while talks continue in parallel.

body: Beitar Jerusalem have moved to secure one of their most promising academy prospects, signing right-back and winger Itay Deel to a three-year contract, according to a report from ONE.
Deel, who turns 15 in September, has spent six seasons inside the Beitar Jerusalem youth system and has established himself as one of his age group's captains, the report said.

His breakout campaign explains the club's eagerness to tie him down. In the 2025/26 season he made 31 appearances across all competitions, contributing seven goals and 12 assists in 1,911 minutes on the pitch - a marked rise from his 2024/25 return of 11 goals and 15 assists.

The youth side he features for reached the semi-final of the State Cup in their category this past season before their run ended with a 3-1 defeat to Maccabi Netanya.

The signing keeps Deel inside Beitar's development pipeline as the club continues to lean on its academy production line, with the Jerusalem side hoping his form as a teenage captain translates into a route toward senior football in the coming years.

title: Cycling, athletics and taekwondo unions cry foul over new equipment fund criteria
dek: Israeli sports federations say a revived Ministry of Culture and Sport grant is scoring applicants by their home municipality's statistics rather than the equipment they actually need.
body: Several of Israel's Olympic-sport unions are protesting the way the Ministry of Culture and Sport is handing out a revived equipment-purchase fund, arguing the new scoring model rewards where a club's town sits on a national statistics table rather than what gear its athletes actually need, ONE reports.

The fund is worth 60 million shekels a year and had sat dormant for four years before the ministry restarted it, releasing the first 30 million shekel tranche under a new "ongoing competitive" model published this week, according to the report. Clubs and unions applied, and are now, per the ministry's own account, in the appeals stage.

The complaint, as relayed by ONE, is about the yardstick rather than the money itself. Instead of weighing an association's actual level of activity or how many athletes it serves, applications are being ranked largely by the Central Bureau of Statistics' socio-economic cluster rating of the municipality where the club or union is registered.

That has produced what unions call an absurd outcome: clubs based in strong, central cities such as Tel Aviv and Jerusalem are being turned down for equipment funding even when their need is genuine, simply because their home authority scores well on the national index.

"Most associations from strong cities in the center of the country that have needed equipment for years aren't eligible for the budget," one association manager told ONE, speaking anonymously. "It turns out we're being judged on a statistical figure and not on the substance of what we do, and that's disappointing."
Israel's Cycling Union, Athletics Union and Taekwondo Union are among the bodies named in the report as having had applications rejected under the new criteria.

Yehuda Maayan, chairman of the Taekwondo Union, was the most pointed critic quoted. "The new fund doesn't suit this period," he said. "It strips most unions of the right to purchase equipment." He also questioned the fund's own branding, asking why a model that filters applicants by municipal statistics rather than merit is being called "competitive" at all.

The Ministry of Culture and Sport, responding to ONE, said the model was designed and vetted properly: it went through a public-comment period and was approved by the National Sports Council before being published for the first time since 2022. The ministry noted that with applications now in, the process is currently at the appeals stage — leaving open the possibility that rejected unions could still see funding released if their objections are upheld.

For federations such as taekwondo, which has repeatedly flagged threadbare training budgets and equipment shortages even after producing an Olympic bronze medallist in Tokyo, the stakes in getting the criteria right are not abstract. A union locked out of a national equipment fund has few other places to turn for the basics — protective gear, mats, training equipment — that keep a small-budget sport running.

ONE's report does not detail how many applications were rejected in total or give a full breakdown of the scoring formula beyond the municipal statistics component, and the ministry has not yet said whether the criteria will be revised. The appeals process now under way is likely to determine whether any of the rejected unions receive funding from this first tranche.

title: Hapoel Lod chairman hit with restraining order over lawyer death threats
dek: Ophir Regev, who leads the lower-division club, denies sending the messages after attorney Ohad Cohen reported threats linked to Hapoel Lod's unpaid arbitration debts.

verificationSources.label: Hapoel Lod Beni Regev — Hebrew Wikipedia

body: A court has issued a restraining order against Ophir Regev, chairman of lower-division club Hapoel Lod Beni Regev, after a sports lawyer accused him of threatening his life during a dispute over the club's unpaid debts, ONE reported.

Attorney Ohad Cohen, who co-chairs the Israel Bar Association's law-and-sport committee, told police he received threatening text messages last Thursday night, shortly before 11pm, tied to his role in blocking Hapoel Lod's registration for the 2026/27 season.

Cohen represents clients owed money by the club under arbitration rulings that Hapoel Lod has still not paid. Israeli clubs cannot register squads for a new season while such debts are outstanding, and the deadline to do so was fast approaching — Monday at 5pm — when the messages arrived, according to ONE.
Cohen filed a police complaint that same evening, consulting the Bar Association before doing so. Within hours, a restraining order was granted barring Regev from approaching him.
"Red lines have been crossed," Cohen said, according to ONE. "Threatening a lawyer's life for doing his job is a serious crime."
Regev denied any involvement when put to him by ONE. "I have no idea what you're talking about," he said. "If he finds one message from me in the last two years, I'll go to jail myself."

The order threatens to complicate a hearing due before the Israel Football Association's court this week, where Cohen and Regev were both set to appear over the same registration dispute — a session ONE said may now need to be postponed.

Hapoel Lod took the Beni Regev name in 2024 in tribute to Ophir Regev's late father, the club's longtime chairman and a dominant figure in Lod football for decades. Ophir Regev has led the club in the years since.

title: What would it cost you to watch Israel's stars play abroad this season?
dek: From a $7 seat in Washington to a $684 night at Selhurst Park, ONE surveyed ticket prices for every club now employing an Israeli international.
body: Following the Israeli contingent scattered across European and North American football is no longer a niche pursuit, but doing it in person carries wildly different price tags depending on which end of the map you're standing at. A survey published by ONE this week put hard numbers on the gap, comparing ticket prices at every club now employing an Israeli international.

The cheapest way in, by some distance, is MLS. Tai Baribo, who scored the winner on his D.C. United debut against his old club Philadelphia Union earlier this year, plays in front of fans who can get through the gate at Audi Field from as little as $7, with a typical resale price around $13 and an average across the market of roughly $66.

New England Revolution, home to defender Ilay Feingold and forward Dor Turgeman, aren't far behind: tickets start around $10.20, with a typical price near $16 and an average of about $99. Charlotte FC, where Liel Abada and Idan Toklomati now play, sit a little higher again, with a typical seat around $30 and an average closer to $102.

FC Dallas, who signed Israeli Premier League title-winning midfielder Ran Binyamin from Hapoel Tel Aviv this year, complete the American picture — MLS remains, across the board, the most affordable place to watch an Israeli abroad.

Cross the Atlantic and the numbers climb sharply. West Ham, who this month agreed a deal to sign Manor Solomon from Tottenham, offer the cheapest route into a Premier League ground among the clubs surveyed: a typical ticket around $67 and an average of about $125, though ONE notes the cheapest individual fixture on their calendar can be found for as little as $45.

Daniel Peretz's Southampton is next up the scale. The Israeli goalkeeper, who impressed enough on loan last season to earn a permanent four-year deal from Bayern Munich reportedly worth around £6 million, now plays in front of fans paying a typical $95 and an average of roughly $144 for a home ticket.

Oscar Gloukh's move to Ajax last year has proven the priciest regular fixture for Israeli fans wanting to watch from the stands: a typical Johan Cruyff Arena ticket runs about $115, with the average across the market reaching some $353 — by far the steepest of any club surveyed on a game-by-game basis.

But no single club tops the list once opponent is factored in. Anan Khalaili's arrival at Crystal Palace — a deal ONE and Sport5 both report is close to being finalised after his move from Union Saint-Gilloise collapsed at Inter over a heart-rhythm irregularity found in his medical — puts him on course to play at Selhurst Park against Arsenal, a fixture ONE lists as the single most expensive ticket in the entire survey, averaging around $684.

As one industry expert quoted in the report put it, the identity of the opponent moves the price far more than the identity of the home club itself, capable of pushing entry costs up by a factor of twelve or more depending on the visiting side's pull.

Put together, the picture is a reminder of just how far Israeli football's export list has spread this year — from a Championship promotion battle on the south coast of England to an MLS play-off race in Texas — and of how differently each of those leagues prices a night watching one of their own.
facts: West Ham, who agreed to sign Manor Solomon from Tottenham, offer a typical home ticket around $67 and an average of about $125, the cheapest typical price among the European clubs surveyed.
Daniel Peretz's Southampton, where he signed a permanent four-year deal after a loan spell, has a typical ticket price of about $95 and an average of roughly $144.
Oscar Gloukh's Ajax has the highest average ticket price among clubs surveyed on a per-game basis, at around $353, despite a typical price of about $115.

New England Revolution (Ilay Feingold, Dor Turgeman), Charlotte FC (Liel Abada, Idan Toklomati) and FC Dallas (Ran Binyamin) also field Israeli internationals in MLS.

title: Ironi Tiberias hand youth department to a staff of homegrown coaches
dek: Kfir Ben David becomes professional director as the Ligat Ha'al club fills 11 coaching and support posts almost entirely with former Tiberias players ahead of 2026/27.

body: Ironi Tiberias have rebuilt their youth department from the ground up ahead of the 2026/27 season, naming Kfir Ben David as professional director in a reshuffle that hands almost every coaching post to people with roots in the club, ONE reports.

Ben David, who has coached in Tiberias's youth ranks before, keeps a foot on the touchline as well as in the office: alongside the administrative brief, he remains head coach of the club's top representative Youth team.

Underneath him, the department has been restructured across its age-group sides. Eitan Pchima takes charge of the Youth A team, Mushiko Asor the Youth B side, and Roei Sarah both coaches Youth C and coordinates the club's academy programme.

Adi Tadmor has been appointed goalkeeping coach across the department, while Shalo Ochana joins as the youth section's analyst - a role increasingly common at clubs looking to professionalise their development pathway.

The three children's age-groups have also been filled: Shlomi Ben David takes Children A, Niv Suyba Children B and Matan Dagni Children C, rounding out an 11-strong staff alongside fitness coach Bar Nikton and operations manager Shlomi Chachmon.
The common thread, according to the club, is background: the large majority of the new appointees are former Tiberias players who came up through the same age-groups they will now coach.

"The future of Ironi Tiberias begins here," the club said in a statement carried by ONE, describing the group as "professionals with one clear goal: developing players, nurturing excellence, and building the club's next generation."

The overhaul comes as Tiberias prepare for another season in Ligat Ha'al, Israel's top flight - a reminder that for a smaller-budget club, a well-staffed academy built on homegrown coaches is as much a competitive necessity as a sentimental choice.

title: Israeli athletics body's excuse-laden statement on U20 worlds flops draws fire
dek: The Israeli Athletics Association's wrap-up of a disappointing showing in Eugene leaned on a string of explanations, from missing poles to early starts, that critics say dodge the real story.

verificationSources.label: World Athletics - Oregon26 men's high jump qualification

body: The Israeli Athletics Association's own summary of its team's showing at the World Athletics U20 Championships in Eugene was supposed to be a routine recap. Instead, ONE reports, it read as a list of justifications for a difficult week, and the framing has drawn criticism from within the sport rather than the sympathy the federation may have hoped for.

The championships ran August 5-9 at the University of Oregon's Hayward Field, drawing well over a thousand athletes from more than 140 national teams. Israel's junior squad came home without the medals or breakthrough results some had hoped for, and the association's statement tried to account for why, event by event.

The most pointed case involves pole vaulter Jordan Mantel, who failed to clear her opening height of 3.80 metres in qualifying. According to the association's own account, she competed without her personal poles after a mix-up on the federation's end, competing instead under what it described as "less than ideal conditions."

That explanation did not land well with Mantel herself. She had already pushed back publicly on an earlier version of the federation's account of the pole mishap, calling it a whitewashed retelling of what actually happened rather than a straight accounting of the error.

In the women's and men's 400m hurdles, Hila Varsano and Gal Nathanel both missed out on the semi-finals, each running slower than their personal bests. The association pointed to the early-morning slot for the preliminary heats as a factor working against the Israelis' chances of peaking.

Liam Akwa, the Israeli under-20 record holder over the hurdles, also fell short of his own benchmarks. He clocked 10.62 seconds in the 100m, off his personal best of 10.39, and in the 110m hurdles finished two hundredths of a second slower than the national junior record he set earlier this year, again without progressing to the next round despite a promising position.

High jumper Joshua Harel produced the closest thing to a bright spot, clearing 2.14 metres in qualifying to advance among the top twelve, then improving to 2.17 metres in the final for eighth place. He picked up an iliopsoas (hip-flexor) injury during that 2.17m attempt, the association said.

Taken individually, each explanation is plausible enough - a scheduling quirk here, a piece of misplaced equipment there, a niggling injury. Strung together in a single statement, ONE's framing suggests, they read less like context and more like an institution unwilling to simply say the championships did not go well.

For an athlete of Mantel's stature, the added friction with the federation over how the pole vault episode was described is likely to keep the story alive beyond a single results wrap-up, especially with the outdoor season and future selection decisions still ahead.

title: Khalaili could win a starting spot at Crystal Palace under new boss Pierre Sage
dek: The Israeli winger, closing in on a move that would make him the country's most expensive footballer ever, may open the season ahead of free-transfer signing Óscar Mingueza in Palace's back three, with Daniel Muñoz expected to leave.
body: Anan Khalaili is closing in on a move to Crystal Palace, and with the transfer all but agreed, ONE has turned its attention to a sharper question: will the Israeli winger actually start for the newly crowned European trophy holders, or spend his first Premier League season fighting for minutes?

Khalaili, 21, is set to leave Union Saint-Gilloise for a fee in the region of €28-30 million, according to reporting from Ynet, N12 and ONE — a figure that would make him the most expensive Israeli player in the sport's history. Crystal Palace are yet to confirm the deal, but Israeli and English outlets alike describe it as effectively done, with a signing expected within days.

The move follows a summer of turbulence. A transfer to Inter Milan, agreed at a similar fee, collapsed at the last moment after Khalaili reportedly failed the Italian club's medical examinations, with an irregularity picked up in his heart rhythm. Palace's interest emerged soon after and has moved quickly since.

He arrives at an unusually good moment for the south London club. Palace, founded in 1905 and long a model of self-sustaining, sell-to-buy football, won both the FA Cup and the UEFA Conference League in the 2025/26 season and will play in the Europa League this coming campaign — a first taste of continental football for many of the squad.

The manager who built that side, Oliver Glasner, left in the summer and has been replaced by Pierre Sage, who arrives from Ligue 1 side Lens after winning that division's Manager of the Year award. Sage has kept the back-three, 3-4-3 shape Glasner used to such effect, which is central to how ONE frames Khalaili's prospects: the system needs an athletic, attack-minded body in the right wing-back slot, and that happens to be Khalaili's best position.

His most direct competition there is Óscar Mingueza, a 27-year-old Spanish defender who joined Palace on a free transfer from Celta Vigo in July — Sage's first signing as manager. A La Masia graduate with Barcelona first-team experience, Mingueza is comfortable at right-back, left-back or as a third centre-back, giving Sage license to use both players at once rather than treat it as a straight either-or.

ONE's assessment is that Khalaili's attacking instincts and directness suit what Sage wants from that role more naturally than Mingueza's more conventional defensive profile, which could hand the Israeli an early advantage for the starting shirt even as a newcomer to the Premier League.

The picture is complicated further by Daniel Muñoz, the Colombian who has been one of Palace's standout performers at right-back and wing-back over the past two seasons. ONE's report says the club expects him to leave amid interest from elsewhere in Europe, with the outlet putting Palace's valuation of him as high as €50 million — sale proceeds that would help fund the Khalaili deal and open the very slot he is being lined up to fill.

Khalaili made his name in Belgium over two seasons at Union Saint-Gilloise, contributing six goals and six assists in 52 appearances last season while also representing Israel's senior national team. His versatility — comfortable as a winger, wing-back or full-back — is precisely what has made him attractive to a club like Palace that prizes tactical flexibility over rigid specialism.

Nothing is confirmed yet in terms of a starting shirt, and pre-season form and fitness will ultimately decide what Sage does. But the combination of Muñoz's likely exit, Mingueza's positional flexibility and a system that rewards exactly Khalaili's skill set means the Israeli could be thrown into Palace's first team from the opening weeks of the season, not eased in from the bench.

body: Hapoel Petah Tikva's pre-season has produced a promising league finish to build on and a Toto Cup campaign that has done little to inspire confidence, and now a club source has admitted openly what the results have suggested for weeks: Omer Peretz's squad is too thin to compete on the level the club is aiming for.

"The league will look better, because we also weren't fully connected in the Toto Cup last year either," the source told ONE. "But there's no question that three or four more players have to arrive here — it's screaming out for it, so that we have options and a deeper squad."

The comments followed a 3-1 defeat to Hapoel Jerusalem on Sunday in the teams' final Toto Cup group match, in which Nir Daffa scored twice for the winners and Yzan Nasar turned the ball into his own net for Petah Tikva, who could only pull one back through Avishay Cohen.

It was the latest underwhelming display in a competition Peretz's players have never taken too seriously, but the club source's message was less about the cup itself than about the size of the group heading into the new Ligat Ha'al season.

The stakes are real. Peretz, who signed a contract extension through 2027/28 after leading Petah Tikva up from the second division and then, last season, into the top-six playoff for the first time in more than two decades, now has to defend that standing with a squad short on depth in key positions.

Defender Alex Musonda, who put pen to paper on a new two-year deal at HaMoshava Stadium, is only just back in full training after a hamstring strain, and it remains unclear whether he will be fit for the upcoming Toto Cup fixture away to Bnei Sakhnin.

The most advanced piece of transfer business hangs on a decision in Ukraine: Bolivian centre-back Diego Arroyo, signed by Shakhtar Donetsk from Bolívar for a reported seven-figure sum last year, will only be released to join Petah Tikva if the paperwork clears before the club moves on to alternative options at the back.

Two more names are on the club's list. Maccabi Haifa's Itay Ahuod, who is also drawing interest from Hapoel Jerusalem, and Maccabi Tel Aviv's 19-year-old midfield prospect Lotam Asers, who scored heavily in the youth leagues over the past two seasons, remain candidates for a loan move to Petah Tikva.
The club is hoping to have at least one of those deals done before the week is out, with time running short before the league campaign begins in earnest.

title: Liverpool 2-3 Monaco: Iraola admits his side lack the energy for 90 minutes on Anfield bow
dek: The new Liverpool manager saw a two-goal lead vanish in his first match in charge at Anfield, and conceded afterwards that his squad's match fitness still has a way to go.
body: Andoni Iraola's first game in the Anfield dugout was supposed to be a gentle pre-season formality. Instead, Liverpool blew a two-goal lead and lost 3-2 to Monaco, and the new head coach walked out afterwards to admit, bluntly, that his players simply cannot last a full match yet.

Liverpool were excellent for most of the first half. Alexander Isak opened the scoring in the 16th minute and Florian Wirtz doubled the lead in the 29th, giving the Anfield crowd an early glimpse of the front two Iraola inherited from Arne Slot's title-winning squad. Monaco pulled one back right on the stroke of half-time when Aleksandr Golovin converted a penalty in the 44th minute.

The second half belonged entirely to the visitors. Mika Biereth levelled in the 56th minute and Paris Brunner completed the turnaround with a late strike in the 88th, sending Iraola to defeat in front of his own supporters for the first time.

"Those who played their first or second match showed energy — the problem is that right now they probably don't have the energy for 90 minutes," Iraola said afterwards, quoted by ONE. He added that Liverpool had produced "a good first half" but lacked "much more" once the intensity was required for a full 90.

The Basque coach made wholesale changes at the interval, a pattern he has followed throughout pre-season as he tries to build up conditioning across the squad rather than chase clean results in friendlies. It meant a Liverpool side that looked sharp and cohesive for 45 minutes was unrecognisable by the final whistle.

It is not an isolated problem. A week earlier, on their pre-season swing through the United States, Liverpool led Leeds United 2-0 at half-time before collapsing to a 4-2 defeat, conceding three times inside 13 second-half minutes as their opponents introduced fresh legs off the bench. Iraola later described that defeat as the most "useful" of the tour precisely because of what it exposed.

The recurring theme — a bright first half undone by a second-half fade — is now the central concern of Iraola's early tenure. He took over at Anfield in June, succeeding Arne Slot, and has been open throughout the summer about needing time to adapt his squad, tactically and physically, to the demands he expects.

Sunday's defeat was still only a friendly, and Iraola's priority in these matches has been minutes and fitness over results. But with the Premier League season about to begin, twice losing a two-goal cushion in the space of a week is the kind of pattern he will want to have eliminated well before it starts to cost points that count.

title: Aviv Barzelay and Tom Minis advance to 200m backstroke semi-finals at European Championships

body: Israel had two swimmers through to the evening semi-finals of the 200 metres backstroke on the opening day of the pool programme at the European Aquatics Championships in Paris, with Aviv Barzelay and Tom Minis both coming through Monday morning's heats at the Centre Aquatique Olympique in Saint-Denis, ONE reports.

Barzelay, the Tokyo 2020 Olympian, went 10th fastest overall in a time of 2:11.55 to book her semi-final place. Minis, 21, followed her into the next round after touching in 2:12.40 - a personal best, according to the report.

The pair's progress came on the first day of a swimming programme that runs at the purpose-built venue in Saint-Denis through August 16, as the centennial European Aquatics Championships move into their pool phase after weeks of open-water, diving and artistic swimming events elsewhere in Paris.

Israel's team had a mixed morning elsewhere in the same session. In the men's 50m butterfly heats, none of Miron Haruti, Martin Kartabi, Michael Leytrovsky or Tom Sale advanced, with Kartabi's 23.77 a personal best despite falling short of the semi-final cut, ONE reported.

There was also no progression for Israel in the women's 100m freestyle, where Daria Golovati and Leah Polonsky were eliminated in the heats, and in the men's 100m breaststroke, where Mark Teller shaved his own personal best down to 1:00.80 but did not advance.

The best individual news of the morning outside the backstroke came in the pool's team events: Israel's men's 4x200m freestyle relay quartet qualified directly for the final, going through with the fourth-fastest time of the morning in 7:06.71, per ONE.
Barzelay and Minis will return to the pool on Monday evening for the 200m backstroke semi-finals, looking to build on the morning's swims and push for a place in the final later in the week.

body: Maccabi Petah Tikva finally have something to smile about in the Toto Cup. The Israeli top-flight club beat Hapoel Ramat Gan 2-1 on Sunday night to close out the group stage with their first win of the competition, after opening with three straight defeats.

The result lifted Maccabi Petah Tikva to third in their group table, and while it came too late to change their standing in the pre-season tournament, the club felt it was a meaningful marker ahead of the league campaign.

With a fuller squad available, Petah Tikva looked a different side. Ghanaian winger Samuel Owusu was again the team's central attacking threat and drew praise for his performance, while English midfield signing Kyle Spence showed his first real flashes of quality in the win.

"When we're together with the full squad for a longer stretch, we'll look a lot better. Another player joining will push us forward. In the end this win gave a bit of a good feeling, but the league is what matters most," the club said, according to ONE.

Eitan Taibi is expected to make his first appearance of the pre-season this weekend when Maccabi Petah Tikva face Ironi Tiberias, while midfielder Li-Yam Dan, who has been working back from injury, could also be included in the squad for that game.
Ariel Lugasi's return was another welcome sight at the club — the player was back involved with the squad after going a full year without any official minutes.

Petah Tikva are also still working the transfer market. As previously reported, the club expects to complete the signing of midfielder Yoav Koren once Hapoel Be'er Sheva's European fixture against Red Star Belgrade is out of the way, with the move targeted for before the end of the week.

One deal that appears to be off, however, is a move for Noam Schwartz. Petah Tikva had wanted the player to fill their right-back slot, but he is instead expected to sign for Hapoel Ramat Gan — the very team Petah Tikva beat on Sunday.

title: Maccabi Tel Aviv recalls center Shane Hunter from his loan spell at Legia Warsaw
dek: The 25-year-old American, signed to a three-year deal last summer, will now try to break into Oded Kattash's rotation after a season sharpening his game in Poland.
body: Maccabi Tel Aviv have ended Shane Hunter's loan spell early, recalling the 25-year-old center-forward from Legia Warsaw and folding him straight into Oded Kattash's preseason roster, the club confirmed via ONE on Sunday.

Hunter, a 2.08-metre American big man, signed a three-year contract with Maccabi in the summer of 2025 but was immediately sent out on loan for a season of continued development rather than joining the parent club's rotation right away.

That loan took him to Legia Warsaw in the Polish league, where he posted solid numbers: 9.2 points per game on 63 percent shooting from inside the arc, five rebounds and 1.3 blocks a night. In the Basketball Champions League he averaged 8.8 points and 6.5 rebounds per game.

"He completes a deep and versatile frontcourt for us," Kattash said of the recall, according to the report. "He gained important experience in Europe last season. He is a big man who moves very well without the ball, shoots at a high percentage from two-point range, rebounds well, is highly mobile in the pick-and-roll and affects opposing shots with his blocking."

Before joining Maccabi, Hunter built his reputation with Norrköping Dolphins in Sweden, where in his rookie professional season he averaged 14.3 points and 8.6 rebounds across 30 regular-season games, then lifted his output to 16.4 points per game in the finals as the club won its fifth consecutive Swedish league title.
A New York native, Hunter played his college basketball at Nova Southeastern University before turning professional in Scandinavia and eventually landing on Maccabi's radar.

With the loan now over, Hunter gets his first real chance to make Maccabi's roster for the coming EuroLeague and Israeli Premier League season, competing for minutes in a frontcourt Kattash has been steadily reshaping heading into the new campaign.

title: UEFA, AFC and CONCACAF accuse Infantino of 'deception' over World Cup rights sale
dek: In an extraordinary joint letter, football's three most powerful confederations tell FIFA president Gianni Infantino he placed himself above the game he was entrusted to serve, and demand a fully independent inquiry into his abandoned plan to sell a stake in World Cup commercial rights.
body: UEFA, the Asian Football Confederation and CONCACAF have taken the extraordinary step of jointly accusing FIFA president Gianni Infantino of "deception," publishing an open letter on Monday that amounts to the sharpest and most coordinated challenge to his authority since he took charge of world football's governing body a decade ago, ONE reported.

The letter was signed by UEFA president Aleksander Čeferin, AFC president Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa and CONCACAF president Victor Montagliani, along with the three confederations' general secretaries. Between them, UEFA, the AFC and CONCACAF represent the overwhelming majority of the world's national football associations and clubs.

At the heart of the dispute is a now-scrapped FIFA plan, reportedly floated in late July under the name FIFA Forward Enterprise, to sell an interest of roughly 20 percent in a new company that would commercialize World Cup and other major tournament rights, in a deal said to be worth in the region of $4.2 billion to private investors.

The confederations' letter calls the episode a "profound failure of judgment" and a "fundamental breach of trust" with the football institutions FIFA is meant to serve. In its most pointed passage, it states: "When trust is broken through deception, when an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority, that duty has been abandoned."

Rather than accept an internal FIFA review of how the plan was drawn up and nearly pushed through, the three confederations are demanding a fully independent investigation carried out by outside parties, with no role for FIFA's own administration or staff.

The letter also raises pointed questions about a leadership meeting held in Morocco during the affair, noting that only FIFA management figures were present and that no elected FIFA Council members or representatives of member associations were invited — a detail the confederations frame as symptomatic of a wider breakdown in consultation.

FIFA abandoned the World Cup rights sale at the end of July after the plan drew fierce internal opposition, but Monday's letter shows the confederations are not satisfied that the retreat settles the matter. They want to know how the proposal got as far as it did without their knowledge.

The pressure on Infantino has been building for weeks. UEFA has separately confirmed it served FIFA with a legal "preservation" letter, a formal step that keeps open the option of further legal action over the collapsed deal.

"Football's strength has always been in its unity, and we call on leaders to serve the game instead of trying to control it," the confederations wrote, in a line that reads as a direct rebuke of Infantino's leadership style after nearly ten years in the FIFA presidency.

It is an unprecedented alignment of continental power against a sitting FIFA president, and one that leaves Infantino facing simultaneous pressure from Europe, Asia and North and Central America over how — and for whose benefit — football's most valuable commercial asset, the World Cup, is run.

title: Amit Arazi signs new contract with Maccabi Haifa after loan spell
dek: The academy product, who spent last season on loan at Hapoel Kfar Saba, has committed to a further two years with the option of two more.
body: Maccabi Haifa have tied down one of their own academy graduates, confirming that midfielder Amit Arazi has signed a new contract that runs for two years with the club holding an option for a further two, ONE reports.

It is a reward for patience on both sides. Arazi, a defensive midfielder who wears the No. 31 shirt, joined Maccabi Haifa's youth setup at the age of eight and worked his way through every rung of the club's development ladder before breaking into the senior squad roughly two years ago.
Last season he was sent out on loan to Hapoel Kfar Saba, where he picked up regular first-team minutes that the Haifa hierarchy believes have sharpened him into a more complete player.

"Maccabi is my home since I was a small child," Arazi said after putting pen to paper. "I'm very excited to sign a long-term contract, and I'll do everything I can to prove myself and help the team achieve its goals."

The club's professional director, Lior Refaelof, credited the loan move for accelerating the 21-year-old's progress. He said Arazi had shown "excellent growth" during his time away and returned to Haifa a sharper player, adding that the club was "very satisfied with the ability he displayed in training camp" ahead of the new season.

The new deal ends any lingering uncertainty over his future, after Arazi had been the subject of loan interest from other Israeli clubs in the past. For Maccabi Haifa, keeping him in-house fits a broader pattern this summer of prioritizing academy graduates as the squad is reshaped under Slobodan Drapic.

title: Hapoel Tel Aviv basketball map out pre-season tour through Bulgaria, Serbia and Sardinia
dek: Dimitrios Itoudis's side face Balkan Botevgrad, Partizan Belgrade, FMP and a Cagliari tournament field including Bayern Munich before the Israeli Super Cup and a Sofia-hosted EuroLeague opener.

verificationSources.label: FIP Sardegna (Italian Basketball Federation, Sardinia committee)

body: Hapoel Tel Aviv's basketball team have mapped out a pre-season itinerary that will take Dimitrios Itoudis's squad through three countries in barely three weeks, ONE reported, ahead of a competitive schedule that opens with two heavyweight fixtures in quick succession.
The trip begins in Bulgaria, where Hapoel will play BC Balkan Botevgrad twice — on August 29 and again on August 31 — giving Itoudis an early chance to test rotations and combinations away from home.
From there the squad moves on to Serbia for a demanding back-to-back: Partizan Belgrade on September 5, followed a day later by FMP, two of the country's established Adriatic League sides.

The most eye-catching stop comes in Sardinia, where Hapoel will take part in the City of Cagliari International Basketball Tournament at the PalaPirastu on September 12 and 13. The event brings together Hapoel, German outfit Bayern Munich, Tony Parker's ASVEL Villeurbanne and the newly formed Italian club Maxima Roma, with Hapoel scheduled to face two of the other three sides.

The preparation window is short. Hapoel's competitive season begins on September 17 with the Israeli Super Cup against city rivals Maccabi Tel Aviv at the Menora Mivtachim Arena, the traditional curtain-raiser to the domestic basketball calendar.

Only a week later, on September 24, Hapoel open their EuroLeague campaign against Bayern Munich — their first taste of the continent's top competition after winning last season's EuroCup, which earned the club promotion. Officially a home fixture, the game will nonetheless be staged in Sofia, where Hapoel have continued to host their European matches because of the security situation in Israel.

That means Itoudis's players will face Bayern Munich twice inside a fortnight — once in the Sardinian tournament and again in the competitive EuroLeague opener — a demanding but useful gauge of where a reshaped roster stands against a genuine continental contender before the results start to count.

title: NBA legend Don Nelson, second-winningest coach in history, dies at 86
dek: The Hall of Famer, who won five titles as a Celtics player before reinventing coaching with small-ball, died at his Maui home surrounded by family.
body: Don Nelson, the second-winningest coach in NBA history and one of basketball's great tacticians, has died at the age of 86, his family announced. He passed on Sunday morning at his home in Maui, Hawaii, surrounded by relatives.

"On Sunday morning our beloved husband, dad, grandfather and great-grandfather Don Nelson peacefully went to be with the Lord, surrounded by his loving family," the Nelson family said in a statement. No cause of death was disclosed.

Nelson spent 31 seasons as an NBA head coach across four franchises — the Milwaukee Bucks, the Golden State Warriors in two separate stints, the New York Knicks and the Dallas Mavericks — finishing with a regular-season record of 1,335 wins and 1,063 losses. Only Gregg Popovich has won more games on an NBA bench.

He was voted NBA Coach of the Year three times, but for all the wins, a trip to the NBA Finals eluded him as a head coach across 18 playoff appearances — one of the enduring quirks of an otherwise decorated résumé.

Before he coached, Nelson won as a player. He spent 11 seasons with the Boston Celtics and collected five championship rings, part of the Bill Russell-era dynasty. The Celtics retired his No. 19 in 1978.

It was as a coach, though, that Nelson left his deepest mark on the sport. He pioneered what became known as "Nelson-ball": smaller, more athletic lineups, a faster pace and a relentless search for mismatches — principles that anticipated the spacing- and pace-driven NBA of today.
He was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 2012, and in 1994 he coached the United States national team to gold at the World Championship.

After stepping away from coaching, Nelson settled full-time in Maui, where he ran a farm and became a fixture of the local community. When wildfires devastated Lahaina in August 2023, he opened his rental properties to six displaced families free of charge, saying the sight of friends losing homes and businesses — including Bob Longhi, owner of the local restaurant Longhi's — felt like "a spike in my heart."

Tributes poured in from the sport he shaped. Mavericks governor Patrick Dumont called Nelson "a true original whose impact on the Dallas Mavericks and the game of basketball will endure for generations... His influence can be seen throughout Mavericks history and across the NBA today."
The Nelson family said a celebration of life will be held on Thursday, August 13, at Preston Hollow Presbyterian Church in Dallas.

title: Israeli sports bodies ordered to pay 1.6 million shekels to gymnasts left disabled by training injuries
dek: A Tel Aviv court found the gymnastics union, the Olympic committee and the Wingate Institute failed in their duty of care after two apparatus gymnasts developed shoulder injuries that ended their careers and left them permanently disabled.
body: Three of Israel's leading sports institutions have been ordered to pay a combined 1.6 million shekels to two former apparatus gymnasts who say years of intensive national-team training left them permanently disabled, ONE reported.

The Tel Aviv District Court found the Israel Gymnastics Union, the Israel Olympic Committee and the Wingate Institute jointly liable for shoulder injuries suffered by the two gymnasts during their time training with Israel's national artistic gymnastics squad between 2008 and 2016.

According to the ruling, both athletes repeatedly complained of shoulder pain during that period but were only ever sent for physiotherapy, never referred to an orthopedist or a sports-medicine specialist for a fuller diagnosis.

The pain worsened over years of high-intensity apparatus work until both gymnasts required complex shoulder surgery. Neither fully recovered, and both were left with lasting impairment that ended their competitive careers.

The court, presided over by Judge Dr. Menachem Klein, set disability at 23.05% for the first gymnast and 19.25% for the second. The first was awarded roughly 1,118,000 shekels and the second about 505,000 shekels, ONE reported.

Attorney Yaniv Gavish, who represented the pair, argued that the gymnastics union, the Olympic committee and Wingate had consistently prioritized results and national-team achievement over athlete welfare, and had failed to carry out the comprehensive annual medical examinations required under Israeli sports law.

The defendants pushed back hard during the proceedings. Some argued that apparatus gymnastics inherently carries a risk of injury and physical wear, and that the athletes knowingly accepted that risk by choosing the sport; others denied they bore responsibility for the gymnasts' medical oversight at all.

The court did not accept those defenses, finding instead that the three bodies had collectively failed the athletes at a formative stage of their careers, when repeated warning signs from their own bodies went unheeded.

The ruling lands as a rare and pointed rebuke of how Israel's national sports institutions manage the health of young athletes on Olympic-track programs, and is likely to be closely read by other federations that oversee high-load training environments for minors and young adults.

body: The final four of this season's Toto Cup are set. Maccabi Tel Aviv will face Maccabi Netanya, and Hapoel Tel Aviv will meet Ironi Kiryat Shmona, with both semifinals kicking off simultaneously on Sunday, August 16 at 20:00, ONE reports.

The draw pairs the two Tel Aviv giants against provincial opposition rather than against each other, meaning the only way Maccabi and Hapoel Tel Aviv can meet in this competition is in the final, which Sport5 reports is pencilled in for December.

According to ONE, the ties will be played at neutral venues — Netanya's Miriam Stadium and Petah Tikva's HaMoshava Stadium — though the report does not specify which semifinal has been assigned to which ground.

Ironi Kiryat Shmona booked their place in some style. The northern club topped their group with four straight wins in the round-robin phase and completed the job with a 3-1 comeback victory over Hapoel Haifa on August 8, according to Walla Sport.

Hapoel Tel Aviv reached the semifinal after finishing on top of their own group, a section they navigated with wins including a 2-0 result over Ashdod, setting up what looks a competitive tie against a Kiryat Shmona side in good early-season form.
Maccabi Netanya arrive off a strong group phase of their own, having gone through the round-robin stage unbeaten to finish top of their section and earn the trip to face Maccabi Tel Aviv.

The same weekend carries the rest of the Toto Cup's ranking playoffs, which decide final placings for clubs eliminated at the group stage. Ironi Tiberias host Maccabi Petah Tikva for 11th and 12th place, and Sakhnin host Hapoel Petah Tikva for 13th and 14th, both on Saturday at 20:15, ONE and Sport5 report.

Hapoel Haifa and Hapoel Beersheva are separately scheduled to meet in a fifth-place playoff, while Monday's card features Maccabi Haifa hosting Hapoel Jerusalem and newly promoted Hapoel Ramat Gan hosting Beitar Jerusalem, the latter played in Rehovot.

For now, though, the headline draw is the last four: Maccabi Tel Aviv-Netanya and Hapoel Tel Aviv-Ironi Kiryat Shmona, both live on Sunday evening in a week that will decide two of the four finalists chasing this season's Toto Cup.

title: Maccabi Tel Aviv sued by longtime Kiryat Shalom cafeteria operator for 520,000 shekels
dek: Zion Blas ran the training-ground kiosk for two decades before it was demolished; his lawyer says everyone at the club was in shock at how the eviction was handled.

verificationSources.label: ONE — follow-up report with attorney's radio comments

body: For the best part of two decades, generations of Maccabi Tel Aviv players and staff grabbed a coffee or a sandwich from the small cafeteria Zion Blas ran at the club's Kiryat Shalom training complex. Now Blas is suing the club at the Tel Aviv District Court for 520,482 shekels, saying his life's work there ended with a demolition notice and nothing to show for it.

According to the claim, filed through attorney Shay Elias and reported by ONE, Blas found what had been a neglected, abandoned shed on the training ground and rehabilitated it himself into a working cafeteria, operating it for years with the club's knowledge. The suit describes Blas, who says he cannot read or write, as a simple, devoted fixture of the site who helped out with maintenance and equipment care well beyond his role running the kiosk.

At the centre of the dispute is a licensing agreement Blas signed on 19 May 2002. Elias says his client signed it under rushed circumstances while boarding a team flight, believing he was securing long-term rights to run the cafeteria, when the document he was later shown differed from what he understood he had agreed to and technically expired within a year. Maccabi nonetheless let him continue operating for another two decades.

The cafeteria's operations stopped during the Covid-19 pandemic and never fully resumed. On 31 December 2023, Blas received a formal letter from the club giving him 14 days to vacate the building, stating that the permission granted under the 2002 agreement had long since lapsed and that Maccabi intended to demolish the structure to build something else for internal club use. The building has since been torn down.

Blas's claim breaks down to 420,482 shekels in lost profits, calculated from the cafeteria's average net income between 2014 and 2020 and projected forward, plus 100,000 shekels for emotional distress and non-pecuniary harm. He is also asking the court to void both the 2002 licensing agreement and a 2016 'volunteer declaration' he signed, arguing neither reflects a genuine, informed agreement given his inability to read.

Speaking on ONE's Sicha HaYom programme, Elias said Blas tried for a long time to resolve the matter quietly through letters before turning to lawyers, and described his client, now in poor health, as someone who gave the club decades of loyal, largely unpaid service. "Everyone who was at the club was in complete shock at this conduct," Elias said of the reaction to how the eviction was carried out.

Maccabi, represented by attorney Yael Margelit, maintains that no employer-employee relationship ever existed between the club and Blas and has suggested the dispute be resolved privately rather than in court. "The door will always remain open to return and meet with club management to discuss matters cordially," Margelit said. According to Elias, Maccabi offered in 2024 to forgive any outstanding debt and provide some compensation, but he says that offer never materialised into anything concrete for his client.
The case now awaits Maccabi's formal response. Both sides, per ONE's report, expect the matter to end in a negotiated settlement rather than a full trial.

title: Kiryat Yam coach Siso vows to aim high despite one of Liga Leumit's smallest budgets
dek: Fresh off a 3-1 Toto Cup win over relegated Maccabi Bnei Reineh, Maor Siso says his newly promoted side will not be defined by its budget as it begins a second season in Israel's National League.
body: Maor Siso, the coach who steered M.S. Kiryat Yam from the fourth tier to the National League inside a few remarkable seasons, is already talking like a man who expects more from a club still working with one of the smallest budgets in Israel's second flight.

Kiryat Yam opened its Toto Cup campaign with a 3-1 win over Maccabi Bnei Reineh, a club freshly relegated from Ligat Ha'Al, in the competition's second round on Monday night. Siso sat down for an interview with ONE afterwards to lay out his ambitions for the club's second season in the National League.

"We always aim to play positive, attacking football and to win every match," Siso said, according to ONE. "I aim for the highest, even if the budget is among the lowest in the league. I don't focus much on that."

The remark speaks to the scale of what Kiryat Yam pulled off last season. The club, refounded in 2021 after an earlier version folded, began its historic first campaign in the National League with a four-point deduction imposed over contract irregularities, yet still climbed clear of trouble and advanced through both the league and cup.

This time, Siso is promising less turbulence. "There will be quiet this year, I can promise you," he said, framing calm and continuity as the priority after a debut season defined by crisis management.

On the squad, the coach struck a balanced tone: a "good group with healthy internal competition," he said, while acknowledging the club is still "looking for two players to complete the puzzle" before the window closes.

Siso has been open before about the gap in resources he is working against. In an earlier interview with Walla Sport, he said some rivals in the National League operate with budgets two to three times the size of Kiryat Yam's, while insisting his players don't feel inferior for it. His stated long-term aim remains reaching Ligat Ha'Al, Israel's top flight.

ONE described the club as a "family-oriented organisation" run by a professional staff, several of whom have top-flight experience. Kiryat Yam plays its home matches at the Toto Acre Stadium in Akko, a 5,000-capacity ground, as it prepares to open its 2026/27 National League campaign.

title: Silva suffers from instability and makes too many mistakes, says Beitar great Dayan
dek: Former Hapoel Jerusalem captain turned pundit Michel Dayan questions whether goalkeeper Miguel Silva has the consistency for a title-chasing Beitar Jerusalem side, while hailing new signing Daniel Worko as the find of the season.

body: Beitar Jerusalem sit well placed heading into the new season, but their goalkeeper is dividing opinion. Michel Dayan, the former Hapoel Jerusalem captain who spent nine seasons as the club's midfield leader and is now a football pundit, used an appearance on ONE's "Sicha HaYom" programme to deliver a blunt verdict on Miguel Silva.

"He suffers from a lack of stability and he makes many mistakes," Dayan said of the Portuguese goalkeeper, who has been Beitar's first-choice since joining in January 2023 and was part of the squad that won the State Cup. Dayan noted that despite Silva's penalty-save heroics, the real question is whether his game management is good enough for a club with genuine title ambitions.

Dayan pointed specifically to what he called errors of irresponsibility — moments where Silva has given the ball away cheaply under pressure rather than clearing his lines safely. It is a recurring theme for the 30-year-old, who has occasionally been the subject of fan frustration in Jerusalem over costly individual errors.

The picture was far rosier when Dayan turned to Beitar's newest addition. Daniel Worko, signed from Hapoel Ramat Gan for a reported 240,000 shekels after the player-status committee set his valuation, was singled out as "the discovery of the season." Dayan praised the young midfielder's dribbling and his tireless work rate across matches, calling him close to a bargain at the fee Beitar paid.

Winger Atzili also drew praise from Dayan as part of a Beitar group he believes has real quality, even if he suggested the club's fields and infrastructure lag behind the level of the talent now on show. Manager Almog Cohen, who first identified Worko while the midfielder was still at Hapoel Ramat Gan, was credited with an eye for unpolished talent in Israel's lower tiers.

Dayan's conversation ranged beyond his old rivals in Jerusalem, too. He touched on Hapoel Jerusalem's mixed start — a 1-0 win over Maccabi Petah Tikva alongside a 3-1 defeat to Netanya — and flagged defensive gaps he thinks the club still needs to address before the season gathers pace.

He was less complimentary about Maccabi Petah Tikva under new manager Ziv Arie, describing the team's level as weak in its current form, while praising the broader pool of overlooked players turning up in Israel's lower divisions. "There are such talented players in these leagues," Dayan said, "you just need to find them."

For Beitar Jerusalem, the takeaway is a familiar one: a squad with genuine attacking upgrades in Worko and Atzili, but with a question mark between the posts that a respected Jerusalem football voice is not shy about raising in public.

body: Hapoel Jerusalem have strengthened their midfield for the season ahead, confirming the signing of Omer Abuhav from Bnei Sakhnin, ONE reports. The 22-year-old has put pen to paper on a one-year contract that carries a club option for an additional season.

Abuhav arrives in the capital having spent the past two seasons at Sakhnin, a stint capped by a standout final campaign in which he made 37 appearances across all competitions and established himself as an automatic starter, according to ONE.

It is his second senior move. Abuhav broke through at Hapoel Ramat Gan at 18, racking up 58 league appearances and two goals over two seasons there before Sakhnin signed him in July 2024. Before that he had come through the youth ranks at Hapoel Tel Aviv, Maccabi Tel Aviv and Maccabi Petah Tikva.
Hapoel Jerusalem, who ended last season in the bottom playoff and finished 12th, are turning to the two-footed, ball-playing midfielder to add energy and passing range through the middle of the park.

"I'm very happy to join Hapoel! This is a great honour," Abuhav said, quoted by ONE. "I believe in this club's direction, the quality here, and the team. I'm coming with high energy and look forward to playing soon."

Abuhav, who is the son of Israeli actress Rotem Abuhav, becomes one of the more experienced additions so far to Lior Zada's squad as Hapoel Jerusalem look to rebuild ahead of the new Ligat Ha'al campaign.

title: Liga Leumit reveals opening fixtures for 2026/27 season
dek: The National League's first three rounds are set for August, with newly relegated Maccabi Bnei Reineh opening on the road against Bnei Yehuda Tel Aviv.
body: Israel's second-tier National League now has a start date. The league management has published the fixture list for the opening three rounds of the 2026/27 Liga Leumit season, with the campaign kicking off midweek on Tuesday, August 18.

According to ONE, all eight matches of round one will kick off simultaneously at 19:30, a scheduling quirk the league uses to keep the opening round on a level playing field before staggered kickoff times return from round two onward.

The headline fixture pairs two clubs with contrasting fortunes: Maccabi Bnei Reineh travel to face Bnei Yehuda Tel Aviv. Reineh's trip to Tel Aviv comes just weeks after their relegation from Ligat Ha'al was confirmed, ending a four-season stay in the Israeli top flight that ended with results elsewhere - Hapoel Jerusalem and Hapoel Haifa's wins - sealing their fate, as reported by Israel Hayom.

Elsewhere in round one, Hapoel Ra'anana host Maccabi Ahi Nazareth, Hapoel Afula welcome M.S. Ashdod, and Maccabi Jaffa take on M.S. Kiryat Yam. Hapoel Kfar Shalem meet M.S. Kfar Qasim, Hapoel Acre host Maccabi Kiryat Gat, and Ironi Modi'in face Maccabi Herzliya to round out the card.

Also on the opening night, Hapoel Rishon LeZion host Hapoel Kfar Saba, who play their home games at the modest Levita Stadium in Kfar Saba - one of the league's smaller grounds and a fixture of the second tier for years.
Rounds two and three have also been locked in: the second round is split across August 23-24, and the third across August 30-31, both with matches kicking off at 19:00 local time.

The league management noted that scheduling beyond round three will follow once the top-flight Ligat Ha'al calendar is finalised. "Additional round assignments will be published later, in parallel with the publication of the Premier League's schedule, due to shared stadiums," the league said in comments carried by ONE - a reference to the several grounds used by both divisions across the country.

Walla! Sport reported separately that the league board approved the wider 2026/27 calendar at a meeting at Sammy Ofer Stadium in Haifa, with league chairman Araz Kalpun saying the aim was to give clubs "as much certainty as possible at the earliest opportunity" so they can plan pre-season training and squad building around firm dates.

For Bnei Reineh, the visit to Bnei Yehuda's Hatikva Neighbourhood ground will be the first real test of a squad manager Lior Reuven is having to rebuild from scratch after an expected exodus of players following relegation, with the club working to keep hold of forward Antonio Sefer, who remains under contract for two more seasons.

title: Aarhus, Atalanta, Braga and OFI Crete: who could stand between Israel's four clubs and Europe
dek: Hapoel Beer Sheva, Maccabi Tel Aviv, Beitar Jerusalem and Hapoel Tel Aviv are all still alive in continental qualifying — ONE previews the heavyweight opponents waiting in the playoff round

verificationSources.label: Maccabi Tel Aviv FC official site
LaPresse — Atalanta to face Hapoel Tel Aviv or Katowice
A Bola — Braga's possible Conference League play-off opponents

body: It is the busiest fortnight of the Israeli football calendar, and by the time it is done all four clubs still standing in European qualifying will know exactly who they are chasing a place in the group stage against. ONE has run the rule over the opposition lying in wait for Hapoel Beer Sheva, Maccabi Tel Aviv, Beitar Jerusalem and Hapoel Tel Aviv, and the names range from a giant-killing Danish champion to last season's Europa League winners.

Hapoel Beer Sheva are first into action. Having overturned a first-leg deficit to eliminate Vikingur Reykjavik, they host Red Star Belgrade on Tuesday in the second leg of their Champions League third qualifying round tie. Win that, and the reward is a playoff-round meeting with Aarhus of Denmark for a place in the league phase itself, with legs scheduled for August 18-19 and 25-26.

Aarhus arrive as newly-crowned Danish champions, their first title since 1986, and have already produced one of the summer's great European comebacks, coming from three goals down on aggregate to eliminate Lech Poznan. They have lost key men in Felix Bijou and Patrick Mortensen since winning the league, and coach Jakob Poulsen — a former Danish international — sets his side up in an attacking 3-4-3. Their own stadium is being renovated, so any home leg would likely be staged in Randers instead.

Lose to Red Star, however, and ONE reports Beer Sheva would drop into the Europa League qualifying picture against Viktoria Plzen, the Czech side who are regular top-three finishers at home and reached the Europa League's round of 16 as recently as 2024-25 — a considerably tougher assignment than the Aarhus alternative.

Maccabi Tel Aviv face an equally pivotal tie of their own against CSKA Sofia in the Europa League's third qualifying round. Advance, and the playoff-round opponent is already confirmed as OFI Crete of Greece, with the first leg on August 20 and the return a week later — a draw the club itself has flagged to supporters. The Greek side are a mid-table outfit in their own league but arrive off the back of a dramatic domestic cup triumph under coach Christos Kontis, despite going without a European away win since the year 2000.

Should Maccabi instead fall to CSKA Sofia, they would parachute into the Conference League playoff round against the winner of Switzerland's Lugano and Runavik of the Faroe Islands — confirmation, straight from Maccabi Tel Aviv's official site, that even a bad night in Sofia would not end their European summer outright. Lugano finished third in Switzerland last season, reached the Conference League quarter-finals under coach Mattia Croci-Torti, and would represent a stern late test for whichever Israeli or Faroese side reaches them.

Beitar Jerusalem's route runs through Austria first. They face FK Austria Wien in their own third qualifying round tie on August 6, with the winner then meeting Sp. Braga in the Conference League playoff — assuming the Portuguese club see off Belarus's Dinamo Minsk in their own tie. Braga would host the first leg on August 20, before the return in Jerusalem on August 27.

Braga are no ordinary Conference League name. They are regular top-four finishers in Portugal and reached the Europa League semi-finals as recently as 2024, under coach Carlos Carvalhal, a former Manchester City assistant. Their squad still features captain Ricardo Horta and the 39-year-old Joao Moutinho, the veteran former Portugal international who remains a fixture in midfield.

Hapoel Tel Aviv, meanwhile, must first get past GKS Katowice of Poland in the Conference League third qualifying round, with legs on August 6 and 12. Win that tie and the prize — reported by Italian outlets including LaPresse and Calcio e Finanza after Sunday's draw in Nyon — is a playoff meeting with Atalanta, the 2024 Europa League champions, home first in Bergamo on August 20 and away in Tel Aviv on August 27.

It would be a daunting draw on paper. Atalanta remain one of Italian football's genuine powers and have just appointed Maurizio Sarri as coach in succession to Gian Piero Gasperini, the architect of their European breakthrough. ONE puts Hapoel Tel Aviv's chances of springing an upset at around five percent should the tie materialise — a reflection of the gulf in resources rather than any lack of ambition from the Israeli side.

Taken together, the picture is of four Israeli clubs each one result away from knowing whether their August ends against realistic, winnable opposition or against clubs with recent continental pedigree of their own. Beer Sheva's tie with Red Star is the most live of the four, kicking off Tuesday evening with a Champions League place still within reach either way.

None of the ties involving CSKA Sofia, Austria Wien, Katowice or the Beer Sheva-Red Star return leg have yet been decided, so every playoff pairing described here remains conditional on results still to be played out over the coming days.

If Beer Sheva beat Red Star, their Champions League playoff-round opponent would be Danish champions Aarhus; UEFA's playoff draw pairs the Beer Sheva/Red Star winner with the Aarhus/Sabah winner, with legs on August 18-19 and 25-26.
