body: Maccabi Ahi Nazareth's return to Liga Leumit is being shaped by a busy week in the transfer market, one that brought two new forwards through the door and, less happily, an injury blow to a player who had barely finished signing his contract.

ONE reports that the club, based in Ilut and managed by Maher Hamed, has brought in Panama international forward Stefan Alfredo, 31, who has 27 caps for his country and was most recently playing in Japan's professional league. His arrival marks a second stint in Israeli football and was arranged through agent Adam Kidan, with the forward landing in the country earlier in the week, according to the report.

Alongside him comes Mohammed Taha, a forward who came through the Maccabi Tel Aviv youth ranks before spending last season at Hapoel Nof HaGalil. His move was brokered by the Fisher Sports agency, with agents Roi Simoni and Stiav Chachmon handling the deal, ONE reports.
Both signings fit a club that won its way back into Israel's second tier and has been recruiting with an eye on competing rather than merely surviving in the division.

The good news, though, was undercut by a much less welcome development involving defender Ashraf Rabah, who had put pen to paper with the club only the day before. According to ONE, Rabah was involved in a car accident overnight and was taken to hospital, where doctors diagnosed a broken hand.
The defender is expected to be sidelined for two to three weeks, the report says, meaning he will miss the early stretch of preparations just as he was set to begin working with his new teammates.

For a promoted side trying to build depth quickly, the timing is unfortunate: Rabah's fitness for the run-in to the new campaign will now be monitored closely, even as the club presses ahead with strengthening the squad around him.

title: More confederations could side with UEFA against FIFA
dek: CAF, CONMEBOL and CONCACAF are weighing their own stance after UEFA's 55 members voted to boycott FIFA competitions over Gianni Infantino's plan to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors.
body: The confrontation between UEFA and FIFA that erupted this week over Gianni Infantino's plan to sell a stake in the World Cup is no longer confined to Europe. ONE reports that other continental confederations are now weighing whether to follow UEFA's lead and shun FIFA's flagship tournament themselves.

UEFA's 55 member federations agreed this week that no European national team will take part in any FIFA competition, including the men's or women's World Cup, unless Infantino's plan is dropped entirely and FIFA gives binding assurances it will never again open its competitions to private ownership.

At the heart of the dispute is a proposal to spin off FIFA's commercial operations into a new entity valued at roughly $20 billion, with around a fifth of it sold to outside investors reportedly including Josh Kushner's Thrive Capital and the bank JPMorgan. In exchange, FIFA has offered each of its 211 member associations a payment of about $20 million, with sign-off required by mid-September.

ONE, citing reporting from Talksport, says UEFA figures view the standoff as effectively a referendum on Infantino himself ahead of FIFA's next presidential election in 2027 — with the suggestion that senior football figures could push for him not to seek another term if the private-investment plan collapses under pressure.

CONCACAF, the 41-member confederation covering North and Central America and the Caribbean, called an emergency meeting this week to decide its own position, voicing concern over what it called a lack of due process and transparency in how the plan was drawn up and shared publicly.

Attention has now turned to CAF and CONMEBOL. CAF's executive committee is due to meet next week to evaluate the proposal, while CONMEBOL, the South American confederation that includes reigning champions Argentina, has yet to state a public position of its own.

Should either of those confederations follow UEFA's example, FIFA would face the prospect of a World Cup without some of the sport's biggest nations. Germany, France, England and world champions Spain are already effectively barred from competing under UEFA's current stance.

Infantino has led FIFA since 2016, when he succeeded Sepp Blatter, and was re-elected in 2023. The row over the private-investment plan is shaping up as the most serious challenge to his leadership since he took charge of the governing body.

How the confederations outside Europe respond in the coming weeks will determine whether this becomes a genuine global revolt against FIFA's ownership plans — or remains, for now, a distinctly European rebellion.

body: Maccabi Tel Aviv's route through Europa League qualifying continues to run through Georgia rather than Bloomfield. The club confirmed on Thursday that it will host the first leg of the third qualifying round in Batumi on August 6, with the second leg away a week later, on August 13.

The fixture caps a comfortable passage past Sheriff Tiraspol. Maccabi won 5-0 in Moldova on July 23 and closed out a 1-0 second leg at the Batumi Stadium on July 30 — settled by a Samba Kone own goal in the 29th minute — for a 6-0 aggregate victory that sent them through to the next stage without much drama.

As with every Maccabi Tel Aviv "home" European fixture this season, the August 6 game will not be played in Tel Aviv. The club has been staging its continental ties in Batumi because of the security situation in Israel, meaning supporters in Georgia rather than at Bloomfield Stadium will see the third-round opener in person.

Maccabi's opponent for that tie was still undecided at the time of writing. Azerbaijan's Qarabag and Bulgaria's CSKA Sofia drew 0-0 in the first leg of their own second-round qualifier in Baku on July 23, with the return leg in Sofia taking place the same day as Maccabi's win over Sheriff — meaning the winner would only be confirmed once away goals and, if needed, extra time or penalties settled the tie.
Whichever side advances, Maccabi will have home advantage — in name if not in geography — for the opening leg, before travelling to Azerbaijan or Bulgaria for the decider on August 13.

The stakes are significant. Winning the third qualifying round would send Maccabi into the Europa League playoff round, the last hurdle before the competition's revamped league phase, and would guarantee the club a place in the Conference League phase at minimum even if they fall short there.

It continues a now-familiar pattern for the Yellow-and-Blue, who have had to treat continental qualifying as an away-from-home campaign in all but name while playing their notional "home" legs in Georgia.

title: Flares halt Hapoel Tel Aviv's Conference League return leg in Bulgaria
dek: Smoke grenades lit by traveling fans forced the referee to stop the Ludogorets fixture early on Thursday, the second successive leg of the tie disrupted by pyrotechnics.
body: Hapoel Tel Aviv's Conference League second qualifying round return leg in Bulgaria was stopped inside the first few minutes on Thursday, after supporters inside Ludogorets Razgrad's stadium set off a wall of smoke grenades and flares, ONE reports.

The referee pulled play up as thick smoke drifted across the pitch roughly two and a half minutes after kick-off, unable to let the match continue in the conditions. It did not restart until the smoke had cleared, close to six minutes later.

It was the second successive leg of this tie in which pyrotechnics forced an interruption. In the first leg on 23 July, staged at the DVTK Stadium in Miskolc, Hungary — the neutral venue Hapoel Tel Aviv used for their "home" fixture — the referee likewise stopped play, in the sixth minute, for around five minutes because of flares lit in the stands.
Hapoel won that first leg 2-0, Omri Altman heading in a first-half opener before Chico Alves added a second late on to give the Israeli side a cushion to defend in Razgrad.
Thousands of Hapoel Tel Aviv supporters again made the trip for the return fixture, filling out a sizeable away end that has followed the club through a demanding European run this summer.

Repeated pyrotechnics use carries disciplinary risk: UEFA routinely opens cases against clubs whose fans ignite flares or smoke devices inside stadiums, and back-to-back stoppages in the same tie are likely to draw scrutiny regardless of the eventual outcome.

Both interruptions were relatively brief and neither leg was abandoned or suspended. Hapoel Tel Aviv are chasing a place in the third qualifying round of the Conference League, a competition the club has targeted as a route back into regular European football after a lean run domestically.

title: LeBron James nears deal with ESPN for his own "Last Dance" documentary
dek: According to ONE, LeBron James is in advanced talks with ESPN for a docuseries tracking his final NBA chapter with the Philadelphia 76ers, drawing inevitable comparisons to Michael Jordan's celebrated series
body: LeBron James's move to the Philadelphia 76ers earlier this month may end up being remembered for more than just a jersey change. According to ONE, James and ESPN are in advanced negotiations for a documentary series that would follow him through what could be the final act of his NBA career — a project already being framed as basketball's answer to "The Last Dance."

ONE reports that talks between James's camp and ESPN are described as being on "the last yard line," with a film crew set to trail him throughout the coming season in Philadelphia. The plan, according to the report, is to blend that fresh footage with archival material spanning his entire career, including previously unreleased content.

The comparison writes itself. "The Last Dance," the 2020 ESPN docuseries chronicling Michael Jordan's final championship season with the Chicago Bulls, became a cultural phenomenon and won an Emmy for outstanding documentary series. Jordan and James are widely regarded as the two greatest players in NBA history, even if their careers unfolded in very different media eras — Jordan's largely before the internet age, James's under constant digital scrutiny almost from the day he entered the league.

That difference is central to why a James documentary has long felt inevitable. He has been filmed extensively since his rookie season in Cleveland, giving any production team an unusually deep archive to draw from — far beyond what was available to Jordan's chroniclers a generation ago.

The project reportedly gained momentum after James's free-agency decision this summer. He signed a two-year, $8 million contract with the 76ers, a deal that includes a player option and represents a steep pay cut from the nearly $53 million he earned with the Los Angeles Lakers last season — underlining that this stage of his career is no longer about the paycheck.

James had spoken openly about weighing retirement before opting instead for one more run at a championship, this time in Philadelphia. He said he believed he could still help turn the 76ers into contenders, pairing his experience with a roster built around Joel Embiid and Tyrese Maxey.

No release date has been set, and the deal has not been finalized, but if it closes as expected, cameras will be rolling on James from the opening days of training camp. For a player who has spent more than two decades as one of the most documented athletes alive, the only surprise may be that the definitive account of his career has taken this long to come together.

title: Hapoel Ussishkin board dispute rolls on as Tel Aviv court hearing ends without a ruling
dek: A three-hour hearing over control of the Hapoel Tel Aviv-linked association's management committee broke up without agreement, with the case adjourned to September.

verificationSources.label: Walla Sport – Hapoel Ussishkin suing Ofer Yanai for over 10 million shekels
Ynet – Hapoel Ussishkin managers demand huge sum from Yanai

body: A Tel Aviv District Court hearing meant to settle who sits on the management committee of Hapoel Ussishkin Tel Aviv, the association that runs Hapoel Tel Aviv's youth and women's basketball programmes and holds a 19% stake tied to the senior men's team, ran for three hours on Thursday and broke up with nothing resolved, ONE reports.

Judge Iris Lushi-Avodi tried repeatedly to steer the two camps — the faction aligned with Hapoel Tel Aviv owner Ofer Yanai and the group representing the association's members — toward a compromise on the committee's makeup. At one point she warned the sides, "if you don't reach agreements, it will never end," according to the report.

Yanai's side pushed a specific slate for the committee, including attorney Amit Pines, former player Gilad Shimchoni, supporters' representative Roni Tal and an additional, more junior nominee — an attempt, in effect, to shape who oversees the body that runs the club's grassroots and women's basketball operations.

The judge rejected a request from Yanai's camp to summon former association chairman Rami Cohen to testify. Pines, for his part, initially offered to join the committee himself as a way to break the deadlock, but withdrew the offer once other parties objected.

Lushi-Avodi's own compromise proposal — selecting committee members without disclosing which side had nominated them, to strip out factional politics — also failed to win support from the parties, ONE reports.
As the hearing closed without a decision, the court ordered Yanai's side to pay 30,000 shekels toward costs. The case is now set to resume in early September.

The committee fight is the latest flashpoint in a long-running feud between Yanai and the association since he took control of Hapoel Tel Aviv's basketball operations. Hapoel Ussishkin has separately gone through insolvency proceedings over debts of roughly 4 million shekels, with court-appointed trustees working on a recovery plan, and has filed its own claim against Yanai for more than 10 million shekels, including about 7.7 million shekels in tax liabilities it says he should have covered.

title: Kalvin Phillips never recovered from Guardiola's comments — and now he's back at Sheffield United
dek: Five years after leaving Leeds as England's Player of the Year, the midfielder is finalising a full-season loan to the Championship club, still trying to escape the shadow of one press conference.
body: There was a time, not so long ago, when Kalvin Phillips was English football's model of homegrown value: Leeds United's Player of the Year for 2020/21, a World Cup semi-finalist, the defensive midfielder Pep Guardiola paid £45 million to bring to Manchester City in the summer of 2021. Five years on, ONE reports he is finalising a return to Sheffield United on loan, a Championship club, still hunting for the form that once made him one of the most coveted players in the Premier League.

The turning point, as ONE and others have chronicled, traces back to a single set of remarks. After the 2022 World Cup in Qatar — where Phillips made only fleeting appearances for England, barely 40 minutes across two substitute outings — Guardiola told reporters his midfielder had come back overweight and unfit to train alongside his City teammates.

It was a public dressing-down of a player who, by most independent accounts, including reporting from The Athletic, had barely strayed from his usual conditioning. Guardiola later admitted the comments were partly designed to jolt Phillips into shape rather than a literal complaint about his fitness. The damage, though, was done.

"That was probably the toughest moment," Phillips himself said afterwards, of the period when his manager's words became public property. "It knocked my confidence and how I felt at the club." Guardiola eventually apologised, in February 2024, more than a year after the original comments — but by then Phillips's standing inside the City dressing room had already collapsed.

What followed were two loan spells that did little to arrest the slide. West Ham took him in during the 2023/24 season, and Ipswich Town a year later; neither reversed his trajectory, and City's midfield only got more crowded around him. Last September, Phillips's entire City season amounted to seven minutes as a substitute in a League Cup tie against Huddersfield.

In January this year he found an escape route to Sheffield United, joining the Blades on a deadline-day loan for the rest of the campaign and making three appearances before the season closed. It was enough, evidently, to convince both player and club that the arrangement was worth extending.

Phillips, now 30, was left out of City's squad for their pre-season tour of Asia this summer while the loan to Bramall Lane was finalised — as clear a signal as any of where he currently sits in Guardiola's plans. Sheffield United manager Chris Wilder has been pushing to bring him back for a full 2026/27 season, and the two clubs are understood to be close to an agreement.

For a player once seen as the long-term heir to Fernandinho in City's midfield, a second Championship loan four years after his big-money move is a stark marker of how far his career has drifted — and how hard one manager's words, however brief, can be to shake off.

title: UEFA members vote to boycott FIFA competitions over World Cup privatization plan
dek: All 55 UEFA nations back a boycott threat unless Gianni Infantino abandons his plan to bring private investors into the World Cup, ONE reports.
body: Every one of UEFA's 55 member federations has agreed to boycott FIFA's competitions, including the World Cup, unless FIFA president Gianni Infantino scraps his plan to bring outside investors into football's showpiece tournament, ONE reported.

The unanimous vote came out of an emergency virtual UEFA meeting called after Infantino unveiled a proposal to spin off the World Cup's commercial and operational rights into a new subsidiary company designed to attract private investment reportedly worth as much as $20 billion, according to CNN and ESPN.

UEFA framed its response in stark terms. "The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product," the confederation said in a statement cited by ONE. "It's one of football's greatest heritages, built across generations by players, teams and fans worldwide."

UEFA president Aleksander Čeferin, who chaired the crisis meeting, accused FIFA of "governance through fear" and called the plan "coercion unbecoming of an institution managing world football." He dismissed Infantino's framing of the process as a "democratic consultation," telling members that "this is not a 'democratic decision.'"

The boycott threat, as reported by CNN and Al Jazeera, is sweeping: European federations, meaning reigning world champions Spain along with semi-finalists France and England, would sit out FIFA tournaments entirely unless the plan is abandoned "in its entirety" and FIFA gives binding guarantees it will never again open its competitions to private ownership.

At the centre of the dispute is a venture reportedly fronted by Thrive Eternal, the investment firm founded by Joshua Kushner, which CNN identified as the lead partner FIFA has lined up for the new subsidiary.

UEFA's objection goes beyond the money itself. The confederation argues that once outside shareholders hold a stake in football's flagship competitions, the sport changes permanently: a commercial return becomes a fixed obligation, and investor expectations start to dictate decisions that were once football's own to make.

Whether the standoff ends in an actual boycott or a climbdown by FIFA remains to be seen, but Thursday's vote marks one of the deepest rifts between Europe and world football's governing body in years, and puts Infantino's flagship project on the clock.

title: NBA scraps Middle East preseason games amid US-Iran tensions
dek: The league will stage no exhibition games in Abu Dhabi or Qatar this year for the first time in five years, even as it presses ahead with long-term plans in the region, including the 2027 World Cup in Doha.
body: The NBA will not stage a single preseason game in the Middle East this year, the first time in five years the league has skipped the region, with the ongoing war between the United States and Iran cited as the reason for pulling the plug.

Abu Dhabi had been lined up as the primary host, with Qatar also under consideration as an alternative or co-host venue. According to the report, the league had been in talks with the Cleveland Cavaliers, Miami Heat, Brooklyn Nets and Washington Wizards about taking part in exhibition fixtures.

One scenario under discussion would have split the games geographically: two teams would have played one exhibition in Qatar and another in the United Arab Emirates, giving both Gulf states a slice of the NBA's preseason showcase.

It marks a sharp change of pace from last October, when the New York Knicks and Philadelphia 76ers played out two preseason games in Abu Dhabi as part of the league's now well-established autumn swing through the Emirates.

The NBA insists the broader relationship with the region is intact despite the pause. The league reaffirmed its partnership with Abu Dhabi's Department of Culture and Tourism, an agreement extended as recently as January that covers joint marketing initiatives and the launch of an NBA Global Academy in the Emirati capital.

Qatar's stake in the picture runs deeper than just hosting games: the Qatar Investment Authority holds a minority interest in the Wizards' parent company, giving Doha a commercial as well as sporting incentive to stay in the NBA's Gulf plans long-term.

The Gulf region's basketball ambitions extend well past the NBA's preseason calendar. Qatar is set to host the FIBA Basketball World Cup in August 2027, and FIBA's secretary general has said there are currently no plans to relocate that tournament, though the situation is being monitored and adjustments remain possible if regional security conditions do not improve.

For now, the league is treating the preseason freeze as a pause rather than a permanent withdrawal, saying games in Abu Dhabi and, potentially, Qatar will return once conditions allow. No target date has been set.

title: Yermakov leaves Maccabi Haifa for Metallist Kharkiv, says he'll never rule out a return
dek: The Ukrainian goalkeeper, sold for a big profit after a single season as Haifa's number one, tells ONE he has "warm feelings" for the club and unfinished business there.
body: Heorhiy Yermakov has said goodbye to Maccabi Haifa after just one season as the club's first-choice goalkeeper, completing a move back to Ukraine with Metallist Kharkiv this week.

The 24-year-old, who grew up in a Jewish family in Kyiv before his parents relocated to Holon after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, made 37 appearances for Haifa last season and kept 12 clean sheets as the team's regular number one.

Maccabi Haifa had originally signed him from Oleksandriya in August 2024 for a modest fee reported at around €100,000, loaning him straight back to the Ukrainian club before he returned to Israel roughly a year ago to establish himself between the posts.

That single campaign has now produced a considerable financial windfall for Haifa. Sport5 reported the sale to Metallist was agreed at €2.8 million plus a 15% sell-on clause on any future transfer, after Haifa had opened talks demanding closer to €5 million; Walla Sport put the fee at nearer €3 million.

Speaking to ONE as the deal was finalised, Yermakov was asked directly whether he could see himself back in Haifa one day. "In football you never say never," he said. "I have warm feelings toward the club, and if circumstances are right in the future, I will definitely consider it."

He described leaving as "a very emotional moment" despite the brevity of his stay, saying he was proud of his own development but admitted "a sense that more could have been achieved" — a reference to the club falling short of silverware during his time there.
Yermakov also touched on the disruption caused by the security situation in Israel during the season, saying it had affected the team's rhythm and momentum at points.

He singled out veteran forward Nikita Rukavitsya for helping him settle in Haifa, and spoke warmly of a near-brotherly relationship with the club's young goalkeeper Mark Golankov. He worked under two head coaches during his time at the club, Barak Bakhar and Diego Flores.
Looking ahead, Yermakov said his ambitions now centre on forcing his way into Ukraine's national team and helping Metallist Kharkiv challenge for its own targets back home.

title: Hapoel Jerusalem loan rising guard Rani Belaga to Hapoel Galil Elyon
dek: The 20-year-old Israel U20 captain, fresh off a historic triple-double at the European Championship, will get top-flight minutes on loan in the Upper Galilee.
body: Hapoel Jerusalem have officially loaned guard Rani Belaga to Hapoel Galil Elyon for the coming season, ONE reports, giving one of Israeli basketball's most closely watched young prospects a shot at regular minutes in the Premier League.

Belaga, 20, is a product of the Hapoel Emek Hefer academy who signed with Hapoel Jerusalem in the summer of 2024 but has spent the last two seasons out on loan with A.S. Ramat Hasharon in the National League, developing away from the capital's senior spotlight.

The move to the Upper Galilee club, according to the report, is meant to fast-track that development at the top level. Hapoel Galil Elyon, based in Kfar Blum and historically nicknamed "the college of Israeli basketball" for the string of national-team players it has produced, has long built its identity around developing young guards.

The 1.97-metre guard arrives with real momentum. He captained Israel's U20 national team through the European Championship this summer, a tournament in which he became, according to reports, the first Israeli player to record a triple-double at the event.

In his most recent National League season with Ramat Hasharon, Belaga averaged around 11 points, four rebounds and roughly 3.6-3.7 assists per game in limited minutes, numbers that helped establish him as one of the league's most promising young ball-handlers.

ONE quotes the Galil Elyon organisation describing what it expects Belaga to bring to the roster: leadership, intensity, and the ability to create shots for himself and teammates, alongside character on and off the court.

For Hapoel Jerusalem, the loan keeps Belaga's rights in the capital while letting him test himself in a senior Premier League rotation before, the club will hope, a fuller integration into its own squad down the line.

body: The first half of Maccabi Tel Aviv's Europa League second-leg tie with Sheriff Tiraspol ended goalless at Bloomfield Stadium on Thursday, ONE reported, though the Israeli champions arrived at the interval already in total command of the qualifying round.

That comfort comes courtesy of the first leg: Maccabi thrashed Sheriff 5-0 in Tiraspol on 23 July, a result that leaves them needing only to avoid a heavy reversal in Tel Aviv to progress to the next round of Europa League qualifying.

Sayed Abu Farchi scored twice in that first-leg rout, opening the scoring in the fifth minute and adding a second-half penalty in the 74th, either side of goals from Dor Peretz, Sagiv Yehezkal and Issouf Sissokho as Maccabi ran riot in Moldova.

title: Ben Yechezkel drops to Liga Alef, signs for Yermiyahu Holon
dek: The 21-year-old winger, once a prolific scorer for Hapoel Tel Aviv's youth ranks and an Israel U19 international, joins the third-tier club through the end of the season.
body: Ben Yechezkel, a 21-year-old attacking talent who once looked destined for the top of Israeli football, has signed for Holon Yermiyahu of Liga Alef South, ONE reported.
The deal runs through the end of the season for the winger, who has spent the last few years searching for a settled home after an eye-catching run through the youth system.

Yechezkel came through the ranks at Hapoel Tel Aviv and Hapoel Ramat Gan before turning senior with Maccabi Jaffa, where he spent two seasons in Liga Leumit. A move to Bnei Yehuda followed, yielding three goals in half a season, before a brief stop at Hapoel Kfar Shalem that brought him just a single appearance.

The pedigree that once made him one of the more talked-about prospects of his age group is real: he scored 17 goals for a Hapoel Tel Aviv under-19 side that finished runner-up in the national championship under coach Omer Damari, and he won two caps for Israel's U19 national team, scoring twice.

This will be his third season as a senior professional, and the switch to Liga Alef South represents a significant step down the pyramid from where he was expected to be at this stage of his career — but also, potentially, a route back to regular first-team football.
At Yermiyahu Holon he will play under Naor Barkol, who returns to senior coaching this season after spending more than a decade working exclusively with youth teams.

For a club in the third tier, landing a player with Yechezkel's underage résumé and international pedigree is a notable coup, and one that will be watched closely to see whether regular minutes can revive a career that has so far promised more than it has delivered.

title: Bnei Sakhnin complete signing of free-agent defender Kabara as Salman eyes contract upgrade
dek: The Guadeloupean international joins on a free transfer after weeks of talks, while Sakhnin move to reward breakout forward Ahmad Salman amid interest from Hungary's Debrecen.

verificationSources.label: ONE - Kabara signs officially, Salman set for upgrade
ONE - Sakhnin in talks with defender Dimitri Kabara
ONE - Debrecen want Salman, who awaits a wage upgrade

body: Bnei Sakhnin have wrapped up one of their more pressing pieces of preseason business, confirming the signing of free-agent defender Dimitri Kabara, according to ONE, ending weeks of negotiation as the Galilee club rebuilds its back line ahead of the new Israeli Premier League campaign.

Kabara, 31, arrives without a transfer fee. His contract with Turkish side Esenler Erokspor ran out on 30 June, leaving the Guadeloupe international and dual French citizen a free agent from 1 July. Standing 1.84 metres and capable at right-back or in the centre of defence, he becomes the latest arrival to emerge from Sakhnin's training camp in Hungary.

ONE first reported Sakhnin's interest in Kabara several weeks ago, describing a club still hunting for defensive reinforcements after failing to extend the stay of Hassan Hilu. Kabara's career has taken him through French football and, most recently, Turkey's second tier with Esenler Erokspor.

His arrival adds to a summer rebuild that already includes Cameroonian forward Kevin Soni, who returned to the Premier League after a season with Hapoel Jerusalem, as coach Yossi Abukasis reshapes the squad that finished last season.

Elsewhere at the training base, attention has turned to one of last season's genuine breakout stories. Ahmad Salman, the 22-year-old forward who has become a firm favourite with the Sakhnin crowd, missed two training sessions this week with illness but returned to full work with the group, ONE reports.

Salman has attracted interest from abroad: Hungarian club Debrecen have made contact and, per ONE, have offered him a contract worth in the region of €200,000 a season - a significant sum for a player still only in his early twenties.

Sakhnin, however, are not entertaining a sale. Salman signed a three-year deal with the club not long ago, and its leadership regard him as central to their plans. ONE reports that officials intend to sit down with him soon to discuss upgrading his terms rather than cashing in on outside interest.

It is a mark of how highly the club now rates him: last season's performances are said to have convinced Sakhnin's board that Salman has outgrown his existing contract, even with a European suitor circling.

Between a free-transfer addition in defence and a reward for a player already established in the first team, the two stories capture the balancing act Sakhnin face every summer - bringing in cover cheaply while trying to protect their own academy-bred talent from a bigger payday elsewhere.
The club's preseason continues in the Toto Cup, where Sakhnin face Hapoel Haifa in their next outing after picking up one defeat so far in the competition.

title: World Cup final referee Vinčić breaks silence: "Messi behaved sportingly"
dek: Slavko Vinčić, the Slovenian who took charge of Spain's 1-0 win over Argentina in the World Cup final, says he'll keep his pitch-side exchange with Messi private — but insists the Argentina captain's conduct was exemplary.
body: Slavko Vinčić has finally spoken about the moment that will define his refereeing career — a quiet word with Lionel Messi in the middle of the World Cup final. And true to the discretion he showed on the pitch that day, the Slovenian is not giving up the details.

"I will leave the conversation between us on the grass," Vinčić said in his first extended remarks since the final. "But I can say that Messi behaved sportingly." It is as close as the 46-year-old has come to describing what passed between the two men during a tense, high-stakes afternoon in New Jersey.

The comment carries weight given the occasion. Vinčić took charge of the July 19 final at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, where Spain edged Argentina 1-0 in what was widely assumed to be Messi's last World Cup appearance, at 38 years old.

The match itself will be remembered for late drama beyond the scoreline. Argentina were reduced to ten men in stoppage time when Enzo Fernández was shown a second yellow card — his tackle sending Spain's Pau Cubarsí flying — and had to see out the closing minutes a man short as Spain held on for the title.

Vinčić described the assignment itself as overwhelming before it became a source of pride. He becomes the first Slovenian referee to take charge of a men's World Cup final, and he spoke of the responsibility of representing his small country on football's biggest single stage.

On the technology that shaped his performance and so many other games at the tournament, Vinčić was unequivocal: modern refereeing, he said, is no longer conceivable without VAR, given the speed and complexity of the way the game is now played at the highest level.

The final turned out to be Vinčić's last match in the middle. The Slovenian Football Association has confirmed he has hung up his whistle, closing out an international career at its absolute peak. He said the decision to retire had already been made before the tournament began — he simply never imagined his farewell would come in a World Cup final.

For Messi, the episode is another footnote in a tournament defined by fine margins — a final lost by a single goal, a red card that changed its complexion late on, and now, from the man who oversaw it all, a word of praise for how he carried himself in the moment that mattered most.

title: Tokyo, 1 August 2021: The Tie-Break That Made Artem Dolgopyat Israel's Second Olympic Champion
dek: A boy who arrived from Dnipro not knowing the word 'Israel' left Ariake Gymnastics Centre with the gold medal in men's floor exercise — won on a countback after two identical scores split by a single decimal of difficulty.

verificationSources.label: The Times of Israel — 'Artistic gymnast Artem Dolgopyat wins Israel's 2nd-ever Olympic gold'
The Jerusalem Post — 'Israeli gymnast Artem Dolgopyat wins an Olympic gold medal in Tokyo'
The Times of Israel — 'From Ukraine to Israel to Tokyo: Journey of an Olympic gold medalist'
Olympics.com — 'Artistic Gymnastics World Championships 2023: Artem Dolgopyat claims floor title'

body: The scoreboard at the Ariake Gymnastics Centre did something strange that afternoon: it produced a tie for the gold medal, and then, a few tense seconds later, it produced a winner. Artem Dolgopyat, a 24-year-old born in Dnipro, Ukraine, and raised in Rishon LeZion, had just finished his floor exercise routine at the Tokyo Olympics with a score of 14.933. Spain's Rayderley Miguel Zapata, competing later in the same final, matched it exactly: 14.933.

Under FIG tie-break rules, when two totals are identical the routine with the higher declared difficulty score is awarded first place. Dolgopyat's exercise carried the steeper degree of difficulty, and by that margin — not by execution, not by artistry, but by a technical coefficient buried in the code of points — he became Olympic champion. China's Xiao Ruoteng took bronze.

It was only Israel's second gold medal in Olympic history, following windsurfer Gal Fridman's victory in Athens in 2004, and it was the country's first-ever Olympic medal in gymnastics of any color. In Jerusalem, Prime Minister Naftali Bennett interrupted a cabinet meeting to relay the news; President Isaac Herzog called it a moment that would be remembered for generations.

Dolgopyat himself seemed almost apologetic about how he'd won it. "I didn't do the best routine," he said afterward. "I did the routine much better in the qualifying round." It hardly mattered. "I don't really have the words, I am still in heaven," he told reporters, before adding, in the disarming way that would define his public persona for years afterward, that he wanted to thank everyone who had helped him get there.

The journey to that podium had begun far from Tel Aviv. Dolgopyat started gymnastics at six, in Dnipro, encouraged by his father Oleg, himself a former gymnast. At twelve, his father told him the family was moving to Israel. "I knew we were Jewish," Dolgopyat later recalled, "but we didn't celebrate the holidays, and until that moment I hadn't even heard of Israel."

The adjustment was not easy. "For the first two months I sat in class in Rishon Lezion and didn't understand a word," he said, until a transfer to a school with Russian-speaking teachers eased the isolation. Gymnastics became the constant that carried him through it: "For me gymnastics was always the most important — it's what I did all the time and what helped me acclimate to Israel."

He built his career through the Israeli system from there — mandatory IDF service balanced against training under coach Sergei Vaisburg, with fellow Israeli floor specialist Alex Shatilov serving as an early mentor. The results accumulated steadily rather than suddenly: silver at the 2017 World Championships in Montreal, silver again at the 2019 Worlds in Stuttgart, gold at the 2020 European Championships in Mersin. Tokyo was the culmination, not a bolt from nowhere.

Vaisburg, watching from the stands, put it plainly afterward: "We were prepared for a medal, but of course we didn't expect the gold. That is a dream." For a small country whose Olympic medal cabinet had, until that afternoon, held exactly three pieces of silverware in judo and windsurfing, a gold decided by a tie-break in gymnastics was a new kind of history — earned in a sport Israel had never before medaled in at all.

The story did not end at Ariake. Two years later, in Antwerp, Dolgopyat became world champion on floor for the first time, and at the Paris Olympics in 2024 he returned to add a floor exercise silver to his collection — proof that the Tokyo gold, however narrow its margin, had been no fluke. But it is the tie-break in the summer of 2021, the identical scores on the board and the single decimal that separated a Ukrainian-born boy from Rishon LeZion from the rest of the world, that remains the moment Israeli sport marks as the turn.
facts: Artem Dolgopyat won gold in the men's floor exercise final at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics on 1 August 2021, at the Ariake Gymnastics Centre.

He tied Spain's Rayderley Miguel Zapata on 14.933 points; gold was awarded to Dolgopyat under FIG tie-break rules because his routine carried the higher difficulty score. China's Xiao Ruoteng won bronze.
It was Israel's second-ever Olympic gold medal, after windsurfer Gal Fridman's win at Athens 2004, and Israel's first Olympic medal of any color in gymnastics.
Dolgopyat was born in Dnipro, Ukraine, and moved to Israel with his family at age 12, settling in Rishon LeZion; he began gymnastics at age six, encouraged by his father Oleg.
Before Tokyo he had won silver at the 2017 and 2019 World Championships and gold at the 2020 European Championships; he trained under coach Sergei Vaisburg with Alex Shatilov as a mentor.
In October 2023 Dolgopyat won his first world title on floor exercise at the World Championships in Antwerp, and at the Paris 2024 Olympics he added a floor exercise silver medal.

title: Israel's U18 girls open bid to escape basketball's Division B in Romania
dek: Roei Eisenberg's squad begin the FIBA U18 Women's EuroBasket Division B tournament in Tulcea on Friday, a year after relegation from the top tier, with promotion the only real target.

verificationSources.label: FIBA U18 Women's EuroBasket 2026, Division B — official event page

body: A year after dropping out of Europe's top tier, Israel's under-18 girls' national basketball team lands in Romania this week with a single, unambiguous job: get back to Division A.

The squad, coached by Roei Eisenberg, opens the FIBA U18 Women's EuroBasket Division B tournament on Friday against Switzerland in Tulcea, the Black Sea-adjacent city hosting all 20 competing nations from July 31 to August 9.

Israel was relegated to Division B last summer, and ONE reports that the mission this time around is explicit: finish among the group that earns an immediate return to the senior European division rather than another year in the second tier.

The format gives Eisenberg's players a narrow but clear path. The 20 teams are split into four groups of five, with Israel drawn into Group B alongside Bulgaria, Norway, Ukraine and Switzerland. The top two from each group advance into the knockout quarterfinals, and ONE reports the top three finishers overall are on course for promotion back to Division A.

The squad's headline name is Maya Zilbershlag, a guard who finished as the second-leading scorer at last year's U18 European Championship and has since committed to play college basketball at Purdue. Her form at this level has made her one of the more closely watched prospects to come through Israel's youth basketball pipeline in recent years.

She is joined by Meyan Gorin, Adi Gutshtadt, Rotem Shtiklerov, Mica Yinai, Or Gadot, Meyan Aviram, Liam Yasso, Mica Kanitz, Hatiana Jeraisi, Tamar Karmi and Savion Kamar in a 12-player squad assembled specifically to reverse last summer's slide.

There is no margin for a slow start. A stumble in the group phase risks pushing Israel into the lower classification bracket and, with it, a second consecutive season outside Division A — a outcome the federation and coaching staff are clearly trying to avoid by fielding their strongest available roster in Tulcea.

Friday's tip-off against Switzerland will set the early tone for a nine-day tournament in which every result carries direct consequences for where Israeli girls' basketball sits in Europe's pecking order next summer.

title: Moyyal warns Beitar fans: flares against Larnaca could hurt the team
dek: Former Beitar Jerusalem midfielder Kobi Moyyal wants supporters to leave the pyrotechnics at home for Thursday's Conference League second leg against AEK Larnaca in Romania, and predicts a tight 2-1 win for the Jerusalem side.

verificationSources.label: Ynet - Beitar warns fans ahead of Romania return leg
Beitar Jerusalem FC - official recap of first leg win in Larnaca

body: Ahead of Thursday's Conference League second leg against AEK Larnaca, former Beitar Jerusalem midfielder Kobi Moyyal used his slot on ONE's "Today's Talk" to send a pointed message to the club's travelling support: leave the flares and fireworks at home.

Moyyal, who made 120 appearances for Beitar's first team before retiring, argued that pyrotechnics carry a real risk of hurting rather than helping the club's push toward the group stage. "Don't try to bring in flares and fireworks," he said, warning that any resulting punishment from UEFA "could really hurt the team."

The warning comes with the tie delicately poised. Beitar go into the return leg holding a 1-0 advantage from the first meeting in Larnaca on July 23, when substitute-turned-hero Brayan Carabali curled home a free kick in the 77th minute, moments after AEK defender Mike van der Hoorn was sent off for hauling down a Beitar attacker breaking clear on goal.
That result means Beitar need only avoid a two-goal defeat on Thursday to advance to the next qualifying round, having controlled the second half in Cyprus once Larnaca were reduced to ten men.

The return fixture will not be played in Jerusalem. Beitar's "home" leg is being staged in Ploiești, Romania, roughly an hour from Bucharest, with more than 3,000 Beitar supporters reported to be travelling in support - one of the largest away followings the club has taken to Europe in recent years.

Romanian police have echoed the club's message with warnings of their own, telling fans that anyone caught carrying pyrotechnic devices into the stadium risks arrest and possible imprisonment under Romanian law, independent of any disciplinary action UEFA might take against Beitar.

The club's own pre-match guidance to supporters largely mirrored that message, prohibiting flares, fireworks, alcohol, weapons and other combustible or illegal materials, while also urging fans to steer clear of racist chanting - the kind of conduct that has drawn UEFA fines against Beitar in the past.

On the football, Moyyal was upbeat about Beitar's prospects. He described the squad as deeper and better balanced than Larnaca's, with enough quality in reserve to cover for absences even away from Teddy Stadium, and forecast a tense contest ending in a 2-1 Beitar win.

Larnaca, who arrive in Romania knowing only a comfortable win will turn the tie around, retain the continental pedigree Moyyal credited them with. But for Beitar, keeping Thursday night about the football - rather than any repeat of pyrotechnic trouble - is now as much a part of the build-up as the team news.

title: Mourinho suffers first injury blow at Real Madrid as Asencio is ruled out for weeks
dek: Young centre-back Raúl Asencio has picked up a rectus femoris muscle injury in his right leg during preseason, with reports putting him out for around a month to six weeks just as José Mourinho settles into his second spell at the Bernabéu.
body: José Mourinho's second coming at Real Madrid has hit its first speed bump: young centre-back Raúl Asencio has been ruled out for several weeks after suffering a muscle injury in preseason training.

The club's medical department confirmed Asencio has a rectus femoris strain in his right leg, ONE reports, sustained after he started Real Madrid's preseason friendly against Leganés at Valdebebas, where he partnered new signing Dean Huijsen at the heart of defence.

ONE's report puts the layoff at around a month, while Spanish outlets including OK Diario and Goal.com have cited estimates of up to six weeks, which would keep Asencio out until roughly mid-September. Real Madrid have not publicly attached an exact return date to the diagnosis.

Either way, the timing stings. Mourinho only returned to the Santiago Bernabéu in June, 13 years after his first spell in charge between 2010 and 2013, signing a three-year contract to replace Álvaro Arbeloa. This is being described in the Spanish press as the first fitness setback of his new reign.

The injury rules Asencio out of the remainder of Real Madrid's preseason programme, which still includes friendlies against Fiorentina, Ferencváros, Deportivo La Coruña and Schalke, and puts his availability for the opening weeks of the La Liga season in doubt.

Asencio, a Canary Islands-born academy graduate, forced his way into Mourinho's defensive plans on the back of a breakout 2024-25 campaign in which he became a first-team regular for Madrid's title and Copa del Rey campaigns.

The setback also complicates his situation off the pitch. Asencio had been made available for a summer move as one of Real Madrid's transfer-listed squad members, and an injury of this length makes any deal before the window closes considerably harder to broker.

For now, Mourinho will have to manage his backline without one of the options he had been trusting in preseason, with Huijsen, Antonio Rüdiger and Éder Militão among those set to carry a heavier load at centre-back until Asencio is fit again.

title: Beitar Jerusalem fans flock to Ploiești for Conference League decider against AEK Larnaca
dek: Thousands of supporters travelled to Romania as Beitar Jerusalem defend a 1-0 aggregate lead over AEK Larnaca in the second qualifying round of the Conference League.

verificationSources.label: Beitar Jerusalem FC - official match recap
ESPN - AEK Larnaca 0-1 Beitar, first leg

body: Thousands of Beitar Jerusalem supporters converged on Ploiești on Thursday, turning what might have been a modest European away leg into, in the words of one fan, "one big madness, a thriller." The Conference League second qualifying round tie against AEK Larnaca kicks off at 20:30 Israel time at the Ilie Oană Stadium, with Beitar defending a narrow 1-0 aggregate lead.

That advantage was forged in Cyprus a week earlier. AEK defender Mike van der Hoorn was sent off in the 72nd minute for hauling down a Beitar forward clean through on goal, and from the resulting free-kick Brayan Carabali curled a finish into the top corner to settle the first leg 1-0 in Beitar's favour.

Thursday's return is being staged in Romania rather than Jerusalem for the second year running. Beitar, like other Israeli clubs in European competition, has continued to host its home continental fixtures abroad because of the security situation in Israel. Romanian outlets reported heightened security around the match, involving both local and Israeli authorities given the profile of the fixture.

None of that deterred the travelling support. ONE reported thousands of Israeli fans made the trip, with Romanian media putting the crowd inside the stadium at more than 2,500, after scenes of Beitar supporters marching and singing through the streets of Bucharest in the build-up to kickoff.

Among them was Oz Lieberman, a 30-year season-ticket holder who has followed Beitar since he was six and brought his own children along for the journey. "It's one big madness, a thriller," he told ONE amid the crowds gathering in Romania. "There are thousands of us here... this is a love you can't give up on."

Meira Sigal, who says she has not missed a Beitar match in 25 years, described a "crowded march" through the city before kickoff. "Fans just want to support the team to success," she said. Her devotion runs deep enough to shape her calendar: as a Sabbath-observant supporter, she said she and others rent Airbnb apartments to make away trips work around religious observance, rather than miss a match.

Sigal suggested even more fans would have made the trip had flights allowed, noting some supporters were still arriving in the hours before kickoff. Both she and Lieberman said they expected Beitar to get the job done, regardless of how AEK Larnaca - missing the suspended van der Hoorn - set up for the second leg.
A win, however narrow, sends Beitar Jerusalem through to the third qualifying round of the Conference League, extending the club's European run into August for a second successive summer.

title: Basketball chief Steinberg: 'A team unworthy of the league won't be here'
dek: The Israeli Basketball Super League management chairman toughened his line on arena standards, waved away a referees' strike threat and admitted he and Hapoel Tel Aviv 'don't see eye to eye on everything'

verificationSources.label: ONE - referees' strike threat over lawsuits
Israeli Basketball Super League - Board of Directors
ONE - Ari Steinberg named league management chairman

body: With the new Israeli basketball season bearing down and a facilities row still simmering from last year, league management chairman Ari Steinberg used a sit-down interview on ONE's "Today's Conversation" program to draw a hard line: clubs that cannot meet the top flight's arena standards simply will not be allowed to compete in it.

"A team unworthy of the top league won't be here. We're determined," Steinberg said, making clear the management intends to enforce facility requirements strictly rather than grant the exemptions that have periodically let under-equipped clubs limp through a season.

Steinberg, who has chaired the Israeli Basketball Super League's management board since 2023, used the same interview to address a more immediate crisis: a threat by top-flight referees that they may refuse to open the season at all.

As ONE reported separately, referees' representatives sent an urgent letter warning that a wave of personal lawsuits against officials over on-court decisions has become untenable, demanding legal protection and financial cover from the league and the basketball federation. One case cited involves a defamation suit filed by a Hapoel Tel Aviv fan against the officials who worked last season's playoff final.

Steinberg dismissed the referees' ultimatum as overblown. "It's not serious," he said of the threat not to open the season, likening a personal lawsuit over a refereeing call to suing a judge for handing down a verdict.

Asked about Hapoel Tel Aviv's habit of voting against management proposals at board level, Steinberg did not deny the friction. "We don't see eye to eye on everything," he said, a rare on-record acknowledgement of the rift between the league office and one of its flagship clubs.

On the sensitive question of foreign players gaining Israeli citizenship to count as locals on club rosters, Steinberg said he backs a balanced policy but pushed back on the idea that naturalisations are distorting competition, rejecting characterisations of the practice as having an "artificial" impact on the league.

He also confirmed a tightening of the rules governing player recruitment: clubs are now barred outright from approaching players who remain under contract elsewhere, with breaches carrying a fine of NIS 350,000 — a sharp deterrent aimed at curbing the tampering disputes that have flared between rival clubs in recent seasons.

Steinberg closed on a more hopeful note, saying a return of Israeli clubs to regular European competition would be the surest way to reignite fan interest in the domestic league, which has operated for two seasons under security-related restrictions on venues and crowds.

Taken together, the interview reads as a chairman trying to project control over a league facing pressure on several fronts at once — from officiating to club finances to the naturalisation debate — heading into a season still short of a start date.

title: Tomer Haren signs for Hapoel Ramat Gan as Omer Nir'on deal edges closer
dek: The newly promoted Ligat Ha'al club has landed a well-travelled goalkeeper on a one-year deal, with ONE reporting a second, more prominent shot-stopper is close to following him through the door.

body: Hapoel Ramat Gan Givatayim have made their first goalkeeping signing since winning promotion to Ligat Ha'al, confirming that Tomer Haren has joined on a one-year contract with a club option for a second season, ONE reports.

The 27-year-old arrives after a season with Maccabi Jerusalem and brings an unusually well-travelled résumé for an Israeli stopper, with spells at Cerro Largo in Uruguay's top flight, Rudar Velenje in Slovenia's second tier and Babelsberg in Germany's fourth division.
"I'm happy and excited to join Hapoel Ramat Gan," Haren said on signing, according to ONE. "I love working hard and being part of a club aiming high."

Haren's arrival is unlikely to be the end of the story between the posts, however. ONE reports the club is closing in on a separate deal for Omer Nir'on, son of former Israel international goalkeeper Danny Nir'on, with the aim of making him the team's first-choice keeper.

Nothing has been signed on that front yet, but according to the report talks are at an advanced stage as manager Masai Dogo shapes his goalkeeping department ahead of the club's return to the top flight.

Dogo, retained after guiding Ramat Gan to promotion following a second-place finish in Liga Leumit last season, is overseeing a broader squad rebuild during pre-season training as the club prepares for its first Ligat Ha'al campaign in years.
Elsewhere in that rebuild, ONE reports Ibrahim Fard is expected to fly in to Israel shortly to begin training with his new teammates.
Dogo is also pushing to bring in Noam Schwartz, with Hapoel Ramat Gan waiting on Maccabi Tel Aviv to decide whether they will release the midfielder to join the newly promoted side.

title: Barda warns Hapoel Tel Aviv against complacency with Ludogorets tie in the balance
dek: Ahead of Thursday's Conference League return leg in Razgrad, coach Elyaniv Barda is guarding against overconfidence despite a 2-0 first-leg lead over Ludogorets.
body: Hapoel Tel Aviv carry a comfortable-looking 2-0 lead into Thursday night's return leg against Ludogorets in Razgrad, but coach Elyaniv Barda is doing everything he can this week to stop his players believing the tie is already won.
"If we arrive thinking the first-match victory is enough, we'll pay dearly for it," Barda said, according to ONE. "One goal from them, and we can get into trouble."

The warning is rooted in simple arithmetic. Ludogorets need only a two-goal swing to force extra time, and a three-goal winning margin would send them through outright, so Barda has spent the week on the group's mentality as much as its tactics, determined that his squad treats Thursday's second qualifying round tie in the Conference League as a contest still very much alive.

The first leg, played last Thursday, produced a landmark night for Hapoel Tel Aviv regardless of what happens in Bulgaria. It marked the club's first competitive European fixture in twelve years, though UEFA scheduling meant the nominal "home" leg was actually staged in Miskolc, Hungary rather than at Bloomfield Stadium.

Israeli media, including Israel Hayom and Ynet, reported that Omri Altman put Hapoel ahead right on the stroke of half-time, before a second goal in stoppage time — attributed to Chico — sealed a 2-0 win that sent the Reds to Bulgaria with a healthy cushion.

Roughly 1,450 Hapoel Tel Aviv supporters snapped up the club's full ticket allocation for the away leg at Ludogorets' Huvepharma Arena, a modest reminder of how much appetite there is among the club's fanbase for a first genuine European run in over a decade.

Ludogorets arrive at the tie diminished from their usual continental standing. The Bulgarian side finished only third domestically last season, ending a run of fourteen straight championships, and needed penalties to see off Lokomotiv Plovdiv in the playoff round just to reach this stage against Hapoel.

Barda's side will lean on the same core that delivered the first-leg win — Altman, Stav Turiel, Emmanuel Boateng and the rest of the attacking group that gave Ludogorets problems in Hungary — but the manager's message this week has been about discipline rather than personnel changes.

Victory on Thursday would send Hapoel Tel Aviv into the third qualifying round of the Conference League, another step in a European comeback that, on the pitch in Hungary a week ago, already looked better than most in Israel had dared hope for.

title: Israeli basketball referees threaten to boycott new season over surge in personal lawsuits
dek: Officials' representatives warn Ligat Ha'Al games cannot go ahead unless league chiefs curb legal action against referees, after a Hapoel Tel Aviv fan filed a 640,000-shekel suit against the officials from June's playoff final.
body: Israel's top basketball division is heading toward a fresh crisis before a ball has even been bounced in the new season, with referees' representatives warning they will not officiate preseason friendlies or league games unless club chiefs act to stop personal lawsuits being filed against officials over their on-court decisions.

In a letter to league leadership reported by ONE, the referees' representative body did not mince words: "if the phenomenon is not handled immediately and effectively... referees will not be able to open the league season." It is an unusually stark ultimatum from a group whose independence, they argue, is being eroded case by case.

The trigger is a lawsuit that has rattled the sport. Shimon Zitron, a Hapoel Tel Aviv businessman and former club board member, filed a 640,000-shekel ($175,000) suit at the Tel Aviv Small Claims Court against five officials from the June 16 Ligat Ha'Al playoff final between Maccabi Tel Aviv and Hapoel Tel Aviv at Menora Mivtachim Arena.

Named in Zitron's claim are referees Amit Black, Ofer Manheim and Omer Estron, along with game supervisor Meir Portal and observer Gil Gordon. The suit stems from an incident in which Zitron called out to fallen Hapoel player Jimmy Clark from his front-row seat, prompting Maccabi's Jalen Hood to approach him in what Zitron describes as a threatening manner before security removed him from the arena. He alleges the officials' subsequent reports on the episode were defamatory and misrepresented what actually happened.

For the referees' body, that case has become the flashpoint for a wider grievance: a growing pattern, they say, of individuals turning to the courts to relitigate calls and incidents that used to stay on the scoresheet. Their letter frames it as a threat not just to individual officials but to "judicial independence" within the sport itself.

The demands are specific. League leadership, the referees say, must move to stop personal lawsuits being filed against officials, guarantee full legal representation and financial compensation for any referee who is sued over decisions made in the line of duty, and put in place lasting mechanisms to shield officiating from that kind of legal pressure.

The letter was addressed to the men who run the professional game in Israel: Basketball Association chairman Amos Frishman, league management chairman Ari Steinberg and league CEO David Basen, with the referees' association headed by Asi Shalem. None of the three had issued a public response by the time ONE's report was published.

It is not the league's only labor flashpoint this year. Just weeks earlier, Israeli players staged their own strike action in the closing stretch of the season, in a dispute over reduced court time for domestic players under the foreign-player quota, an episode that briefly threatened to force clubs to field foreign and youth players alone.

With preseason friendlies looming and the new Ligat Ha'Al campaign due to get under way in the coming weeks, the referees' warning leaves league leadership facing a decision it cannot easily postpone: find a way to shield officials from personal legal exposure, or risk a season that cannot open on time.
facts: Referees' representatives in Israel's top basketball division, Ligat Ha'Al, have warned they will not officiate preseason or regular-season games unless league leadership curbs personal lawsuits against officials.

The trigger is a 640,000-shekel lawsuit filed at the Tel Aviv Small Claims Court by Hapoel Tel Aviv businessman and former board member Shimon Zitron against five officials from the June 16, 2026 playoff final between Maccabi Tel Aviv and Hapoel Tel Aviv at Menora Mivtachim Arena.

Zitron's suit names referees Amit Black, Ofer Manheim and Omer Estron, game supervisor Meir Portal and observer Gil Gordon, alleging defamation over their account of an incident that led to his ejection from the arena.

The referees' representatives, headed by Asi Shalem, are demanding league leadership stop personal suits against officials, guarantee legal representation and compensation for sued referees, and protect referees' 'judicial independence.'
The letter was addressed to Basketball Association chairman Amos Frishman, league management chairman Ari Steinberg and league CEO David Basen.

It is the second major labor dispute to threaten the league's calendar in 2026, after Israeli players struck in the closing weeks of last season over reduced playing time under the foreign-player quota.

title: Maccabi Tel Aviv communications VP Roey Gladstone to step down after nine years
dek: The basketball club's VP of communications and digital, who built the department from scratch in 2017, is parting ways with Maccabi at the end of his term.

body: Roey Gladstone, the vice-president of communications and digital at Maccabi Tel Aviv's basketball club, is leaving his post after nine years in charge of a department he built from the ground up, ONE reported.

Gladstone joined Maccabi in September 2017, a few months after stepping down as head of the basketball desk at the Sports Channel, where he had covered the club as a journalist. He was brought in to set up a modern communications and digital operation for one of Israeli sport's most closely watched franchises.

According to ONE, the exit comes at the end of his current term and was framed by both sides as an amicable, planned departure rather than a dismissal. Gladstone is expected to stay on through a transition period to help hand the department to his successor, who has not yet been named.
"I want to thank everyone for an unforgettable, challenging and fascinating period, in which every day brought a new adventure," Gladstone said, according to the report.

Club CEO Avi Ben Tal, who took over at Maccabi last August after a long career at Yedioth Ahronoth and as CEO of Channel 13 and Ynet, credited Gladstone with shaping the club's public voice. "Roey's contribution over the years was hugely significant in establishing our communications department and leading Maccabi Tel Aviv's digital activity," Ben Tal said, per ONE.
Over nine years, Gladstone became one of the more recognizable off-court figures at Yad Eliyahu, fronting the club's response through championship runs and controversies alike.
No timetable for a successor has been set, and ONE did not report where Gladstone is headed next.

title: Haifa radio voice Itzik Ahronovich hits back at critics: 'Maccabi Haifa is my life, I take it to heart'
dek: The veteran Haifa football commentator, criticised online for an emotional, raised-voice outburst about the club's rocky start, insists his frustration was aimed squarely at the coaching staff, not the players.
body: Itzik Ahronovich has spent the better part of two decades as one of the loudest, most recognisable voices covering Maccabi Haifa on local radio, and this week that voice became the story itself. A day after raising his tone emotionally on air while discussing the club's difficult start to the campaign, the veteran commentator went back on ONE's phone-in programme to explain himself, after clips of the outburst drew concern and criticism on social media.

"Maccabi Haifa is my life, I take it to heart, I feel good," Ahronovich told listeners, according to ONE, pushing back on the idea that the moment reflected anything more than a burst of frustration from a fan who happens to also be a broadcaster.

He was unapologetic about the passion itself, but keen to correct what he described as a misreading of his target. "I raised my voice for a few seconds. The blame isn't on the players, only on the professional staff," he said, distinguishing between his patience for Haifa's coaching setup and his loyalty to the men wearing the shirt.

To make the point concrete, he named names. "It doesn't matter who the players are — whether it's Yarin Levi, Zohar Zesano or Goni Na'or — the fault isn't with the players, only with the professional staff," Ahronovich said, rattling off three men from Haifa's dressing room to underline that his criticism was never meant to land on them.

Levi, a young striker, returned to Sami Ofer Stadium this year after an eye-catching loan spell in green-and-black-turned-yellow-and-black at Beitar Jerusalem, where he established himself as a first-team regular. Zesano, a right back, joined Haifa in a swap deal involving Beitar Jerusalem, while Na'or is a well-travelled defender who has featured for the club in recent seasons after arriving from Hapoel Jerusalem.

Ahronovich also used the interview to address the wider concern his outburst had triggered, saying he had messaged colleagues directly to reassure them. "I sent you a WhatsApp and said I feel good. Maccabi Haifa is my life and I take it to heart," he said, according to ONE, before recalling an earlier scare: he needed medical attention at Rambam Hospital during a tense past encounter against Kazakhstan's Aktobe, a club Haifa fans associate with one of the most dramatic nights in the team's European history.

None of it, he made clear, was intended as a signal that he was stepping back from the microphone or from the club he has followed for years. If anything, the episode was a reminder of how closely local radio in Haifa is stitched into the emotional life of the fanbase — for better and, this week, briefly, for worse.
Maccabi Haifa have not commented publicly on the commentator's remarks, and ONE's report did not detail specific results behind the "crisis" Ahronovich referenced on air.

title: AC Milan deny false rumours of Franco Baresi's death, say club great is 'going through a difficult period'
dek: The club moved quickly to quash false reports spreading on social media that the former captain and three-time European champion had died, saying he and his family have its full support.
body: AC Milan were forced into an unusual and uncomfortable statement on Wednesday night, publicly denying false reports that had begun circulating on social media claiming that club legend Franco Baresi had died.

The rumours, which spread quickly across Italian social platforms, prompted the club to intervene directly rather than let the false claims linger. Milan's official statement was blunt: it denied "the false reports concerning Franco Baresi that have begun circulating in recent minutes," adding that "Franco is going through a difficult and delicate time, and the club stands firmly alongside him and his family," while asking for his privacy to be respected.

Baresi, 66, is one of the most decorated defenders in football history. He spent his entire 20-year playing career at Milan between 1977 and 1997, captaining the club for 15 of those seasons, and won three European Cups (1989, 1990 and 1994) along with six Serie A titles. He also captained Italy to the final of the 1994 World Cup. Since 2020 he has served as the club's honorary vice-president.

The panic around his health traces back to last August, when Baresi underwent surgery to remove a nodule from his lung after routine examinations flagged the issue. The operation was described as successful, with no complications in his recovery, though doctors recommended a course of immunotherapy afterwards. Baresi himself said at the time that he would "need some time to get back in shape," thanking Milan and supporters for their encouragement.
He was seen back at San Siro in December, attending a Milan match as he continued his recovery, which had offered some reassurance to fans before this week's false alarm reignited concern.

Milan's decision to issue a formal club statement, rather than leave the denial to individuals close to Baresi, underlines how seriously the club took the spread of the misinformation and its sensitivity given his ongoing health situation.

ONE reports that among those initially caught out was Italian deputy prime minister and prominent Milan supporter Matteo Salvini, who posted a tribute to Baresi online before deleting it once the false premise became clear.

title: Adeyemi: I'm not afraid of Lamine Yamal or anyone else
dek: The new Barcelona forward says he won't be intimidated by competition for a starting spot from the club's young stars as he settles in after his move from Borussia Dortmund.
body: Karim Adeyemi has wasted no time addressing the elephant in the room at his new club: how does a newly arrived German winger expect to get minutes in a Barcelona attack already stacked with teenage sensation Lamine Yamal and company?

"I'm not afraid of any player, not Lamine or anyone else. I know my abilities," Adeyemi said, according to ONE, when asked directly about the competition for playing time he will face up front at Camp Nou. "If I'm at my best and give my hundred percent on the pitch, I will play. Everything depends on me."

It is a blunt answer from a player who arrived at Barcelona this month carrying no shortage of pressure. The 24-year-old completed his move from Borussia Dortmund in a deal worth around €22 million plus roughly €9 million in add-ons, with the Bundesliga club retaining a 35 percent sell-on clause and Adeyemi signing a contract through 2031.

He was formally unveiled at a Barcelona press conference on July 23, telling reporters that expectations at his new club are simply part of the deal. "I'm joining the best club in the world," he said, adding that when he first heard of Barcelona's interest, "I couldn't believe it; my last season wasn't the best."

The move reunites Adeyemi with head coach Hansi Flick, who first capped him for the German national team. "Flick has been a pillar of support; he told me to give it my all," Adeyemi said of the manager who convinced him the switch to Spain made sense.

On Yamal specifically, Adeyemi was warm rather than wary. "I think he's an incredible footballer; I can connect with him," he said, describing himself as the kind of runner who thrives off exactly the sort of passes Yamal supplies. "He scores goals and you've got to feed him the ball."

Asked to weigh Yamal's rapid rise against the club's greatest icon, Adeyemi kept his answer grounded rather than hyperbolic. "Lamine wouldn't mind if I said it's difficult to reach Messi's level," he said, before naming his own footballing heroes: "My role models and idols at Barça are Messi and also Ronaldinho."

Adeyemi also praised the production line behind Yamal and Barcelona's other academy graduates, saying the young players to have broken through are technically outstanding and relentless workers on top of their talent — a nod to a Barcelona squad now blending marquee signings with homegrown stars as it targets a serious Champions League push this season.

title: Hapoel Ramat Gan open with 2-1 comeback win, but club says squad 'still needs to strengthen'
dek: Fresh off a Toto Cup win to start pre-season, the newly promoted club is chasing six to eight more signings before its Ligat Ha'al return — including Maccabi Tel Aviv defender Noam Schwartz and goalkeeper Omer Niron.
body: Hapoel Ramat Gan Givatayim opened its pre-season with a comeback 2-1 win over Hapoel Petah Tikva in the second round of the Toto Cup, but the mood inside the club afterwards was less about the three points than about what still has to happen before the real season starts.

Playing at the municipal stadium in Rehovot, Ramat Gan fell behind before Idan Barnes leveled and Luan Campos struck late to seal the win — a fitting way, ONE reports, for a squad in transition to open the campaign.

This is a significant season for the club: Ramat Gan Givatayim returns to Ligat Ha'al for the first time in 13 years, having climbed back after Michael Zandberg was dismissed as head coach last October and Masai Dago, fresh from his exit at Bnei Yehuda, took over and drove the promotion push.

Despite the winning start, a club source told ONE the group "still needs to strengthen significantly," adding pointedly that "if we succeed, the lineup in the league will look very different" from the one that beat Petah Tikva.

The numbers behind that statement are striking for a club only weeks from its top-flight return: Ramat Gan is targeting six to eight further additions to the squad, with at least four of them expected to be foreign players, and the club wants the bulk of that business wrapped up before the league opens rather than waiting on the January window.

Top of Dago's wish list, according to the report, is Noam Schwartz, the young Maccabi Tel Aviv defender — the coach wants him in Ramat Gan, and the club is now waiting on Maccabi Tel Aviv's decision on whether to let him leave, likely on loan given his contract in Tel Aviv.
Ramat Gan is also closing in on a deal for goalkeeper Omer Niron, whom ONE describes as close to being finalized as the club's first-choice option between the posts for the coming season.

The incoming business already has some shape to it. Brazilian forward Luan Campos, 24, a product of the Palmeiras academy, has signed a two-year deal with an option for a third, and made an immediate impact with the winning goal against Petah Tikva. Portuguese centre-back Jota Gonçalves, 26, a former Portugal youth international who captained Vizela before his contract there expired, has also joined, along with midfielder Ibrahim Fard, who was due at the club for his first training session the day after the Petah Tikva win.

For a club rebuilding a squad capable of surviving in Israel's top division after over a decade away, Wednesday's win was a welcome start — but by the club's own admission, the version of Hapoel Ramat Gan that takes the field for the league opener in three weeks' time is still very much a work in progress.
facts: Hapoel Ramat Gan Givatayim beat Hapoel Petah Tikva 2-1 in the second round of the Toto Cup, coming from behind.
