title: Hungarian side Debrecen chase Bnei Sakhnin's Salman as forward eyes pay rise
dek: Debreceni VSC have reportedly offered around €200,000 a season for the in-form attacker, but Bnei Sakhnin are refusing to sell — and Salman says he would stay for the right salary.

verificationSources.label: ONE - דברצן ההונגרית רוצה את סלמן, שמצפה לשדרוג שכרו

body: Hungarian top-flight club Debreceni VSC have set their sights on Bnei Sakhnin forward Ahmad Salman, ONE reports, with the young Israeli attacker growing increasingly frustrated at his modest wages despite a productive campaign for the Ligat Ha'al side.

According to the report, Debrecen have moved quickly, informing Sakhnin of their interest and putting an annual contract worth roughly €200,000 on the table for the 22-year-old — several times what he currently earns in Israel.

Sakhnin, ONE says, are refusing to entertain a sale and have no intention of releasing Salman midway through his development at the club, where he has become one of the more influential attacking figures over the past season.

The player's frustration, per the report, centres on pay rather than a desire to leave: despite being heavily involved in Sakhnin's goals last season, Salman is said to be among the lowest earners in the squad. He has indicated he would be willing to stay put if the club moves to upgrade his contract.

Salman, born in March 2004, came through the Hapoel Katamon and Hapoel Jerusalem youth system before senior spells at Hapoel Jerusalem and Maccabi Netanya, joining Bnei Sakhnin in 2024. He has also represented Israel at under-19 level, including in the side that won silver at the 2022 European U-19 Championship.

A move to Debrecen, regular participants in Hungary's NB I and occasional European qualifiers, would represent a significant step up in profile as well as salary for the forward — but for now, ONE's report frames this as an approach rather than a deal in motion, with Sakhnin standing firm.

The situation leaves Salman's future unresolved for now: a club unwilling to sell, a suitor offering a substantial pay rise, and a player who says money — not a move abroad for its own sake — is the real issue at stake.

title: Suspect arrested over arson at Givatayim restaurant owned by Beitar Jerusalem's chairman
dek: Police detained a man from Rehovot over the July 12 fire at a Japonica branch, the latest in a wave of attacks on the chain owned by Beitar Jerusalem controlling owner Barak Abramov.
body: Tel Aviv District Police's Central Unit (Yamar) has arrested a suspect over the arson attack on a Japonica restaurant branch in Givatayim, a chain owned by Beitar Jerusalem's controlling owner, Barak Abramov, ONE reports.

The suspect, a man in his 20s from Rehovot, was taken into custody and transferred for questioning. Police are due to bring him before the Tel Aviv Magistrate's Court to request an extension of his remand.

The fire at the Givatayim branch broke out in the early hours of July 12. It is one of a string of attacks that have hit Japonica outlets across the country in recent weeks, with other branches targeted by explosive devices, pepper-spray grenades and gunfire, according to Israeli media reports.

Abramov bought the Japonica chain in 2015 and has separately owned Beitar Jerusalem, one of Israeli football's most prominent and fan-driven clubs, since 2022, when he took over the club along with its debts.

Ynet reported that the wave of attacks has been linked by police sources to a feud between rival crime organisations, with one faction allegedly targeting Abramov's business after concluding he had grown closer to a rival family. Abramov himself is not a suspect in any wrongdoing.
The unrest has had commercial fallout too: a planned stock exchange listing for Japonica has reportedly been postponed as a result of the ongoing attacks.

The Givatayim arrest marks the first announced breakthrough in the investigation into the chain's targeting, though police have not said whether they believe the case is connected to organised crime or is being treated as an isolated act.

title: Belgium's second tier to let coaches challenge referees instead of using full VAR
dek: The Challenger Pro League will trial Football Video Support next season, handing the power to trigger video reviews to coaches rather than a video assistant referee
body: Belgium's second-tier Challenger Pro League will scrap the idea of full VAR coverage next season and instead hand referees' decisions over to a coach-driven challenge system, becoming one of the first senior men's competitions in the world to test it in a full domestic season.

The system, known as Football Video Support (FVS), flips the usual VAR model on its head. Rather than a video assistant referee proactively scanning replays for every goal, penalty shout and red card, it is the coaches on the touchline who decide whether a decision is worth contesting.

Each coach will get two challenges per match, with a third available should the game go to extra time. To use one, a coach makes a rotating-finger gesture and hands a review card to the fourth official, who relays the request to the referee. The referee then goes to a pitchside monitor to review the footage before making a final call.

Reviews are limited to four categories: goals, penalty-box incidents, direct red cards, and cases where a card has been shown to the wrong player. If the original decision is upheld, the coach loses that challenge for the rest of the match; if it is overturned, they keep it in reserve.

Belgian Pro League chief executive Lorin Parys explained the move as a practical one rather than a philosophical rejection of VAR. Running a full video assistant referee setup across every fixture in a second division, he said, simply is not financially realistic — the same reasoning that has kept the Dutch second tier without VAR altogether. The aim, in his words, is not to leave clubs and supporters at the mercy of officiating errors just because the top-flight technology is out of reach.

FVS is not a Belgian invention. The concept was developed for futsal and made its first official appearance at the 2021 FIFA Futsal World Cup in Lithuania, having already been tested in Spain's domestic futsal league. It has since crossed over into 11-a-side football, with trials at FIFA youth tournaments including the 2024 Blue Stars/FIFA Youth Cup and the 2024 FIFA Under-20 Women's World Cup.

On the professional club stage, Italy's Serie C began testing FVS in October 2024, and Spain's Liga F — the country's top women's division — adopted it for the current 2025-26 season. Canada's domestic top flight has trials pencilled in for 2026, and Germany's federation, the DFB, has signalled openness to introducing the system domestically.

The Challenger Pro League's adoption pushes FVS further into the mainstream of men's senior football than it has gone before, and will be watched closely by other cash-strapped second and third divisions weighing up whether full VAR is worth the cost — or whether a cheaper, coach-led compromise can deliver similar accuracy without the price tag.

The comparison being drawn locally is with challenge systems already familiar in other sports: tennis players contesting line calls, or ice hockey coaches asking for a review, both operating on a similar use-it-or-lose-it principle rather than constant official oversight.

title: Ironi Tiberias lawyer accuses IFA spokesman of acting as 'judge and executioner'
dek: Attorney Kobi Levi has demanded a retraction from Israel Football Association spokesman Shlomi Barzel, warning against prejudging a fresh indictment over alleged player IV infusions ahead of Wednesday's hearing.
body: Ironi Tiberias has opened a new front in its long-running battle with Israeli football's disciplinary machinery — this time aimed not at a judge, but at the Israel Football Association's own spokesman.

Club attorney Kobi Levi sent a sharply worded warning letter to the IFA this week, ONE reports, accusing spokesman Shlomi Barzel of behaving as "an arbiter, judge and executioner" over public comments he made about a fresh indictment filed against Tiberias barely a day earlier.

That indictment, lodged around July 27, centres on allegations that club officials arranged improper intravenous infusions for players before a bottom-of-the-table relegation playoff against Ashdod last season — reportedly more than the permitted 100 millilitres of saline solution, administered in what prosecutors allege breached IFA bylaws on assisting the use of drugs and stimulants "in aggravated circumstances."

According to ONE, Levi's letter took particular issue with Barzel invoking an entirely separate case while the new charges remain untested. "We had evidence and because of the war we decided to give up. Ultimately 14 league points, the harshest penalty," Barzel was quoted as saying — a reference to Tiberias's earlier disciplinary saga over so-called double contracts.

That case ended in a plea deal approved by the IFA's disciplinary tribunal on April 1, with Tiberias accepting an eight-point deduction with immediate effect and six more in the coming season, a fine of 500,000 shekels payable in seven instalments, and a ban on registering new players from the January 2027 window. Club owner Miki Bitan was separately barred from all football activity for seven years, beginning June 1.

Levi's letter argues that citing that 14-point precedent while a new, unrelated indictment is pending amounts to prejudging Tiberias's guilt before the case has been heard — a breach, he wrote, of the presumption of innocence. It formally demands a public clarification that the club remains innocent until proven otherwise, a retraction of Barzel's remarks, and confirmation of whether the spokesman's comments reflect the IFA's official position or his own.

The club has given the association until next Tuesday to respond — one day before a scheduled hearing on Tiberias's legal standing in the new case, with Levi noting that the indictment "has only just been filed."

Tiberias has separately dismissed the substance of the new charges. In a statement carried by Walla Sport, the club called the indictment "a document full of assumptions... without solid facts and evidence," insisting prosecutors have no scientific documentation of the quantities involved and are relying instead on "conservative assumptions and average calculations." The club also alleged the investigation was marred by bias and procedural failures, including a failure to properly question key officials.

With Tiberias already facing a six-point deduction and a transfer ban carried into the new season from the double-contracts case, any further sanction from the new indictment threatens to leave the club fielding what it has itself warned could be an under-strength side. Wednesday's hearing looks set to be the first real test of how the IFA's disciplinary court handles the case — and how much weight, if any, it gives to the war of words now breaking out around it.

title: The day Leganés' owner told his coach: "We have the new Messi"
dek: A home video of a 16-year-old on a US academy pitch convinced Jeff Luhnow he had found a gem. Two years on, Yan Diomande is closing in on a Real Madrid move worth well over €100 million.
body: Before Yan Diomande had kicked a ball for CD Leganés' first team, the club's owner was already telling people he had unearthed the next Lionel Messi. Borja Jiménez, the coach who took Leganés into La Liga and later into the Bernabéu on the night Diomande would debut, has now told the story in detail — and ONE picked it up this week under the headline that gives away the punchline: "We have the new Messi."

According to Jiménez's account, Leganés owner Jeff Luhnow — the American businessman better known in the US for his years running the Houston Astros — pulled up a YouTube clip on his phone and showed it to his coach. It was grainy home footage of a 16-year-old Diomande playing for a boys' academy team in the United States. Luhnow's verdict, as Jiménez remembers it, was blunt: "We have the new Messi."

Diomande, an Ivorian winger, had been training with Leganés' academy set-up but was nowhere near the first-team picture when Jiménez first laid eyes on him in the flesh — by his own telling, barely a week before Leganés were due to travel to face Real Madrid at the Santiago Bernabéu in March 2025. Jiménez threw him into that squad anyway.

The teenager's senior debut came in Madrid, in front of the club he would eventually be linked with buying him. Jiménez has described the instant impact: in Diomande's very first involvement he raced down the wing, beat two defenders and nearly won a penalty. Leganés were relegated from La Liga that season regardless, but Jiménez has since said he believes an earlier introduction for Diomande — rather than a late-season cameo — might have been enough to drag the club to safety.

What happened next moved fast even by modern transfer-market standards. In the summer of 2024, Leganés sold Diomande to RB Leipzig for a reported €20 million, a fee that looked full value at the time for a player who had barely established himself. Leganés reportedly kept a resale clause worth somewhere between five and eight percent of any future transfer, a detail that is about to look extremely shrewd.

Just over a year later, Real Madrid have agreed a deal to sign Diomande from Leipzig. Fabrizio Romano and multiple outlets in Spain, Germany and England reported this week that the two clubs have struck an agreement worth well in excess of €100 million, with figures cited ranging from a fixed fee near €120 million to a package — including add-ons — closer to €135 million. Neither club had confirmed final terms at the time of writing.

Whichever number lands, the trajectory is staggering: a player sold for €20 million barely twelve months ago is now being valued at five to seven times that figure. Jiménez himself predicted the leap, telling Spanish media he expected Diomande's value to "double or triple" within a year or two of leaving Leganés — a forecast that has already been comfortably exceeded.

Diomande, born on 14 November 2006, made his mark in his single season at Leipzig and has also become a fixture for Ivory Coast at international level. Real Madrid, under Jose Mourinho, are said to be closing in on completing the paperwork before the squad departs for their pre-season training camp in Austria, with an official announcement expected imminently.

For Leganés, the deal is a bittersweet footnote — vindication for the recruitment call Luhnow made on nothing more than a phone video, and a reminder of how far a lower-table Spanish club's discovery can travel once a giant like Real Madrid decides it wants in.

title: Kozuk weighs lineup changes for Hapoel Beer Sheva's Vikingur return leg
dek: Training sessions this week have pointed the Hapoel Beer Sheva coach toward personnel changes for Wednesday's Champions League qualifier, though his staff insist the players' approach must shift too.
body: Ran Kozuk is weighing changes to his Hapoel Beer Sheva starting eleven for Wednesday's Champions League second qualifying round return leg against Vikingur Reykjavik, with the Israeli champions needing to overturn a first-leg deficit to keep their European campaign alive.

Beer Sheva lost the opening leg 2-1 in Reykjavik last week. Kings Kangwa pulled a goal back for the visitors, but two second-half strikes from the Icelandic champions left Kozuk's side with work to do heading into the second leg.

Because Hapoel Beer Sheva cannot currently stage UEFA competition matches at Turner Stadium, the return fixture has been moved to Szombathely in Hungary, the venue that has become the club's de facto home ground for European nights.

According to ONE, this week's training sessions have pushed Kozuk toward using Zahi Ahmed and Javon East in place of Mohamed Abu Romi and Amir Ganah in the starting lineup, based on what the coaching staff have seen on the training pitch.

Niv Yehoshua is expected to keep his place in the side, while Matan Baltaxa, who is working back from a mild concussion, is being considered either at left-back or in central defence, the report said.

Before any talk of personnel, though, ONE reported that the coaching staff have stressed to the squad that the real shift needs to come in the players' approach — that this is a Champions League tie and Beer Sheva must play with far greater intensity than they showed in Iceland.

That message echoes what Sport5 reported from inside the camp: after a tactical debriefing following the first leg, Kozuk held individual conversations with several players before turning to the training ground, where he deliberately avoided running a full XI in practice — sticking to small-sided scrimmages instead — so as not to tip off the starting lineup while training on the actual matchday pitch.

There is squad business unfolding in parallel. ONE reported that Pedro Amador, set to join as a new left-back, was undergoing medical evaluations in Israel, with a note of concern over an Achilles tendon issue before his signing could be finalised. Walla Sport has since reported the move as agreed, with Amador expected to land in Israel shortly.

For Kozuk, Wednesday is as much about mentality as selection. A repeat of the passive display in Reykjavik would end Beer Sheva's hopes of advancing in Europe; a response built on intensity, he and his staff believe, is what gives them a chance of erasing the aggregate deficit on home — if borrowed — turf.

title: Pirlo's son hits back as Italy's coaching search turns to Mancini and Conte
dek: Nicolò Pirlo says "noise" beat competence and values after his father's candidacy for the Azzurri job collapsed, with Roberto Mancini now favoured over Antonio Conte to take the bench.
body: Nicolò Pirlo has broken his silence over the humiliating collapse of his father's candidacy to coach Italy, accusing the federation of letting "noise" drown out competence and values.

The 23-year-old, who works for the football agency Gersh Sports, posted a statement on social media on Monday defending Andrea Pirlo after the former World Cup winner was dropped from contention for the national team job amid a row over his commercial ties to a Russian betting firm.

"As a son, but also as a young man who dreams of building a future in football, all of this hurts," Nicolò wrote, adding that "noise seems to count more than competence, respect and values today." He said his bitterness was not about losing a coaching post — "that can be won and lost in sport" — but about the climate created around a man who, in his words, has "always let his work speak, without seeking shortcuts."

Andrea Pirlo, the 2006 World Cup winner turned coach of Fatih Karagümrük in Turkey, had emerged as a surprise front-runner for the Azzurri bench only after Carlo Ancelotti and Pep Guardiola both turned the job down. ESPN reported that his candidacy then unravelled over a sponsorship arrangement linking him to Fonbet, a Russian betting company, through a deal with a club in the UAE.

The saga has been chaotic even by Italian football's standards. Paolo Maldini and Leonardo, the technical directors who had championed Pirlo as a long-term project builder, are reported to have resigned once his appointment was shelved, leaving federation president Giovanni Malagò to take the final call on the appointment himself.
With Pirlo gone, the race has reverted to the two men most observers expected to be fighting for the job all along: Roberto Mancini and Antonio Conte.

Mancini, who led Italy to the Euro 2020 title (played in the summer of 2021) before a shock resignation in 2023, is reported to be in pole position and remains close to Malagò and to several senior players from his old squad. He has been out of work since leaving Qatari club Al-Sadd last month and has made no secret of his ambition to lead Italy at a World Cup, having missed out on the 2022 tournament after the team's playoff elimination.

Conte, who steered the Azzurri to the Euro 2016 quarter-finals before his current spell at Napoli, remains the preferred option of several Serie A clubs. His trademark 3-5-2 system would mean a tactical overhaul from the back-four setup Italy have used in recent cycles, a factor understood to be weighing on Malagò's thinking.
Giorgio Chiellini, the former Juventus and Italy defender, is separately reported to be the leading candidate to take over the technical director's role vacated by Maldini and Leonardo.

Whoever gets the job inherits a national team in genuine crisis: Italy have failed to qualify for three consecutive World Cups, an unprecedented run of failure for a four-time champion, and the federation is under pressure to end the chaos with a swift, credible appointment.

title: Torino and Genoa keep close watch on Maccabi Tel Aviv's Sayed Abu Farhi
dek: ONE reports the Serie A pair are tracking the 20-year-old striker, with scouts expected in Batumi for Thursday's Europa League qualifying return leg against Sheriff Tiraspol.

verificationSources.label: Ynet - Maccabi Tel Aviv 5-0 Sheriff Tiraspol report

body: Two Serie A clubs are circling one of Israeli football's brightest young forwards. ONE reports that Torino and Genoa are following Maccabi Tel Aviv striker Sayed Abu Farhi closely, with both sides expected to have scouts watching when Maccabi complete their Europa League qualifying tie away to Sheriff Tiraspol on Thursday.

The interest comes on the back of a red-hot start to the campaign for the 20-year-old. Abu Farhi scored twice in Maccabi's 5-0 demolition of Sheriff in the first leg, heading in a cross from Ido Shahar in the fifth minute before converting from the penalty spot in the 74th to cap a one-sided night.

It was his second brace in as many outings. According to ONE, Abu Farhi also scored twice against Hapoel Be'er Sheva as Maccabi lifted the Israeli Champions Cup with a 3-1 win at the start of the season under new manager Kenny Miller.

That run of back-to-back doubles is what has put him on the Italian radar, per the report, with Torino and Genoa said to be monitoring him closely enough that they could send representatives to Georgia for Thursday's return leg, which Sheriff are hosting in Batumi rather than Tiraspol.
Neither club has made contact over a formal move, and no fee or contract details were mentioned in the report - this is scouting interest at an early stage, not a confirmed approach.

Abu Farhi, born in Baqa al-Gharbiyye in May 2006, made his senior debut for Maccabi in August 2023 as a substitute against Celje in Conference League qualifying, before loan spells at Kafr Qasim and Maccabi Bnei Reineh helped sharpen him for first-team football. He nailed down the starting striker's role last season and has also represented Israel's under-21 side under Guy Luzon.

Speaking to Walla Sport after the Champions Cup final, he made no secret of his hunger for more. "I'm always aspiring for more," he said. "Even if I score 30 goals, next season I want 31." He also credited Miller's preparation for the team's fast start and named the league title as the trophy he most wants to win with Maccabi.

For now, Abu Farhi remains focused on Europe with Maccabi, who carry a five-goal cushion into Thursday's second leg. Any decision on his future is likely to wait until the Israeli champions know how far this season's qualifying run takes them - but with two Serie A scouting departments now paying attention, his stock is rising fast.

title: Commanders fire tight ends coach Ben Steele on the eve of training camp after DUI arrest
dek: Ben Steele never coached a single practice for Washington after joining the staff in February — the club cut ties days before camp opened following a June drink-driving arrest in Virginia.
body: The Washington Commanders parted ways with tight ends coach Ben Steele on Monday, cutting short a tenure that never even reached its first training-camp practice, after the club learned he had been arrested last month on suspicion of driving under the influence.

Steele, 48, was stopped by police in Loudoun County, Virginia, in the early hours of June 7, not far from the Commanders' training facility, and was arrested on charges that included driving while intoxicated, refusing to submit to a blood or breath test, obstructing or resisting an officer without force, and an improper lane change, according to Virginia court records cited by multiple US outlets.

Steele reported the arrest to the organisation himself, prompting the Commanders to place him on leave and inform the NFL league office, several reports said. He stayed on leave through the following weeks before the club decided to sever ties entirely on Monday, just before training camp opened for the 2026 season.
"We are parting ways with tight ends coach Ben Steele," the club said in a brief statement. "The team will have no further comment at this time."

The Israeli outlet ONE, in reporting the firing, framed the timing starkly: Steele arrived after last season ended only to be dismissed a day before the very camp he was hired to help run, never getting the chance to coach a single practice session with his position group.

Steele had joined Washington in late February as part of head coach Dan Quinn's offseason staff moves, brought in to replace David Raih, who was promoted to pass-game coordinator. Before that, he spent three seasons as tight ends coach of the Arizona Cardinals, where he was credited with helping develop Trey McBride into one of the NFL's most productive tight ends and an All-Pro selection.

The Commanders, who reached the NFC Championship game last season under Quinn, must now fill the position quickly, with the full roster set to report for training camp this week ahead of the 2026 campaign.

title: Hapoel Tirat Carmel build their Liga Alef push around homegrown youngsters
dek: Newly promoted to the third tier, the Haifa-area club are handing first-team roles to academy graduates Sahar Mansour and David Swissa under new coach Lidan Deloya

verificationSources.label: ONE/Walla - Lidan Deloya coaching background at Hapoel Acre

body: Hapoel Tirat Carmel are entering their maiden season in Liga Alef with a squad plan built more on patience than spending: hand the ball to the kids the club raised itself.

The Haifa-district side, promoted after finishing runner-up in Liga Bet, have installed Lidan Deloya as head coach for the third-tier campaign. Deloya arrives with a coaching CV that includes a spell as assistant coach at Hapoel Haifa and time working with both youth and senior teams at Hapoel Acre, according to ONE.
He will be flanked by Amit Peretz as assistant coach, who also works with the Under-18 side at MK Neve Yosef Haifa, and by Paz Ron as fitness coach.

The headline decision, though, is upstairs rather than on the touchline: club officials have chosen to fast-track two academy products straight into senior contention rather than shop exclusively in the transfer market.

Forward Sahar Mansour, 20, is promoted after six years working through the youth ranks, in which he scored 102 goals, ONE reports. The club's framing of the move leaves little ambiguity about how highly he is rated internally, with the sky reportedly described as the limit for where his career could yet go.

Goalkeeper David Swissa, who turns 19 later this year, is the other academy graduate handed a first-team opportunity. He has been with Hapoel Tirat Carmel for close to a decade, progressing through every age group before this promotion.

"There is no greater pride than a club seeing a homegrown player grow from the youth leagues into the senior team," the club said in comments carried by ONE, framing the promotions as a statement of identity rather than a short-term fix.
Around that academy core, the rebuilt squad also brings back experience: forward Michael Ashkenazi and defender Ron Applebaum both return for the new campaign.

The recruitment outside the club has stayed local and modest in scale, in keeping with third-tier budgets. Defenders Omer Liyad and Barak Englister arrive from Liga Bet side Or Akiva, while defender Uriel Cohen joins from fellow Liga Alef club Tira.

It is a deliberately unglamorous roster build for a club making its first appearance at this level, one that leans on continuity in defence and faith in what the academy has produced rather than a marquee signing to headline the return.

title: Puzzle still incomplete: Mourinho weighs Real Madrid's next moves
dek: Four marquee arrivals are already in Madrid, but ONE reports the Portuguese coach must now decide who leaves before his rebuild is truly finished.

verificationSources.label: ONE - הפאזל עוד לא שלם: השלב הבא בפרויקט של מוריניו

body: Real Madrid's summer rebuild under José Mourinho was supposed to be the easy part of the job — sign four proven internationals, hand the Portuguese a squad built for his football, and let him get on with reclaiming the title. According to ONE, that phase is done. The harder one is only just starting.

The arrivals have been emphatic. Marc Cucurella joined from Chelsea in a deal reportedly worth up to €55 million, Bernardo Silva walked in for free after his contract at Manchester City expired, Ibrahima Konaté signed as a free agent through June 2030, and Denzel Dumfries completed a four-year move from Inter Milan. Four internationals, four positions strengthened, and a clear signal that Florentino Pérez has backed his new coach.

But ONE's report on Mourinho's project makes clear the puzzle isn't finished — it has simply moved from who comes in to who goes out. Weeks ago, the outlet reported that Mourinho had already handed Pérez a list of six players he does not consider part of his plans: Rodrygo, Eduardo Camavinga, Franco Mastantuono, Fran García, Raúl Asencio and Dani Ceballos.

Of that group, Asencio is now described as the most likely to leave. The young centre-back was one of the breakout stories of last season's Castilla-to-first-team pipeline, but Mourinho reportedly wants another established defensive option brought in, and a sale would help fund it.

Camavinga's situation is murkier. The Frenchman is one of the more talented and versatile midfielders in the squad and remains under contract until 2029, but ONE reports genuine interest from clubs in England. Real Madrid would demand a substantial fee for a player of his profile and age, but his standing under the new coaching staff appears far from secure.

Endrick's path back into the picture is also complicated. The Brazilian forward, returning from a loan spell, faces stiff competition for minutes in an attacking group already stacked with senior options, and there is no guarantee Mourinho will give him the regular football he needs at this stage of his development.

Mastantuono presents a similar dilemma. Real Madrid invested roughly €60 million in the young Argentine, but a player of his age typically needs consistent first-team minutes to develop — something that may be hard to guarantee behind the club's more established forwards this season.

Not every story is heading for the exit, though. Gonzalo García had been expected to be moved on before Mourinho arrived, but the coach is reportedly a fan of his distinctive style and profile as a forward, and the striker now looks set to stay and fight for a role rather than be sold.

The immediate backdrop to all of this is preparation, not paperwork. Real Madrid face Leganés on Tuesday at 19:00 in their second preseason friendly at Valdebebas, having opened their preseason schedule against Alcorcón — exactly the kind of low-stakes fixture Mourinho is expected to use to run his eye over the fringe players whose futures are still being decided.

None of the departures ONE describes are confirmed sales, and no fees have been reported for any of the six names on Mourinho's list. But the shape of the message from Madrid is consistent: after four heavyweight arrivals, the next test of the project is how cleanly Mourinho can trim a squad built for someone else's system into one built for his.

title: Father's claim adds a twist to Liran Sardal's Hapoel Haifa exit saga
dek: The homegrown defender is technically a free agent after rejecting a reduced contract offer, but his father insists a deal was actually struck – and rival Ligat Ha'al clubs are already circling regardless.
body: Even by the standards of a Ligat Ha'al summer full of contract stand-offs, the situation around Liran Sardal and Hapoel Haifa has taken a strange turn: the club and the player's own family cannot agree on whether a deal has actually been done.

Sardal, a fixture of the team for a generation, featured in only seven of Hapoel Haifa's 24 league matches during a difficult 2025-26 campaign. When the two sides sat down over a new contract, the club offered him a reduced salary reflecting his diminished role rather than terms befitting an automatic starter. According to Sport5, Sardal did not sign, subsequently missed the squad's pre-season training camp in Bulgaria, and is now, technically, a free agent for the first time in his career.

Hapoel Haifa's version of events is straightforward. "Nobody said we don't want him, we made an offer, he chose not to take it," the club said, according to Sport5, framing the impasse as a simple case of a player unwilling to accept a pay cut that reflects reduced playing time.

Sardal's father tells a different story. He countered that his son had, in fact, accepted the club's lowered terms and is simply waiting on the paperwork to be finalised — a version that, if accurate, would turn the saga into a misunderstanding rather than a genuine parting of ways.

According to the father, other Ligat Ha'al clubs have already made approaches for Sardal, but the player has no interest in leaving. He described Hapoel Haifa as his home since the age of five and said that is where he wants to stay.

That framing captures why the story resonates in Haifa. Sardal joined Hapoel Haifa's youth ranks at five years old and has spent 25 years at the club in total, the last 13 of them in the first team, without ever pulling on another side's shirt. He has won the State Cup with Hapoel Haifa, earned caps for Israel's senior national team, and previously represented the country's Olympic team — the kind of one-club résumé that is increasingly rare in Israeli football.

The stand-off also lands amid a wider shake-up at Sammy Ofer Stadium. Owner Yoav Katz has been pushing for a squad capable of finishing third and reaching Europe on merit, and several other contracts, including that of Tomer Yosefi, are also due to expire, pointing to a summer of significant turnover regardless of how the Sardal situation resolves.

For now, nothing is signed. Whether this becomes the quiet ending of a homegrown career or, as his father suggests, a paperwork delay before Sardal extends his quarter-century at the club, remains genuinely open — which is precisely the twist Sport5's report points to.

title: Three Gordon brothers win on the same historic night in Tel Aviv
dek: Ahavat Hashem, Ruach Hashem and Kibudei Gordon all triumphed at GFN 1 in Tel Aviv, and each now says the UFC is the target.
body: Three brothers, three fights, three wins — and one last name that was suddenly everywhere in Tel Aviv. On Monday night at the Menora Mivtachim Arena, Ahavat Hashem, Ruach Hashem and Kibudei Gordon each stepped into competition on the same card and each walked away victorious, turning a family surname into the story of Israeli combat sports.

The event, GFN 1: Israel vs. the World, was the first fight night staged in Israel under the family's own Gordon Fight Nights banner, a 12-bout card built around the trio and billed, fittingly, as a showcase for the Gordons' own rise, Sport5 reported.

The headline result belonged to Ahavat Hashem Gordon, who outpointed the veteran Brazilian John Lineker — a former ONE Championship bantamweight world champion with deep UFC pedigree — by judges' decision in the main event. The win pushed Gordon's Muay Thai record to 13-0, according to Sport5 and Ynet's coverage of the night.

Beating a fighter of Lineker's résumé in front of a packed hall was, by any measure, the biggest scalp of Gordon's career so far. Sport5 frames it as a genuine step toward wider recognition, though the outlet is careful to note his path to the UFC still runs through sharpening his ground game and stacking more high-level wins.

The eldest brother, Kibudei Gordon, produced the night's most explosive moment. Competing in a Muay Thai-rules bout rather than his usual MMA format, he knocked out Jose Alberto Quiñones — an opponent with UFC experience — in under a minute, Sport5 reported. The result lifts his overall MMA record to 8 wins and 2 losses.

Kibudei is the one brother who made the full switch to MMA while Ahavat Hashem and Ruach Hashem have stayed in Muay Thai. He has fought for organisations including LFA and FFC, and trains out of the Fighting Nerds gym in Brazil, where his training partners include UFC fighters Jean Silva and Carlos Prates alongside fellow Israelis Eilai Brazili and Sean Paro, per Sport5's reporting.

After the knockout, Kibudei used the moment to address the UFC directly, a message Sport5 describes as a call for the promotion's leadership to notice him and bring him into the organisation. It is a pitch he has made before, but rarely with a stoppage this emphatic behind it.

The youngest of the three, Ruach Hashem Gordon — born in 2004, according to Sport5 — closed out the family sweep with a unanimous decision over the Moldovan Maximus Bejenuta across three rounds. It was his second straight win, continuing a comeback after a break from competition, and adds to a Muay Thai résumé that already includes the 2023 King's Cup and recognition as an outstanding athlete at that year's IFMA World Championships.

Taken together, the night amounted to more than three individual results. Sport5's framing of the card as a launching pad for the family is hard to argue with: for one evening at least, Tel Aviv had front-row seats to what the Gordons hope becomes a recurring fixture, and each brother now carries a very public case to make to the sport's biggest stage.

title: Zidane pushes for four-tournament, eight-year deal as France's new coach
dek: Sport5 reports the incoming coach wants — and is set to get — a contract running to 2034 and covering four tournaments, though other outlets describe a shorter deal that ends after the 2030 World Cup.

verificationSources.label: Sport5 – Four tournaments guaranteed: Zidane's demand from the France national team

body: Zinedine Zidane, poised to be confirmed as France's new head coach, has told the French federation he wants — and is set to receive — a long-term commitment running all the way to 2034, according to Sport5. The Israeli outlet reports the terms amount to an eight-year contract covering four major tournaments, a striking length for an international manager's deal.

Zidane is stepping into a job Didier Deschamps held for 14 years, since 2012. Deschamps's reign delivered the 2018 World Cup title and a run to the 2022 final, but it ended painfully this summer: a 2-0 semi-final defeat to Spain at the 2026 World Cup, followed by a wild 6-4 loss to England in the third-place play-off in Miami.

Zidane, 54, won the World Cup himself as a player with France in 1998 and reached another final with Les Bleus in 2006. He has been out of coaching since his second spell at Real Madrid, where he won three straight Champions League titles between 2016 and 2018.

Per Sport5's report, the contract on the table would keep Zidane in charge through two European Championships — 2028 and 2032 — and two World Cups: the 2030 tournament co-hosted by Spain, Portugal and Morocco, and the 2034 edition awarded to Saudi Arabia.

Two familiar faces from Zidane's Real Madrid backroom staff are expected to follow him to the federation: David Bettoni, his long-time assistant since their days together at Cannes, and Hamidou Msaïdie, who worked as a fitness and rehabilitation aide under Zidane in the Spanish capital.

Sport5's account of the length and scope of the deal does not fully match other reporting on the appointment. Goal.com and ESPN, among outlets describing the terms, have reported Zidane signing on for a shorter stretch, through the 2030 World Cup, with his brief covering the 2027 Nations League, Euro 2028 and that World Cup — three tournaments rather than four. Which version reflects the final, signed terms has not been settled publicly.
The French federation has yet to formally confirm the appointment, though federation president Philippe Diallo has indicated an announcement is imminent as the process is finalised.

Either way, the broad shape of the story is not in dispute: Zidane is on his way to the France job for the first time since retiring as a player, inheriting a squad built around Kylian Mbappé and Aurélien Tchouaméni as the federation turns the page from Deschamps's long, trophy-laden era.

title: Israel's under-18s go 3-0 in Italy and draw Denmark in bid to rewrite basketball history
dek: A perfect group stage at the FIBA U18 EuroBasket sets up a last-16 tie with Denmark on Wednesday, with a place at the world championship — and a shot at Israel's best-ever youth finish — still on the table.

verificationSources.label: Sport5 — The opponents are set: the youth team's road to history

body: Israel's under-18 boys' national team closed out the group phase of the FIBA U18 EuroBasket with a perfect 3-0 record on Monday, and now knows exactly who stands between it and a place among Europe's final eight: Denmark, in Wednesday's round of 16.

The group-stage run, in Group A alongside Austria, France and Greece, included a gritty 93-84 overtime win over a Greek side considered one of the continent's strongest youth programmes, played at the A. Marchetti Sports Hall in Rovereto. Beating France in the same group only added to the sense that this squad, coached by Nadav Zilberstein, is built for a deep run.

The format is unforgiving: beat Denmark and Israel not only reaches the quarterfinals but guarantees itself a place in Division A next time out, sparing the programme the drop into the survival playoffs that awaits the loser. There is no margin for a slip.

Should Israel get past the Danes, the reward is a quarterfinal against either Slovenia, runners-up in Group C, or Latvia, third in Group D — both sides Israel would enter as underdogs on paper, but not by much given the form shown so far in Trento and Rovereto.

The tournament, running from 25 July to 2 August across the two Italian cities, carries stakes well beyond seeding. A top-five finish books a berth at the 2027 U19 World Cup in the Czech Republic — a prize Israel has claimed only once, in 2024, when it finished fourth in Tampere behind a team headlined by tournament MVP Ben Saraf and forward Omer Mayer.

Go one round further this time — a semifinal or a bronze-medal finish — and Israel would surpass even that, eclipsing the country's long-standing benchmark: fourth place at the 1972 U18 European Championship in Zadar, where Miki Berkovich's scoring carried a Ralph Klein-coached side to what had stood for more than half a century as Israeli youth basketball's high-water mark.

The current group has the individual numbers to match the collective run. Aviv Aronov leads the scoring at 26.7 points per game, David Musis is averaging a near double-double at 24.0 points and 12.0 rebounds, and Lior Hershko has been the pest at the other end, leading the team with 2.7 steals a game to go with 8.3 points.

None of that guarantees anything against a Denmark team that reached the knockout rounds out of a group including Serbia, Turkey and Slovakia. But for a programme that has spent decades chasing the shadow of 1972, Wednesday's game is the kind of test — win it, and history is genuinely in view.

title: Ruach Hashem Gordon grinds out points win as brothers' promotion debuts in Tel Aviv
dek: The middle Gordon brother needed all three rounds and the judges' scorecards to see off Moldova's Maximus Bejenuta as the family's new GFN promotion staged its first show at Menora Mivtachim Arena.
body: Ruach Hashem Gordon needed all three rounds and the judges' scorecards, but he got the job done — outpointing Moldovan Muay Thai fighter Maximus Bejenuta on Monday night at Menora Mivtachim Arena in Tel Aviv, as the Gordon brothers' own promotion staged its debut event on home soil.

The card, billed as GFN 1: Israel vs. the World and organised by the brothers together with Yaniv Kaminski, marked the first time all three fighting Gordons — Ahavat Hashem, Ruach Hashem and Kibedy — appeared on the same bill, each matched against an international opponent in Muay Thai and kickboxing bouts.
In the main event, the youngest brother, Ahavat Hashem Gordon, faced former ONE Championship flyweight king John Lineker, while Kibedy Gordon also picked up a win by knockout elsewhere on the card.

Ruach's fight went the distance. Bejenuta, a stubborn opponent who according to ONE.co.il's report worked his low kicks and pressed forward when he sensed he was behind late on, could not turn the fight around, and the judges scored it unanimously for the Israeli after three rounds and fifteen minutes.

By the outlet's account, Gordon controlled the pace from the opening round with repeated low kicks to Bejenuta's lead leg and a sharp elbow combination late in round one, leaving his opponent visibly marked by round two. Bejenuta raised his output in the third as he searched for a finish, but Gordon defended calmly and kept working behind his combinations to close out the win.
"Thanks to faith and hard work this happened. I want to thank everyone — your support helped me greatly," Gordon said afterwards, quoted by Sport5.

He also spoke about the road back to the ring. "It was a difficult year for me personally, with almost no fights, and I searched to rediscover myself. It wasn't simple at all. Although I didn't finish the fight with a knockout as I wanted, I proved to everyone who I am, and I'm very proud."
It was Gordon's second win in a row after that quiet stretch, following an earlier victory over Hussein Dolo on a UTMA card as he worked his way back to full fitness and form.

Bejenuta is no journeyman gatekeeper: the 24-year-old Moldovan made his ONE Championship debut in April at Lumpinee Stadium in Bangkok, where he lost by TKO to Tomyamkoong Bhumjaithai, giving Monday's result some added weight for a fighter still building his record.

The Gordons — sons of American-born chiropractor Azriel Gordon and Hong Kong-born mother Chaninat Hashem, who converted to Judaism — have become one of the more recognisable families in Israeli combat sports, with the trio fighting under the Team Gordon Fighters banner out of the Silapa Thai Gym. GFN's organisers have described the venture as an attempt to build an annual, internationally produced fight night in Israel.

title: Hapoel Tel Aviv and Tamir Blatt revive contract talks after ten-day pause
dek: Sport5 reports both sides expect the long-running saga to be resolved soon, though Hapoel is still weighing a loan-out option and has warned the guard he won't immediately be in the EuroLeague rotation.

verificationSources.label: Sport5 – On the way to signing: progress between Hapoel Tel Aviv and Tamir Blatt
Walla Sport – Blatt agrees terms with Hapoel Tel Aviv on lucrative three-year deal
Sport1/Maariv – For a huge salary: Tamir Blatt crosses town to Hapoel Tel Aviv

body: Hapoel Tel Aviv's pursuit of point guard Tamir Blatt is moving again. Sport5 reported on Monday that negotiations between the club and the 29-year-old guard, frozen for more than ten days, have resumed, with both sides now expecting the saga to reach a conclusion soon.

The two parties had already found broad agreement earlier this month on the shape of a long-term contract worth roughly $1.6 million a season, including hundreds of thousands of dollars in equity stakes. But the deal stalled amid internal disagreement inside Hapoel's basketball department over how Blatt fits into head coach Dimitris Itoudis's system, delaying any official announcement.

Blatt became a free agent after three seasons at Maccabi Tel Aviv, and Hapoel's interest is tangled up with the noisiest domestic story of the Israeli off-season: Yam Madar's departure from Hapoel across town to Maccabi, which opened the point guard spot the Reds want Blatt to fill.

According to Sport5, one option still on the table is for Hapoel to sign Blatt to a long-term contract while loaning him out elsewhere for the coming season, rather than keeping him in the first-team squad straight away.

Even if he does stay in Tel Aviv, the club's staff have made clear internally that Blatt would not be part of the initial EuroLeague rotation — a notable caveat given the money on offer. Last season in that competition he averaged 7.1 points and 5.2 assists in 19.5 minutes per game.

Blatt began his senior career at Hapoel Tel Aviv between 2014 and 2017, including a loan spell at Ramat Hasharon, before moves to Hapoel Holon, Hapoel Jerusalem, Alba Berlin and finally Maccabi Tel Aviv. A return to Hapoel would bring him back to where he started, nine years after he first left as a young player.
Blatt is also a regular in the Israel national team setup, having featured in EuroBasket and World Cup qualifying windows.

Itoudis, the Greek coach and two-time EuroLeague champion with CSKA Moscow, is entering his third season in charge of Hapoel Tel Aviv, and his read on Blatt's fit appears to have been the sticking point in the drawn-out talks.

As things stand, no contract has been signed and Hapoel has issued no official statement, but Sport5's report suggests renewed momentum after the stand-off — with both camps now sounding confident of getting the deal over the line.

title: Assago, 18 May 2014: The Overtime Night Maccabi Stunned Real Madrid
dek: Written off before the Final Four even began, Maccabi Tel Aviv beat CSKA Moscow and then Real Madrid on Italian soil to claim a sixth European crown — in the first Euroleague final to need overtime in 45 years.

verificationSources.label: Times of Israel — "Maccabi Tel Aviv win Euroleague final 98-86"
Maccabi Tel Aviv official site — 2014 Final Four game recap

body: The Forum di Assago sits in an unglamorous industrial suburb just outside Milan, a hall built for concerts and conventions as much as basketball. On the evening of 18 May 2014 it turned, improbably, into an extension of Tel Aviv. Blue-and-yellow flags hung from every tier, Hebrew chants rolled down onto the court, and by tip-off close to twelve thousand fans packed a building whose capacity had been stretched to fit them — a large share of them Israelis who had crossed the continent on short notice, some buying up tickets originally allocated to Barcelona and CSKA Moscow supporters once those clubs were eliminated.

Nobody outside that crowd gave Maccabi much of a chance. Real Madrid arrived as the tournament's clear favourite, still chasing its first European title since 1995 and fresh off a runner-up finish the year before. Coached by Pablo Laso and stacked with talent — Sergio Rodríguez, Rudy Fernández, Nikola Mirotić, captain Felipe Reyes — Madrid had dismantled Barcelona 100–62 in the other semi-final. Maccabi, by contrast, had spent the season fending off criticism of head coach David Blatt after a rough patch domestically, and had needed a last-gasp basket from guard Tyrese Rice to squeeze past CSKA Moscow 68–67 in their own semi-final two nights earlier.

The final itself refused to break either way. Maccabi's starting five — Yogev Ohayon running the point, David Blu and Devin Smith on the wings, Alex Tyus and Sofoklis Schortsanitis, the giant Greek-Cypriot centre known across Europe simply as "Big Sofo," inside — matched Madrid basket for basket. Regulation time ended locked at 73–73, forcing the first overtime period in a Euroleague championship game since 1969.

It was in that extra five minutes that Rice, a lightly regarded American guard who had spent parts of his career bouncing around Europe's second tier, produced the performance of his life. He poured in a string of clutch shots as Maccabi pulled away, finishing with 26 points and claiming the Final Four MVP award. He did not do it alone: Ricky Hickman added 18, David Blu 14, Devin Smith 15, and Alex Tyus contributed 12 points, 11 rebounds and three blocks in the paint. When the buzzer sounded, the scoreboard read Maccabi Tel Aviv 98, Real Madrid 86.

"Unbelievable," Yogev Ohayon told reporters afterward. "I'm in complete shock." Devin Smith said the noise inside the Forum reminded him of Maccabi's own home floor, then known by its sponsor name as the "Nokia" arena in Tel Aviv. Blatt, who only months earlier had been fending off calls for his job, called it simply "an unbelievable season."

The scale of what had happened only became clear the next morning. This was Maccabi Tel Aviv's sixth European championship, joining the club's earlier titles from 1977, 1981, 2001, 2004 and 2005 — a run matched by only a handful of clubs in the competition's history. And it had come against the odds, on the road, against a Real Madrid side that many assumed was about to reclaim its old place at the top of the continent (Madrid would indeed do exactly that the following year, winning the 2015 title under Laso).

For a club and a country whose basketball glories had, by 2014, started to feel like distant memories from the Tal Brody era of the 1970s or the golden Final Four run of 2004 and 2005, the Assago final was proof the story wasn't finished. It was won not by a roster of superstars but by a group of journeymen and role players — Ohayon, Hickman, Tyus, Schortsanitis, Rice — welded together by a coach fighting for his own credibility, in front of a travelling support that had turned a suburban Italian arena into the loudest room in European basketball for one overtime period in May.

David Blatt would leave Maccabi within months to coach the Cleveland Cavaliers in the NBA. Real Madrid got its revenge a year later. But the banner from Assago still hangs in Tel Aviv, a reminder of the night the underdogs simply refused to lose.

title: Chelsea's 180-degree turn: Xabi Alonso eyes Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson
dek: After years of stockpiling teenage prospects, Chelsea are reportedly chasing two players in their mid-thirties as their new manager looks for leadership his young dressing room has lacked.
body: Xabi Alonso is redrawing Chelsea's recruitment blueprint, and the two names now attached to his rebuild say everything about the change in thinking: not teenage prospects from the club's global scouting network, but a pair of veterans closer to retirement than their prime.

Sport5 reports that Chelsea are pursuing a "180-degree turn" from the approach that has defined the Todd Boehly-Clearlake ownership era, when the club signed wave after wave of young players on long contracts and repeatedly fell short of expectations. The new targets are Brighton striker Danny Welbeck, 35, and free-agent-in-waiting midfielder Jordan Henderson, 36.

Welbeck enjoyed another productive season on the south coast, scoring 13 Premier League goals in 37 appearances for Brighton — his second successive campaign in double figures. He signed a new one-year contract at the Amex in March that runs to the end of 2026-27, meaning any move would require Chelsea to negotiate a fee rather than wait for a free transfer.

Sky Sports reports that Chelsea have already held "positive talks" with Brighton over Welbeck, alongside their interest in Henderson. According to those reports, personal terms have been discussed with both players as the club tries to push the double deal through.

Henderson's situation is different. The former Liverpool captain has a year left on his contract at Brentford, but Sky Sports and TNT Sports both report the Bees would be willing to let him leave on a free transfer. He made 34 appearances for Brentford last season after a brief spell at Ajax, and was part of England's World Cup squad.

At Liverpool, Henderson lifted the Champions League, the Premier League and a string of domestic trophies as captain — the kind of dressing-room pedigree Sport5 says Alonso feels Chelsea's academy-heavy squad has been missing, even if neither veteran is expected to be a guaranteed starter.

Alonso took charge at Stamford Bridge on July 1 on a four-year contract, arriving after spells at Bayer Leverkusen, where he won Leverkusen's first-ever league title, and Real Madrid. On his unveiling he said the ownership shared his ambition to build "a team capable of competing consistently at the highest level and fighting for trophies."

That ambition, according to the Sport5 report, now extends to actively seeking out experience rather than avoiding it — a striking reversal for a club whose transfer strategy under Boehly and Clearlake has been built almost entirely around signing players in their late teens and early twenties on seven- and eight-year deals.

Neither move has been confirmed by Chelsea, Brighton or Brentford, and a fee for Welbeck — who only signed a new deal three months ago — still has to be agreed. But the fact that two of English football's most decorated thirty-somethings are simultaneously in Chelsea's sights has become one of the more unusual storylines of the club's pre-season.

title: Why fighters smeared Vaseline on their faces before GFN 1
dek: A small backstage ritual, repeated before all 12 fights on the Gordon brothers' historic Tel Aviv card, left first-time viewers asking questions — the answer is simple skin science, not superstition.

verificationSources.label: Sport5 - "אהבת השם והאחים גורדון: מה מורחים הלוחמים על הפנים?"
Ynet - GFN 1 recap, Menora Mivtachim Arena

body: In the minutes before each of the 12 fights on Monday's GFN 1 card at Tel Aviv's Menora Mivtachim Arena, a member of every fighter's corner performed the same quiet routine: working a thin, glistening film into the cheekbones, brow and nose of the athlete about to walk out. To anyone new to combat sports watching from the stands or the broadcast, it looked almost like make-up being applied backstage.

It was Vaseline, Sport5 reported from ringside. The petroleum jelly reduces friction on the skin while keeping it soft and elastic, and stops it drying out before a fighter takes a punch or a kick to the face.

That matters because dry skin splits far more easily than lubricated skin. The smoother and more supple the surface, the outlet explained, the less damage a strike does for the same amount of friction and impact — which in practice means fewer cuts and less bleeding over the course of a fight.

No fighter wants to walk into the cage or ring already carrying broken skin, and none wants to come out of a bout looking like they went through a war if it can be avoided. The Vaseline is a small, almost invisible piece of preparation aimed squarely at preventing that.

It is not a GFN quirk. Cutmen and cornermen apply it before bouts in boxing, kickboxing, Muay Thai and MMA gyms worldwide, as routinely as wrapping hands or checking gloves — a habit so ordinary to those inside the sport that it rarely gets explained to those outside it.

At GFN 1, the ritual bookended a night that made history for Israeli combat sports regardless of what was on anyone's face. All three Gordon brothers — Ahavat Hashem, Ruach Hashem and Kibedy — fought in front of a sold-out house and won, the first time the family had appeared together on one professional card.

For all the noise around that result, it was this understated backstage habit that had newcomers to the sport asking the same question all evening: what exactly are they putting on their faces? The answer, as Sport5 laid out, turned out to be refreshingly unglamorous — a jar of Vaseline, and a job cutmen have quietly been doing for as long as people have been hitting each other for a living.

title: Kibedy Gordon knocks out former UFC fighter, then calls out Dana White
dek: The Jerusalem-born striker starched Jose Alberto Quiñonez in under a minute at Gordon Fight Nights in Tel Aviv, then used the microphone to lobby for a UFC contract.

verificationSources.label: Sport5 - כיבדי גורדון: הישראלי שלח מסר ל-UFC
Tapology - GFN 1: Israel vs. The World

body: Kibedy Gordon needed less than a minute to make his point. Fighting on home soil at Gordon Fight Nights' inaugural card in Tel Aviv on Monday, the Jerusalem-born striker dropped former UFC fighter Jose Alberto Quiñonez with a single shot, then turned to the cameras with a message for the sport's biggest promotion.

"Dana White, Sean Shelby, look at me," Gordon said afterward, according to Sport5, addressing the UFC president and the matchmaker who signs new talent to the roster. "See what we did here, bring me to the big league and see what I can do. I threw one punch and stunned myself."

The bout was contested under Muay Thai rules rather than standard MMA, part of GFN 1: Israel vs. The World, a card promoted by the Gordon family at the Menora Mivtachim Arena. Kibedy's brother Ahavat "Golden Boy" Gordon headlined the same show against Brazilian striker John Lineker, while a third sibling, Ruach Gordon, also fought on the undercard.

For Kibedy Gordon, the knockout was the latest data point in an 8-2 professional MMA record built mostly outside Israel. He relocated to São Paulo, Brazil, in 2022 and trains at the Fighting Nerds gym alongside current UFC roster members, including welterweight contender Carlos Prates and featherweight Jean Silva, as well as fellow Israelis Eilai Barzilai and Sean Pro.

That gym is no small credential. The Fighting Nerds have become one of the UFC's most talked-about pipelines in recent years, producing several ranked fighters out of a single Brazilian training camp, and Gordon, who fights under the nickname "Slingshot," has made clear he wants to be the next name out of it to reach the Octagon.

Sport5 reports that the realistic route to UFC attention for a fighter like Gordon runs through promotions plugged into the UFC's Fight Pass streaming system, the pipeline the organization increasingly uses to scout talent outside its own cage. Gordon has already fought under that umbrella, competing in LFA and FFC and picking up his first FFC win in August 2024.

His team is not treating Monday's win as a one-off showcase. Sport5 reports Gordon is expected back in MMA competition within the coming months, with the Tel Aviv knockout intended partly to build his profile, both for the home crowd and for the American matchmakers he name-checked in his post-fight interview.

Gordon's on-camera pitch to White and Shelby is a familiar move in combat sports, where fighters routinely use a big finish and a live microphone to lobby for a contract. Whether it moves the UFC is untested, but the knockout itself, and the reel it produced, are real, and now part of the case he is building.

title: Ahavat Hashem Gordon beats John Lineker as all three Gordon brothers win on historic Tel Aviv card
dek: GFN 1 sold out the Menora Mivtachim Arena for Israel's biggest combat-sports night yet, headlined by Ahavat Hashem Gordon's unanimous decision over former ONE Championship world champion John Lineker.

verificationSources.label: Sport5 — Ahavat Hashem Gordon wins after a huge fight
MMAmania — GFN 1: Israel vs. The World fight card

body: Ahavat Hashem Gordon moved to 13-0 on Monday night, outpointing former ONE Championship bantamweight world champion John Lineker over three rounds of Muay Thai to headline GFN 1, the biggest combat-sports card Israel has staged, at a sold-out Menora Mivtachim Arena in Tel Aviv.

The judges scored it unanimously for the Israeli in what Sport5 called the best fight of the night. Lineker, 36, arrived with a genuine pedigree that made the win count for something: a UFC veteran who beat the likes of John Dodson, Michael McDonald and Marlon Vera before crossing to ONE Championship, where he knocked out Bibiano Fernandes for the bantamweight MMA title in 2022. Facing him in a striking-only ruleset, rather than the cage, Gordon still had to survive three rounds against one of the hardest hitters his sport has produced.

GFN — Gordon Fight Nights — is built around Ahavat Hashem and his brothers, part of a family whose parents gave several of their children Hebrew names invoking God, according to profiles in Ynet and Israel Hayom: Ahavat Hashem means "love of God," Ruach Hashem "spirit of God" and Kibdei roughly "my honours." Monday's card, billed as Israel vs. the World, was the promotion's first show and drew international broadcast interest, streamed abroad via the Millions.co platform.

The other two brothers delivered too. Ruach Hashem Gordon won a judges' decision over Maximus Bejenuta in a Muay Thai bout, while Kibdei Gordon needed only the first round to stop Jose Alberto Quiñonez by knockout — meaning all three Gordons won on the same night they headlined together for the first time at home.

On the women's portion of the card, Nili Blok outpointed Brazilian opponent Isabel Monique de Oliveira over the distance in Muay Thai, one of the featured bouts Sport5 flagged in its build-up coverage.
In the evening's lone MMA contest, Ilay Barzilay defeated Brazil's Lucas Almeida by decision.

The card also carried Natan Levy, only the second Israeli fighter to compete in the UFC, against American Lando Vannata in a kickboxing bout — a pairing MMAmania listed among the main-card fights, though the result had not been confirmed in the reporting reviewed at time of writing. Levy has become a prominent voice against antisemitism in combat sports abroad after facing hostile crowds at a recent bout in South Korea, where he said winning by knockout was "the best answer" to the abuse.

Further down the bill, Israeli fighters largely swept the preliminary card: Max Bernis stopped Alexander Skokov by first-round TKO, Guy Haj outpointed Natas Stopak, Zohar Chayot finished Rarek Stadler inside the first round, Or Moshe won on the cards against Panaiotis Kousis, and Guy Moor Alon took a decision in his professional debut.

For a country with no established top-tier kickboxing or Muay Thai promotion of its own, an event of this scale — a sold-out arena, an international broadcast deal and a card stacked with fighters carrying real résumés from the UFC and ONE Championship — marks a genuine attempt to plant a permanent striking-sports scene in Tel Aviv.

Israeli media have credited Ruach Hashem, 22, as the first Israeli man to win a Muay Thai world title, while Kibdei, 26, has spoken of UFC ambitions in the coming years. On the night their promotion launched, both backed that reputation up alongside their older brother — giving GFN a result to build its next show around.

title: Beer Sheva's night race returns with reworked routes and a Skazi finish-line party
dek: The 2026 Light Run through the Negev capital will feature a faster, recertified course, family fun-runs and a live electronic set from veteran Israeli DJ Skazi at the finish.

verificationSources.label: Official Light Run Beer Sheva site

body: Beer Sheva's Night Race is coming back on September 9, 2026, and organisers say this year's edition has been rebuilt from the ground up — new, recertified routes and a finish-line concert from Israeli psytrance veteran Skazi headlining the after-party.

The course overhaul is the headline change. Organisers describe the reworked track as quicker and cleaner, with the half marathon (21.1km), 10km and 5km competitive routes all remeasured and certified by the Israel Athletics Association, meaning times run there will count for personal bests and qualifying standards.

Alongside the competitive distances, the event keeps its community side intact: shorter fun-runs of 2.5km, 1km and 500m are aimed at families and younger runners who want to take part without racing the clock.

The entertainment package is built around Skazi — the stage name of Asher Swissa, one of Israel's best-known psytrance producers since the late 1990s — who will play a live electronic set at the finish line. The band Rockville is also billed to perform, with organisers promising further surprises around the event's expo village.

There's prize money on offer too: a total pool of 18,000 shekels, with half-marathon podium finishers collecting 3,000, 2,000 and 1,000 shekels for first through third, and the top three in the 10km sharing 1,500, 1,000 and 500 shekels.

Sport5 will broadcast live from the race, which is being staged by production company Shvoong. Beyond the running itself, the night is billed as a broader festival — an expo area themed around sport and healthy living, interactive activity zones, and a tribute segment saluting Israel's security forces.

The Beer Sheva Night Race has been a fixture on the Negev's sporting and social calendar for well over a decade, drawing thousands of runners and spectators to the city after dark each year. Registration for the 2026 edition is open now through the event's official site.

title: Adam Ramsay-Peaty questions it all after bitter Commonwealth bronze
dek: Racing under his new married name for the first time at a major championship, the three-time Olympic champion broke down in Glasgow and asked aloud whether the 5:30am starts are still worth it.

verificationSources.label: Yahoo Sports — full post-race quotes and context
The Star (Malaysia) — race result and further quotes
ESPN — explainer on the name change
Hello! Magazine — marriage to Holly Ramsay

body: Adam Ramsay-Peaty — the swimmer the world has known for a decade as Adam Peaty — stood in Glasgow on Sunday night with a Commonwealth bronze medal round his neck and, for once, did not sound like a champion talking about small technical fixes. He sounded like a man asking why he still gets up before dawn at all.

Racing under his new name for the first time at a major championship since marrying Holly Ramsay, daughter of chef Gordon Ramsay, in December, the 31-year-old finished third in the men's 100m breaststroke final in 59.65 seconds — his slowest time in a major championship final in a decade. Australia's Sam Williamson took gold in 59.17, with Jersey's Filip Nowacki edging him for silver in 59.34.

Ramsay-Peaty broke down in tears afterwards, and rather than the usual talk of stroke rate or race plan, he turned the interview into something closer to a confession about the cost of a life built around a pool.

"What's the point of all the 5.30am starts?" he asked. "What's the point of all the metres every single day? What's the point of being exhausted all the time, or missing family events because you have to train?"

It was a striking admission from a man who has spent nearly two decades as the most dominant breaststroker in history — Olympic champion in Rio and Tokyo, world record holder, the face of British swimming through three Games cycles. He made no apology for showing it. "I'm never afraid to show emotion," he said. "It's important because it helps create stronger people, stronger men, stronger fathers and stronger husbands."

He was adamant the time on the board did not reflect the work behind it. "This cycle especially, I've worked harder than ever," he said. "To get a result like that hurts because I know I'm better than that." Pressed further, he put it more bluntly still: "I work a lot harder than what it says on the scoreboard."

The bronze has left him reassessing not just his weekly schedule but his entire event programme. "It hurts too much. I have got to approach training differently now because it hurts too much," he said, before raising a question that would have been unthinkable from him a few years ago: "Is the 100 even viable any more? I don't know."

He floated a possible shift toward the 50m breaststroke, the sprint distance added to the Olympic programme for Los Angeles 2028. "The 50 is probably my super strength with my power," he said. "With the Olympics, that's probably going to be more realistic, but it's too early to tell."

Even so, he stopped short of writing off the event that made him famous. "I know I'm a sprinter. I know I can do very well because I've done it. It doesn't disappear overnight," he said. "It requires me to look at the formula and see how I can get to that speed again."

There is little time to dwell on it. Ramsay-Peaty said he intends to race again within a fortnight. "I'm a fighter," he said. "We've got another opportunity at the Europeans in two weeks, and I do enjoy a scrap."

The scene in Glasgow underlined how much has shifted for a swimmer who once looked unbeatable over 100m breaststroke — a new marriage, a new name, and a body absorbing the toll of nearly two decades at the top, all now shaping the conversation about what comes next on the road to a fourth Olympics.

title: Ex-Karpaty coach: Bruninho is special, but he doesn't believe in himself yet
dek: Fran Fernández, who managed the Brazilian at Karpaty Lviv, tells Sport5 that Maccabi Haifa's new signing has the talent for Spain or Italy — if he can trust it.

verificationSources.label: Ynet — Bruninho signs for Maccabi Haifa on a three-year deal

body: Fran Fernández spent only half a season working with Bruninho at Karpaty Lviv, but the Spanish coach has been left in no doubt about what Maccabi Haifa have signed — and what still needs to change. "He's a special footballer, a very versatile player," Fernández told Sport5. "But he still doesn't fully believe in himself."

It is a striking assessment of a player Maccabi Haifa spent months chasing before finally landing him this summer. Bruninho, 26, signed a three-year contract with the Israeli champions in a deal Israeli outlets including Ynet and Israel Hayom valued at roughly €1.6-1.7 million, with a reported salary of around €450,000 a season.

Fernández, who took charge of Karpaty in January after replacing Vladyslav Lupashko, worked with the Brazilian through the second half of last season before his sale to Israel. Asked to rate him purely on ability, the coach didn't hedge: Bruninho, he said, is "the strongest footballer I've trained."

The coach's real point, though, was about the gap between talent and conviction. He said that if Bruninho builds genuine belief in his own qualities, he has what it takes to play in Spain or Italy before long — a suggestion that Maccabi Haifa may end up being a staging post rather than a destination.

Karpaty, for their part, are still working out how to cover for him. Fernández indicated the Ukrainian club's incoming recruits are being assessed partly on whether they can collectively replace the individual quality Bruninho took with him to Haifa Bay — a sign of how central he had become to the team.

Bruninho's route to Israel ran through Belo Horizonte and Lviv. He came up through the Atlético Mineiro academy, breaking into the senior side in 2018, before Karpaty signed him on loan and later made the move permanent for a reported €800,000.

He arrives in Israel off a productive stretch in Ukraine, where he established himself as one of Karpaty's leading attacking outlets over two seasons before Maccabi Haifa's interest turned serious this year.

Speaking after the move went through, Bruninho made clear what drew him to Haifa. "I'm very happy to be here. I think this is a huge opportunity for me," he said, according to Sports Rabbi — adding that watching the club's Champions League tie against Paris Saint-Germain last season made him "even more eager to come."

He was direct about his own ambitions, too, saying he believes "this could be the moment to bring trophies back" to Haifa through attacking, attractive football — a target that will only sharpen the scrutiny on Fernández's caveat about self-belief.

For now, Maccabi Haifa are banking on a player his former coach considers the most naturally gifted he has worked with. Whether that translates into results in the Israeli Premier League, and eventually beyond it, may come down less to his feet than to his head.

title: Hapoel far outrank Maccabi in bookmakers' EuroLeague title odds
dek: Panathinaikos are favourites and defending champions Olympiacos are second, while a big-spending Hapoel Tel Aviv sit fifth — well clear of a struggling Maccabi Tel Aviv.

body: The first bookmakers' odds for the 2026/27 EuroLeague title, compiled by Basketball Sphere and reported by Sport5, expose a wide gulf between Israel's two clubs in the competition: Hapoel Tel Aviv sit among the genuine contenders, while Maccabi Tel Aviv are grouped deep in the also-ran pack.

Hapoel are priced at 12.00 to win the title, the fifth-best odds of any of the 20 teams in the field. Maccabi, by contrast, are all the way down at 34.00, tied for 14th — the gap that gave the Sport5 report its headline, framing Maccabi as "far from" their crosstown rivals this time out.

Panathinaikos head the market as 4.00 favourites, just ahead of defending champions Olympiacos at 4.25. Olympiacos beat Real Madrid 92-85 in Athens in May to win their fourth European Cup and first since 2013, but bookmakers rate the Greek club as a marginal second choice behind their compatriots for the coming campaign. Real Madrid and Fenerbahçe are tied for third-favourites at 8.00.
Hapoel sit just below that group, ahead of Barcelona and the newly moneyed Dubai Basketball, both priced at 15.00.

Sport5's analysis points to spending as the reason for Hapoel's rise up the market: alongside Dubai, the report says, Hapoel made the single biggest financial investment of any club in the competition this summer, in a squad rebuild aimed squarely at Europe's traditional powers.

That investment is visible on Hapoel's roster sheet. The club signed Vasilije Micic, the former EuroLeague MVP, alongside Czech veteran Tomas Satoransky, forward Zach LeDay and ex-Los Angeles Clippers wing Amir Coffey, while extending Ish Wainwright's contract through 2028 — a squad now built with genuine Final Four ambitions rather than simply another EuroLeague campaign to survive.

Maccabi's positioning tells the opposite story. Israel's most decorated club, six times champions of Europe, finished the 2025-26 EuroLeague regular season with a losing 18-20 record, and the bookmakers now rank them level with Valencia, Olimpia Milano and Partizan Belgrade — clubs Maccabi have traditionally finished above, not alongside.

Sport5's report does not write Maccabi off entirely, noting the squad still has the individual quality to trouble the favourites over the course of a long season, even if the odds imply their realistic title chances are slim.

The rest of the market runs Žalgiris Kaunas at 21.00, ASVEL Villeurbanne at 26.00, Andorra and Red Star Belgrade at 29.00, then the group of Valencia, Milan, Partizan and Maccabi at 34.00, Beşiktaş at 41.00, Baskonia at 81.00, and Virtus Bologna, Bayern Munich and Paris Basketball closing out the list at 101.00 apiece. The 2026/27 EuroLeague regular season is due to open in October, when the numbers will start to move for real.

title: Kibedy Gordon flattens former UFC fighter Quiñones in under a minute
dek: The eldest of the fighting Gordon brothers delivered a stunning knockout on the debut card of Gordon Fight Nights in Tel Aviv, then called out Dana White for a UFC shot.

verificationSources.label: Tapology - José Alberto Quiñones fighter page
