body: It took Kibedy Gordon less than a minute to make his case for the UFC. Fighting on the debut card of his family's own promotion, Gordon Fight Nights, the eldest of the Gordon fighting brothers blitzed former UFC bantamweight José Alberto Quiñones with a single, fight-ending strike in their Muay Thai bout on Monday evening at Menora Mivtachim Arena in Tel Aviv.

The knockout, confirmed by Sport5, capped a Muay Thai clash that formed one third of a triple main event at GFN 1: Israel vs. The World, the first show staged by the Gordon brothers under their own banner. Gordon needed under 60 seconds to put Quiñones away, according to the outlet's report.

Quiñones, nicknamed 'El Teco', is no journeyman. The 35-year-old Mexican fought professionally in the UFC's bantamweight division, compiling a 5-4 record inside the Octagon after emerging from the promotion's Ultimate Fighter: Latin America reality series in 2014. His presence on the card was meant to be a genuine measuring stick for Gordon — instead, he became the latest name on Gordon's highlight reel.

Sport5 quoted Gordon addressing UFC leadership directly in the aftermath, calling out the promotion's president and matchmaker by name. 'Dana White, Sean Shelby, look at me. See what we did here, bring me to the big league and see what I can do. I threw one punch and shocked myself,' Gordon said, according to the outlet.

The victory was Gordon's first appearance on an Israeli card and continues a hot run for the family. His MMA record stands at 8-2, built across stints with the LFA promotion and, since August 2024, the FFC organisation, before Monday's move into a Muay Thai bout on home soil.

GFN 1 itself was billed as a statement event for Israeli combat sports, headlined by John Lineker against Kibedy's brother Ahavat Gordon, with a second Gordon brother, Ruach, also fighting Maximus Bejenuta in the triple-main-event structure. The card also featured former UFC lightweight Natan Levy against Lando Vannata in a kickboxing bout, plus additional Muay Thai and MMA fights.

For a family that has built its profile fight by fight — often against confrontational or higher-profile opposition — Monday's card in Tel Aviv was as much about establishing Gordon Fight Nights as a promotion as it was about any single result. Kibedy Gordon's knockout gave it an early highlight reel moment, and a fresh talking point aimed squarely at the UFC's front office.

body: Ilay Barzilay banked the best win of his career on Monday night in Tel Aviv, out-pointing Brazilian veteran Lucas Almeida over a judges' decision at GFN 1 to put himself back in the UFC conversation.

The Israeli lightweight, fighting for the first time in more than a year, needed the full distance at the Menora Mivtachim Arena before the scorecards went his way, Sport5 reported, in what the outlet framed as the clearest statement yet of his readiness for the sport's top promotion.

Almeida is no journeyman gatekeeper. The 35-year-old Brazilian has fought in the UFC itself and is ranked among the top 100 lightweights in the world, according to Sport5 — making Barzilay's win over him the most significant result of his career to date.
The loss was Almeida's sixth as a professional, dropping his record to 15-6 by Sport5's count, while Barzilay improved to 8-1.

For Barzilay, the win closes out a frustrating stretch away from the cage. He had been slated to challenge Christian Spian for the UWC lightweight title, and later to fight American Landry Ward in June, but both bouts fell through before he could step in against Almeida instead.

Sport5 cast the performance as proof to Dana White's organisation that Barzilay is ready to test himself against the sport's elite — the latest marker in a rise that began at Souko Gym in Herzliya, where the Brazilian jiu-jitsu specialist first built his amateur pedigree before turning professional and fighting on cards in Las Vegas.

GFN 1: Israel vs. The World, staged by the Gordon brothers' promotion, brought a heavyweight international fight card to Tel Aviv, and Barzilay's win over a recognised UFC name gave the home crowd one of its headline results of the night.
With his name already said to be on the UFC's radar, Barzilay will hope this result — rather than another cancelled date — is what finally gets him signed.

title: Sydney Opera House to host inaugural Padel Invitational with Pat Rafter
dek: Former world No. 1 Pat Rafter headlines a two-day padel spectacular beside Sydney Harbour as the sport chases a place at the Brisbane 2032 Olympics.

verificationSources.label: International Padel Federation (FIP), Patrick Rafter profile

body: Sydney's most famous silhouette is about to host a very different kind of show. On August 15 and 16, 2026, the sails of the Sydney Opera House will frame a custom-built padel court for the inaugural Padel Invitational, presented by UBS — the first time the sport has taken over one of the world's most photographed venues.

The event is being staged by Padel Australia in partnership with Premier Padel and the International Padel Federation (FIP), with organisers building a temporary arena on the Opera House's Northern Broadwalk, right on the edge of Sydney Harbour.

Heading the bill is Pat Rafter, the Australian former world No. 1 and two-time US Open champion who has become one of the sport's most visible ambassadors since retiring from tennis. He will play as part of the 'Aussie Crocs' team over the weekend.

"Padel is fast, dynamic, incredibly entertaining to watch and fun and social to play," Rafter said of the sport's appeal, adding: "To be able to showcase the sport at the Sydney Opera House is pretty special."

FIP president Luigi Carraro framed the event as part of a broader strategy. "Creating a padel event at the Sydney Opera House is a powerful way to showcase the sport and build momentum towards our Olympic dream," he said.

That Olympic dream centres on Brisbane 2032. Padel is not yet on the programme, and the full sports list for the Games will not be confirmed until 2027, but the FIP has been lobbying the IOC directly — Carraro met earlier this year with Kit McConnell, the IOC's chief sport officer for Brisbane 2032.

The Sydney weekend is designed to sell the sport to a broader Australian audience rather than just diehard fans. The programme mixes professional exhibition matches from the Premier Padel circuit with a finals series for Australia's leading club players, plus celebrity one-point matches modelled on the format popularised by the Australian Open's '1 Point Slam'.

Organisers have also built in live music, food and fan activations around the court, with tickets starting at 30 Australian dollars — including sessions where spectators can pay to play alongside Rafter and the visiting professionals.

Padel has been one of the fastest-growing racket sports worldwide over the past five years, and Sydney becomes the latest landmark venue enlisted to sell the game as it pushes for wider global, and eventually Olympic, recognition.

title: Ironi Tiberias face "most serious indictment ever" over unsupervised player infusions
dek: The Israel Football Association has charged Ironi Tiberias with helping players receive unauthorised intravenous infusions before a relegation playoff last season. The club's lawyer insists calling 40 or 50 millilitres illegal is absurd, and predicts the case will "end in nothing."
body: The Israel Football Association has filed what it is calling the gravest indictment ever brought against a club in the country's history, accusing Ironi Tiberias of arranging unauthorised intravenous infusions for players before a lower-league playoff match last season.

The charge sheet, drawn up by federation prosecutor Gal Bergman, accuses club figures of assisting in the use of prohibited substances and stimulants under aggravating circumstances, breaching federation regulations, and failing to comply with a prior disciplinary ruling. The federation says players were injected with saline solution without any medical professional present to supervise or monitor the process, ahead of a bottom-of-the-table playoff against Ashdod.

Shlomi Barzel, who heads the federation's public relations department, did not mince words in describing the scale of the case. "This is the most serious indictment ever filed against a club in the history of Israeli football," he said.

Named in the proceedings are suspended club owner Miki Bitan, head coach Eliran Chodeda, director Gavriel Cohen, fitness coach Shlomi Vadrero, technical director Chen Sol and staff member Aviv Givli — a roster that spans the club's ownership, coaching staff and administration.

Ironi Tiberias's lawyer, Eyal Yafe, dismissed the case as a wild overreaction to a routine medical procedure. "This is entirely legal — the federation is making a mountain out of a molehill," he said, pushing back hard when pressed on the legality of the infusions. "You're calling it illegal because someone received 40 or 50 millilitres without medical supervision?"
Yafe said he was standing by that position regardless of how the case unfolds. "I'm not changing my opinion. In my view, this will end in nothing," he said.

The federation's account of the quantities involved is notably higher than the figure Yafe cited in his defence: prosecutors allege that some players received well over 100 millilitres of fluid, though they have acknowledged working from what they describe as conservative estimates rather than exact medical documentation, since no clinician logged the doses at the time.

This is not Tiberias's first brush with sanction over the affair. The club's head coach and five players were previously suspended once the infusions came to light, and the club has already been handed a points deduction and a transfer ban in connection with the wider case — with relegation-adjacent consequences given how tightly it was fighting to avoid the drop.

The dispute has also spilled beyond the pitch and into open hostility with the federation's investigators. Tiberias has separately threatened a defamation lawsuit worth 500,000 shekels against the investigator handling the file, accusing him of prejudging the club's guilt and applying undue pressure on a young player during questioning — allegations the federation has rejected as a politically motivated media campaign.

With the indictment now formally filed, the case moves to Israeli football's disciplinary tribunal, where sanctions on the table reportedly range from further points deductions to relegation, depending on how the panel weighs the club's role in what happened before that fixture against Ashdod.

title: PSG walk away from Diomandé chase, blast "completely inflated" fee as Real Madrid move in
dek: Paris Saint-Germain say they will not "break their principles" over Yan Diomandé's asking price, clearing the runway for Real Madrid to land the RB Leipzig winger for a fee that could top €120 million.
body: Paris Saint-Germain pulled the plug on their pursuit of Yan Diomandé on Sunday evening, and they didn't go quietly about it — releasing a blunt statement that torched the numbers being asked for the RB Leipzig winger just as Real Madrid moved into pole position to sign him.

"The asking transfer fee and salary demands were completely disproportionate and distortive," the French champions said in a statement given to Sky in Germany, "and PSG will not break its principles of rational financial management and squad balance." It's a pointed way of bowing out of one of the summer's biggest transfer sagas.

The withdrawal effectively hands the 19-year-old Ivorian to Real Madrid, who reached agreement with Leipzig on personal and club-to-club terms the same evening — a deal multiple outlets, including transfer reporter Fabrizio Romano, put at more than €100 million, with add-ons that could push the total beyond €120 million.

That would make Diomandé one of the most expensive signings in Real Madrid's history, ranking behind only Jude Bellingham and Eden Hazard and ahead of Gareth Bale — an extraordinary price tag for a player who had never featured for a European giant before this summer.

Diomandé's rise has been rapid even by modern football's standards. Leipzig paid Spanish second-tier side Leganés only around €20 million for him last summer, a fee that looks like a bargain twelve months on.

He repaid that investment immediately, posting 12 goals and eight assists in 33 Bundesliga appearances and picking up the league's Rookie of the Season award in a breakout campaign at the Red Bull Arena.

The World Cup then turned him into a genuine global name. Diomandé played the full 90 minutes as Ivory Coast opened with a 1-0 win over Ecuador, set up their goal in a 2-1 defeat to Germany, and teed up Nicolas Pépé for the winner in a 2-0 victory over Curaçao.

PSG had been credited with strong interest of their own, reportedly tabling a bid in the region of €100 million before deciding the numbers had spiralled beyond what the club were prepared to justify — hence Sunday's statement making clear they were stepping back on principle rather than being outbid.

For Real Madrid, the move continues a summer in which the transfer market as a whole has been pushed to fresh extremes, with Manchester City and Chelsea both setting new British transfer records earlier in the window.

Diomandé is expected to travel to Madrid this week for a medical, with reports suggesting a contract running through June 2031 is on the table. Formal confirmation from Real Madrid and Leipzig is still to come.

title: Real Madrid submit opening offer for Rodri worth up to €60m
dek: The World Cup-winning Spain captain has reportedly agreed personal terms with the European champions, but Manchester City's valuation — and a looming back operation — could complicate the move.
body: Real Madrid have made their opening move for Rodri, submitting a bid in the region of €50-60 million for the Manchester City and Spain midfielder, ONE reports, citing the Italian transfer journalist Nicolò Schira.

The approach comes only weeks after Rodri capped one of the finest summers of his career, captaining Spain to the 2026 World Cup title and picking up the Golden Ball as the tournament's outstanding player.

According to ONE, Rodri has already agreed personal terms with Real Madrid and would prefer a return to his home country, having spent his career in England since leaving Atlético Madrid for City in 2019.

The midfielder is heading into the final two years of his City contract, which runs to 2027, and has so far resisted the club's efforts to tie him to a new deal — a stalemate Madrid believe gives them an opening.

That opening is not straightforward. City are said to value Rodri at closer to €80 million, leaving a substantial gap with Madrid's opening bid and setting up a negotiation that could stretch deep into the summer.

Complicating matters further is Rodri's fitness. He is set to undergo back surgery with no firm return date yet given, a blow that could see him miss the start of the new season regardless of where he ends up playing it.

City sources have pushed back on the scale of the reports, with the club said to deny having received any formal offer from Madrid at this stage — a reminder that talks, if they are happening, remain at an early stage.

ONE also notes Paris Saint-Germain have been mentioned as a possible alternative suitor, viewing Rodri's contract situation as a rare opportunity to land a player of his calibre without a huge structural outlay.

For Real Madrid, adding a player of Rodri's profile — a World Cup-winning defensive midfielder in career-best form — would address a long-standing need in the middle of the park as Xabi Alonso's side define what a post-Bellingham-era midfield looks like.
Nothing is close to done. But with Rodri's preference reportedly clear and his contract clock ticking, this is a saga Madrid appear determined to push through before City's leverage hardens further.

title: Bataille returns to full training as Tsunami primed for Maccabi Haifa debut start
dek: The Belgian defender's recovery from a training-camp knee injury gives Barak Bakhar a timely boost before Tuesday's Toto Cup opener against Ironi Kiryat Shmona, where new signing Wanderson Tsunami is set to start at left-back.
body: Maccabi Haifa have a piece of good news to carry into their Toto Cup opener: Jelle Bataille, the Belgian defender who missed the closing stretch of pre-season training camp with a knee injury, is back in full training, ONE reports.

Bataille, 26, joined Haifa from Antwerp and has become one of Barak Bakhar's more valuable defensive options precisely because of his versatility — he can slot into either a back-four or a back-three, a flexibility the coach has leaned on while shaping his system for the new campaign.

The squad picture is not entirely clean, though. Captain Yirin Levi was sent straight home upon arriving at the training complex after showing signs of a virus, while forward Andrea Novaković trained separately from the group for the same reason, according to the report.

Attention now turns to Tuesday's Toto Cup fixture against Ironi Kiryat Shmona, kicking off at 20:00. ONE reports that Brazilian left-back Wanderson Tsunami — signed on a two-year deal earlier this month — is set to make his first competitive start for the club in that slot, with Shon Goldberg's recent form at left-back said to be behind the change.

There is also a first squad involvement on the way for Nigel Lonwijk, the Dutch centre-back signed from Wolverhampton Wanderers via a loan spell at Luton Town, who could see some minutes off the bench against Kiryat Shmona as he continues settling into the group.

Not everyone is close to a return. Winger Manuel Benson is expected to rejoin full training only next week, while defender Elad Amir remains sidelined for roughly five months following surgery in London, leaving Bakhar to manage a squad still finding its full strength this early in the season.

For a club that spent the summer rebuilding parts of its back line — Bataille, Tsunami and Lonwijk all arrived within recent weeks — the Toto Cup game offers an early, low-stakes look at how those new pieces fit before the Israeli Premier League season proper gets under way.

title: Israeli FA spokesman: Tiberias's conduct in doping case 'among the most disgraceful I've seen'
dek: Shlomi Barzel says the club's public offensive against the investigation into banned infusions has only worsened its position, as Ironi Tiberias awaits an August 5 disciplinary hearing.

verificationSources.label: ONE - "מבחינת התנהלות, של טבריה מהמחפירות שראיתי"
ONE - יש כתב אישום: טבריה תעמוד לדין בפרשת העירויים

body: Shlomi Barzel does not usually pick fights in public. But asked about Ironi Tiberias's handling of the banned-infusions scandal now threatening the club's future, the Israeli Football Association's head of communications did not hold back. "In terms of conduct, Tiberias's is among the most disgraceful I've seen," he said on air, days after the Association filed its indictment against the club.

The case centres on an incident on April 29, when Tiberias drew 1-1 in a match that left the club facing relegation. According to the indictment, filed by Association prosecutor Gilad Bergman, owner Miki Bitan directed coach Eliran Hod'da to arrange intravenous infusions for players before their next fixture, despite having no medical authorisation to do so.

Six players are said to have received the infusions, with one player initially refusing before being pressured into compliance. The doses allegedly ran well beyond the 100ml-per-12-hours limit set by the World Anti-Doping Agency, administered without a doctor present or any medical documentation kept.

The club's coach, five players and members of its staff were provisionally suspended in July while the investigation ran its course. The Association is now seeking serious sanctions at a disciplinary hearing scheduled for August 5, with a heavy points deduction, fines and a transfer ban all on the table, on top of possible multi-year bans for individuals involved.

Barzel's frustration was aimed less at the substance of the case than at how Tiberias has fought it in public. He accused the club of publishing statements that only deepen its legal exposure, likening its approach to "a fish caught in a net, thrashing about" rather than engaging with the actual charges.

He also pushed back hard on Tiberias's campaign against the Association's lead investigator, Din Prager, whom the club has accused of bias, leaking to the press and pursuing a predetermined outcome to relegate the team. Barzel dismissed the accusations as an attempt to discredit the investigation rather than answer it, calling some of the club's claims about a "contaminated" process distorted and misleading.

Aryeh Kalmenson, who has spoken publicly in the club's defence, has said he sat with the investigator for forty minutes after the story broke and has heard nothing from Association leadership since. Barzel rejected the club's framing of that episode too, saying Tiberias has confused separate bodies - anti-doping authorities and the Football Association itself - to muddy the picture.

Asked whether chairman Shino Zoaretz had any hand in pushing the case forward, Barzel denied any interference from the top, saying the prosecution has run on its own merits. "We lost our innocence about this group," he added, a pointed reference to what he described as a pattern of conduct from the club rather than a one-off dispute.

It is not Tiberias's first brush with the Association's disciplinary machinery this year. In April, the club was docked eight points over a separate case involving the management of double contracts - a sanction that, combined with the infusions case, leaves the second-tier club fighting on multiple fronts to survive the season intact.

With the August 5 hearing approaching, the stakes for Tiberias could hardly be higher: a points deduction on top of April's penalty, transfer restrictions and suspensions for key staff would be a serious blow to a club already fighting to stay competitive. Barzel's comments suggest the Association intends to press the case without softening its stance, whatever pressure Tiberias applies in the meantime.

title: Ahavat Hashem Gordon edges John Lineker to stay unbeaten in Tel Aviv main event
dek: The 20-year-old Muay Thai fighter survived a bloody, back-and-forth battle with the Brazilian veteran to improve to 13-0 in front of a packed Menora Mivtachim Arena.
body: Ahavat Hashem Gordon kept his unbeaten record intact on Monday night, outlasting Brazilian veteran John Lineker over a bruising three rounds to win a unanimous decision in the main event of GFN 1: Israel vs. The World at Tel Aviv's Menora Mivtachim Arena.

The win pushed the 20-year-old Muay Thai fighter to 13-0 as a professional, and it came against the sternest test of his young career: Lineker, a former UFC and ONE Championship title contender nicknamed "Hands of Stone," arrived in Israel with a combat-sports record of 37 wins and 11 losses and a reputation for heavy hands.

It showed early. Lineker opened the fight the stronger man, working the body with hard, accurate punches that drew blood from Gordon inside the first round, according to ONE's ringside account of the bout.

Gordon regrouped in the second, and the fight's momentum swung as Lineker began to tire and struggled to keep up the pace he had set at the opening bell. The Israeli took control of the round as his more experienced opponent's work rate dropped off.

The third and final round turned into the kind of fight Gordon's unbeaten record had not yet been tested by: a genuinely tight, draining exchange in which, by ONE's telling, the Israeli came close to suffering the first defeat of his career before the horn sounded.

When the scorecards were read, all three judges sided with Gordon. He was visibly emotional in the aftermath, and his older brother Ruach Hashem Gordon — himself a Thai boxer and part of the same fighting family — was seen moved to tears at ringside.

The bout capped a card built around the Gordon name. GFN 1 featured a triple main event, with Ruach Hashem Gordon facing Maximus Bejenuta and a third brother, Kibedy Gordon, taking on Jose Alberto Quiñonez, before Ahavat Hashem closed the night against Lineker.

Gordon, born in Shiloh in 2006 to an American father and a Hong Kong-born mother, fights under one of the more distinctive names in world combat sports — Hebrew for "Love of God" — a naming choice shared by his brothers that has made the family a talking point well beyond the ring.

For Lineker, this was a rare venture into pure Muay Thai rules after a long career built mainly in mixed martial arts, where he held the ONE bantamweight world title and fought for years on the UFC roster. The step into a Thai-boxing ring in Tel Aviv, against a fighter more than a decade his junior, was framed locally as exactly the kind of crossover test that could have derailed Gordon's perfect record.

Instead, the Israeli crowd that filled the arena got the outcome it came for, and Gordon's win adds another high-profile scalp to a resume that has already included Turkish and Lithuanian opponents earlier this year on his way to a 13-0 start.

title: Ironi Tiberias to stand trial as football association charges club over banned infusions
dek: Six club figures, including suspended owner Miki Bitan, face aggravated doping-assistance charges after players were given unauthorised intravenous infusions before a relegation play-off match last season.

verificationSources.label: ONE — There is an indictment: Tiberias will stand trial in the infusions case

body: Ironi Tiberias will stand trial after the Israeli Football Association's disciplinary prosecutor filed an indictment against the top-flight club and six of its senior figures, formally charging them over an affair in which players were given unauthorised intravenous infusions before a relegation play-off match last season.

Attorney Gilad Bergman, the federation's prosecutor, brought charges of assisting athletes to use prohibited substances and stimulants under aggravated circumstances, violating the association's medical regulations, and failing to comply with a disciplinary ruling — among the most serious indictments filed against an Israeli club in years, ONE reported.

The six defendants are the club's suspended owner, Miki Bitan; head coach Eliran Chuddah; technical director Chen Sol; team manager Gabriel Cohen; fitness coach Shlomi Wadraro; and a staff member, Aviv Jibli.

According to the indictment, Bitan approached Chuddah on April 29, 2026, and proposed reviving the players with intravenous infusions to help them recover from a heavy schedule ahead of a bottom-of-the-table play-off fixture against Ashdod. Sol then arranged to obtain a dozen ampoules and IV equipment from Migdal HaEmek.

Six players were given infusions lasting 20 to 35 minutes in the away team's dressing room, administered by a club associate who worked as a paramedic rather than a doctor. The indictment states three players initially refused before being told the treatment was mandatory.

No physician was present or consulted, and prosecutors say there was no documented medical justification for the procedure. The doses are estimated at 120 to 240 millilitres per player — well above the 100-millilitre threshold permitted within any 12-hour window under the World Anti-Doping Agency's code without medical exemption.

A further charge stems from what the indictment describes as attempts to obstruct the investigation. Despite a June 2026 agreement under which Bitan was meant to step back from running the club because of his suspension, prosecutors allege he continued to manage its affairs and moved to coordinate testimony, handle evidence and contact witnesses once the case was opened.

The indictment does not spell out a specific punishment request for the club, but prosecutors have signalled they will seek severe sanctions, from heavy points deductions to removal from competition, while individual defendants could face suspensions from several years up to a lifetime ban depending on their role in the affair.

Ironi Tiberias rejected the charges in a statement carried by Walla Sport, describing the indictment as "a document filled with speculation, circumstantial assessments and attempts to create an atmosphere, instead of relying on solid facts and evidence."

The case, which ONE first brought to light, now moves to the football association's disciplinary tribunal, adding a legal cloud over Ironi Tiberias just as the Ligat Ha'al club prepares for a new season already shadowed by the fallout from one of Israeli football's most serious doping-adjacent scandals in years.

Prosecutors also allege Bitan kept running the club and interfered with witnesses despite a June 2026 agreement for him to step back given his suspension.

body: The source article at one.co.il/Article/529155.html, headlined "האם חגורת בטיחות תעזור בתאונה בכביש מהיר?" ("Will a seatbelt help in a highway accident?"), is not a sports story.
It is a general automotive safety explainer, written by Shai Lev, a former editor of ONE's autos section, examining how seatbelts function in high-speed crashes.

The piece explains that when a car stops suddenly at speed, an unrestrained occupant keeps moving forward under inertia, striking the car's interior with a force the article compares to falling from a multi-storey building.

It describes modern seatbelts as integrated safety systems with pre-tensioners that tighten before impact and load limiters that release gradually to reduce the risk of rib fractures, spreading crash force across the pelvis and ribcage.
The article includes guidance on correct fit for women — the lap strap should sit low across the hip bones rather than the abdomen, and the diagonal strap should cross the chest rather than the neck.

It also stresses that seatbelts and airbags work as a paired system, warning that an unbelted occupant risks skull or spinal injury from airbag deployment, and it dismisses common myths that belts are dangerous in fire or submersion scenarios, noting these account for a negligible share of highway collisions.

title: No exceptions to the timetable, presiding judge warns in Tiberias infusions case
dek: The Israeli football disciplinary tribunal has put Ironi Tiberias's banned-infusions case on a strict, non-negotiable schedule, with presiding judge Noam Liubin telling the parties the proceeding will not be allowed to drag on.
body: Israel's football disciplinary tribunal has drawn a hard line under the Ironi Tiberias banned-infusions case, warning the club, its former officials and the federation's own prosecutor that there will be no room to stretch the calendar as the hearing gets under way.

Presiding judge Noam Liubin, who chairs a three-judge panel handling the case, said the court "does not intend to allow this case to drag on indefinitely," according to ONE. He went further, stating that no deviations from the established timelines would be permitted "except for circumstances related to the court or extraordinary situations alone."

The panel's first concrete order was procedural but pointed: the Israel Football Association's prosecutor must hand over a clear, organised physical copy of the incriminating evidence by the following Monday, giving the defence a firm date to work against from the outset.

The case has been classified for complex proceedings, which is why it is being heard by three judges rather than a single adjudicator — a reflection of both the volume of material involved and the seriousness of the allegations against the club.

The tribunal's involvement follows an indictment filed this week against six people connected to Tiberias: head coach Eliran Hodeda, club manager Gabriel Cohen, fitness coach Shlomi Vadraro, technical manager Chen Sol, suspended owner Michael "Micki" Bitan, and staff member Aviv Jibli.

The charges include aiding the use of banned drugs and stimulants in aggravating circumstances, breaching the Israel Football Association's medical regulations, and non-compliance with a ruling of a judicial body, with additional allegations touching on the club's conduct once the affair came to light.

The case centres on events after Tiberias's 1-1 draw with Hapoel Haifa on April 29, 2026. Bitan is alleged to have approached Hodeda and proposed reviving fatigued players with intravenous infusions ahead of a decisive lower-playoff match against MS Ashdod — a game Tiberias went on to lose 0-3, deepening the club's fight against relegation from Ligat Ha'al.
Ironi Tiberias has pushed back publicly on the case. "A lot of speculation, without facts or evidence," the club said in response to the indictment, according to Walla Sport.
With the schedule now locked in and the evidentiary deadline looming next week, the tribunal has signalled it wants this case resolved on its own terms and its own clock — not the parties'.

title: Ahavat Gordon outlasts John Lineker, then tells Kaminski: get to work on GFN 2
dek: The unbeaten Israeli improved to 13-0 with a hard-fought decision over the Brazilian veteran at a sold-out Menora Mivtachim Arena, then used his post-fight microphone to demand a sequel.
body: Ahavat Gordon walked out of the Menora Mivtachim Arena on Sunday night with his unbeaten record intact and, within minutes, was already talking about the next one. Moments after his hand was raised over John Lineker in the main event of GFN 1, the Israeli fighter grabbed the microphone and put the promotion's co-founder on notice: want a GFN 2? Kaminski, get to work.

The line, aimed at Yaniv Kaminski — the ONE broadcaster who partnered with the three Gordon brothers to build the promotion from scratch — closed out the biggest night yet for Israel's fast-growing kickboxing and Muay Thai scene. GFN 1 was billed as 'Israel vs. The World,' and Gordon's headline bout delivered exactly that test.

Fighting under Muay Thai rules, Gordon needed the judges to separate himself from Lineker, a Brazilian veteran and former UFC and ONE Championship bantamweight world champion who represented by far the toughest name on his résumé. Gordon was awarded the decision, pushing his professional record to 13-0.

"Every strike I took, I saw black. He hit so hard," Gordon said afterwards, according to Sport5. "I knew I had to survive. I gave everything and listened to the instructions." He described the contest itself as close: "It was a 50-50 fight. I'm very happy."

He was in no rush to make it about himself alone. "I dedicate this fight to the people of Israel," Gordon said. "There are all kinds of people here, but everyone came to cheer and show that the people of Israel live. A great privilege."

It was a family night in the truest sense: Gordon's brothers, Ruach and Kibedy, also fought on the card and both won, Ruach by decision and Kibedy by knockout, according to Ynet's recap of the event. All three had a hand in organizing the show alongside Kaminski, making GFN as much a family production as a fight promotion.

That backdrop is what gave Gordon's closing message its punch. Kaminski, a familiar face to Israeli sports fans from his broadcasting work, has been credited by the Gordon camp with helping professionalize the sport locally before GFN existed at all. Turning to him in front of a packed, sold-out arena and calling for an immediate sequel was Gordon's way of signaling that Sunday's show was a beginning, not a peak.

For a combat-sports scene in Israel that has long operated on the margins of the country's sporting conversation, a full house at Menora Mivtachim Arena for a card headlined by an Israeli family act, against genuine international opposition, is itself the story. Whether Kaminski answers Gordon's challenge with a GFN 2 date will be the first test of whether Sunday's atmosphere can be repeated.

title: World Cup final referee Slavko Vinčić announces retirement
dek: The Slovenian official who took charge of Spain's extra-time win over Argentina steps away from the game a week after the biggest match of his career, capping a decade at the sport's elite level.
body: Slavko Vinčić, the Slovenian referee who took charge of the 2026 World Cup final, has retired from professional officiating just a week after the biggest match of his career, the Slovenian Football Association has confirmed.
Vinčić, 46, was the man in the middle when Spain beat Argentina 1-0 after extra time at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey on July 19, sealing the tournament in the United States.

The final was not without controversy. Vinčić sent off Argentina midfielder Enzo Fernández in stoppage time at the end of normal time for two bookable offences, a decision that fed into a bad-tempered finish to the match involving several Argentina players, including Leandro Paredes.

Despite the criticism that followed his handling of a fractious final, Vinčić still leaves the game garlanded. The International Federation of Football History and Statistics (IFFHS) named him the World Cup's outstanding referee, and Italy's referees' association, the AIA, gave him its Giulio Campanati award.

"One week after the World Cup final in the USA, Slavko Vinčić officially concluded his historic refereeing career at the top of the world," the Slovenian Football Association said in a statement announcing his retirement.

Vinčić had been one of UEFA's elite-listed referees since 2019 and built a résumé few of his peers can match. He took charge of the 2024 Champions League final, when Real Madrid beat Borussia Dortmund 2-0 to lift a 15th European Cup, and the 2022 Europa League final between Eintracht Frankfurt and Rangers.
He also officiated at Euro 2020 and reached the semi-final stage again at Euro 2024, cementing his reputation as one of the continent's most trusted whistlers for the biggest occasions.

At this World Cup, Vinčić took charge of four matches in total, including Mexico's 2-0 round-of-32 win over Ecuador, where he sent off Ecuador defender Piero Hincapié under FIFA's newly introduced rule mandating a red card for covering the mouth during a confrontation with an opponent.

That willingness to apply the letter of the law was ultimately what defined his final assignment as well, and now marks the last chapter of a career that made him the first Slovenian referee to take charge of a World Cup final.

title: Avi Nimni: Maccabi Tel Aviv still need a winger and a defender
dek: The club's all-time top scorer, now an agent and ONE pundit, says Kristijan Belić's foot fracture has exposed gaps in a squad already rebuilt this summer around Ester Sokler and Belić's own permanent transfer.

body: Avi Nimni knows this club better than almost anyone alive, having scored more goals for Maccabi Tel Aviv than any player in its history, and his verdict on this summer's rebuild carries weight: the squad, he says, is not finished yet.
"The team needs to bring in another winger and a new defender," Nimni said on ONE's Sicha HaYom programme, where he now appears regularly as a pundit alongside his work as a players' agent.

His comments came with the injury to Kristijan Belić fresh in mind. The Serbian midfielder fractured a metatarsal in his foot after coming on as a substitute in Maccabi's 5-0 win over Sheriff Tiraspol in Europa League qualifying, a knock that could keep him out for up to three months.

That is a blow to a squad Maccabi have otherwise spent the summer strengthening. Belić himself was only just turned into a permanent Maccabi player, with the club paying AZ Alkmaar roughly €1.3 million to make his loan move official for the new season after 23 appearances in yellow last term.

The club has also brought in Slovenia international striker Ester Sokler from Serbian side Radnički Kragujevac, a deal reported at around €1 million, with Sokler having scored 15 goals in 29 appearances for Radnički last season and earned his senior Slovenia debut in June.

Nimni was cautious about passing judgement on the new striker just yet, saying he wants to see more of Sokler alongside Sayed Abu Farchi before assessing how the forward line fits together — but his broader point stood: even with Belić and Sokler in, he believes Maccabi are still short a winger and a defensive body, particularly with Belić now sidelined.
Asked about Roy Revivo, whose future has been a recurring subject of transfer talk, Nimni offered nothing new: "not for now," he said, declining to elaborate further on the winger's situation.

The interview also touched on family news. Nimni's 19-year-old son, Amit, has signed his first senior contract, joining second-tier Hapoel Kfar Shalem after a prolific youth season with Shimshon Tel Aviv. Avi Nimni said he tries to stay out of his son's career decisions, hoping only that Amit will "learn, work hard and enjoy himself" under new coach Noam Shoham.

For Maccabi Tel Aviv, though, the headline message from one of the club's most respected voices is a note of caution heading into the new season: reinforcements already made are welcome, but in Nimni's eyes, the rebuild is not complete.

title: Kivdei Gordon opens family's Tel Aviv card with 45-second knockout
dek: The eldest of Israel's fighting Gordon brothers dropped Mexico's José Alberto Quiñones with a slingshot head kick before the first minute was up, setting an early tone on Gordon Fight Nights' debut show.

verificationSources.label: MMAmania - GFN 1: Israel vs. The World card, time and location

body: Kivdei Gordon needed less than 45 seconds to finish his night's work. Fighting at the Menora Mivtachim Arena in Tel Aviv on Monday, the eldest of Israel's Gordon fighting brothers stopped Mexico's José Alberto "Taco" Quiñones by knockout, becoming the first of the family to step into the cage on their own promotional card, ONE reported.

Gordon, 26, dictated the pace from the opening bell, hammering Quiñones's legs with kicks that had the 35-year-old Mexican badly off balance within seconds. The finish arrived before the 45-second mark: a thudding high kick to the head — the kind of strike that has earned Gordon the nickname "Slingshot" on the professional circuit — put Quiñones down and unable to continue, according to ONE's account of the bout.

The win came on GFN 1: Israel vs. The World, the debut event of Gordon Fight Nights, a promotion built around the Gordon family itself. The card, held in Tel Aviv, was topped by a Muay Thai main event pitting Kivdei's brother Ahavat Hashem Gordon against the well-travelled Brazilian striker John Lineker, according to MMAmania's preview of the show.

Gordon arrived at the bout on an 8-2 professional record and a hot streak: his previous outing also ended in almost identical fashion, a 45-second knockout of Peru's Alexis Ramos at FFC 102 in March, a result that had already made him one of the more talked-about young Israeli fighters on the regional scene.

The Gordons are among the more distinctive stories in Israeli combat sports. The children of Dr. Azriel Gordon, an American-born chiropractor, and his Hong Kong-born wife, the siblings were given Hebrew names built around phrases of faith — among them Otzmat Hashem, Kivdei, Simchat Hashem, Ruach Hashem and Ahavat Hashem — and several have gone on to build fight careers of their own, drawing large and vocal Israeli crowds wherever they compete.

Kivdei began training in Muay Thai at 11 and won European kickboxing gold as a teenager before turning to MMA, honing his game in gyms in Boston and São Paulo. Monday's finish, delivered in front of a home crowd for the first time on a card the family itself promoted, extends his run of fast finishes and keeps alive his stated ambition of eventually testing himself in the UFC.

title: Ruach Hashem Gordon makes it two from two for the Gordon brothers in Tel Aviv
dek: The Muay Thai world champion outpointed Moldova's Maximus Bejenuta over three rounds at the Menora Mivtachim Arena, setting the stage for youngest brother Ahavat Hashem Gordon's headline clash with Brazilian great John Lineker.

body: Ruach Hashem Gordon made it two wins from two for the fighting Gordon brothers on Monday night, grinding out a unanimous decision over Moldova's Maximus Bejenuta in a Muay Thai bout at the Menora Mivtachim Arena in Tel Aviv.

Gordon, Israel's reigning IFMA world champion, built his win on a relentless low-kick game plan. By the end of the first round he had already found his range, closing the stanza with what ONE described as a powerful combination that finished with an elbow to Bejenuta's back.

The Moldovan's left leg was visibly bruised by the second round as Gordon kept chopping away with kicks and mixed in sharp punches, controlling range and tempo against an opponent who struggled to find an answer.

Bejenuta lifted his work rate in the third, sensing he was behind on the cards, but Gordon refused to let up and kept the pressure on to the final bell. The judges scored it clearly in the Israeli's favour.

The victory completed a 2-0 start to the night for the Gordon family, coming minutes after older brother Kibadi Gordon needed less than a minute to blast out Mexico's José Alberto Quiñones with a head kick in the evening's opening bout.

Ruach Hashem Gordon, 22, is one of the most decorated fighters Israeli Muay Thai has produced. He won the IFMA World Championship at 57kg in Bangkok in 2023, becoming the first Israeli man to claim a Muay Thai world title, and the same year became the first Israeli to win a stadium championship in Thailand, at Omnoi Stadium.

Monday's card, staged under the banner GFN 1: Israel vs. the World, was billed as the largest event of its kind ever held in Israel, built entirely around the three Gordon brothers appearing on the same professional bill for the first time.

The night's headline act was still to come: youngest brother Ahavat Hashem Gordon was set to face Brazil's John Lineker, the former UFC fixture and ex-ONE Championship bantamweight world champion, in what was framed as the toughest test yet of his young career.

The three brothers grew up in a national-religious family of seven children from Nachliel in the Binyamin region, with an American-born father and a mother from Hong Kong - a background that has made their rise through combat sports one of the more unusual stories in Israeli sport this year.

title: Ginat to 2030 is not sentiment. It is Hapoel Tel Aviv's whole strategy in one signature
dek: A 31-year-old forward four months out of knee surgery has been tied down until 2030 by a club that spent part of last season in exile. The romance is real, but so is the calculation behind it.

source.name: ILSP Columns
source.originalTitle: ILSP column
source.author: ILSP Sports Desk

verificationSources.label: Ginat extension through 2030 announced 27 July 2026 after eight seasons; Malcolm departure; Sofia/Israel dual-base plan; Motley to Crvena Zvezda; reported Kleber pursuit
Elijah Bryant extension to 2029 (11 July 2026), his 2025-26 EuroLeague statistics, play-off qualification in debut season, Itoudis as coach
Ginat knee surgery on 16 March 2026 (trapped-nerve release, Ichilov Hospital), season-ending for the regular season, his 10.0 pts / 5.0 reb in ten EuroLeague games, squad relocation to Sofia
Ginat career history: born November 1994, Hapoel 2016-2020, Metropolitans 92 2020-22, return in 2022, 2025 EuroCup title

body: Hapoel Tel Aviv's announcement on Monday that Tomer Ginat has signed a new contract running to 2030 invites an easy reading: a beloved forward, eight seasons into his association with the club across two spells, rewarded for devotion with a deal that should carry him to the end of his career. The easy reading is not wrong. It is simply incomplete. Look at what Hapoel have done this month, and this extension stops being a love letter and starts looking like doctrine.

Consider first what Ginat is, in cold accounting terms. He is 31, a power forward who joined the club as a young player in 2016, left for Metropolitans 92 in France in 2020, and returned in 2022 on a five-year agreement. He was part of the side that won the 2025 EuroCup, and in Hapoel's first EuroLeague campaign he was productive in a reduced role, averaging 10.0 points and 5.0 rebounds across ten appearances. Then, in March, he underwent surgery at Ichilov Hospital to release a trapped nerve in his right knee, an operation that ended his regular season with the club hoping, at the time, for a play-off return.

Most European clubs do not respond to that profile with a contract stretching four more years. The market logic of continental basketball is ruthless about players on the wrong side of 30 coming off knee operations; the standard instrument is the one-year deal with a club option, risk parked firmly on the player's side of the table. Hapoel have done the opposite, and they have done it deliberately, because this is now a pattern rather than a gesture.

On 11 July the club extended Elijah Bryant to 2029. Bryant had earned it on the floor — 15.4 points, 5.2 rebounds and 3.3 assists across 38 EuroLeague games, with an efficiency rating among the competition's top five — but the structure of the deal matters as much as the merit. Two core players, two long horizons, announced within a fortnight of each other. Clubs that intend to live hand to mouth do not draft contracts that expire in 2029 and 2030.

The context that makes this genuinely striking is geographic. Hapoel played part of their debut EuroLeague season in Sofia, and on 20 July the club confirmed that the coming campaign will again be run from both Bulgaria and Israel, with security conditions to be reassessed as the season progresses. This is a club that cannot currently promise its players a settled home floor, a settled commute, or a settled life. What it can promise is time — and time is precisely what these contracts distribute.

That is the strategic insight buried in the Ginat announcement. When a club's physical circumstances are unstable, the roster becomes its only reliable geography. Dimitris Itoudis's squad spent last season proving that a first-year EuroLeague club could reach the play-offs while living out of suitcases; the lesson the front office appears to have drawn is that the thing which made that possible — a core that did not fracture under itinerant conditions — is the asset most worth overpaying to keep. Continuity is cheap to praise and expensive to buy. Hapoel are buying it.

It is a selective purchase, and honesty requires saying so. The same month that produced the Bryant and Ginat extensions also saw Johnathan Motley leave for Crvena Zvezda and Colin Malcolm depart after 40 EuroLeague appearances in the debut season. This is not indiscriminate loyalty. It is a two-tier model: an identity layer of players bound to the club on long paper, and a flexible layer that can be refreshed each summer as the competitive picture demands. The reported pursuit of Maxi Kleber, a free agent out of the NBA, belongs to the second tier — and the first tier is part of the sales pitch, because a recruit weighing a move to a club without a guaranteed home city needs evidence that the project is not a pop-up.

None of this makes the Ginat deal safe. A contract to 2030 for a player who turns 32 in November, months after nerve-release surgery on his knee, can age badly, and the financial terms have not been disclosed, so we cannot judge how much risk Hapoel have actually absorbed. European deals are renegotiated more readily than their NBA equivalents, which softens the downside, but a club carrying long commitments to declining players has less room to move than one that kept its powder dry. If Ginat's knee does not fully co-operate, this becomes an expensive piece of symbolism.

Yet even that scenario may be priced in. Ginat's value to this particular club was never purely his box score. He is one of the few players who connects the Hapoel that scrapped through domestic seasons in the late 2010s to the Hapoel that now sells itself as a EuroLeague institution, and for a fanbase that followed its team to Sofia, that thread has worth a spreadsheet struggles to capture. A club in exile needs custodians of what it is; you cannot recruit those on the open market.

There is also a wider Israeli argument here. The league's persistent condition is export: its best players leave, usually young, usually westward, and the domestic game is narrated as a departure lounge. A club demonstrating that a serious European career can be housed in Israeli colours — play-off basketball in a debut EuroLeague season, contracts that treat players as long-term partners rather than seasonal inventory — changes the terms of that conversation, at least at the margin. Whether it changes behaviour across the league depends on money most rivals do not have, which is the caveat that should temper any triumphalism.

The test of Monday's announcement is therefore not how it feels this week. It is whether, in two or three seasons, Hapoel's core is still intact, still competitive and still recognisably the group that carried the club through its strangest year — or whether the long contracts have calcified into obligations. Judged today, on the evidence available, the bet is coherent, on-pattern and braver than the market norm. That is more than can be said for most transfer news in July.

body: Israel's under-16 women's handball team barely let Mexico into the contest on Monday, running out 19-3 winners at the IHF Women's U16 World Championship in Zagreb to make it two wins from two at the tournament.

It was one-sided from the opening whistle. Israel controlled 79 percent of possession over the 50 minutes, according to ONE, and set up all but a handful of their goals with 13 assists, the kind of clinical, unhurried numbers that speak to a gulf in class rather than a scrappy blowout.

Yahali Rokach and Yara Huino-Garcia each finished with three goals to lead the scoring, with Tamar Orhan, Galia Wright, Rotem Bar, Tamara Salmon and Hila Korsia all chipping in twice. Shani Yaakubovitz, Inbar Yanko and Alma Tauber rounded out the goal charts with one apiece — ten different players got on the scoresheet, underlining just how comprehensively Israel's bench contributed.

"The players did their job in a game where they were favourites," coach Idan Kaftori said afterwards, according to ONE, before turning his attention immediately to what comes next. "Tomorrow we expect a tough and important match against Holland."

That warning is not just coach-speak. Israel faces the Netherlands on Tuesday at 15:30 local time, a side ONE describes as one of the strongest teams in the world at this age group and by some distance the sternest test of Israel's group.

Monday's win followed an opening-day victory over South Africa, 12-7, in which Israel had to work harder for the result — trailing 0-2 early before reeling off five unanswered goals to lead 6-4 at the break, then pulling clear with a 4-1 third quarter. Rokach was named player of the match in that game too, alongside Uri Grodman, each scoring three.

Israel's group in Zagreb also includes Hungary, giving the teenage squad a demanding run of fixtures before the tournament's knockout stages, but two wins from two — one comfortable, one hard-fought — is as good a start as the coaching staff could have asked for.

For a Handball Federation of Israel age group that rarely gets attention outside its own community, a 79-percent-possession demolition of a fellow world-championship entrant is a notable result, and one that raises the stakes for Tuesday's meeting with the Dutch.

title: Hapoel Petah Tikva strengthen their Youth A attack with two prolific teenage scorers
dek: ONE reports the club has signed wingers Liel Azoulai and Idan Kostaki, who scored a combined 39 goals between them in last season's Youth B league, ahead of coach Bar Cohen's first campaign in charge.
body: Hapoel Petah Tikva's Youth A squad is getting sharper teeth up front. ONE reports the club has added two attacking wingers, Liel Azoulai and Idan Kostaki, who between them scored 39 goals in last season's Youth B league — a striking return that has followed both players across the country this summer.

Azoulai arrives on a three-year deal after a prolific campaign with Beitar Tiberias Netanya, where he scored 14 goals in the Youth B league before a spell with Beitar Yehuda Tel Aviv. According to ONE, his path through Israeli youth football began at Hapoel Be'er Sheva's academy, before stops at Ashdod SC and eventually Beitar Tiberias, where his scoring form made him a wanted man. He is represented by agent Oren Sterling of the PLAY IT agency.

Kostaki, meanwhile, joins from cross-town rivals Maccabi Petah Tikva on a two-year deal with a club option for a third season, ONE reports. He was the more prolific of the pair last season, scoring 18 goals in the Youth B league for Maccabi, and his numbers were even more eye-catching earlier in his development — 22 goals at the Under-12 level for the same club, after starting out at the Gadna Tel Aviv academy and playing for the Nes Tziona youth section. His agent is Ran Rosenthal.

The double capture gives new Hapoel Petah Tikva Youth A coach Bar Cohen, who previously worked with the youth ranks at Kiryat Yam and Hapoel Herzliya, a pair of proven finishers to build his attack around as preparations continue for a season ONE says is roughly three weeks from kicking off.

For a club whose senior side has spent recent seasons fighting for promotion back to the top flight, investment in the academy pipeline carries obvious long-term appeal — and two wingers who have already shown they can find the net at every age group they have passed through give Cohen's group a clear head start heading into the new campaign.

title: Beersheba's Nir Katz: "I'm not giving him to you, not even for 10 million euro"
dek: The Hapoel Be'er Sheva chief refused to sell Kings Kangwa out of a Champions League qualifier for any price, and watched Panathinaikos complete the transfer instead of AEK Athens on Beersheba's own terms.
body: Nir Katz doesn't usually need to raise his voice to end a negotiation. When AEK Athens called Hapoel Be'er Sheva one final time to try to prise away Kings Kangwa, the Beersheba chief executive simply told them no — in terms blunt enough that they've become the story. "I'm not giving him to you, not even for 10 million euro," Katz said, according to ONE, and with that the Greek club's pursuit of Beersheba's best player was over.

The stand-off centred on a single fixture: Beersheba's Champions League qualifying tie against Icelandic side Vikingur Reykjavik. AEK's sporting director, Javier Ribalta, first approached Beersheba with a fee attached to a condition — he wanted a 50 percent discount on Kangwa's asking price if the Zambian midfielder was allowed to play for Beersheba against Vikingur before completing his move to Athens.

Beersheba said no. Katz was not willing to let his club's own European campaign be discounted away in someone else's transfer math, and the club held firm that Kangwa would stay available for the qualifier regardless of what any suitor was offering.

Ribalta called back with a revised proposal, according to ONE: AEK would now pay the full, undiscounted fee, but still wanted assurances Kangwa would be withheld from the Vikingur match to protect their incoming asset. That was the point at which Katz drew the line for good, delivering the refusal that has since done the rounds in Israeli football media.

It wasn't really about money by that stage. Katz's point, as ONE reported it, was that no fee — real or hypothetically doubled to ten million euro — would buy Kangwa out of a match that mattered to Beersheba itself. The AEK deal collapsed there.

Panathinaikos, who had also been tracking Kangwa through the summer, stepped into the opening AEK left behind. Unlike AEK, the Greek giants agreed to Beersheba's condition outright: Kangwa would remain in the Beersheba squad and be free to face Vikingur Reykjavik in Champions League qualifying before formally switching clubs.

That concession sealed it. Beersheba confirmed the sale to Panathinaikos, with Walla Sport reporting the package at roughly €4.5 million — around €3.8 million paid upfront plus a further €700,000 in add-ons, a deal Israel Hayom described as a historic fee for the club.

It caps a rapid rise for the 27-year-old. Kangwa arrived at Beersheba in the summer of 2024 from Red Star Belgrade for a reported fee in the region of €800,000 and quickly became the team's creative fulcrum, contributing 12 goals and 11 assists across 40 appearances last season by some Israeli media tallies.

For Katz, the episode is as much a statement about Beersheba's leverage as it is about one player. AEK arrived with a bigger financial pull than most Israeli clubs are used to negotiating against, and still left empty-handed because it wouldn't meet Beersheba on the one term the club actually cared about.
facts: Hapoel Be'er Sheva CEO Nir Katz rejected a final offer from AEK Athens for midfielder Kings Kangwa, telling the Greek club "I'm not giving him to you, not even for 10 million euro," according to ONE.
AEK Athens sporting director Javier Ribalta initially sought a 50 percent discount on Kangwa's fee if he was allowed to play for Beersheba against Vikingur Reykjavik in Champions League qualifying.
Beersheba rejected the discount; when Ribalta later offered the full fee but wanted Kangwa withheld from the Vikingur match, Katz refused and the AEK deal collapsed.
Panathinaikos agreed to Beersheba's condition that Kangwa remain available for the Vikingur qualifier and completed the transfer instead.
The Panathinaikos deal is reported at roughly €4.5 million (about €3.8 million upfront plus €700,000 in bonuses), per Walla Sport.
Kangwa, a Zambia international, joined Beersheba in 2024 from Red Star Belgrade for a reported fee of around €800,000.

title: Maldini and Leonardo quit Italian federation roles over Pirlo saga
dek: The pair resigned as Italy's technical director and advisor just 16 days into the job after federation president Giovanni Malagò refused to approve Andrea Pirlo as head coach over his ties to a Russian betting firm.
body: Paolo Maldini and Leonardo have resigned as the Italian football federation's technical director and advisor, walking away from the project just 16 days after taking up the posts, in a collapse triggered by a dispute over who should coach the national team.

The two AC Milan greats were installed on July 11 by Giovanni Malagò, the former Italian Olympic Committee chief who was elected FIGC president in June and tasked with rebuilding a federation still reeling from Italy's World Cup play-off exit to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Maldini and Leonardo were meant to lead that reconstruction, starting with the choice of a new head coach to replace Gennaro Gattuso.

Their pick was Andrea Pirlo, the 2006 World Cup winner and former Juventus and Milan midfielder now coaching in Turkey. But Malagò refused to sign off on the appointment, citing Pirlo's role as a global ambassador for Fonbet, a Russian betting company, at a moment when Italian officials and politicians have been wary of any commercial association with Russian-linked brands.

With their preferred candidate blocked, Maldini and Leonardo chose to leave immediately rather than pursue an alternative they had not championed, according to reporting from Sky Sports and several Italian outlets including ANSA and Corriere dello Sport.

Pirlo himself addressed the affair publicly, saying that "during my career... I have always carried out my activity in full respect to the laws," and describing his Fonbet arrangement as "exclusively commercial and sporting in nature."

Before the collapse, the federation had also sounded out other names for the vacant bench job. Pep Guardiola turned down an approach for personal reasons unrelated to football, while Carlo Ancelotti was contacted but remains contracted to coach Brazil.

The abrupt departures leave Malagò needing to rebuild the technical set-up for a second time in barely two weeks. Roberto Mancini, who previously led Italy to European Championship glory in 2021, has re-emerged as the president's favoured option, with Antonio Conte also under consideration. Giorgio Chiellini's name has surfaced as a possible replacement for Maldini in the technical director's chair.

It is the latest upheaval for a federation still absorbing the fallout from missing next year's World Cup. Gattuso, team manager Gigi Buffon and former federation president Gabriele Gravina all left their posts after Italy fell at the play-off stage, a failure that prompted Malagò's own move from Olympic sport into football administration.

Malagò had previously said the federation was working through a "Plan A, Plan B and Plan C" for both the head coach and technical director roles. That contingency planning now looks set to be tested in full, with a new appointment expected within days as Italy tries to steady itself before European Championship qualifying begins.

title: Nachmias goes the full 90 as Ludogorets stay top before Hapoel Tel Aviv return leg
dek: The Israel international centre-back played every minute of a routine league win over Dunav Ruse, three days after Ludogorets fell 2-0 to Hapoel Tel Aviv in their Conference League qualifier.
body: Idan Nachmias played every minute of Ludogorets' 2-0 win away to Dunav Ruse in the Bulgarian league on Monday, a routine result that kept the champions top of the table but mattered for a much bigger reason: it was the Israel international's last outing before the biggest 90 minutes of his club season.

Ludogorets go into Thursday's Conference League return leg against Hapoel Tel Aviv needing to overturn a 2-0 deficit from last week's first leg, and Nachmias's manager clearly wanted his defensive lynchpin fully match-sharp rather than rested for it.

According to ONE, Bernard Tekpetey put Ludogorets ahead in the 14th minute and Rwan Cruz doubled the lead in the 47th, goals that stretched the Bulgarian side's unbeaten domestic run and left bottom club Dunav Ruse still searching for their first points of the campaign.

The result offered Ludogorets a measure of reassurance after a bruising European night three days earlier. Hapoel Tel Aviv won the first leg of their UEFA Conference League second qualifying round tie 2-0, with Omri Altman converting a Stav Turiel pass just before half-time and Chico adding a second after the break.

That match, like other recent European fixtures involving Israeli clubs, was not played on home soil in Israel but at a neutral venue in Miskolc, Hungary — a continuing arrangement UEFA has required for Israeli teams' home ties amid the ongoing security situation.

It leaves Ludogorets with a genuine mountain to climb at their own Huvepharma Arena in Razgrad on Thursday, needing at least a two-goal margin simply to force extra time against a Hapoel Tel Aviv side that travelled to Hungary and did exactly the job it needed to.

For Nachmias, the tie carries an unusual personal dimension: an Israel international lining up for a foreign club against an Israeli team desperate to eliminate him. The 29-year-old centre-back, born in the Golan Heights kibbutz of Ein Zivan, moved to Ludogorets in 2025 after spells at Maccabi Tel Aviv and Ironi Kiryat Shmona, and has been a full Israel international since his 2020 debut.

His manager's decision to play him the full 90 against Dunav Ruse, rather than rotate ahead of a season-defining European night, suggests Ludogorets have no intention of treating Thursday's second leg as a lost cause — whatever the size of the deficit they must overturn.

title: Hapoel is my home, I want to retire here, says Ginat after new deal
dek: Tomer Ginat has extended his contract with Hapoel Tel Aviv through the 2029/30 season, stretching his stay at his boyhood club to 12 years, with a first league championship now the one prize he still wants.

verificationSources.label: EuroLeague/EuroCup - Hapoel reunites with Ginat on multi-year deal

body: Tomer Ginat has put his name to a new contract with Hapoel Tel Aviv that runs through the 2029/30 season, and the power forward made no secret of how he wants the story to end: in the same red jersey he has worn since he was a young pro.

"Hapoel has always been my home, a place I love very much, very dear to my heart," Ginat said in an interview with ONE published after the signing. "I have felt like I belong and am very connected to this place, since I was a child I remember myself as a Hapoel fan."

Asked directly about how he pictures the finish line of his career, he did not hedge. "I would be very happy to retire in the uniform of Hapoel Tel Aviv," he told the outlet. Under the new terms, Ginat will be 35 when the deal expires.

By the club's own count, relayed through ONE, the extension takes Ginat's total tenure in Tel Aviv to 12 years - an initial four-year spell followed by eight more years now locked in. He first signed with Hapoel in July 2016, turning down other offers to join the club he supported as a boy, and has already committed to multiple extensions since.

For all the loyalty on show, Ginat was clear that sentiment alone will not satisfy him. The one prize missing from his run at Hapoel is a domestic league title, and he framed that as the remaining item on his personal list. "This is the most important thing... I believe that when we win a championship it will be closing a circle, a very important milestone," he said.

The context for that ambition is a club that has been transformed on the European stage. Hapoel won the EuroCup in 2025 and are about to begin their second season competing in the EuroLeague, basketball's top continental competition - a rise Ginat described in the interview as remarkably quick. "The jump was incredibly fast and here we are today as a EuroLeague team entering its second year there," he said.

Ginat's own numbers reflect a player who has taken on a heavier European workload without being the headline scorer: he averaged 8.9 points, 4.8 rebounds and 1.4 assists during Hapoel's EuroCup-winning campaign, and 3.3 points and 1.9 rebounds once the step up to EuroLeague competition arrived.

Head coach Dimitris Itoudis, who has led Hapoel through its European climb, praised Ginat's durability through a run of injuries and said he hoped the forward would stay healthy and keep helping the club for years to come, according to ONE.
There was a personal note too. Ginat has recently become a father, and he described the summer break around the birth as, in his words, the most fun vacation he has ever had.

Ginat captains Israel's senior national basketball team and has been named the country's Player of the Year twice and Player of the Month five times over his career, alongside four selections to the Israeli league's All-First Team. With this deal, Hapoel Tel Aviv have again shown a preference for building continuity around homegrown, boyhood-supporter figures rather than churning through imports at forward - a policy the club will hope pays off first in the EuroLeague, and then, if Ginat gets his wish, on the domestic table.

title: Point guard Yuval Schneiderman signs with Hapoel Ironi Eilat
dek: The 23-year-old playmaker joins the National League club after a season at Hapoel Galil Elyon, with coach Oren Aharoni hailing a "real point guard" for the roster.
body: Hapoel Ironi Eilat have added a new floor general for the 2026/27 season, confirming the signing of 23-year-old point guard Yuval Schneiderman, ONE reports.

Schneiderman arrives in the Red Sea city after a season with Hapoel Galil Elyon, where he averaged 8.3 points, 4.0 assists, 3.3 rebounds and 1.5 steals per game — numbers that made him one of the more productive young playmakers outside Israel's top flight.

It is the latest stop in a well-travelled career for the Jerusalem-born guard, who came up through Hapoel Jerusalem's youth system before spells at Hapoel Galboa Gilboa, Maccabi Ironi Ramat Gan, Ironi Kiryat Ata and, most recently, Galil Elyon.

Eilat head coach Oren Aharoni made no secret of his excitement over the addition. "A real point guard, a quality game manager with excellent character, who fits the style we want this team to play," Aharoni said of his new floor leader, according to ONE.

Sport1/Maariv separately confirmed the signing, with the outlet also carrying comments attributed to Schneiderman describing himself as a "quality game manager" — echoing the club's framing of the move as a direct upgrade at the point guard position.
Neither ONE nor Sport1 disclosed contract length or financial terms of the deal.

Eilat's basketball project has been on the rise: the club, formed via the 2024 merger of Hapoel Eilat and Maccabi Eilat into Ironi Eilat, won promotion after topping the 2025/26 National League table and now returns to a higher tier, where a steady, experienced hand at the point should be a priority for Aharoni as he builds his roster for the step up.

title: Three Gordon brothers to fight on the same card as Tel Aviv hosts Israel's biggest combat sports night
dek: GFN 1 brings John Lineker and 12 bouts to the Menora Mivtachim Arena on Monday, with broadcaster Yaniv Kaminsky calling it a night the whole fighting world is watching.
body: For one night, the Yad Eliyahu district of Tel Aviv becomes the center of the combat sports world. GFN 1 — billed by its organisers as "Israel vs. the World" — fills the Menora Mivtachim Arena on Monday evening for a card built around a feat Israeli fight fans have never seen: three brothers, all from the same family, all fighting professionally on the same card, on the same night.

The broadcast goes out live on ONE, and the channel's ringside voice, Yaniv Kaminsky, previewed the night on ONE's "Conversation of the Day" podcast in unambiguous terms. "We did something crazy here," he said, according to ONE. "It's going to be madness, the whole world is talking about it — we're hours away from history."

The headline act belongs to Ahavat Hashem Gordon, who closes the show against John Lineker, the well-travelled Brazilian who fought for years at the top of the UFC's bantamweight and flyweight divisions before becoming a former ONE Championship bantamweight MMA world champion. It is by some distance the highest-profile international name an Israeli combat-sports card has landed.

His brother Ruach Hashem Gordon fights earlier on the same bill against Maximus Bejenuta, a Moldovan Muay Thai and kickboxing fighter reported by Sport5 to be carrying one professional Muay Thai bout on his record, a loss inside ONE Championship. Ruach Hashem did not hide his confidence in comments carried by Sport5: "I'm going to hunt him down ... apply tremendous pressure. I saw him in the sauna, we were there together, and he looked very weak."

The third brother, Kibdei Gordon, meets Jose Alberto Quiñonez in the third of the family's bouts. Kibdei arrives on a high; Ynet reported he stopped Alexis Ramos in well under a minute at an FFC card in Peru his last time out, and a win in Tel Aviv would make it back-to-back knockouts on home soil.

Around the family's three fights, GFN 1 is a genuinely sprawling card — 12 bouts in all, pitting Israeli fighters against opponents brought in from across the Muay Thai and kickboxing world under the promotion's "Israel vs. the World" framing. Doors and the early prelims were set for the late afternoon, with the marquee bouts, including the Gordon brothers' fights, expected to run through the evening.

ONE reported the undercard will also include showcase bouts involving wounded veterans from the Beit Hagibor organisation, Israelis who lost limbs in recent years, alongside a run of musical performances woven into the broadcast — production touches the promotion has leaned on to sell the night as more than just a fight card.

ONE reports the arena is expected to draw a crowd of roughly 11,000, a number that, if it holds, would make it one of the largest paying crowds an Israeli combat-sports event has assembled, reflecting the pull of having three siblings from one Israeli fighting family on a single marquee.

GFN — Gordon Fight Nights — is a new promotion built around the family's profile, and organisers have talked about turning Monday's show into an annual fixture rather than a one-off. Its ambition is unmistakable: import a genuine former UFC and ONE Championship name in Lineker for a market that has rarely, if ever, hosted a fighter of his résumé.

Kaminsky, for his part, was open about wanting a clean sweep. He said he was hoping for three wins from the three brothers by the end of the night, while acknowledging on the podcast that pulling off all three would be difficult given the calibre of the opposition Gordon Fight Nights has brought in.

title: Real Madrid ready to loan out Asencio to Marseille as Chelsea explore Welbeck return
dek: Raúl Asencio looks set for a temporary move to Ligue 1 after falling down José Mourinho's pecking order, while Chelsea open talks to bring Danny Welbeck back from Brighton.
body: Real Madrid are prepared to send Raúl Asencio out on loan this summer, with Marseille pushing hardest for the young centre-back after the Spanish champions made clear he no longer figures in José Mourinho's plans.

The proposed structure, first reported by ONE and corroborated by Spanish and English outlets, has Marseille taking the 23-year-old on loan with a mandatory obligation to buy — reported at around €15 million — that would be triggered if certain appearance conditions are met over the season.
Real Madrid are also said to have insisted on keeping a 25 percent sell-on clause, meaning the club would benefit further if Marseille later sold Asencio on for a profit.

Asencio was one of the breakout stories of Real Madrid's 2024-25 campaign, forcing his way into the first team amid a defensive injury crisis, but his path back into the side has narrowed considerably since Ibrahima Konaté's arrival strengthened the centre-back options at Mourinho's disposal.

Benfica had also explored signing Asencio earlier in the window, but those talks stalled after the Portuguese club balked at Real Madrid's demand for a buyback option, clearing the way for Marseille to advance their interest.

Separately, Chelsea have opened talks over a possible return for Danny Welbeck, with David Ornstein of The Athletic reporting that the west London club are exploring a deal to bring the 35-year-old forward back from Brighton & Hove Albion.

According to Ornstein's report, discussions are at an early stage, but there is said to be optimism on all sides that an agreement could be reached, with Welbeck's experience and leadership in the dressing room appealing to Chelsea.

Welbeck, who began his career at Manchester United before spells at Sunderland, Arsenal and Brighton, enjoyed one of the most productive Premier League seasons of his career in 2025-26, scoring 13 league goals under Fabian Hürzeler. His contract on the south coast runs until 2027, and Brighton are not expected to let him go easily.

Neither move has been finalised, and both remain reports rather than confirmed transfers at this stage, but the two threads point to a busy end to the window for Real Madrid's fringe squad players and for Chelsea's search for attacking depth and experience.
