title: Haifa Labour Court Rejects Bnei Sakhnin Bid to Freeze Arbitration in Mimer Pay Dispute
dek: A regional labour court has cleared the way for arbitration to continue in former coach Sharon Mimer's roughly NIS 920,000 claim against Bnei Sakhnin, rejecting the club's request to halt the process.

verificationSources.label: ONE - report on the court ruling
ONE - background on the Mimer-Sakhnin dispute

body: A regional labour court in Haifa has rejected Bnei Sakhnin's attempt to freeze arbitration proceedings brought by former head coach Sharon Mimer, who is seeking roughly NIS 920,000 in compensation from the club, ONE reported.
Judge Dania Drori found no grounds to suspend the process, dismissing the club's argument that letting the arbitration run its course would cause it irreparable harm.

Mimer, who took charge of Sakhnin again in 2025, filed the claim in March 2026, according to ONE. It covers termination compensation, wage differences, unpaid pension and insurance contributions, and severance pay.

Sakhnin had argued that these are statutory rights over which only the labour courts have jurisdiction, not a private arbitrator, and asked the court to pause the arbitration while it pursued that argument through the appeals process.

The judge disagreed, reasoning that even if Sakhnin's underlying claim eventually succeeds, any arbitration ruling issued in the meantime would automatically be voided - meaning the club faces no irreversible damage from letting the process continue, per the ruling cited by ONE.

The dispute is being arbitrated by retired judge Oren Shgav, appointed under regulations the Israel Football Association amended after the Eli Babayev affair, which saw retired judges brought in to rule on disputes between clubs and their coaches and players.

It is the second setback in a row for Sakhnin in the case: the arbitrator already rejected the club's bid to have Mimer's claim thrown out entirely on 22 June, and a full arbitration hearing is now due in August 2026.
Mimer is represented by attorneys Amir Cohen and Sharon Braverman Atiya, while Sakhnin's case is being handled by Anan Frou and Amal Khinawi, according to ONE.

The rupture between Mimer and the club turned public and bitter after chief executive Yosef Badarna suggested that parting with the coach sooner would have helped Sakhnin's push up the table; Mimer has said he felt exposed to hostility during his time in Sakhnin, and his claim reportedly also cites breach of contract and damage to his professional reputation alongside the financial demands.

title: The man who eliminated Maccabi and Red Star is closing in on a move — to Red Star
dek: Free agent Derrick Lukassen, once of Maccabi Tel Aviv, is reported close to a three-year deal with Red Star Belgrade — a club he knocked out of the Champions League himself last summer, and one that could yet meet Hapoel Beer Sheva in this year's qualifiers.

verificationSources.label: ONE — ידיח את הפועל ב"ש? לוקאסן מתקרב לכוכב האדום

body: It is one of those transfer stories that only football could produce: the centre-back who spent last August knocking Red Star Belgrade out of the Champions League is now, by all accounts, on the verge of signing for them.

Derrick Lukassen, the 31-year-old Ghana international, has been a free agent since his contract at Cypriot champions Pafos expired on July 1. According to Serbian outlets hotsport.rs and tportal.hr, picked up by ONE, Red Star have reached an agreement with him on a three-year deal with no transfer fee involved.

Lukassen's history with Red Star runs deeper than a passing rumour would suggest. Last August, still wearing Pafos colours, he was part of the side that eliminated the Serbian champions 3-2 on aggregate in the Champions League play-off round — a result that sent Pafos into their first-ever league-phase campaign and dropped Red Star down into the Europa League.

It was not his only scalp that summer. In the second qualifying round, Pafos had already knocked out Maccabi Tel Aviv, Lukassen's own former club, winning 2-1 on aggregate before going on to eliminate Dynamo Kyiv and then Red Star themselves.

Born in Amsterdam and a product of the AZ Alkmaar academy, Lukassen moved to PSV Eindhoven in a reported €5 million deal in 2017 before spells at Hertha Berlin, Anderlecht and two Turkish clubs, Kasımpaşa and Fatih Karagümrük. He joined Maccabi Tel Aviv before his switch to Pafos, where he became a key figure in the Cypriot club's historic European run.

Qualifying for Ghana through ancestry, Lukassen earned his senior international debut and went on to start at this summer's World Cup, scoring against Croatia in the group stage and featuring against Colombia and England as the Black Stars made their mark in the United States.

That Dutch passport carries a practical benefit for Red Star, too: as an EU national, Lukassen would not occupy one of the club's limited foreign-player slots in the Serbian Superliga, making him an unusually low-risk addition for a team also plotting a fresh European qualifying campaign.

Should the move go through, Lukassen would link up with Muhammad Abu Fani, the Israel international midfielder who signed a three-year contract at Red Star in June after moving from Ferencváros. Red Star's Israeli contingent has shifted this summer in the other direction too — goalkeeper Omri Glazer, who spent three seasons in Belgrade, has agreed to return to Maccabi Haifa.

The Israeli interest in this story does not end there. Red Star's Champions League qualifying draw has them lined up to face Northern Ireland's Larne in the second round, with the winner set to meet Hapoel Beer Sheva in the third qualifying round — provided the Israeli champions first get past Iceland's Vikingur Reykjavik in ties being played this week.

Should both Red Star and Hapoel Beer Sheva advance, and should Lukassen's transfer be finalised in time to be registered, the same player who eliminated Maccabi Tel Aviv from Europe less than a year ago could find himself lining up against another Israeli champion in the very next Champions League campaign.

Nothing has yet been confirmed by Red Star Belgrade or by Lukassen himself — the report so far rests on Serbian outlets, relayed by ONE — but the outline of the deal, a straightforward free transfer on a three-year contract, is being described in Belgrade as close to done.

title: Spain baffled as FIFA leaves Cubarsí and Laporte off World Cup Best XI shortlist
dek: Despite anchoring the tournament's meanest defence, the centre-back pair who started every Spain knockout game were missing from FIFA's Team of the Tournament nominees — with the full-backs picked instead.

verificationSources.label: ESPN — Rodri wins World Cup Golden Ball
CBS News — Spain wins 2026 World Cup

body: Spain is still basking in a second World Cup title, but a strange piece of FIFA paperwork has needled the celebrations back home: the ballot for the tournament's official Team of the Tournament left out the two centre-backs who marshalled the meanest defence at the 2026 finals.

ONE reports that when FIFA published its list of nominees for the World Cup 2026 Team of the Tournament, Pau Cubarsí and Aymeric Laporte — Spain's first-choice central defensive pairing through the knockout rounds — were nowhere on it.

It is a curious omission on the numbers alone. Spain conceded a single goal across the entire tournament, the best defensive record of any of the 48 teams, with Cubarsí and Laporte at the heart of it in every game that mattered.

The snub looks stranger still next to Cubarsí's other silverware from the summer: the 19-year-old Barcelona defender was named the tournament's Young Player of the Tournament, an award FIFA itself handed him for exactly the kind of composed, high-volume defending that somehow didn't earn him a place on the Best XI shortlist.

Goal.com's Saudi Arabia edition carried the same story, reporting that FIFA "sparked a wave of fierce criticism in Spain" by leaving the pair off the voting list, even as it nominated Spain's two full-backs, Marc Cucurella and Pedro Porro, for defensive slots instead.

Porro's attacking numbers — among the highest chance-creation figures of any full-back at the finals — and Cucurella's assist tally made their inclusion easy to defend. But Spanish pundits and fans, according to the reports, struggled to square attacking output outweighing a defence that shipped almost nothing all tournament.

Laporte's absence carries its own subplot. The 32-year-old, born and raised in France, qualified for Spain through residency after years at Athletic Bilbao and Manchester City, and has spent this World Cup as vice-captain of the back line — a late-career vindication now shadowed by the snub.

None of it changes what actually happened on the pitch. Spain beat Argentina 1-0 after extra time in the final at MetLife Stadium on July 19, with Ferran Torres settling it in the 105th minute to hand Luis de la Fuente's side the country's second World Cup, its first since 2010.

Rodri collected the Golden Ball as the tournament's outstanding player, Kylian Mbappé took the Golden Boot, and goalkeeper Unai Simón won the Golden Glove — a haul that underlines just how dominant this Spain side was, even before FIFA's own paperwork became the story.

title: Champions of Israel Fly Furthest: Beer Sheva Cover 5,315km to Reach Reykjavik Qualifier
dek: Hapoel Be'er Sheva have travelled further than any other side in Tuesday's Champions League qualifying round, ONE reports, adding logistics to the list of obstacles facing Ran Kozuk's team in Iceland.

verificationSources.label: UEFA.com — Víkingur R. vs H. Beer-Sheva match page
UEFA.com — H. Beer-Sheva vs Víkingur R. match page

body: Hapoel Be'er Sheva's Champions League campaign gets under way in Reykjavik on Tuesday night, and by the time the Israeli champions reach Víkingsvöllur they will already have logged more air miles than anyone else in this round of qualifying. According to ONE, the club's journey to Iceland totals 5,315 kilometres — the longest trip of any team playing in the second qualifying round this evening.

The first leg against Víkingur Reykjavík kicks off at 22:00 Israel time, with Beer Sheva facing the Icelandic champions on their artificial pitch in a city where midsummer conditions are about as far removed from a Negev summer as European football gets.

It is not simply a case of an away trip taking its toll. ONE notes that Beer Sheva, like several other Israeli clubs, still cannot host UEFA fixtures on home soil while European football's governing body withholds approval to stage matches in Israel over the security situation. Maccabi Tel Aviv, Beitar Jerusalem and Hapoel Tel Aviv all face the same arrangement, meaning even a nominal 'home' leg for Beer Sheva later this summer would likely be staged on neutral ground abroad rather than at Turner Stadium.

Coach Ran Kozuk has already flagged the cumulative toll of all this before a ball has been kicked, according to the report, pointing to the unfamiliar weather, the synthetic surface and the travel itself as factors his squad must absorb on top of the football.

Víkingur are no soft touch for a team carrying that kind of fatigue. The Reykjavik side eliminated Hungarian champions Győr in the previous qualifying round to reach this stage, and they arrive at this tie unbeaten and dominant domestically — leading the Icelandic top flight by eight points after 14 rounds this season, having lost none of their league matches.

For Beer Sheva, reigning Israeli champions, the reward for navigating both the travel and the opposition is a step closer to the group phase of Europe's premier club competition — and the financial windfall that comes with it. The return leg is scheduled for next week, with Beer Sheva hoping home advantage of a sort can help erase whatever the long flight to Iceland costs them on Tuesday.

title: LaLiga chief Tebas: Infantino 'must go, he's destroying football'
dek: Days after Spain's World Cup triumph, LaLiga president Javier Tebas tore into FIFA's leadership, calling in-match hydration breaks 'a farce' and arguing the Folarin Balogun red-card reversal nearly cost Gianni Infantino his job.

body: Javier Tebas has never been shy about picking fights with football's governing bodies, but this week the LaLiga president went further than usual: Gianni Infantino, he said flatly, "must go" because FIFA under his watch is "destroying football."

Tebas made the remarks in an interview with an Italian sports daily, days after Spain beat Argentina 1-0 in extra time to win the 2026 World Cup final in New Jersey, and he used the moment to lay out a lengthy charge sheet against FIFA's stewardship of the game.

"FIFA organises things for its own interests, not for football, and if they need a 27-minute break, they take it," Tebas said, taking aim specifically at the mid-half hydration breaks introduced for matches at this summer's tournament.

He dismissed the pauses as "a farce, an advertising break," pointing out that LaLiga only uses similar stoppages in genuine heat emergencies, whereas several World Cup venues — among them stadiums in Dallas, Los Angeles and Atlanta — had air conditioning. Infantino has defended the breaks throughout the tournament, insisting the heat across U.S. host cities made them necessary for player welfare.
Tebas reserved some of his sharpest words for what he called the "Balogun affair," the FIFA disciplinary saga that became one of the tournament's most contentious sideshows.

USMNT forward Folarin Balogun was sent off with a straight red card in the group stage against Bosnia and Herzegovina, triggering an automatic one-match ban for the last-16 tie against Belgium. President Donald Trump then phoned Infantino personally to ask for a review, saying publicly that he "didn't think it was a foul." FIFA responded by suspending the ban for a year-long probationary period, clearing Balogun to play. The United States lost the match anyway, 4-1, but the reversal drew accusations that FIFA had bent to political pressure on the eve of a knockout game.

Tebas argued the episode could have cost Infantino his job outright. "They were lucky Belgium eliminated the United States," he said, suggesting a deeper American run would have kept the Balogun ruling — and the call behind it — in the headlines through the rest of the tournament.

The LaLiga president also took aim at FIFA's push to expand the World Cup to 64 teams, arguing the plan would further squeeze a calendar already strained by domestic competitions that employ far more players, coaches and staff than international football does.

Yet Tebas conceded that removing Infantino is, in practice, close to impossible. He described FIFA's internal structure as "a system sick from its origin," in which national federations remain loyal to the incumbent and no credible rival is willing to run only to lose.

It is not a new fight. Tebas has clashed publicly with FIFA and UEFA for years over the international calendar and the concentration of power at the top of the game, and his comments this week add another chapter to a rivalry that has only sharpened in the days since Spain lifted the trophy.

title: Yarmakov out, Glazer in: Maccabi Haifa's rebuild starts in goal
dek: As Giorgi Yarmakov heads to Ukraine, veteran coach Slobodan Drapić says Haifa have not weakened between the posts — but he wants the wider rebuild built on patience and youth, not panic.

verificationSources.label: ONE — Yarmakov agrees Metalist Kharkiv move, €3.2m fee

body: Maccabi Haifa's summer has crystallised around a position that, on paper, ought to be a downgrade: the goalkeeper's gloves that carried Giorgi Yarmakov to Israel's goalkeeper-of-the-year honours last season are heading back to Ukraine, with Metalist Kharkiv agreeing a fee reported at around €3.2 million for the 24-year-old.

Yet Slobodan Drapić, the veteran Serbian-Israeli coach who spent years on Maccabi Haifa's bench, told ONE he does not see it that way. Haifa moved fast to bring back Omri Glazer, the Israel international goalkeeper, from Red Star Belgrade — and in Drapić's reading, that swap leaves the position stronger, not weaker.
"Excellent signing. An outstanding goalkeeper and a national team player. I think Maccabi Haifa gained, and did not weaken," Drapić said of the Glazer deal, according to the interview.

Glazer, 30, is no stranger to Sammy Ofer Stadium. He spent five seasons in Haifa's goal between 2016 and 2021, making 58 appearances, before leaving for Serbia, where he won three championships and three domestic cups with Red Star across three campaigns. His return gives Haifa a goalkeeper with continental pedigree and full senior caps for Israel — a rare commodity in a squad the club is now trying to rebuild.

Drapić's authority on the subject comes from history rather than punditry alone. He served as Maccabi Haifa's assistant coach under Ronny Levy in the mid-2000s, before going on to manage Maccabi Netanya, Hapoel Kfar Saba and Hapoel Haifa in his own right — giving him an insider's read on a club he knows from the inside of the dressing room.

His message to Haifa's hierarchy went beyond the goalkeeper debate. Drapić urged the club to resist the urge to fill every gap with a rushed marquee signing, arguing instead for a rebuild rooted in patience and in players coming through the club's own youth system rather than knee-jerk purchases in the transfer market.

The goalkeeper reshuffle is not the only piece of business Haifa have completed this summer. The club also announced the signing of Andrija Novakovich, an American-Serbian centre-forward, from Reggiana of Italy's Serie B. The 29-year-old, born in Wisconsin to Serbian parents and previously capped by the United States, arrives as a physical presence up front after a modest campaign in which Reggiana were relegated.

The turnover in personnel comes as Maccabi Haifa's football department also settles its leadership for the new campaign. Barak Bachar, who has already won three straight Israeli titles with Haifa once before and steered the club to a Champions League group-stage win over Juventus in 2022/23, signed on for a third stint as head coach, while club legend Lior Refaelov was appointed sporting director.

For Drapić, that stability at the top only sharpens the point about how the squad beneath it should be shaped. Losing a goalkeeper of Yarmakov's calibre — one good enough to draw a seven-figure European offer inside a year of arriving in Israel — would ordinarily read as an alarm bell. Bringing back an Israel international with a winning pedigree in his place, Drapić argues, turns that alarm into a genuine upgrade, and a platform the rest of the rebuild can be judged against.
What happens next in Haifa's transfer business will show whether the club heeds his advice on patience, or whether the goalkeeper swap proves the calm before a busier, more reactive summer.

title: Reuven Atar: Rafaelov must come down to the grass to help Bachar
dek: The Maccabi Haifa great says the club's new sporting director can't run the Bachar era from an office chair alone — he needs to be out on the training pitch too.

body: Reuven Atar knows Maccabi Haifa's dressing room better than most, and his verdict on the club's newly split command structure comes with a condition attached: it only works if Lior Rafaelov is prepared to leave the office and get his tracksuit dirty.

Speaking to the sports outlet ONE, the former Haifa midfielder said he expects Rafaelov, the club's incoming sporting director, to be hands-on with Barak Bachar's staff wherever he can help — including out on the training pitch — rather than treating the job as a purely administrative one.

The comment lands weeks after Haifa finally settled its management structure for 2026-27. Bachar, back for a third spell in the dugout, keeps his job as head coach, while Rafaelov — one of the most decorated attacking players in the club's recent history — moves into the newly created sporting director role, overseeing recruitment and the wider football operation.
Bachar's return itself came in October 2025, when he replaced Diego Flores in his third stint in charge of the club, having previously left the job before returning less than half a year later.

Atar has been tracking the Bachar-Rafaelov relationship since that reappointment. Back in October, he said Bachar's success would hinge on how well the pair worked together, urging both men to settle disagreements directly rather than trade messages through the press — a pointed reference to friction that had occasionally spilled into public view during Bachar's earlier spells at the club.

His latest comments push that argument further: it is not enough, in Atar's view, for Rafaelov to sign off on transfers and squad planning from a distance. A sporting director who built his reputation as a player through graft on the pitch, Atar argues, needs to bring that same visibility to preseason work if the new structure is to earn the dressing room's trust.

For Haifa, the stakes are straightforward. After a campaign that fell well short of expectations, the club has opted for a shared leadership model instead of concentrating power in one figure — and pundits like Atar are already framing the coming season as a joint test of whether Bachar and Rafaelov can make that division of labour work in practice, not just on an organisational chart.

body: NBA Summer League wrapped up in Las Vegas this week, and the box scores from Thomas & Mack Center have already rippled back to Israeli basketball circles. Two Americans who spent last season on Israeli Premier League rosters — Darin Green Jr. and Nathan Mensah — are once again being talked about as candidates for a step up to Europe's top competitions, a pattern Sport5 flagged in its own reporting on the post-Summer League market.

Green Jr. is the more eye-catching case. The Florida State product played for Hapoel Holon in the Israeli Premier League in the 2024-25 season before moving on to Serbia's Radnički Kragujevac, where in December he set a career high of 52 points — going 13 of 23 from three-point range — in a 111-102 win over OKK Beograd.

That form carried into Las Vegas. Signed for Summer League by the Dallas Mavericks, Green Jr. scored 18 points off the bench, with five assists, three rebounds and two steals, in a 96-88 win over Memphis. Two days later he matched that with another 18 points and five rebounds as Dallas beat Oklahoma City 97-87, then closed his week with 21 points on 6-of-13 shooting, including 6 of 12 from deep, against the Knicks.

None of that guarantees Green Jr. an NBA training-camp invite, let alone a roster spot — Summer League deals rarely convert directly into regular-season contracts. But performances like his are exactly what gets circulated among European sporting directors once Vegas empties out, and Hapoel Holon's old guard will recognise the type: a scorer the Israeli league helped season before he found his shooting rhythm elsewhere.

Mensah's route has been more circuitous. The Ghanaian-born centre, a product of San Diego State's college program, signed with Olympiacos in December 2024 as the Greek club sought injury cover in the middle of a EuroLeague season. His time in Piraeus was brief and light on minutes — two EuroLeague appearances and six Greek League games, in which he averaged 5.2 points and 4.0 rebounds.

Olympiacos released him that April, and within weeks Maccabi Tel Aviv had signed him for the rest of the 2024-25 season, pairing him with a returning Alex Tyus in the frontcourt. It made him one of a handful of players to wear both an Olympiacos and a Maccabi jersey inside a single EuroLeague campaign.

Maccabi, too, parted ways with Mensah once the season ended, and he resurfaced more recently in Turkey with ONVO Büyükçekmece of the Basketbol Süper Ligi. That makes him, once again, a free agent heading into a European club season — precisely the profile agents are shopping around the EuroLeague and EuroCup markets this month.

The churn isn't unique to players with Israeli-league stints. Cam Reddish, the 10th overall pick in the 2019 NBA draft, spent this past season with Lithuania's BC Siauliai before the two sides parted ways; he then played Summer League with the Orlando Magic, another data point in the same NBA-fringe-to-Europe-and-back cycle Sport5's reporting described as a genuine wave this summer.

For Israeli clubs, the subplot is a familiar one. Hapoel Holon and Maccabi Tel Aviv have long functioned as a proving ground and occasional relaunch pad for American players moving between the NBA's margins and Europe's bigger leagues — and Green Jr.'s Vegas week, in particular, is the kind of tape that Israeli front offices, not just EuroLeague ones, will have pulled up as well.

Nothing here is a signed deal. Both players are, as of this week, without a club for the coming season, and any move to a EuroLeague or EuroCup roster will only become official once rosters are finalised over the coming weeks. What is clear is that the Summer League performances have reopened the conversation — and that Israeli basketball, once again, sits somewhere along the route these players are taking.

title: Olise Denies Involvement With Secret Daughter as Child-Support Dispute Goes Public
dek: A German mother says the Bayern Munich and France winger has refused all contact with their toddler daughter and stopped paying support; his lawyers insist he has offered help from the start.

verificationSources.label: African Football — paternity and child support claims report

body: Michael Olise's stock has rarely been higher — Bayern Munich's back-to-back Player of the Season, a standout of France's World Cup summer, and the subject of transfer talk running into nine figures. Now he is facing a far less flattering headline: a German woman says he has cut off contact with their 20-month-old daughter and stopped paying to support her.

Fatima Zaunbrecher, 34, from Düsseldorf, says she and Olise carried on a long-distance relationship for roughly two years after meeting on Instagram in 2022, when he was still playing for Crystal Palace in the Premier League. By her account, the relationship had already ended by the time she discovered she was pregnant.

Their daughter, whom Zaunbrecher named Aaliyah Noor, is now about 20 months old. She says a paternity test carried out in Munich confirmed Olise as the father and that he legally acknowledged it — but that he has never once visited the child.
"It hurts me to see his cruelty towards his child," Zaunbrecher said, adding that all contact with Olise now runs through his lawyers, who she says advised him against seeing the girl at all.

Money sits at the center of the dispute as well. Zaunbrecher describes the financial offers made on Olise's behalf as inadequate, at one point calling a proposal "ridiculously low." Reported figures vary — an early proposal put in the low hundreds of euros a month, later said to have risen to roughly €2,000 — sums she contrasts with a player reportedly earning close to €14 million a year at Bayern.

Olise's legal representatives have firmly rejected her account. In response to the allegations, they said the player offered assistance "from the outset" and remains open to an amicable settlement, insisting he never refused to support the child financially. They say Zaunbrecher separately pursued a claim of around €60,000 a month through the French courts that was not upheld, and that Olise's own offer exceeds the maximum child-support level allowed under German law.

Neither side has made court filings, the paternity report or a written settlement offer public, so for now the dispute rests on competing accounts — Zaunbrecher's version of events against the firm denial issued by Olise's lawyers.

Olise, 24, was born in London to a Nigerian father and a French-Algerian mother and chose to represent France at international level. He joined Bayern from Crystal Palace in 2024 in a deal worth close to £50 million and has since been voted the club's Player of the Season in consecutive campaigns, alongside a prominent run for France at this summer's World Cup.

The story has broken at an awkward moment for Bayern as well: Real Madrid have been repeatedly linked with a club-record move for Olise, with reported fees north of €200 million, even as the German champions insist he is not for sale and Real Madrid have publicly denied any contact with the player or his camp.

For a player enjoying the best form of his career, the personal fallout is a reminder that off-field scrutiny tends to grow in direct proportion to on-field success — and that, without documents to settle it, this dispute is likely to keep running in parallel with his transfer saga.

title: Spain's Crown, Mbappé's Record and Football's American Makeover
dek: Two days after Ferran Torres settled the final in extra time, the tournament's real legacy is coming into focus — a dominant Spain, a rewritten scoring record for Kylian Mbappé, and a sport visibly bending toward American commercial rhythms.

body: Two days on from Ferran Torres's extra-time strike at MetLife Stadium, the dust is settling on the 2026 World Cup — and the conversation has moved from who lifted the trophy to what the tournament actually revealed about the state of the men's game.

Spain beat Argentina 1-0 in Sunday's final, with Torres converting a Nico Williams assist in the 106th minute after Argentina had played the closing stages of normal time and all of extra time a man down, following Enzo Fernández's second yellow card in second-half stoppage time. Lionel Messi, in what may be his final World Cup appearance, did not score.

It was Spain's second world title, sixteen years after their breakthrough triumph in 2010, and it came with a personal milestone for head coach Luis de la Fuente: at 65, he became the oldest coach to win a World Cup. His side arrived in North America as reigning European champions too, having beaten England 2-1 in the Euro 2024 final in Berlin — with, fittingly, Mikel Oyarzabal scoring the winner both then and again from the penalty spot in this tournament's semifinal.

That semifinal, a 2-0 win over France on July 14 in Arlington, Texas, was Spain's statement result. Oyarzabal opened the scoring from the spot after Lucas Digne fouled teenager Lamine Yamal, and France's vaunted attack did not manage a shot on target until well past the hour mark. Kylian Mbappé's best chance, a 67th-minute effort that deflected off Marc Cucurella, drifted just wide.

That was the one match all tournament in which Mbappé failed to score. He still finished with the Golden Boot — 10 goals, matching Gerd Müller's single-tournament haul from 1970 — and became the first player in World Cup history to win the award in consecutive editions, adding this one to his 2022 tally. His 22 career World Cup goals now put him one clear of Messi's 21, the new all-time record.

The tournament was less kind to two of the sport's most decorated club coaches, hired specifically to end their federations' trophy droughts. Carlo Ancelotti's Brazil were eliminated in the round of 16 by Norway, 2-1, undone by a late Erling Haaland double — Brazil's earliest World Cup exit since a group-stage elimination in 1966. The Brazilian federation chose to keep him on regardless, with Ancelotti calling it "the start of a new cycle" rather than an ending.

Thomas Tuchel's England fared considerably better, beating that same Norway side in the quarterfinals before losing to Argentina in the semifinal — the best run by any team with a foreign-born coach at this World Cup, and the only foreign-coached side to reach the last four. Even so, the pattern that has held since the first World Cup in 1930 continued: no team led by a coach who is not one of its own nationals has ever won the tournament.

The other storyline to follow Spain and Mbappé out of this tournament was FIFA's introduction of mandatory three-minute hydration breaks in each half — ostensibly a player-safety measure for matches played in North American summer heat, but ones broadcasters were permitted to fill with advertising. Britain's press coverage was blunt about what that produced: outlets described the breaks as nudging football toward a four-quarter structure more familiar from basketball or American football than from the sport's traditional 45-minute halves.

Tuchel himself said the breaks altered a match's identity and broke its momentum; Uruguay coach Marcelo Bielsa dismissed them as adding nothing to the game. The commercial logic was straightforward regardless of the football complaints — analysts estimated the breaks generated more than $250 million in US advertising alone, and close to $1 billion worldwide across the tournament's 104 matches.

Layered on top of that was the now-familiar complaint about the expanded 48-team format itself: a bloated group stage that produced more lopsided fixtures and, critics argued, diluted the tension that used to define the tournament's opening weeks. It is a debate that has followed the format since FIFA first approved it, and this World Cup did little to settle it either way.

What is settled, for now, is the hierarchy at the top of the men's game. Spain leave North America with a European and a world title within two years of each other, a squad built around Yamal, Williams and Oyarzabal that looks set to stay together, and a coach who has quietly become one of the most successful in the sport's history. The arguments over how the World Cup is packaged and sold will run into the next cycle; who actually wins it, for now, is not much in doubt.
facts: Spain beat Argentina 1-0 in the 2026 World Cup final on July 19 at MetLife Stadium, New Jersey, with Ferran Torres scoring in the 106th minute of extra time.
It was Spain's second World Cup title, 16 years after 2010; coach Luis de la Fuente, 65, became the oldest coach to win a World Cup.
Spain beat France 2-0 in the semifinal on July 14 in Arlington, Texas, with Mikel Oyarzabal converting a penalty after Lucas Digne fouled Lamine Yamal.

Kylian Mbappé won the Golden Boot with 10 goals, becoming the first player to win it in consecutive World Cups (2022 and 2026); the Spain semifinal was his only scoreless match of the tournament, and his 22 career World Cup goals now lead Lionel Messi's 21.

Carlo Ancelotti's Brazil were eliminated in the round of 16 by Norway (2-1, Erling Haaland scoring twice) — Brazil's earliest World Cup exit since 1966; Thomas Tuchel's England lost to Argentina in the semifinal, the deepest run by any foreign-coached team.

FIFA's new three-minute per-half hydration breaks doubled as advertising windows, drawing criticism in the British press as an 'Americanization' of football and reportedly generating close to $1 billion in worldwide ad revenue.
Spain also won Euro 2024, beating England 2-1 in the final, meaning they hold both the European and World titles simultaneously.

title: Haifa council says Hapoel Haifa owes it 190,000 shekels, threatens training base
dek: City officials say they won't let this one slide, warning the club could lose its Beit Neigler training ground days before the Haifa derby — the latest strain on a club already reeling from a separate 1.485 million shekel court judgment.

body: Haifa's municipality has told Hapoel Haifa it owes the city 190,000 shekels and, this time, has no intention of letting the debt slide, according to a report by the Israeli sports site One.

The message from City Hall reportedly carries a concrete threat attached to it: if the club doesn't settle up, it risks losing the use of Beit Neigler, the training complex near Kiryat Haim Stadium where Hapoel Haifa's senior squad and youth sides currently prepare.
The timing bites. The claim lands just days before Hapoel Haifa travel across town for a Haifa derby against Maccabi Haifa at Sammy Ofer Stadium, a Toto Cup fixture set for Saturday, July 25.

It is also not the club's only financial headache this summer. On June 3, the Haifa District Court ruled in a long-running dispute between Hapoel Haifa and the Histadrut, the labor federation, ordering the club to pay 1.485 million shekels plus VAT for years of use of the Kiryat Haim facility — with the court also fixing monthly rent going forward at 30,000 shekels and giving the club 30 days to pay.
That case centered on a dispute between club owner Yoav Katz and the Histadrut, with the ruling noted at the time as a heavy blow given the club has barely used the facility in recent years.

Squad-building has proceeded modestly against that backdrop. One's reporting describes a roster refreshed mainly with players drawn from the lower divisions alongside some already-established top-flight names, rather than a marquee outlay, with contract talks over the continued participation of some existing squad members still unresolved heading into the new season.

The 190,000-shekel municipal figure has so far been reported only by One, and this desk could not independently corroborate that specific sum with a second named outlet before publication — a gap worth flagging given how quickly financial disputes involving Israeli clubs and local authorities tend to get contested or revised.

What is independently documented is the club's broader financial squeeze: the Histadrut judgment, the loss of significant municipal support in recent budget cycles, and now a fresh dispute over training-ground access, all arriving in the same close season as Hapoel Haifa try to build a squad capable of competing in the derby and beyond.

Separately, the Haifa District Court ruled on June 3, 2026 that Hapoel Haifa must pay the Histadrut 1.485 million shekels plus VAT for years of use of the Kiryat Haim facility, and set monthly rent at 30,000 shekels going forward.

title: Israeli champions Hapoel Be'er Sheva open Champions League bid against unbeaten Víkingur
dek: The newly crowned Israeli title-holders travel to Reykjavik on Tuesday night to face an Icelandic side unbeaten in 23 matches, with Kings Kangwa carrying much of the attacking weight.

body: Hapoel Be'er Sheva begin their Champions League campaign on Tuesday night, travelling to Reykjavik for the first leg of a second qualifying round tie against Víkingur, the runaway leaders of the Icelandic top flight. Kickoff is set for 22:00 Israel time.

The trip caps a whirlwind close to Be'er Sheva's season. They lifted their sixth Israeli championship in May, snatching the title from Maccabi Tel Aviv with a 4-2 win over their rivals in the penultimate round of the 2025-26 Ligat Ha'Al.

The build-up to Europe has been bumpier than the celebrations suggested. Maccabi Tel Aviv beat Be'er Sheva 3-1 in last week's Super Cup, the champions' first competitive outing since sealing the title and a reminder of how close the gap remains between Israel's top two clubs.

Much of Be'er Sheva's attacking hope in Reykjavik rests on Kings Kangwa. The Zambian international, who arrived from Red Star Belgrade in 2024, was named Israeli Footballer of the Year for 2025-26 after scoring 12 league goals and driving the title run — form the club will need again if they are to survive Europe's toughest qualifying ladder.

Víkingur are no soft draw. Founded in 1908, the Reykjavik club won their eighth Icelandic championship last season and arrive at Tuesday's tie unbeaten in 23 matches across all competitions, a run stretching back to a 4-2 defeat to Stjarnan Garðabær last August. They currently lead this season's Icelandic top flight by eight points, having won 13 of their opening 14 league games.
They are also fresh from knocking out a bigger name than themselves. Víkingur eliminated Hungarian champions Győr 3-2 on aggregate in the first qualifying round to reach this stage.

There is an added wrinkle to the tie. According to Israeli reports, Be'er Sheva's own "home" second leg will not be played in Israel at all — it is set to be staged at Győr's stadium in Hungary instead, continuing a pattern in which Israeli clubs have had to host European fixtures abroad in recent seasons.

The stakes are real. Be'er Sheva's best run in the competition remains 2017-18, when they reached the playoff round before a 5-2 aggregate defeat to Maribor ended the bid. Beat Víkingur over the two legs and they advance to the third qualifying round, still two rounds from a first-ever group-stage appearance; lose, and their European campaign continues instead in the Europa League qualifying rounds.

body: Hapoel Be'er Sheva have all but agreed to sell their Zambian playmaker Kings Kangwa to AEK Athens — but the Greek champions are threatening to walk away from the table over what happens on a training pitch in Reykjavík tonight, not in a boardroom.

Kangwa is due to line up for Be'er Sheva this evening against Víkingur Reykjavík in the first leg of their UEFA Champions League second qualifying-round tie. AEK's concern is simple and technical: under UEFA rules, a player who appears for one club in a European competition cannot switch allegiance and be registered for a second club in the same competition in the same season.

If Kangwa takes the field tonight, he would be cup-tied for AEK's own continental campaign this season, wiping out much of the value AEK sees in signing him now rather than in the autumn. Sport5 reported that AEK's camp has made that risk explicit to the Israeli side, warning the deal could unravel entirely if he plays.

Be'er Sheva's response, according to the report, is to go ahead and start him regardless — with the club reportedly prepared to counter that Víkingur themselves could still be an obstacle to AEK's own European ambitions, giving Be'er Sheva leverage of its own in the negotiation rather than a reason to blink first.

The transfer fee has not been pinned to an exact figure across the reporting on both sides, but Israeli outlets have consistently placed it in the €3.5 million to €4 million range — a substantial return on a player Be'er Sheva signed for well under €1 million.

Kangwa, a 27-year-old central midfielder capped by Zambia, joined Be'er Sheva from Red Star Belgrade in the summer of 2024 on a contract that ran to June 2028, according to Transfermarkt's records. He was not a squad afterthought: he became the team's creative hub almost immediately.

His first season in Israel brought 14 goals and eight assists. In 2025-26 he added a further 12 goals and nine assists in 33 league appearances, numbers that underpinned Be'er Sheva's run to the Israeli Premier League title and earned him the league's Footballer of the Year award.

That title is precisely why tonight's fixture carries the stakes it does — Be'er Sheva enter the Champions League picture as Israeli champions, only weeks after opening their new season with a 3-1 Super Cup defeat to Maccabi Tel Aviv.

Víkingur Reykjavík arrive at this qualifying tie in ominous form, unbeaten in 23 matches across all competitions stretching back to last August. A result either way tonight will shape the context in which Kangwa's future is finally settled — the second leg, and the transfer deadline pressure that comes with it, still to follow.

For now, the deal sits in an unusual limbo: personal terms and a fee broadly agreed, but the final signature effectively hostage to a team-sheet decision Be'er Sheva's coaching staff have to make before kickoff this evening.

title: Beer Sheva's leading scorer C.J. Elleby signs with Hapoel HaEmek
dek: The 26-year-old guard, who averaged 18.1 points a game last season, turned down interest from Hapoel Jerusalem to become the fourth import in coach Sharon Avrahami's rebuilt roster.

body: Hapoel HaEmek has landed one of the more eye-catching guards on this summer's Ligat HaAl market, confirming a deal with C.J. Elleby after the American reportedly weighed a rival offer from Hapoel Jerusalem before committing to the Jezreel Valley club.

Elleby, 26, was the standout of last season's Hapoel Beer Sheva/Dimona side, leading the team in scoring at 18.1 points per game to go with 6.9 rebounds and 3.9 assists — numbers that put him among the league's most productive combo guards.

His path to Israel ran through the NBA. Portland picked him 46th overall in the 2020 draft out of Washington State, where he had been the Cougars' first draftee since Klay Thompson in 2011. After time on Portland's roster and in the G League, he moved to Europe, playing in Turkey's top flight for MKE Ankaragücü before joining Beer Sheva/Dimona last season.

At 1.98 metres and comfortable both creating shots and finishing at the rim, Elleby gives Hapoel HaEmek a scoring option who has already proven himself at the top of the Israeli table rather than as an unknown import.

The club he is joining carries a new name but familiar roots. Known for years as Hapoel Gilboa Galil, it rebranded as Hapoel HaEmek this summer after folding in Hapoel Afula's senior operation, and continues to represent the Gilboa region, the Jezreel Valley and Afula in the Ligat HaAl.

Elleby is the fourth import coach Sharon Avrahami has brought in for the coming season, joining Nigerian forward Christian Mekwelle, Malik Hall — arriving after a season with Hapoel Kiryat Ata — and Cameron Henry, who is staying on from last year's squad.

On the domestic side, Hapoel HaEmek has added guard JJ Kaplan from Maccabi Rishon LeZion while holding on to the core of last season's group: captain Roi Natia, Niv Meshgev, Lucas Goldenberg and Gil Noyovitz all remain.

With Elleby's arrival, the club has effectively finished restocking its foreign quota well before the Ligat HaAl season resumes, giving Avrahami a settled group to build around after the rebrand and the roster turnover that came with it.

title: Southern dream: Be'er Sheva chase a first Champions League breakthrough in Reykjavík
dek: Israel's champions face Víkingur Reykjavík in the second qualifying round with an injury-hit squad, a Super Cup defeat behind them and, as ever, no home advantage.

body: Tonight in Reykjavík, Hapoel Be'er Sheva will try to do something the club has never managed: reach the group phase of the Champions League. Kickoff against Víkingur Reykjavík is set for 22:00 Israel time (19:00 UTC), the first leg of a second qualifying round tie that will decide whether Israel's champions move a step closer to Europe's top table or are diverted, as so often before, toward the Europa League instead.

Be'er Sheva travel as reigning champions of Israel, having beaten Maccabi Tel Aviv 4-2 in May to clinch the 2025-26 Ligat Ha'al title under manager Ran Kojok. The club rewarded him afterwards with a new two-year contract, with reported bonuses tied to how far the team goes in Europe this summer.

That title put them in the Champions Path of this year's qualifiers, and it is not the first time Be'er Sheva have come close without completing the job. Their high-water mark remains 2016-17, when Barak Bakhar's side eliminated Sheriff Tiraspol and then Olympiacos before losing the play-off round 5-4 on aggregate to Celtic - a 2-0 win at home wiped out by a 5-2 defeat at Celtic Park that kept them out of the Champions League proper. No campaign since, including this one, has got them further.

Standing in the way now are Víkingur Reykjavík, Iceland's champions, who arrive unbeaten in 23 matches across all competitions - 19 wins and four draws - since a 4-2 defeat to Stjarnan Garðabær last August. They are not easybeats either: they eliminated Hungary's ETO Győr 3-2 on aggregate in the first qualifying round to reach this stage.

Be'er Sheva's build-up has been bumpy. They opened the season by losing the Israeli Super Cup 3-1 to Maccabi Tel Aviv on July 16, with Sayed Abu Farchi scoring twice and Dor Peretz adding a third; Be'er Sheva's only reply came from a backheeled finish by midfielder Kings Kangwa.

Kangwa's own future adds to the uncertainty. The Zambian international was voted the Israeli league's Footballer of the Year for 2025-26 after scoring 12 goals, and Greek club AEK Athens have reportedly offered around €4 million for a player who joined from Red Star Belgrade only two years ago. Nothing is signed yet, and Be'er Sheva will need him sharp in Reykjavík regardless of how the transfer saga ends.

There is also, by now, a familiar complication that has nothing to do with form. UEFA's ban on staging matches inside Israel, imposed in October 2023 and reconfirmed as recently as this February, remains in force, so the return leg on July 28 will again be played away from Turner Stadium and Israeli soil, as with every European tie Israeli clubs have played since.

A defeat would not end Be'er Sheva's European season outright - as with previous Champions Path losers, elimination sends the team into the Europa League play-off round - but that has always been the consolation, not the point, on nights like this.

For a club whose supporters have waited a decade to turn near-misses in Europe into something more, kickoff in Reykjavík is where that particular dream either survives a little longer or is deferred again.

title: Haziza agrees terms to join Maccabi Netanya, ending seven years at Haifa
dek: The Israel international winger has verbally sealed a two-year deal with new head coach Roni Levy, though the formal signing awaits the end of the Tisha B'Av fast.
body: Dolev Haziza is heading to Maccabi Netanya. The Ligat Ha'al winger has agreed personal terms on a two-year contract that will end his seven-year run at Maccabi Haifa, according to a report from ONE on Tuesday, corroborated by Israel Hayom, Sport5 and Walla Sport.

Haifa placed the 30-year-old captain, whose existing contract still had a year to run, on its list of players cleared for departure this summer. That opened the door for Netanya's new head coach, Roni Levy, to make his move.

Israel Hayom reported that it was a single phone call from Levy - who wants Haziza to lead his forward line - that tipped the balance, after the winger had wavered for weeks over whether to try his luck abroad instead of staying in Israel.

Family considerations, including young children, together with his age, were understood to have weighed on his decision to remain in the Israeli league rather than search for a move overseas, per Sport5's reporting.

The formal unveiling has not yet happened. Under Jewish custom, no signing ceremony or official club announcement takes place before the Tisha B'Av fast concludes, so Netanya are working through the last details with a presentation expected once the fast ends this week.

Small gaps over salary were reportedly narrowing between Haziza's representatives and the Netanya hierarchy, with both sides hopeful of closing them within days so the move can be completed and announced.

For Haifa, it marks the end of an era. Haziza joined the club in 2019 and rose to become its captain, lifting three Ligat Ha'al championships - in 2020/21, 2021/22 and 2022/23 - after earlier winning two State Cups with Bnei Yehuda Tel Aviv.

He remains part of the national team picture as well, with 18 caps for Israel since his debut against Poland in a Euro 2020 qualifier in November 2019. Haziza also holds French citizenship through family ties.
For Levy, who took over at Netanya on an 18-month contract, landing an experienced, title-winning attacker gives his rebuilding project immediate substance heading into the new Ligat Ha'al season.

title: Despite the Small Hours, Israel's Toto Says It Had Its Biggest-Ever World Cup
dek: With many matches kicking off in the middle of the night in Israel, the state gambling monopoly says punters wagered more than ever anyway — topped by a record single-day haul on final day.

verificationSources.label: Hebrew Wikipedia — Toto / Council for the Regulation of Sports Betting
FIFA — Spain v Argentina final match report
Sport5 — Toto's preparations for the 2026 World Cup
Ice.co.il — Toto's World Cup prize plans
CBS Sports — 2026 World Cup bracket and semi-final results

body: Kickoff for some of this World Cup's biggest matches fell in the small hours of the Israeli morning, with the tournament staged across the United States, Canada and Mexico and a seven-to-eight-hour time gap back home. On paper, that should have hurt betting turnover. Instead, Israel's state gambling monopoly says it just had the best World Cup in its history.

The Council for the Regulation of Sports Betting — known throughout Israel simply as Toto — says revenue for the tournament period reached roughly 700 million shekels, according to figures it released and that were reported by the Israeli sports site One. That would mark an increase of about 18% on the roughly 590 million shekels wagered during the 2022 Qatar World Cup, though the new total has not yet been corroborated by a second independent outlet.

Of that sum, betting tied directly to World Cup matches is said to have brought in around 450 million shekels, a 36% jump on the previous tournament. More than 70% of all revenue was returned to the public as prizes, the same model Toto has operated under since 2019, when its profits stopped funding sports development in Israel and began flowing straight into the state treasury.

The figures, if they hold up, would exceed even Toto's own pre-tournament expectations, which were themselves record-setting: a forecast of 623 million shekels for the World Cup period, split between 406 million shekels at physical betting stations and 217 million shekels online. That projection reflected a tournament expanded for the first time to 48 teams and 104 matches spread over 39 days, well beyond the 64 matches played over 29 days in Qatar four years earlier.

Sunday's final between Spain and Argentina, settled 1-0 in extra time by a Ferran Torres strike, was reportedly the single biggest betting draw of the tournament: 32.65 million shekels wagered on that match alone, part of what Toto describes as a record 34.4 million shekels taken in across all its coupons on final day — the highest single-day figure in the organization's history.

The semi-finals were not far behind on Toto's own numbers: 18.9 million shekels on Spain's win over France, and 18.7 million shekels on Argentina's late comeback past England, with the France-Morocco quarter-final drawing 13.2 million shekels.

Toto also points to a shift toward digital betting. It puts registered users on its website at 106,000 during the tournament, up from 94,000 in 2022, with 40,000 online submissions logged on final day alone, against 30,000 four years earlier. Online betting is said to have grown to 38% of total revenue, up from 30% at the last World Cup.

Toto chairman Shabtai Tzur credited staff for the results, pointing to a period of intensive work that delivered record income for the treasury, while chief executive Meir Bardogo framed the numbers as proof the organization can hold its ground against illegal betting operators and newer commercial rivals without loosening its responsible-gambling rules.

Whatever the precise final tally, the broader pattern is not really in question: every World Cup under Toto's expanded, tech-heavier setup has out-earned the one before it, awkward kickoff times included. Late nights or not, Israelis kept filling out their coupons — and this time, as every time since 2019, it is the state treasury that banks the difference, not local football.

title: Without Messi, Argentina comes home to a hero's welcome after World Cup heartbreak
dek: Thousands braved cold and rain along the Ricchieri highway to greet Lionel Scaloni's squad a day after Spain's extra-time win in the final — while Messi stayed away from the homecoming.
body: There was no trophy in the hold and no Lionel Messi on the tarmac, but that did not stop Buenos Aires from turning out to welcome its team home.

A day earlier, Argentina had lost the World Cup final 1-0 to Spain, beaten by a Ferran Torres strike deep into extra time after a goalless 90 minutes in which they failed to register a single shot on target. It denied Lionel Scaloni's side the chance to defend the title they won in Qatar in 2022, and left Spain celebrating their first world championship since 2010.

The squad's charter touched down at Ezeiza International Airport on Monday evening, and despite the disappointment of the final, thousands of supporters lined the closed-off Ricchieri highway leading from the airport toward the Argentine Football Association's training complex, waving sky-blue-and-white flags in the cold and rain.
Players made the short journey by open-top bus rather than the full victory parade laid on after 2022, waving back to fans who had waited for hours to see them, win or lose.

Among the crowd, the mood was one of gratitude rather than grief. One fan said she wanted to thank the team's veteran captain for "all the years he made us happy" and urged him not to walk away from the national team; another said simply that the squad had "united us all" and deserved thanks for that alone.

Messi was not among those who made the trip. The Argentine federation said only that some squad members would not be on the returning flight, and local broadcasters showed no sign of him coming down the aircraft steps. His whereabouts and his plans for international football beyond this tournament remain unclear.

For Scaloni, the reception closes an extraordinary run: the same coach who lifted the trophy in Qatar four years ago now becomes one of a small group of managers to have finished both champion and runner-up at a World Cup.

Fans pointed to the road that got them here as much as the final itself — most of all a stirring semi-final win over England, a result that carried extra emotional weight given the two countries' long-standing dispute over the Falkland Islands.

Not every scene on Monday night was as warm. Hours after the airport reception, thousands gathered around the Obelisco in central Buenos Aires for informal celebrations that turned violent when a group breached barriers around the monument. Police responded with tear gas and a water cannon, and at least a dozen people were detained as officers and bystanders were hurt in the chaos.

For a squad that arrived home with silver rather than gold, it was a reminder of how much the run still meant to a fanbase that turned out anyway — cold, wet and without their captain, but not ready to let the team walk home alone.

title: Butterflies and a 12-year wait: Hapoel Tel Aviv lands in Hungary for Europe's return
dek: The Reds flew out Tuesday to Miskolc, where Thursday's Conference League qualifier against Ludogorets Razgrad will be played as a 'home' fixture in front of an expected 5,000 travelling fans.

body: Hapoel Tel Aviv's squad boarded a flight to Hungary on Tuesday morning, the first physical step in a return to European football that the club has waited twelve years for. Thursday's opponent in Miskolc is Ludogorets Razgrad of Bulgaria, in the first leg of the Conference League's second qualifying round.

The tie is technically a home game for Hapoel, but it will not be played anywhere near Bloomfield Stadium. UEFA competition matches involving Israeli clubs are currently being staked out at neutral venues abroad, and Hapoel settled on the DVTK Stadium in Miskolc, roughly an hour and forty minutes from Budapest, as its adopted ground for the campaign.

The stadium itself is a modern 2018-built arena seating around 14,600, home to Hungarian second-tier side Diósgyőri VTK. It is an unglamorous stand-in for a club used to European nights in Jaffa, but it is the venue that will decide whether Hapoel's continental return starts with a lead or a deficit heading into next Thursday's second leg in Bulgaria.

Twelve years is a long gap by any measure. Hapoel Tel Aviv's last European fixture came in Europa League qualifying in the summer of 2014; since then the club has watched the tournament from the outside while rivals like Maccabi Tel Aviv and Maccabi Haifa took turns representing Israeli football abroad. Getting back required finishing last season strongly enough to qualify, and the draw against Ludogorets was not the kind teams hope for at this stage — the Bulgarian champions are a regular continental fixture themselves.

Squad news travelling with the party is thin on transfer activity and heavier on fitness. Winger Roy Kurin and goalkeeper Dor Benyamini are both missing through injury, leaving head coach Elyaniv Barda without a couple of options he might otherwise have leaned on for a first continental test in over a decade.

The mood among the players who did make the trip, relayed through the club's own channels to one.co.il, was described in blunt, human terms rather than the usual pre-match boilerplate: excitement mixed with nerves, players openly admitting to "butterflies in the stomach" before a fixture of this size. The accompanying message was one of focus — a recognition that continental football punishes the kind of lapses that pass unnoticed in the domestic league.

That domestic form, at least, is with them. Hapoel go into the Ludogorets tie fresh off eliminating Beitar Jerusalem from the Toto Cup, needing a penalty shootout to get there after the sides were level 2-2 at full time. It was not the cleanest way to open the season, but it was a win, and Barda is expected to make few changes to the group that saw it through.

Fan interest has been considerable. More than 3,500 tickets had already been sold in the build-up to the trip, with the club anticipating a travelling contingent north of 5,000 supporters descending on Miskolc for Thursday's kick-off — a striking number for a match being played roughly 2,500 kilometres from home, and a measure of how much the club's return to Europe means to its fan base after over a decade away.

Should Hapoel get a result in Hungary, the tie will be settled a week later in Bulgaria, where Ludogorets have long been one of the continent's most difficult away trips for Israeli clubs. For now, though, the story is simpler: a squad short on recent European experience, landing in a country that isn't actually their opponent's, trying to make an adopted stadium feel enough like home to survive the first leg.

title: Kangwa set to start as champions Beer Sheva open Champions League bid in Reykjavik
dek: Israeli champions face Iceland's in-form Vikingur for the first time ever on Tuesday night, with Kings Kangwa's reported move to AEK Athens parked until the tie is settled.

verificationSources.label: Sports Rabbi on Beer Sheva's 2025-26 title

body: Hapoel Beer Sheva open their Champions League campaign on Tuesday night with a trip few in Israeli football would have picked out on a map a year ago: Reykjavik, and a first-ever meeting with Icelandic champions Vikingur, kicking off at 22:00 Israel time in the second qualifying round.

The Israeli champions arrive with more questions than form. They are winless in five of their last six matches and go into the tie fresh off a 3-1 Super Cup defeat to Maccabi Tel Aviv, a game in which Kings Kangwa's equaliser was answered by two second-half goals from the champions of the Israeli cup competition.

Vikingur, by contrast, have barely lost a step at home. The Reykjavik side are unbeaten in 23 consecutive matches at their own ground since August 2025 - 19 wins and four draws - and reached this round by edging Hungary's Győr 3-2 on aggregate, sealed by a stoppage-time winner in the first leg.

The dominant storyline heading into the match, though, is Kangwa's future rather than his form. The Zambian midfielder, named Israeli Footballer of the Year after driving Beer Sheva to the 2025-26 league title, is reported to be closing in on a move to AEK Athens, with the Greek club said to have tabled an offer in the region of four million euros.

Kangwa is under contract in Beersheba until June 2028, and the club has made clear the transfer talk will not be allowed to derail preparations for Europe. "We're dealing only with Vikingur," the club said, as quoted by the Hebrew-language outlet One. "The goal is to get past this hurdle, then we'll look ahead."

That stance is expected to translate into team selection: despite the swirling speculation, Kangwa is set to start in midfield for Beer Sheva in Reykjavik, with the club treating the qualifier - not the negotiating table - as the priority for the next 48 hours.

Coach Ran Kozuch kept his final training session before the trip deliberately guarded, running drills and small-sided games rather than a full tactical rehearsal, aware that Icelandic scouts were reportedly watching. Beer Sheva's players also had to adjust to Vikingur's synthetic pitch and the cooler Reykjavik conditions in the build-up.

A win, or even a narrow defeat, would leave Beer Sheva firmly in the tie ahead of next week's return leg at home, where they would fancy their chances of advancing to the next qualifying round. Lose heavily in Iceland, though, and an already stuttering pre-season would take on a far more troubling shape just as the club tries to keep hold of its best player.

dek: Mid-way through a summer-long public pitch to lure LeBron James to Golden State, Green told a fan on Threads he'd happily hand over the offense and reinvent himself as a corner three-point specialist — reviving a running joke about PJ Tucker's shooting he first made back in 2020.

body: Draymond Green has spent this summer publicly courting LeBron James to Golden State, and on Sunday he took the pitch to a new, self-mocking place: he offered to disappear into the corner and let someone else run the show.

A fan asked Green on Threads who would actually run the Warriors' offense if James signed — Green himself, Stephen Curry, or James. Green's reply: "Bron. I'd become PJ Tucker. Greatest corner 3pt shooter ever."

The Tucker line is a running bit for Green. PJ Tucker built his NBA reputation less on scoring than on spacing the floor and guarding bigger forwards, and by Second Spectrum's count he made 704 corner three-pointers over a 12-season span, more than any other player in that stretch, with most of the damage done during his prime years in Houston. His career three-point mark sits at 36.6 percent, 38.4 percent from the corner specifically.

Green first made the comparison in September 2020, after a playoff series against Tucker's Rockets, calling him "perhaps the best three-point shooter in NBA history." NBC Sports Bay Area dug into that claim at the time and found the numbers didn't really back it up — which hasn't stopped Green from bringing it back out five years later as his own hypothetical role.

Fans and other outlets weren't exactly buying the vision of Green, a career 31 percent three-point shooter built primarily around defense and playmaking, morphing into a corner specialist. The joke spread quickly across social media, with plenty of ribbing rather than agreement.

It lands, though, against a very real backdrop. LeBron James has told the Lakers he intends to leave the franchise this offseason and is working through free agency, with the Warriors, Cavaliers, Heat and 76ers among the teams in the mix. Green has publicly angled for a reunion push all summer, including reportedly declining his own player option to help clear the Warriors' books for a possible James deal.

James, 41, has said he won't drag out his decision much longer. Until he actually picks a team, Green's version of a LeBron-anchored Warriors offense — with himself lurking in the corner, waiting for a kickout — remains exactly what it was on Sunday: a joke with just enough real stakes behind it to make people talk.

body: Hapoel Beer Sheva head into their first competitive test of the new European season priced as anything but favorites, at least in the eyes of Israeli bookmakers. Winner has set match-winner odds of 2.40 for a Beer Sheva victory, 2.30 for Víkingur Reykjavík and 3.15 for a draw in Tuesday's Champions League second qualifying round opener — numbers that treat the reigning Israeli champions as essentially even money against a club most of their fans had barely heard of a month ago.

The first leg kicks off Tuesday evening at Víkingsvöllur in Reykjavík, with the return fixture in Beer Sheva to follow next week. It is the opening assignment of a European campaign the champions hoped would start with more momentum behind them.

Ran Kozuch's side arrive off the back of a rough few weeks by their own recent standards. Having won the league title in May — Hapoel's first championship since 2018 — Beer Sheva then lost the State Cup final to Maccabi Tel Aviv, and opened the new season by losing the Super Cup to the same rivals, 3-1, at Turner Stadium on July 17. Kozuch himself has since signed a two-year contract extension, a vote of confidence from the club despite that pair of domestic reverses.

Víkingur, for their part, are Iceland's champions and were largely unknown on the continent before this summer, but they have already shown European teeth: they eliminated Hungary's Győr in the previous qualifying round, winning 3-2 on aggregate.

The near-identical prices for the two win markets tell their own story — Winner is not treating this as a routine step for the higher-ranked side, but as a genuine toss-up between two national champions.

Beyond the match result, Winner has also priced a head-to-head goal prop pitting Beer Sheva's Zambian winger Kings Kangwa against Víkingur's Gylfi Sigurðsson: Kangwa to outscore Sigurðsson pays 3.60, Sigurðsson to outscore Kangwa pays 3.30, and the pair finishing level — including on no goals at all — pays 1.50.

That pairing comes with its own subplot. Kangwa, who was central to Beer Sheva's title-winning campaign, has been chased by AEK Athens in a transfer reportedly worth several million euros, and no deal had been finalized as of kickoff, leaving open whether he even starts in Reykjavík.

Sigurðsson, by contrast, is the most recognizable name on the Icelandic side. The 36-year-old, who has played for Tottenham and Everton and represented Iceland at the 2018 World Cup, joined Víkingur from Valur last year and remains its most dangerous attacking presence.

A Beer Sheva win, or even a draw with an away goal, would hand the Israeli champions the advantage heading into next week's second leg back home. Lose in Reykjavík, and a European campaign that began with a coronation two months ago could already be in serious trouble.

title: Vinícius Júnior debuts sharper jawline after chin filler procedure
dek: Photos from a Goiânia clinic show the Real Madrid winger with a strikingly redefined profile, the reported result of a minimally invasive facial procedure he sought after weeks of online mockery of his chin during the World Cup.

body: Vinícius Júnior showed up online this week with a face a lot of people needed a second look at — a noticeably sharper, more defined jaw that had fans and rivals alike doing double takes over photos taken at a clinic in Goiânia, Brazil.

The Real Madrid winger underwent a minimally invasive facial harmonization procedure, using injectable fillers to sculpt and add definition to his chin and jawline, according to Brazilian entertainment reporting picked up by outlets including Yahoo and OneFootball. One report named the treating dermatologist as Alessandro Alarcão, working out of a specialized clinic in the city.

The reported trigger was weeks of online mockery. Vinícius's chin and facial features had become a target of memes and criticism during Brazil's run at the 2026 World Cup, and multiple outlets frame the procedure as a direct response to that scrutiny rather than anything medically necessary.

Images of the result spread fast once they surfaced, with the 26-year-old described in several reports as barely recognizable next to photos of him from the tournament just weeks earlier. His former girlfriend, Brazilian influencer Virginia Fonseca, was among those whose posts helped the pictures travel, and social media reaction ranged from stunned to skeptical — one widely shared post on X read, in Portuguese, roughly translated: "My brain can't process that this is Vini Jr now, I swear."

Vinícius has been one of the sport's most talked-about — and most targeted — figures since completing his move from Flamengo to Real Madrid in 2018 for a reported fee near €46 million. He has grown into one of the world's premier attackers and a fixture for Brazil, but his time at the top has also come with relentless outside noise, from provocations by rival fans to running commentary on his celebrations and appearance.

Neither Vinícius nor Real Madrid have issued any official comment on the procedure. He remains on his post-World Cup break and is expected to report back for preseason training with the club in the coming weeks.

title: Omri Glazer lands in Israel to seal Maccabi Haifa return
dek: Israel's national-team goalkeeper touched down with his family Monday night, medicals and a three-year contract awaiting as he rejoins Barak Bakhar for a third time.

body: Omri Glazer walked out of arrivals at Ben Gurion Airport on Monday night with his wife, Shira, and their family in tow, the final leg of a journey that will end, barring a hitch in his medical, with a return to Maccabi Haifa.

The 30-year-old goalkeeper agreed personal terms with the Greens earlier that day, and Israeli outlets reported the contract at three years with a salary in the region of €400,000 a season plus bonuses, one of the higher goalkeeper wages in the Israeli league. Haifa are believed to have paid Red Star Belgrade somewhere between €250,000 and €300,000 to release him, with reports differing slightly on the exact figure.
Before anything becomes official, Glazer has to pass a medical and sign the paperwork that will formally bind him to Barak Bakhar's squad. That process was expected to run through the week.

For Glazer, it's a reunion rather than a first meeting. Bakhar coached him during his first Haifa spell, crossed paths with him again during a short stint in charge at Red Star Belgrade in 2023, and now takes charge of him a third time after being reappointed as Haifa's manager for the upcoming season.

He arrives to replace Georgiy Yermakov as the club's first-choice goalkeeper. Yermakov, a Ukrainian-Israeli dual national who joined Haifa in August 2024, will now compete for the shirt rather than assume it as his own.

Glazer's history with Haifa runs deep. He first joined the club at 20, in 2016, and spent five seasons in green before leaving as a free agent in 2021 — a spell that included a Israeli championship medal in 2020/21.

It was afterward, at Hapoel Beersheba, that he built his reputation. Glazer was the goalkeeper who won Beersheba the 2021/22 State Cup, saving three consecutive penalties — from Dolev Haziza, Godsway Donyoh and Mavis Chibota — in a shootout final against the very club he is now rejoining.

That form earned him a move to Red Star Belgrade in the summer of 2023, where he spent three seasons, won Serbian league titles and picked up Champions League experience, including a 13-save display away to Manchester City. He lost his starting spot during his second season in Belgrade, however, and made only a handful of appearances in 2025 before this move became live.

Glazer has also become a fixture for Israel's national team, with 18 caps to his name, and his arrival gives Bakhar a proven, internationally tested option between the posts as Haifa reshapes its squad for the new campaign.

title: Enzo Fernández speaks out on World Cup final red card, skips the apology
dek: In his first public comments since Argentina's ten-men collapse in Spain's extra-time win, the Chelsea midfielder thanked fans and praised the national shirt — but never mentioned the reckless late foul that triggered his sending-off.

verificationSources.label: NBC News — "A World Cup known for officiating controversy ends with Argentina seeing red"
Yahoo Sports — "World Cup final: Late red card on Enzo Fernández leaves Argentina a man down in extra time of Spain's 1-0 win"
FIFA.com — Official match centre, Spain v Argentina, Final

LadBible — "Enzo Fernandez speaks out after costly World Cup final red card"

body: Enzo Fernández finally addressed Argentina's World Cup final defeat on Monday night, more than 24 hours after his reckless late tackle left his team down to ten men in extra time — but the message he sent contained no reference to the sending-off itself.

Argentina lost the July 19 final 1-0 to Spain after extra time at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, a result that denied Lionel Messi the storybook ending to his international career and handed Spain a second World Cup title.

Fernández, booked once in the first half, picked up a second yellow card in second-half stoppage time for a reckless, studs-up challenge on Spain defender Pau Cubarsí as he chased a loose ball. The referee had little choice but to send him off, leaving Argentina to play the additional 30 minutes a man short.

The damage compounded after the final whistle. Midfielder Leandro Paredes was shown a separate red card once the match had already ended, after grabbing Spain's Eric García by the throat and wrestling Gavi to the ground in a mass confrontation at midfield — Argentina's second dismissal of the night.

Spain made the numerical advantage count. Substitute Ferran Torres scored the winner in the second period of extra time, finishing a move started by fellow substitute Nico Williams, to seal La Roja's second World Cup crown in a final in which Argentina failed to register a shot on target.
It was only the sixth red card shown in a World Cup final in the tournament's history, and the first since Zinedine Zidane's dismissal for headbutting Marco Materazzi in the 2006 final.

In his statement, posted to Instagram, Fernández made no mention of the tackle, the sending-off or its consequences for his team. Instead, he thanked Argentina's supporters and framed the tournament as a source of pride rather than regret.

"As time goes by, you understand there is something much bigger than a result," he wrote, adding: "Wearing my country's shirt is the greatest honor of my career, and I will continue to give everything I have every time I'm called upon to defend it."

The written message stood in contrast to his reaction in the moment. As he walked off the field immediately after his sending-off, Fernández had raised both hands toward the Argentina section of the crowd, an apparent gesture of apology that several outlets covering the match described as more contrite than anything in his eventual public statement.

For a Chelsea midfielder who has built his international career on Argentina's run of major-tournament success — the 2022 World Cup and Copa América titles among them — the final in New Jersey leaves a rare blemish: a red card in the biggest match of his career, and a public response that stopped short of an apology.
