The stated purpose of the moves is playing time. Rather than keeping the group in youth or reserve frameworks, the champions want the six exposed to weekly senior competition, with Weinberg the most prominent of the departing players: he has already travelled with the first team for European fixtures and carries squad number 52 on the club's first-team list.

The mass loan fits an established pattern at the club, which routinely farms out young professionals to gain minutes; Transfermarkt currently lists seven other Maccabi players on loan at clubs in Israel, Hungary and Ukraine, among them teenagers Daniel Tishler and Itay Zafrani.

The timing is no accident. Maccabi opened their trophy season on Wednesday with a 3-1 Super Cup victory over Maccabi Be'er Sheva, and the coaching staff are trimming and shaping the squad ahead of the league campaign and European qualification rounds, making a clear runway for the academy group elsewhere the logical step.

Loan durations and any recall or option clauses were not disclosed in the report, and at the time of publication neither Maccabi Tel Aviv nor Kfar Shalem had posted an official announcement of the six moves on their channels; the transfers are therefore attributed to the reporting outlet pending club confirmation.

body: Beşiktaş president Serdal Adalı has publicly accused Mohamed Salah's agent of derailing the Turkish club's pursuit of the Egyptian forward, claiming an initial understanding with the player was in place before the representative sharply raised his financial demands. Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Adalı directed his frustration not at Salah — a free agent since his Liverpool contract expired — but at agent Ramy Abbas.

According to Adalı, Salah was open to the move to Istanbul and went as far as meeting the club's new head coach, Vincenzo Italiano, together with its sporting director, signalling that he wanted to come. It was only after Turkish media reported that the transfer was close to completion, the president said, that the terms changed.

"After we had already reached an initial agreement, because the media published that the deal was close to being finalised, his agent raised his commission demand to inconceivable levels — around 35 percent," Adalı said, in remarks reported by the Israeli outlet ONE. "From our point of view, there is no chance of accepting such percentages. Moreover, we do not think Salah is aware of these sums."

Adalı also denied that outside intermediaries had been involved in the negotiation, insisting the club had dealt only with Abbas directly. The commission figure is, for now, the president's account alone; the agent's side has not confirmed it, and no fee or contract terms have been made public by either party.

Abbas, for his part, has pushed back on any suggestion that a deal exists. "I personally do not know where Mohamed will play next season," the agent said this week, adding that it is not his practice to hold talks with clubs his client would not want to join. Beşiktaş had earlier issued its own statement dismissing reports of a completed transfer as fiction.

Salah's next destination therefore remains genuinely open. Beyond Beşiktaş, the 34-year-old has been linked with Saudi Arabia's wealthiest clubs and with Major League Soccer, where The Athletic has reported a possible move to Sporting Kansas City — a scenario with a distinctly Israeli subplot, as it would make Salah a teammate of Israel international centre-back Or Blorian, who joined the MLS side from Hapoel Be'er Sheva in June.

If Adalı's version holds, the impasse is about the agent's percentage rather than the player's wishes, and talks could yet be revived; if Abbas's denials prevail, the Istanbul chapter may close before it begins. Either way, one of the most decorated forwards of his generation enters late July without a club, and every stated outcome — Turkey, the Gulf, or America — remains conditional on a negotiation that is still visibly unresolved.

body: Dolev Haziza, the former Maccabi Haifa captain who left the club this summer after seven years, is expected to sign for Maccabi Netanya, Israeli sports outlet Sport5 reported Sunday, adding that the gaps between the two sides have narrowed in recent days.

Haziza's agent met with Netanya officials on Sunday, and the club hopes to complete the deal within days — ideally before Tuesday, when Netanya is due to hold its traditional season-opening training session. The club is said to have pushed that opening back by a week to finish assembling its squad.

Sunday's report fits a steady trail of coverage over the past month. Netanya's interest first surfaced in late June, when the club was said to have opened preliminary talks with the midfielder, and a report last week described significant progress after head coach Ronny Levy spoke directly with the player, though it noted that gaps over salary still remained at that stage.

Haziza, 31, spent seven seasons at Maccabi Haifa after arriving from Bnei Yehuda Tel Aviv in 2019. Sunday's report credits him with 247 appearances, 43 goals and 41 assists for the Greens, along with three league championships won during Haifa's title run from 2021 to 2023 — a period in which he also wore the captain's armband. Last season he scored nine goals and added two assists.

His exit from Haifa was not of his own choosing. Israeli outlets reported earlier this summer that the club informed the attacking midfielder he was not part of its professional plans, and that he initially weighed a move abroad before talks with Netanya gathered pace in recent weeks.

A move to Netanya would carry an element of homecoming: Haziza was born in the coastal city in July 1995. It would also be only the fourth stop of a career that has taken in Bnei Yehuda, a loan spell at Hapoel Ramat Gan and Maccabi Haifa, alongside 18 caps for the Israel national team.

The deal remains unsigned, though the direction of travel is unmistakable. In a conversation with Levy on Monday morning, Haziza said he was "determined to prove myself" and to show he can still lead a top-flight side, according to a follow-up report.

That report added that only small financial gaps remain, centred on two possible ways of bridging his wages: Maccabi Haifa topping up his first-year salary, or a compensation payment from Haifa before the move goes through. Netanya's management was described as optimistic about completing the transfer within days.

body: Ironi Kiryat Shmona have confirmed that an agreement is in place to sell Cristian Martínez to Slovan Bratislava, drawing a line under the Panamanian midfielder's two seasons in the Upper Galilee. The club's confirmation on Sunday was careful in its wording: what exists between the two sides is a concluded understanding rather than an announced transfer.

Martínez himself travelled to Slovakia over the weekend to complete the final formalities. The terms have nonetheless taken shape quickly — reporting in Israel puts the deal at three years, and the player's registration record now lists him at Slovan with a contract running to June 2029 and an arrival dated 19 July. Neither club has disclosed the fee, which remains unreported.
The timing owes everything to this summer's World Cup. Panama went out at the group stage without a point, yet Martínez emerged with his reputation enhanced.
Deployed on the flank rather than in his customary central role, he was named Player of the Match in the 1-0 defeat by Croatia. The interest that followed came from Europe and South America alike.

Slovan officials indicated they had tracked the midfielder across several transfer windows and had to see off considerable competition to sign him — a persistence that finally paid off once Panama's tournament ended.

His Kiryat Shmona record explains the demand. The 29-year-old, who has won 69 caps for Panama, arrived on loan in July 2024 and made 33 appearances in his first season before the club made the deal permanent.
In 2025-26 he added 31 appearances and four goals from central midfield, establishing himself among the more dependable foreign players in the Israeli top flight.

For Slovan the urgency is straightforward: the Slovak champions open their Champions League second qualifying round tie this week and want their new midfielder registered and available as early in the European campaign as possible.

For Kiryat Shmona, who missed the championship playoff last season, the sale continues a familiar and financially necessary pattern — recruit shrewdly, extract a strong season or two, and sell into Europe. The undisclosed fee will now fund the next iteration of that model, and the search for a successor in the middle of the pitch.

body: Maccabi Haifa Women's Basketball has opened an academy with the Hebrew Reali School, giving teenage players a structured way to combine high-level training with their secondary education. The programme is open to players from ninth grade upward, and it hands the city something it lacked: a defined pathway for girls who want serious basketball without stepping outside their normal school life.

The arrangement joins a club already competing inside the Israel Basketball Association system with one of Haifa's established schools. Its ambitions go beyond fielding a strong team. The academy is meant to support athletic, academic and personal development under a single structure, rather than leaving families to piece those elements together on their own.

That distinction carries real weight in youth sport. Training loads typically climb sharply through the teenage years, just as exams and travel start eating into a player's time. A school-club model can manage those competing demands more deliberately than either side working alone, though the academy has yet to publish a full timetable, an admissions process or a coaching roster.

There is already a competitive base to build on. Maccabi Haifa Women's Basketball is registered under team code 2198, with Ilan Beck and Rinat Kahana listed as club representatives and its home venue recorded at 19 Bikurim Street in Haifa. The club's girls' upper-group side finished its most recent campaign with 12 wins and two losses from 14 games, according to the association's published table.

That record matters because it means the academy is extending an active pathway rather than inventing one on paper. A player entering in ninth grade can draw a straight line between structured development work and a club that is already competing in the national girls' framework — a link that narrows the gap between introductory youth basketball and a genuinely competitive setting in northern Israel.

The launch was billed as a regional first and drew Sports Minister Miki Zohar and Haifa mayor Yona Yahav, lending the opening civic weight. But the programme's real test will come later, in details still to be settled: coaching quality, training access, academic coordination, and how many players stay in the sport through their later teenage years.

For Maccabi Haifa, the payoff is a clearer route to identifying and keeping local talent. For the Reali School, it offers a formal structure for students whose sporting commitments already resemble those of elite athletes. The framework is now in place; the evidence that will matter comes with the first full season's intake, staffing and competition schedule.

body: Tamar Steinberg finished sixth and Sharon Kantor eighth in the women's iQFOiL event at the Long Beach Olympic Classes Regatta, leaving Israel without a podium finish at the final Sailing Grand Slam stop of the season. Steinberg advanced one round further than Kantor in Thursday's medal series, but neither reached the four-athlete final that decided the medals on what will be the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic course.

Steinberg had entered the medal series in fourth place, earning a bye straight into the semi-final. A difficult launch off the line cost her the early position she needed to advance, and sixth became her final classification. Kantor arrived in better form, having climbed nine places during the qualifying series to reach eighth and a quarter-final berth, but another compromised start ended her run through the knockout ladder.

Daniela Peleg rounded out the Israeli women's iQFOiL entry in 12th, two places outside the medal-series cut. It was a narrow margin in a fleet that had put Steinberg third and Kantor fifth after the second day of racing. Britain's Emma Wilson, who had led the event from the front throughout, converted that position into the overall win.

The men's iQFOiL campaign fared worse, finishing outside the medal series altogether. Yoav Cohen was the leading Israeli in 21st, with Tomer Vardimon 27th and Olympic champion Tom Reuveny 28th. The week amounted to a development exercise rather than a continuation of Israel's medal record in the class, with the course itself and the afternoon sea breeze offering the most useful takeaways.

Israel also sent two athletes into the women's Formula Kite fleet, where Maya Ashkenazi placed 14th and Gal Zuckerman 15th. Their presence mattered beyond the results: Long Beach brought both Olympic board disciplines together for the first time, with high-speed kiteboards and foiling windsurfers racing side by side off Belmont Shore, on the same waters set to host Olympic sailing in 2028.

The regatta ran from 13 to 16 July and drew more than 100 international competitors across the four iQFOiL and Formula Kite fleets. It was the first of this summer's Los Angeles Olympic-class blocks and the closing round of the 2026 Sailing Grand Slam, giving teams an unusually early look at the Olympic venue two years out from the Games.

For Israel, going without a medal marks a meaningful break in what has otherwise been a strong women's iQFOiL season. The sharper lesson, though, came from the elimination racing itself: in a format where advancement can turn on a single short contest, the opening seconds carry outsized weight. Steinberg and Kantor both had the speed to compete for the podium — Long Beach simply showed how little room the medal series leaves for recovery once the start goes wrong.

body: The winners of Sunday's World Cup final will receive championship rings for the first time in FIFA competition history. Argentina or Spain will still lift the trophy and collect the traditional gold medals at New York New Jersey Stadium, but the winning delegation will also be assigned 30 personalised rings modelled on a familiar North American sporting tradition.

The first presentation will come immediately after the final, when the victorious captain and head coach receive temporary versions during the ceremony. Permanent rings will then be produced to measure and delivered later, each of the 30 team pieces individually numbered and accompanied by a certificate of authenticity.

The design keeps the World Cup at its centre rather than simply importing another sport's jewellery. One side features the tournament trophy, while the opposite face will be completed only after the final, once Argentina or Spain have settled the match and the manufacturer can personalise it to reflect the winning nation.

FIFA has capped the total edition at 2,026 rings, a direct reference to the tournament year. Thirty are reserved for the champions, and the remaining 1,996 will be offered worldwide as officially licensed supporter pieces. No public price had been announced when the collection was revealed.

The initiative adds a commercial product to the most protected symbol system in football, but it also changes how this particular winning group will be commemorated. Medals belong to football's established presentation ritual; rings are designed to be worn and displayed as a continuing marker of membership in a championship team.

American leagues have long made that idea part of their championship culture, with bespoke rings carrying team colours, records and season references. The 2026 World Cup gives FIFA an obvious setting to adopt the practice: the final is being played in the United States, and the tournament itself has been staged across Canada, Mexico and the US.

What remains unchanged is the sporting order of importance. The ring accompanies the trophy rather than competing with it. For the winner of Argentina against Spain, though, the 2026 title will now produce three distinct keepsakes: the game's most recognised cup, the champion's medal and the first personalised ring awarded by FIFA.

body: Giannis Antetokounmpo used his first formal appearance as a Miami Heat player to define the move in championship terms. Introduced at Kaseya Center on Thursday alongside president Pat Riley and coach Erik Spoelstra, the two-time NBA Most Valuable Player said Miami offered the strongest route to competing for another title. What had been transaction news became, in that moment, the opening statement of a new Heat era.

The trade itself was substantial. Miami acquired Antetokounmpo and Bobby Portis from Milwaukee in a deal approved on 6 July, sending Tyler Herro, Kel'el Ware, Jaime Jaquez Jr. and Kasparas Jakučionis to the Bucks along with three first-round picks, a 2030 first-round pick swap and a 2033 second-round pick. That price tag leaves little doubt about the timeline: Miami has traded away a large share of its young core and future draft control in exchange for immediate contention.

Antetokounmpo will wear No. 7 in Miami rather than the No. 34 that followed him through his entire Milwaukee career. The new number, visible during Thursday's introduction and already updated on the Heat's official roster, is a cosmetic detail with real symbolic weight — it marks the line between a 13-season Bucks career and the first major relocation of his professional life.

On the court, the fit starts with Antetokounmpo alongside Bam Adebayo, two elite defenders capable of covering unusual amounts of space and attacking the rim from different angles. That pairing is also Spoelstra's central puzzle. Neither star is primarily a high-volume perimeter shooter, so Miami's spacing, half-court creation and late-game execution will hinge on the guards and wings built around them. The defensive ceiling is obvious; the championship offense still has to be built.

Antetokounmpo brings the credentials to demand that standard be met. He led Milwaukee to the 2021 championship, won back-to-back regular-season MVP awards in 2019 and 2020, and was named Finals MVP during that title run. The NBA's official farewell tally credits him with 21,531 points in a Bucks uniform and ranks him first in franchise history in points, rebounds and assists. Miami is not simply acquiring a superstar's reputation — it is acquiring one whose peak already reshaped a franchise.

His introduction also carried an unmistakable cultural expectation. Riley and Spoelstra have spent years building Miami's identity around conditioning, accountability and postseason ambition, and Antetokounmpo's own reputation for physical preparation and sustained intensity fits that mold closely. That alignment makes the partnership coherent on paper, but it does not resolve the harder questions of health, roster depth or shot creation. Shared standards are a starting advantage, not proof of a championship.

The move also closes the book on the most successful era in half a century of Bucks basketball. Antetokounmpo delivered the championship Milwaukee had waited 50 years to reclaim, then departed as the franchise's all-time leader across its three major cumulative categories. His Miami unveiling did not erase that history — it simply opened the next question: whether his prime can be converted into another title window, now that the Heat has spent one of the summer's largest asset packages to find out.

No game has yet been played with Antetokounmpo in a Heat uniform, and Miami's final rotation remains, for now, a preseason question. Thursday's significance was strategic rather than competitive: the club presented its new centerpiece, the player accepted the pressure of a title mandate, and both sides made clear this trade will ultimately be judged in the postseason. The announcement is finished. The harder work — building a champion around No. 7 — starts now.

body: The NBA is examining the circumstances surrounding Gary Trent Jr.'s new contract with the Milwaukee Bucks, placing a significant free-agent agreement under league scrutiny days after it was reported. A league spokesman confirmed the NBA was continuing to look into the matter.
That is an active review, not a finding that Trent, Milwaukee or his representatives broke a rule.

Milwaukee officially announced Trent's return on Thursday without disclosing financial terms. The agreement has been reported as four years and $64 million, which would keep the 27-year-old guard with the Bucks through the 2029/30 season. NBA.com also records that Trent declined his player option before returning on the new multi-year deal.
At issue is possible salary-cap circumvention through a prior understanding. Trent joined Milwaukee in 2024 on a veteran-minimum contract and returned on another short agreement in 2025.

The reported concern is whether those lower salaries were connected to a promise of a larger contract once the Bucks had acquired the contractual mechanism to retain him above the cap. No such prior arrangement has been proved.

The unusual jump in salary has drawn attention because Trent's production declined in 2025/26. He averaged 8.1 points in 21.2 minutes across 65 regular-season appearances, starting 21 games — both his lowest scoring and playing-time averages since his 2018/19 rookie season. He shot 36 percent from three-point range, down from 41.6 percent the previous year.

Performance alone cannot establish circumvention, however. Teams are free to value shooting, continuity and roster fit differently from the public market, and a player's recent box score does not prove the existence of an undisclosed promise. The league's task is narrower and more evidential: determine how the sequence of agreements was negotiated, and whether any binding commitment predated the point at which Milwaukee was permitted to offer the new deal.

For the Bucks, the timing matters amid a wider roster reset. Trent's contract would create a substantial multi-year commitment to a rotation guard at the same moment Milwaukee are reshaping the team around a younger core. The review does not suspend the agreement, and neither the league nor the club has announced a timetable for a decision or any interim restriction on Trent.

The case also carries significance beyond one player's salary. The NBA's cap system depends on clubs competing within shared exceptions and negotiating windows, and if a team can secure discounted seasons by promising a later reward, that would undermine the intended balance.

Equally, treating every surprising contract as evidence of wrongdoing would interfere with legitimate negotiations — which is why the distinction between suspicion and proof must remain visible throughout the review.

Trent remains a Bucks player while the league gathers information. The verified position is therefore limited but consequential: Milwaukee have re-signed him, the four-year, $64 million terms are reported rather than club-disclosed, and the NBA is examining the surrounding circumstances. Any conclusion about a violation, penalty or contract status must wait for the league's findings.

body: Slavko Vinčić will referee Sunday’s World Cup final between Argentina and Spain at New York New Jersey Stadium. The appointment gives the 46-year-old Slovenian his fourth match of the tournament and places one of European football’s most experienced officials in charge of the game that will decide the world title.

Vinčić will work with Slovenian assistant referees Tomaž Klančnik and Andraž Kovačič. Jordan’s Adham Makhadmeh has been named as the fourth official, with compatriot Mohammed Al-Khalaf serving as reserve assistant referee. The five-man on-field group combines an established Slovenian trio with two Jordanian officials for the final assignment.

This will be Vinčić’s second men’s World Cup. He refereed Argentina’s 2–1 group-stage defeat by Saudi Arabia and Wales’ 2–0 win over Iran in Qatar in 2022. His previous experience with Lionel Messi’s team therefore comes from one of the defining shocks of that tournament, although that historical result supplies context rather than any evidence about how Sunday’s final will be handled.

Vinčić has already taken charge of three games at the 2026 tournament: Brazil’s draw with Morocco, Jordan against Algeria and Mexico’s round-of-32 victory over Ecuador. The last of those included Piero Hincapié’s dismissal. Sunday will be his first appearance since that knockout assignment and his first World Cup final as the referee in the middle.

The scale of the occasion is familiar from club football. Vinčić controlled Real Madrid’s 2–0 win over Borussia Dortmund in the 2024 Champions League final at Wembley. He also refereed the 2022 Europa League final between Eintracht Frankfurt and Rangers in Seville, which Frankfurt won on penalties. UEFA’s official record lists him as an international referee since 2010.

Klančnik and Kovačič were also Vinčić’s assistants at the 2024 Champions League final, giving the Slovenian trio experience together in a comparable one-match showpiece. That continuity is a functional advantage rather than a guarantee of an error-free night: positioning, eye contact and concise radio communication all depend on rehearsed habits when the noise and speed of a final compress decision time.

For Argentina and Spain, the practical significance lies in preparation rather than mythology around past results. Teams use an official’s recent matches to study thresholds for contact, dissent, advantage and time management. Vinčić’s established assistants matter equally: offside decisions and communication across the crew can shape a final long before a major disciplinary call reaches the referee.

Argentina and Spain are scheduled to kick off at 3pm local time on Sunday 19 July. The referee appointment completes another central part of the match operation as both finalists move into their last training days. Vinčić’s task is straightforward to describe and uniquely difficult to execute: keep the world’s largest football match moving, apply the laws consistently and make the officials as secondary to the contest as the contest allows.

body: Spain conducted their World Cup final preparations under a haze of Canadian wildfire smoke in northern New Jersey on Thursday, though the latest outlook points toward improving conditions before Sunday rather than any confirmed disruption to the match itself. The smoke visibly altered the backdrop for the finalists, but it has not produced an official change to the Argentina–Spain schedule.

The Spanish squad trained outdoors in East Hanover, roughly 15 miles from New York New Jersey Stadium, the sun dimmed behind a grey layer overhead. The first 15 minutes of the scheduled hour-long session were opened to media. Argentina, meanwhile, remained at their base in Marietta, Georgia, after reaching the final, meaning the two teams were not preparing under the same local air conditions at that point in the week.

Air quality in East Hanover began Thursday in the 'unhealthy' range before improving to 'unhealthy for sensitive groups' by mid-afternoon. The principal concern was fine particulate matter, PM2.5, carried south by the smoke. Such particles pose a genuine risk around high-intensity outdoor exercise, since players move far more air through their lungs than they do at rest — making the training environment a legitimate performance and welfare issue even in the absence of a postponement.

New York State's official air-quality advisory, covering the New York City metropolitan area, had warned that fine-particle levels could exceed an Air Quality Index value of 100. The National Weather Service's New York office likewise carried smoke in its short-term forecast discussion through Thursday night. Together, those records corroborate the haze witnessed at Spain's session, without elevating a temporary advisory into a forecast for the final itself.

Argentina and Spain are due to meet at New York New Jersey Stadium on Sunday 19 July at 3pm local time. Current projections expect the smoke to clear well before kickoff, with Sunday's air-quality forecast sitting in the 'moderate' range. That category falls short of pristine air, but it marks a clear improvement on the conditions recorded during Spain's Thursday training.

No relocation, postponement or revised kickoff has been officially announced. The evidence therefore supports a narrower conclusion than the most dramatic reading of the skyline would suggest: the smoke complicated part of Spain's preparation and warranted monitoring, even as the match outlook continued to improve. Treating the final as already under threat would run ahead of both the forecast and the tournament authorities.

Spain's staff retain the option to adjust exposure and workload should local readings deteriorate again, though no confirmed change to the training programme has been published. The more immediate asymmetry between the finalists is geographic rather than medical: Spain were already working close to the venue under the haze, while Argentina could continue their recovery in Georgia before travelling north. Whether that difference carries any sporting cost cannot be established from air-quality readings alone.

The next meaningful evidence will come from the weekend forecast and the teams' final training sessions. For now, the responsible position is to separate a real training-day problem from a speculative match-day crisis. The air over northern New Jersey looked troubling on Thursday, but the verified trajectory ahead of the world-title match was toward relief.

body: Houston's pressure took Brooklyn's preferred rhythm away before the game had time to settle, and the Rockets turned a 28–13 first quarter into a 100–83 NBA Summer League win at Cox Pavilion. Houston moved to 3–1. Brooklyn fell to 2–2, leaving the Nets outside the four-team semi-final field after their four scheduled preliminary games.

The opening period did the damage. Houston made Brooklyn work to initiate possessions, then punished the resulting empty trips with a balanced half-court attack. The teams split the second quarter 21–21, but the Nets still trailed 49–34 at the break. Houston took the third quarter 29–23 before Brooklyn rallied to win the fourth 26–22 — a late push that trimmed the margin without changing the shape of the night.

Ben Saraf played 16 minutes and 26 seconds off the bench and finished with two points, one assist and two steals. He missed all three of his field-goal attempts, including his lone three-point try, and made just one of two free throws. Two turnovers and a minus-15 rating rounded out a difficult offensive outing, though the steals reflected defensive activity that held up even as his shot and playmaking stalled.

Danny Wolf started at forward and posted four points, eight rebounds, two assists, one steal and two blocks in 18 minutes and 35 seconds. Six of those boards came at the defensive end. But five turnovers and five personal fouls cut into the value of that work, and Wolf shot just one of three from the floor and one of three from the line, finishing at minus-15 alongside Saraf.

Brooklyn's broader shooting trouble hurt more than either Israeli's individual line. The Nets made 25 of 71 attempts for 35.2 percent and just nine of 38 threes — 23.7 percent. Houston shot 43.1 percent overall and 45.8 percent from deep, sinking two more threes on 14 fewer attempts. The Rockets also won the rebounding battle 41–32, turning their sharper perimeter efficiency into extra scoring chances.

Bruce Thornton led all scorers with 23 points on 7-of-13 shooting, and Tristen Newton added 20 points and six rebounds in 21:32. Egor Dëmin carried Brooklyn with 21 points and five made threes, with Mikel Brown Jr. contributing 14. Those numbers kept the Nets in the game after the early blow, but they were not enough to offset a Houston starting group that shot just 33.3 percent yet still produced 53 combined points.

Brooklyn did generate disruption of its own, finishing with 15 steals and eight blocks — both higher than Houston's totals — and two fewer team turnovers. The issue was conversion. Those defensive plays rarely turned into efficient offense, and Houston kept answering with cleaner shooting of its own.

For Saraf and Wolf, the final preliminary game was a sharp contrast to Tuesday's 115–83 win over Sacramento, and a clear read on the physical and decision-making demands their next stage of development will require.

Kastine Evans, Austin Spiker and Monnazjea Finney-Smithy officiated the contest, played at Cox Pavilion in Las Vegas; no attendance figure was published. Brooklyn now moves into its final placement game, while Houston's 3–1 record keeps the Rockets in the wider Summer League qualification picture.

body: Israel's under-20 men's team shed every trace of relegation anxiety on Thursday, beating Italy 84–59 in Ljubljana to secure its place in the top division of the European championship. Oren Aharoni's side seized control in the second quarter and kept stretching the lead after half-time, delivering its most complete performance since Wednesday's round-of-16 defeat to Greece.

Italy led 16–15 late in the first quarter, but Israel closed it on a 21–16 run and never let the game drift back into one-possession territory. The second quarter went 18–16 in Israel's favor for a 39–32 half-time lead, then a 20–11 third period pulled the contest open. A 25-point fourth quarter sealed it, giving Israel the night's largest winning margin at 25 points.

Yonatan Keller led all scorers with 19 points, and Oren Sahar added 18 while posting the game's highest efficiency rating, 23. Four Israeli players finished in double figures — a spread that mattered as much as the top numbers, since it left Italy unable to load its defense against a single creator while Israel kept pace and pressure flowing through its rotations rather than leaning on one late shot-maker.

The shooting numbers explain why the margin only grew. Israel shot 40 percent from the field to Italy's 31 percent, converting 46.8 percent on two-point attempts and 30 percent from three. Italy managed just 37.2 percent inside the arc and 16.7 percent from long range. Israel was also 81.3 percent from the free-throw line, locking in the advantage whenever the game stopped.

Once ahead, Israel was rarely troubled again. The official lead tracker recorded only one lead change all night, with Israel in front for 37 minutes and 16 seconds against 1:36 for Italy, and its biggest lead reaching 28 points. Those numbers point to a game controlled from the front rather than a late escape — a notable contrast to the 79–66 loss to Greece that had ended the medal path just one night earlier.

The win also resolved the tournament's most pressing competitive question. At this age level, the classification bracket carries real consequences: finishing in the bottom positions means relegation to Division B. By winning the 9–16 classification opener, Israel locked in its spot in the top European division for 2027, with the remaining fixtures left to determine an eventual finish anywhere from ninth to twelfth.

Arena Stožice II hosted a crowd of 100, with Yener Yilmaz, Lukasz Jankowski and Sinisa Prpa officiating — a modest setting that did nothing to ease the stakes. With less than a day to reset after the Greece loss, Israel played with clearer spacing, sharper shot selection and the defensive discipline to hold Italy to 43 points over the final three quarters. Survival was the minimum requirement; the manner of the win restored some authority to the campaign.

body: Maccabi Haifa have reached an agreement with United States striker Andrija Novakovich, adding a proven central-forward profile to Diego Flores's rebuild. The club said the 29-year-old is expected in Israel next week for medical examinations. That condition is decisive: Haifa have an agreement, not a completed registration, and the player should not be described as signed until the medical process is finished.

Novakovich arrives from Italy after a season in Serie B in which he made 33 league appearances and scored five goals. At 1.92 metres, he offers a reference point between centre-backs and a target for deliveries into the penalty area. He has also spent enough of his career working outside the United States to understand the tactical demands of European club football, rather than arriving as a development project.

The move changes the shape of Haifa's forward search. Flores has wanted a striker capable of fixing defenders centrally while the wide players attack the spaces around him. Novakovich's frame can help the team play through direct passes when a high press closes the first build-up route, but his value cannot be measured only through aerial duels.

Haifa also need clean lay-offs, penalty-area occupation and repeat movement across the front line. Five goals in 33 league matches is not, on its own, a guarantee of a high-volume scorer — it is a recent record that requires context. A striker's output depends on minutes, chance quality and role, and Haifa will need to build a service structure that brings him closer to goal.

If he spends too much of each match receiving with his back to goal, far from the box, the physical profile will solve progression problems without necessarily solving finishing. That distinction will matter as the coaching staff design his role.

The medical requirement deserves more than routine wording. Until the examinations are completed, the club retain the ability to evaluate fitness, and the parties have not crossed the final administrative threshold. Presenting the agreement as a finished transfer would erase the exact contingency Haifa placed in their own announcement. The next confirmed step is his arrival; a contract announcement should follow only if the checks are satisfactory.

For Haifa, the timing is useful. The domestic cup phase begins later in July, giving the staff a narrow window to integrate a new number nine before the league programme settles. Training work will need to cover pressing triggers as well as attacking patterns — a tall striker can make a team more direct, but Flores will want that outlet connected to the midfield rather than isolated above it.

Novakovich therefore represents a clear roster decision without yet being a completed one. Haifa have selected size, experience and penalty-area presence for the next stage of their reconstruction. The medical will determine whether that plan becomes a signing; the football afterwards will determine whether the team can turn those traits into more reliable chance creation.

body: Maccabi Tel Aviv will face Sheriff Tiraspol in the second qualifying round of the Europa League after the Moldovan club eliminated Aluminij 1–0 on aggregate. The first leg is scheduled for 23 July with the return on 30 July, giving Maccabi one week to move from the Super Cup celebration into a two-match European assignment.

The tie was already fixed in UEFA's draw as the winner of Sheriff–Aluminij against Maccabi. Thursday's second leg supplied the missing name. After a goalless opening match in Tiraspol, Sheriff won 1–0 in Slovenia through Jaurès-Ulrich Loukou's fifth-minute goal. That early advantage survived the remainder of the match and became the only goal across 180 minutes.

Sheriff's route says something useful about the contest Maccabi should expect. The Moldovan side did not need a high-scoring series to advance. They protected a narrow away lead after a first leg in which neither team scored, a profile that places a premium on patience, rest-defence and avoiding cheap transitions. Maccabi cannot assume territorial control will automatically produce a comfortable margin.

Maccabi enter the tie with competitive rhythm and a trophy. Their 3–1 Super Cup win over Hapoel Be'er Sheva showed the value of Sagiv Yehezkel's delivery and Saied Abu Farchi's penalty-area movement, even after Roy Revivo's dismissal reduced them to ten men. European qualifying will ask for the same threat with greater control, because one poorly managed phase can distort an entire two-leg contest.

The draw order places Sheriff at home in the first leg and Maccabi in the return. Final venue arrangements remain subject to the clubs' and UEFA's operational confirmation, so the useful certainty at this stage is the sequence and dates rather than an assumed stadium. Maccabi's immediate objective is to leave the first game with the tie structurally manageable.

Sheriff carry extensive qualifying experience and have previously reached major UEFA group and league phases. Historical reputation will not decide the tie, but it affects how the Moldovan club approach difficult minutes. A team accustomed to knockout qualifiers is less likely to panic when possession or territory moves against it. Maccabi will need to create chances without allowing frustration to loosen the spacing behind the ball.

The pairing now gives Zarko Lazetic's staff a precise scouting task. Sheriff's compactness, Loukou's early scoring impact and the low-event first-round pattern form the starting evidence. Maccabi have the more recent attacking statement, but the next round will be decided by how well that aggression survives across two matches rather than by the momentum of one domestic final.

title: Israel U20s answered a survival game with grown-up control
dek: The 84–59 score mattered because it preserved Division A status; the way Israel built it showed how quickly a youth team can reset its identity after elimination.

source.name: Sport5
source.originalTitle: עמדה במשימה: 59:84 לעתודה שנשארה בדרג א'
source.author: Sport5 editorial team

verificationSources.label: FIBA official Italy–Israel game page and statistical record

body: Youth tournaments are usually remembered for medals and prospects, but their toughest tests often arrive once both have slipped out of reach. Israel's 84-59 win over Italy was played in exactly that uncomfortable space, less than 24 hours after a round-of-16 loss to Greece had already ended the title route. There was no podium on offer, no glamour attached to the fixture, only the institutional stakes of remaining in Division A. Israel met the moment with the most adult performance of its week.

The first sign was not a spectacular run but the absence of emotional waste. Italy edged ahead in the opening quarter, yet Israel closed it out 21-16 without letting Wednesday's disappointment spill into Thursday's tension. The lead grew to seven by half-time, to 16 after the third quarter and to 25 by the final buzzer. A young team that had lost its primary objective found a secondary one and treated it as non-negotiable.

Control shows up clearly in the official data. Israel led for 37 minutes and 16 seconds against just 1:36 for Italy, with the lead changing hands only once and the largest margin reaching 28 points. Those numbers do not describe a loose classification game settled by a hot final minute. They describe a team that dictated where the contest would be played and held that ground through rotations, stoppages and the inevitable stretches when the first option broke down.

The scoring balance mattered just as much. Yonatan Keller produced 19 points and Oren Sahar added 18, with four players finishing in double figures. In a survival game, that distribution counts tactically and psychologically alike: Italy could not solve the attack by shutting down one guard, and Israel did not need a single player to shoulder the emotional weight of repairing the tournament. The possession belonged to the group before it belonged to any one scorer.

That collective approach translated into genuine shooting efficiency. Israel converted 46.8 percent of its two-pointers, 30 percent of its threes and 81.3 percent of its free throws. No single figure there is extraordinary, but together they built an efficient floor game: enough pressure at the rim to force defensive decisions, enough perimeter touch to punish collapsing coverage, and enough composure at the line to stop Italy buying its way back through fouls.

It was the defensive side, though, that created the real separation. Italy shot just 31 percent from the field and 16.7 percent from beyond the arc. Poor opponent shooting can sometimes be dismissed as variance, but the quarter-by-quarter pattern argues otherwise. Italy scored 16, 16, 11 and 16 across the four periods -- evidence that Israel did not merely survive one cold stretch but kept the 2025 champions below a functional offensive level for the entire night.

None of this erases the Greece defeat, and a classification win should never be mistaken for a medal. A well-run development programme resists that kind of emotional accounting. The failure to reach the quarter-finals still belongs in the evaluation, including how Israel handled Greece's defensive pace and why its own shooting never settled into rhythm. The response against Italy matters precisely because it sits alongside that failure rather than pretending to erase it.

Division A status is not a bureaucratic footnote. It preserves the level of competition available to the next under-20 generation, keeps Israel inside the top championship bracket, and protects a pathway that produced consecutive European titles in 2018 and 2019. Relegation would not have broken the system, but it would have narrowed the competitive environment the next group has to grow through -- and Thursday's players secured that environment for athletes who were not even on the floor with them.

Oren Aharoni and his staff should read the result as evidence of a culture holding up under pressure, not proof that every problem has been solved. Classification games remain, and the tournament still needs a full accounting. But the response revealed something no selection camp or warm-up match can manufacture: how quickly these players can accept a changed reality, narrow their focus, and execute when the reward is responsibility rather than celebration.

That is the part worth carrying forward. Keller's scoring and Sahar's efficiency will sit in the box score, but the larger achievement was structural -- a team that defended without chasing redemption on every possession, shared the scoring load, and widened the margin quarter by quarter. Given one night to move from disappointment to duty, Israel's under-20s did it with the calm of a side that understood exactly what was at stake.

title: 2018–19: the two summers that changed Israeli youth basketball
dek: Israel's first FIBA title in Chemnitz was followed by a home defence in Tel Aviv, turning a breakthrough generation into the benchmark for every U20 team that followed.

source.name: FIBA
source.originalTitle: Israel claim historic title at FIBA U20 European Championship

verificationSources.label: FIBA official 2019 tournament record and standings
FIBA official record of Israel's 2017 silver medal

body: Israel's under-20 championship story did not begin with gold. In 2017, the team reached the European final in Crete and lost 65–56 to host Greece before a sold-out crowd. Tamir Blatt made the All-Star Five, but the silver medal left a generation with evidence that the summit was reachable and a clear account of the final step it had failed to take.

One year later in Chemnitz, Israel completed that step. The tournament opened with a defeat by host Germany, then turned into a six-game winning run. France were beaten 83–57 in the semi-final, and previously undefeated Croatia waited in the final. Israel led 45–34 at half-time, absorbed the pressure after the break and won 80–66. It was the country's first gold medal in any FIBA competition.

Yovel Zoosman supplied the defining senior performance of the 2018 final: 17 points, 11 rebounds, four assists and four steals. Captain Gil Beni also scored 17, while Miron Ruina added 14 points and 14 rebounds. The spread was important. This was not one prodigy dragging a youth team through a final; it was a connected guard-led group turning defence, rebounding and shared decisions into a title.

Zoosman was named tournament MVP after averaging 14.4 points, 4.7 rebounds, 3.6 assists and 2.3 steals. Beside him in the All-Star Five was Deni Avdija, only 17 and the youngest player at the tournament. That combination captured the system's immediate strength: players ready to win at their own age and an exceptional younger talent already capable of influencing matches against older opponents.

The defence of the title in 2019 carried a different pressure. Israel hosted the championship, expectations had replaced surprise and Shlomo Arena sold out for the final in five minutes. FIBA recorded 3,500 spectators inside and more than 20,000 people on the waiting list. Spain arrived with the depth and technical quality to test whether the first gold had been a peak or the start of a standard.

The final was tied 42–42 at half-time. Spain opened the third quarter with four consecutive three-pointers, the kind of burst that can turn a home crowd from force into weight. Israel did not fracture. The hosts scored 50 second-half points and won 92–84, becoming only the second team at that time to defend the U20 European title after Serbia's 2007 and 2008 teams.

Avdija and Yam Madar shaped that victory. Avdija finished with 23 points, seven assists, five rebounds and four blocks; Madar added 17 points on 7-of-11 shooting and eight assists. Tomer Porat scored 11, while Raz Adam and Eidan Alber combined for 20. Israel shot 52 percent in the final. The trophy was retained through star quality, but the supporting scores again stopped the opponent from reducing the game to one matchup.

Avdija's tournament numbers explain why the 2019 title became part of a larger basketball story. He averaged 18.4 points, 8.3 rebounds, 5.3 assists, 2.4 blocks and 2.1 steals and was named MVP. Madar joined him in the All-Star Five. Both would move into major professional roles, but the historical achievement belongs to the complete group and to coach Ariel Beit Halahmy's ability to join talent with a coherent tournament team.

Back-to-back titles changed the reference point for Israeli youth basketball. Before Chemnitz, a medal run could be described as an exceptional breakthrough. After Tel Aviv, every strong generation inherited proof that Israel could win at this level, recover inside a final and defend a championship under home expectation. That proof is empowering, but it can also make later teams seem disappointing when development follows a less spectacular route.

The better legacy is not a demand that every under-20 side reproduce gold. It is the pathway those summers made visible: play elite opposition, give young guards responsibility, defend collectively and treat a youth championship as both a competition and an education. The 2026 team's Division A survival win over Italy belongs much lower in the medal hierarchy, yet preserving top-level status protects the environment from which another Zoosman, Avdija or Madar generation might eventually emerge.

title: Hapoel Jerusalem badge vote meets 1,300-signature backlash
dek: Season-ticket holders received alternative designs as part of a wider rebrand, but a fast-moving petition has turned the club’s identity project into a test of supporter trust.

source.author: Sport5 editorial team

body: Hapoel Jerusalem's attempt to refresh their basketball identity has met immediate resistance. A supporter petition against changing the club badge has reached about 1,300 signatures, after season-ticket holders received alternative designs as part of a wider rebranding process — turning what might have remained a marketing exercise into a public argument over who has authority over a club's most recognisable symbol.

The process has already changed course once. A branding company produced an initial design meant to form part of a larger presentation of the club's plans, but that event was postponed and the first proposal did not advance. Revised alternatives were then circulated to season-ticket holders instead. No replacement badge has been adopted, so the current position is consultation under pressure rather than a completed identity change.

The speed of the response is what gives the dispute its weight. An initial count put the petition above 1,200 signatures within roughly two hours of launch; a later update placed it at about 1,300. Those figures do not prove that every supporter opposes a redesign, and they should not be read as a formal referendum. But they do show that a substantial, organised group considers continuity more important than the club expected.

A badge is unusually difficult brand property because it works in two directions at once. Management use it across tickets, merchandise, digital products and sponsorship inventory. Supporters carry it across generations, often long before the current owner, executive team or design agency arrived. Legal control may sit with the organisation, but emotional ownership is distributed through the community.

That tension is sharper because Hapoel have made supporter reconnection a stated strategic goal. In January, chief executive Oren Arieli described returning fans to the Arena, improving transparency and listening more systematically as central parts of the club's long-term plan. The new 2026/27 season-ticket model was also presented as a supporter-centred project designed to reward loyalty and bring families back.

Rebranding can still serve a legitimate purpose. A clearer mark can work better on small screens, simplify merchandise and give commercial partners a consistent system to build around. But design efficiency is not the only measure of success for a sports badge — if the process weakens trust among the very people the club wants to bring home, a technically stronger logo can become a strategically weaker asset.

Hapoel now have several defensible routes open to them: retain the existing badge, modify one of the alternatives, or continue consultation before selecting a new mark. The strongest next step would be to explain the problem the redesign is meant to solve, and to publish how supporter feedback will shape the decision.
Until the club chooses and announces a final badge, the alternatives remain proposals — and the petition remains a warning rather than a verdict.

body: Ironi Ness Ziona have signed Paris Lee to a two-year contract, placing one of the Israeli league's most experienced new guards at the centre of their rebuild. Three reports carry the completed move and contract length, and the 31-year-old arrives directly from a season with UNICS Kazan. This is not a developmental lottery ticket. Ness Ziona are buying decision-making, ball pressure and a large body of elite European work.

EuroLeague's official record lists Lee as a 1.84-metre guard with 128 appearances across Monaco, Panathinaikos and ASVEL between 2021 and 2025. He started 77 of those games, averaging 9.5 points, 3.7 assists and 1.3 steals. Those numbers describe a lead guard who has repeatedly handled possession against switching defences and aggressive pick-and-roll coverage, not a scorer being asked to learn the position.

His most distinctive strength sits at the other end of the floor. Lee led the 2023/24 EuroLeague with 1.7 steals per game, an official competition marker that fits Ness Ziona's need for a guard who can change tempo without waiting for a defensive rebound. Steals alone are not a defensive system, but his ability to disrupt the first pass can create the open-floor possessions that make an athletic roster easier to organise.

UNICS provide the immediate career context. The Russian club's official profile records Lee with the 2025/26 team and identifies him as a VTB United League and WINLINE Basket Cup runner-up. Moving from that environment to Ness Ziona changes both role and expectation: he should receive more control of the offence, but he will also carry greater responsibility for late-clock choices and for developing the guards around him.

The tactical fit begins with pace kept under control. Lee can advance the ball quickly, attack a high screen and still pull a possession back when the first advantage disappears. Ness Ziona need that judgement as much as his individual production, because a roster full of new pieces can look fast while actually playing rushed.

The point guard's job is to tell the difference between an early opportunity and an early mistake. That is the discipline the new-look backcourt will lean on most as it comes together over the season.

The surrounding build is not finished. Adam Ariel and Vincent Amsalem have already been attached to the new group, while Spencer Weisz and T.J. Cline provide continuity from before. If completed, that group would give Lee another ball-handler and a vertical interior target, rather than forcing every possession through a single creator.

Ness Ziona have made a high-upside commitment with a clear test attached. Lee's EuroLeague past raises the floor of the backcourt, but reputation will not space the court, protect the rim or keep the full roster healthy. The two-year term gives the club time to build an identity around him, and the first season will show whether that identity becomes an organised, disruptive team or simply the league's most eye-catching collection of summer names.

body: Tiemoko Diarra has signed for Kasımpaşa, closing off the route that had appeared set to bring him back to Israeli football with Hapoel Tel Aviv. The Istanbul club announced his transfer from Stade de Reims and staged the signing at its Kemerburgaz training facilities, with chief executive Ceyhun Kazancı present. The statement did not specify the length of the contract, so no term should be inferred from the announcement.

Hapoel's failed move was more advanced than casual interest. Three separate accounts agree that the Tel Aviv club had reached a club-to-club understanding with Reims before the negotiation stalled over the player's personal terms. Two of those reports put the proposed fee at €1.7 million, plus a 20 per cent share of any future sale. Neither club has confirmed those financial details, so they remain reported terms rather than a published contract.

That distinction explains the apparent reversal. Agreement between a buying and a selling club can open a transfer, but it cannot complete one without the player accepting his employment terms and clearing the remaining registration steps. Hapoel had a route to Diarra's rights; it never had his signature. Kasımpaşa now do, and their official announcement is the decisive record of where he has landed.

The 23-year-old was an attractive target for the Israeli market because his adaptation risk looked unusually low. Diarra previously played for Hapoel Haifa, and the two most detailed accounts of the move agree on a return of six goals and four assists in 32 appearances during that spell. He can attack from wide positions, threaten the space behind a full-back and carry the ball through transition — qualities Hapoel Tel Aviv still need to find elsewhere.

Kasımpaşa offer a different competitive context. The club's own table records a 13th-place finish in the 2025/26 Turkish top flight, which is neither European qualification nor a protected elite role, but it does keep Diarra in a strong league with a fresh route to senior minutes after his time at Reims. His familiarity with Israeli football may well have strengthened Hapoel's case, but it did not outweigh the package he ultimately accepted in Istanbul.

For Hapoel, the useful lesson is not simply that a target chose another club. A proposed transfer of this size consumes planning time, an international-player slot and a meaningful share of the recruitment budget before it is even completed. When personal terms remain open, the sporting department needs to keep a parallel shortlist alive rather than treat a club-to-club agreement as the finish line.

The collapse also reframes how any replacement should be judged. Matching Diarra's reputation matters less than replacing the functions the squad expected him to provide: direct running, one-against-one threat and a credible scoring contribution from the flank. A central creator or a possession winger would be a different kind of signing, even if the market value looked comparable.

There is no longer any uncertainty about where Diarra will begin the season — Kasımpaşa have made the transfer public and put him under contract. The open question now belongs to Hapoel Tel Aviv: whether the work already invested in this deal can be converted quickly into a player who fits the same tactical need, without paying a premium for having lost its first choice so late in the process.

Two separate reports carry the same figure and the same immediate consequence: the administrative barrier that had kept the 21-year-old out of Beitar's match squad has been lifted.

The number stands out because Ramat Gan had reportedly sought NIS 1.2 million — the award lands at one fifth of that claim. It should not be read as a conventional transfer fee negotiated between clubs. The dispute concerned training and development compensation tied to a player's move, with the figure set through the status process rather than a completed sale agreement.

Warku signed a three-year contract with Beitar in February but stayed with Ramat Gan through the end of their promotion campaign, and that season forms the sporting backdrop to the disagreement. Beitar secured a developing player ahead of the summer; Ramat Gan, in turn, sought recognition for the years spent bringing him through to senior level.

A useful identity check comes from the Israel Football Association's 2022 under-19 squad list, which places Daniel Warku at Hapoel Ramat Gan. It confirms both the spelling of his name and his long association with the club's youth pathway, and it rules out confusion with other similarly named players turning up in registration searches.

Beitar's next league assignment is away to Hapoel Tel Aviv in Netanya on Saturday evening. Reports say the ruling makes Warku eligible to be included, though eligibility is not a promise of selection or minutes — the coaching staff still has to judge whether a player only now emerging from an administrative wait is ready for the match plan.

In tactical terms, Warku represents a different kind of squad option to an established starter. His value lies in mobility, development upside and the capacity to grow into a role across a long season. Beitar do not need this ruling to make him an instant focal point; they need it to restore the normal football process, in which training form and tactical fit decide a player's place.

The gap between the claim and the award will invite scrutiny, but on its own it proves nothing about either club acting unreasonably. Cases like this turn on regulations, documented training history and a player's registration status. Until a public decision record sets out the full reasoning, the safe conclusion is the one both reports agree on: NIS 240,000 was awarded, and registration can now proceed.

Even so, it is a meaningful outcome all round. Ramat Gan receive compensation for a player they developed; Beitar gain certainty at a fraction of the reported demand; and Warku can go back to being judged as a footballer rather than an unresolved file. The registration question is settled. His place in Beitar's team is still his to earn on the pitch.

The contract also balances commitment with control. His recent record supplies evidence of senior competition, not a guaranteed goal total.

dek: The 2001 Portuguese champions must vacate their stadium by 31 July after missing a monthly creditor payment, the latest step in a collapse split across club and football company.

body: Boavista have been ordered to cease the activities the insolvent club runs at the Estádio do Bessa, with the Porto institution required to clear its stadium and adjoining premises by 31 July. The insolvency administrator executed the creditors' closure decision after a monthly payment of €55,000 went unpaid, turning a long financial retreat into an operational shutdown.

The order reaches beyond a senior football result or a licensing penalty. It covers everything Boavista Futebol Clube runs at the Bessa complex, including the club's other sports and development structures. Staff and teams may use the short window before the handover to remove personal property and wind down operations, but the direction of travel is unambiguous: the facilities must be delivered free of people and assets by month's end.

Legal precision matters here, because 'Boavista' contains more than one insolvent body. The member club and the SAD that ran professional football follow connected but distinct processes. A commercial court ordered the SAD into liquidation in May after its recovery plan was withdrawn from a creditor vote. This week's instruction concerns the club establishment and its activities at the stadium — it is not, by itself, a single document dissolving every Boavista legal entity.

The separation has not spared either side the same financial gravity. Public reporting places accumulated debts above €150 million. The club was declared insolvent in 2025 and kept operating only under conditions set by creditors, including recurring payments to cover current costs. Missing the latest instalment activated a mechanism that had already been postponed once, rather than creating a new crisis from an otherwise stable position.

That history is why the shutdown carries more weight than another relegation. Boavista broke Portugal's three-club title grip by winning the league in 2000/01. Two years later they reached the UEFA Cup semi-finals, drawing 1-1 away to Celtic before Henrik Larsson's late goal at the Bessa denied them a place in the final. UEFA's record also shows Boavista eliminating Málaga on that run and winning every home match before the semi-final defeat.

The Bessa was the physical expression of that status. Rebuilt around Euro 2004, it staged Champions League football and housed the club's administrative, sporting and commercial functions. Its loss removes more than a pitch from the balance sheet — a club can replace a training base or rent a ground, but rebuilding the daily network that connects academy teams, other sports, staff and members is a different task altogether, especially with liquidation already consuming the institution's assets.

A recovery attempt is still conceptually possible, through new investment, creditor agreement or a reconstructed sporting organisation. None of that should be reported as secured. The current legal act is the closure order, the missed payment and the deadline to surrender the premises; dissolution and the future ownership of Boavista's sporting identity remain open questions, not facts that can be inferred from the administrator's instruction.

Portuguese football has seen historic clubs fall through the divisions, enter insolvency and reappear in altered form. Boavista's position is harsher because the member institution, the professional company and the stadium have all become entangled in overlapping financial failures. The club that once made the Bessa one of Europe's most difficult away grounds now has two weeks to leave it. Any credible rescue must begin by explaining which Boavista it is saving, what liabilities survive, and where its teams would actually play.

body: Israel's men's under-20 handball team lost 33–31 to the Faroe Islands in the M20 EHF EURO cross match for places 9–16, surrendering a two-goal halftime lead but keeping their route to the 2027 IHF Men's Junior World Championship alive. The official tournament record confirms the final score and the 17–15 interval advantage for Israel.

The arithmetic of the two halves tells the story of the reversal on its own. Israel scored 17 before the break and 14 after it, while the Faroe Islands went from 15 goals in the first half to 18 in the second. That four-goal swing over 30 minutes turned a controlled position into a narrow defeat, with the match still close enough that neither side could build a decisive cushion.

Israel arrived in the placement phase after a volatile preliminary group in Romania, where they beat Bosnia and Herzegovina 43–33 but lost 42–33 to Sweden and 39–31 to the hosts. Israel, Romania and Bosnia finished level on points behind Sweden, and Romania went through to the main round on goal difference. Israel continued instead through the intermediate route.

That distinction shaped Thursday's stakes. The Faroe Islands had already reached the main round and were inside the tournament's leading group, while Israel entered the 9–16 cross matches from the intermediate phase. The Faroese win moves them toward the places 9–12 games; Israel now enter the places 13–16 path, where the final ranking carries a consequence larger than the position itself.

The IHF has set the qualification line for the 2027 Men's Junior World Championship at 15th place. Twelve European teams have already secured their tickets by reaching the M20 EURO main round, leaving three places to be settled lower in the ranking bracket. For Israel, one win across the remaining placement sequence would guarantee a finish no lower than 15th and claim one of those last European berths.

That makes the Faroe defeat painful rather than terminal. Israel no longer have the margin to treat the next match as another development fixture: a victory would complete the qualification job, while another loss would push the decision into the final contest for 15th. The team have already shown they can produce sustained attacking stretches at this level; Thursday's second half exposed how quickly a small defensive decline can undo that work.

The broader value of qualification is competitive continuity, moving this group from a demanding European championship directly into another global age-grade tournament and adding high-level matches just as many of these players begin competing for larger senior roles. The immediate task, though, is much narrower: protect the defensive standard that built the 17–15 lead, find enough second-half scoring to avoid another late squeeze, and turn one of the next two opportunities into a World Championship place.

body: Hapoel Tel Aviv have chosen recognition over reinvention for 2026/27. The club unveiled a red home shirt and a white away strip on Thursday, opening a new cycle with Adidas while keeping the two colours that make the team instantly legible. This is a kit launch built around the Hapoel identity, not a design concept looking for a club to inhabit it.

That restraint is a football decision as much as a retail one. Shirts are seen most often at speed, from the stands or through a broadcast camera, where a strong block of colour carries further than intricate detail. The red home strip preserves that instant recognition, while the white change kit supplies the traditional contrast without severing the visual relationship between the two sets.

The most personal detail sits high on the back. The shirts carry a line meaning ‘My beloved, my red’, placing a familiar expression of attachment where a name or slogan can remain visible after a player has turned away from the camera. It turns supporter language into part of the uniform without asking the front of the shirt to carry another decorative element.

There is also technology inside the crest. Hapoel say the badge on the match shirt contains an NFC chip for the first time, and touching a compatible phone to it opens a club page intended to carry changing material and supporter offers. The same system was introduced in June through a season-ticket promotion involving signed match jerseys, but the launch now makes the connected crest part of the wider shirt proposition.

Adidas supplies the playing kit, training wear and professional equipment from this season, alongside club-specific merchandise collections. That broader agreement raises the standard by which the shirts will be judged, since a supplier change is not only a logo switch — sizing, stock, delivery, training wear and the quality of supporter replicas all determine whether the partnership feels substantial once the launch film has passed.

For Hapoel, the timing links a commercial reset to the start of competitive work. The shirts will move quickly from controlled reveal imagery into European and domestic match conditions, where sponsor placement, numbers and names become part of the complete composition. A clean base gives those compulsory elements room, although the final verdict will belong to supporters when they see the material and fit at close range.

The design argument is therefore quite clear. Hapoel have not tried to manufacture novelty from a club whose visual code is already powerful: red at home, white away, three Adidas stripes and a line of supporter language provide the continuity, while the connected crest supplies the new layer. It is less a costume change than an attempt to modernise the way an old identity is worn.

title: World Cup final seats reach $8,680 in Spain's allocation
dek: Official prices expose a dramatic split between a tightly limited $60 supporter tier and the four-figure cost of most federation-allocation seats for Argentina against Spain.

source.name: Sport1 / Maariv
source.originalTitle: שחקן נבחרת ספרד ניסה להשיג כרטיס לגמר המונדיאל. התשובה היממה אותו
source.author: Sport1 editorial team

FIFA official $60 Supporter Entry Tier announcement
FIFA official tournament schedule and final venue

body: A seat in Spain's official federation allocation for Sunday's World Cup final can cost as much as $8,680. The published table for the Argentina–Spain showpiece lists premium tickets at that figure, with standard seats priced at $5,575 and a value category at $4,185. Those are face values in US dollars, not resale mark-ups — and even the cheapest of the three main categories sits far beyond an ordinary matchday purchase.

The allocation mechanism complicates that headline number. Participating federations receive eight per cent of the net saleable capacity for each of their matches. Spain invited supporters to request knockout tickets before knowing whether the team would advance that far, promising refunds if elimination made a booking unusable. Once Spain qualified for a given knockout match, the federation said there would be no further chance to buy from that allocation.

FIFA has built a sharply different entry point alongside it. Its Supporter Entry Tier fixes a limited share of tickets at $60 for every match, including the final, with each national federation setting its own eligibility and distribution rules for that ten per cent slice of its allocation. FIFA says a further 40 per cent goes to the Supporter Value Tier, leaving the remaining half split evenly between Standard and Premier categories.

The $60 offer is real, but it does not make the final a broadly affordable event. It is a narrow, protected route inside an allocation whose other published prices run into four figures, and demand alone decides how many eligible supporters actually secure it. For everyone outside that tier, the official price table shows that face value can rival the cost of a major holiday — before flights, accommodation and local travel are even added.

This structure reflects FIFA's wider pricing policy. The governing body says it can adapt prices between sales phases after reviewing demand and availability, though it distinguishes that process from automatic dynamic pricing. Its stated goals are to optimise revenue and maximise attendance — objectives that, at a final between two global teams under extreme demand, pull hard against the idea that a meaningful share of the stadium should stay within reach of the fans who followed their teams there.

Argentina and Spain meet at New York New Jersey Stadium on Sunday after contrasting semi-finals. The defending champions recovered from Anthony Gordon's goal to beat England 2–1, while Spain controlled France in a 2–0 win. The final gives Lionel Messi a chance to retain the trophy and Spain a shot at a second men's world title — precisely the kind of occasion where demand will overwhelm any affordable supply.

The real issue, then, is not whether a $60 ticket exists or an $8,680 one finds a buyer. Both can be true at once. What matters is how much of the stadium is genuinely reachable at each price point, and how clearly that distribution is communicated to the public. A final presented as a global occasion now runs on radically different access lanes — a small protected supporter tier, expensive federation categories and a wider market shaped by scarcity. The football will decide the champion. The ticket map has already decided who gets to watch from inside.

The placement matters more than it might first appear. Sleeve inventory travels with the team in every televised match and survives in photographs long after perimeter advertising has left the frame, giving RTMI a constant association with Hapoel's playing identity without displacing the club's front-of-shirt position. Multi-team partnerships let a sponsor speak to one supporter community across different competitions and seasons, while the clubs gain a partner already familiar with the culture and expectations around the name. RTMI owner Stav Shaham supplies a personal link to the club. He previously owned Hapoel Kfar Saba and has been publicly involved with Hapoel Tel Aviv basketball as both sponsor and board member. It is a heritage reference, but not a reproduction: the new shirt places the old palette and texture inside a contemporary Adidas template.

title: Sharp scores 12 as Kings fall to Celtics in Summer League
dek: The Israeli guard added two steals without a turnover but shot 4-of-13 in Sacramento's 82–76 loss, two days after scoring 23 against Brooklyn.

source.name: ONE
source.originalTitle: 12 נקודות לעמנואל שארפ בהפסד סקרמנטו
source.author: ONE editorial team

verificationSources.label: NBA official Boston–Sacramento Summer League box score
NBA official report of Sharp's 23-point game against Brooklyn
