title: Konin and Mazor finish 10th in technical duet at European Aquatics Championships
dek: The Israeli pair produced a clean, penalty-free routine on the opening day in Paris and also advanced to Saturday's free duet final.

verificationSources.label: Wikipedia — Artistic swimming at the 2026 European Aquatics Championships, women's duet technical routine results

body: Israel's artistic swimming duet opened the European Aquatics Championships in Paris with its best kind of statement: a routine with nothing to correct. Katy Konin and Aya Mazor finished 10th in the women's technical duet final on Friday, scoring 260.6284 points in a routine that ONE described as executed cleanly, without penalties or falls, despite carrying genuinely difficult elements.

The result placed the Israeli pair ahead of Georgia, Switzerland, Turkey and Bulgaria in a 19-nation field, with the gold going to Greece's Anna-Maria and Eirini-Marina Alexandri (311.4308), ahead of a Russian-flagged neutral-athletes duet and Great Britain's Kate Shortman and Isabelle Thorpe.

Konin, who swims for Hapoel Jerusalem, and Mazor, of Elah Matzeret Batya, were not done for the day. In the free duet preliminaries they scored 245.0557 points for 11th place, enough to book their spot in Saturday evening's free duet final — a second final in two events on the opening day of the meet.

ONE noted it marked the first time the duo had put together a fully clean technical routine at this level, landing the higher-difficulty elements without the deductions that have cost Israeli swimmers in the past. That kind of execution is what separates mid-table finishes from the medal contenders in a sport where difficulty scores mean little if the judges spot a wobble.

The championships opened Friday at the Olympic Aquatics Centre in Saint-Denis, the venue built for the 2024 Paris Games, and run through August 16 across swimming, diving, water polo, open water and artistic swimming disciplines, with 22 member federations sending artistic swimmers to compete for 11 European titles.

Israeli artistic swimming has been building toward moments like this. Shelly Bobritsky and Ariel Nassee delivered the country's best-ever Olympic finish in the discipline, 11th in the duet at Paris 2024, and Konin and Mazor themselves were part of the Israeli team that reached the free routine final at the 2023 European Games. A top-10 continental finish for the newer pairing suggests that depth is not a one-off.

Saturday's free duet final will be the next test, against a field that includes several of the same technical-final rivals Israel has just outscored. For now, though, the clean sheet in the technical routine is the headline: no falls, no penalties, and a climb past half the continent's artistic swimming powers on the opening day in Paris.

title: Messi's status in doubt as Inter Miami prepare to host Columbus Crew
dek: Fresh off Argentina's World Cup final defeat to Spain, the captain trained with his Inter Miami teammates this week — but interim coach Guillermo Hoyos won't confirm he'll play on Saturday night.
body: Lionel Messi trained with his Inter Miami teammates for the first time this week since Argentina's World Cup final heartbreak, but whether he actually takes the field against Columbus Crew on Saturday night remains an open question.

Messi landed back in Fort Lauderdale on Wednesday, only around ten days after Argentina lost the World Cup final to Spain, well inside the 21-day rest window FIFA grants players after the tournament. He was out on the training pitch with the squad within hours of arriving, ONE reports.

Asked directly about Messi's availability, Inter Miami's interim head coach Guillermo Hoyos stopped short of any promise. "He arrived a short time ago, so we haven't had the chance to discuss it properly yet," Hoyos said. "But we are happy he and De Paul returned."

Rodrigo De Paul, Messi's Argentina teammate and international-tournament roommate, returned to training on the same day and finds himself in an identical spot — back with the club, but with no guarantee of a place in the squad this weekend.

Hoyos only took interim charge of Inter Miami in April, after Javier Mascherano stepped down citing personal reasons just four months after leading the club to its first MLS Cup title. He now faces an early selection dilemma over how to handle his two returning World Cup finalists.

US media reports the club may prefer to be cautious with Messi and hold him back for his official comeback in the Leagues Cup, which opens on Wednesday against Atlético San Luis — part of a group stage that also includes Monterrey and León at home.

The timing is not desperate for Inter Miami. The club arrives on a six-match unbeaten run and sits second in the MLS Eastern Conference, two points behind leaders Nashville SC in the race for the Supporters' Shield.

They will still be shorthanded regardless of Messi's status. Forward Germán Berterame remains out after being taken away by ambulance following a head collision in the win over CF Montreal on July 25, while Telasco Segovia and Ian Fray are suspended and Tadeo Allende is sidelined through injury.
For now, Inter Miami fans will have to wait until closer to kickoff to learn whether their captain features — with the club seemingly in no rush to rush him back before he is ready.

title: Maccabi Tel Aviv weigh Oz Bilu alongside foreign options for vacant wing berth
dek: The Maccabi Netanya winger is back on the champions' radar as a contingency plan while the club chases replacements for Amir Sahiti, who is reluctant to return to Israel.

verificationSources.label: ONE - מכבי ת"א בודקת את בילו
Sport5 - עוז בילו הפך למשתכר הישראלי הבכיר במכבי נתניה
Israel Hayom - קיפאון במגעים עם מכבי תל אביב: הצעד של אמיר סהיטי
Maccabi Tel Aviv FC - אסטר סוקלר מצטרף למכבי

body: Maccabi Tel Aviv have quietly reopened a file they closed a year ago. According to ONE, the champions are examining Oz Bilu, the Maccabi Netanya winger, as a possible Israeli solution for the wing spot left open by Amir Sahiti — even as the club continues to send offers to foreign candidates for the same position.

The urgency stems from Sahiti's situation. The winger, who joined on loan from Hamburg in January and impressed enough to earn a permanent move over the summer, has told the club he is reluctant to return to Israel because of the security situation, and talks over his terms for next season have stalled. Maccabi Tel Aviv have publicly played down the crisis, but the practical effect is a hole on the flank that needs filling before the season restarts.

Bilu's name is not a new one at Kiryat Shalom. ONE reports he was on Maccabi Tel Aviv's radar last year too, before the club moved instead for Sahiti and shelved the interest. With that deal now in doubt, the 25-year-old has resurfaced as a fallback option — one the club is described as monitoring regardless of whether a foreign winger is signed first.

The renewed attention is easy to explain on form alone. Bilu just produced the best season of his senior career at Netanya, scoring ten goals and adding four assists in 31 league appearances, output that made him the club's leading Israeli earner and prompted Netanya to lock him into a contract through 2027/28.

Maccabi Tel Aviv's recruitment picture is unusually crowded. The club currently has eight foreign players registered following the arrival of Slovenian striker Aster Sokler, signed this month from Serbia's Radnicki Kragujevac for close to a million euros on a two-year deal with an option for two more. Sokler will wear the number 9 shirt.

That leaves little room to maneuver, and ONE notes the club still has to find solutions for Kervin Andrade, the Venezuelan forward bought from Fortaleza last year, and for Ion Nicolaescu, the Moldovan winger whose roster slot may effectively be frozen until January because of injury.

Separately, Maccabi Tel Aviv are due to learn on Monday whether UEFA will impose sanctions over pyrotechnics let off during their European qualifier against Sheriff Tiraspol in Batumi, with the club already carrying a suspended ban on selling tickets for one away fixture from an earlier incident involving Stuttgart fans.

For now, Bilu remains an option rather than a target with a fee attached. But with the foreign quota nearly exhausted and Sahiti's return in genuine doubt, Maccabi Tel Aviv's interest in one of the league's in-form Israeli wingers is unlikely to cool.

title: Real Madrid's academy graduates hand the club over €180 million this summer
dek: Without a single first-team departure, Real Madrid have banked a fortune from selling on La Fábrica products such as Nico Paz, Gonzalo García and Víctor Muñoz — more than they have spent on new signings, ONE reports.

verificationSources.label: Managing Madrid - Víctor Muñoz to Liverpool

body: Real Madrid have not sold a single first-team player this summer, yet the club's finance department is having one of its best windows in years — courtesy of a production line that never stops paying dividends. ONE reports that La Fábrica, the club's storied academy, has generated more than €180 million in transfer income since June, almost entirely from graduates who spent their careers away from the Bernabéu first team.

The figure, according to the report, comfortably exceeds the roughly €105 million Real Madrid have spent so far on squad reinforcements this summer — meaning the academy alone has effectively bankrolled the club's market activity, before any of the marquee incoming deals still being discussed are finalised.

The single biggest windfall came from Nico Paz. Como paid Real Madrid €60 million to turn the Argentina international's loan spell into a permanent transfer, with Los Blancos inserting a buyback clause reported to be worth around €80 million and a right of first refusal for the summer of 2027 — the classic La Fábrica structure of selling young but never quite letting go.

Paz made only a handful of senior appearances for Real Madrid before joining Como, but his stock has soared since: he starred for Argentina at this summer's World Cup, and Tottenham had been rebuffed by Como in an earlier attempt to sign him for a much larger fee.

Gonzalo García, who scored freely for Real Madrid during last year's Club World Cup run before falling down the pecking order, is moving to Fulham for a fee reported at around €40 million plus add-ons. Real Madrid have kept a 30 percent sell-on clause and a buyback option on the striker, who is set to link up with former Real Madrid Castilla coach Álvaro Arbeloa at Craven Cottage.

Víctor Muñoz's move to Liverpool is worth roughly €40 million in total, with Real Madrid pocketing around half of that fee under the terms agreed when the winger left the club. It is another example of the model: Madrid parts with a player it is not ready to promote to the first team but keeps a stake in his next transfer.

Smaller sums add up too. A sell-on percentage from Mario Gila's move — his rights were split between Madrid and Lazio after his 2022 departure — brought in a further payment when he was transferred on to Milan this summer, while the Uruguayan forward Álvaro Rodríguez's switch to Bournemouth is reported to have added roughly another €15 million to the academy's summer haul, again on a shared-rights basis.

ONE frames the number as "incomprehensible" for a graduate pipeline that, on paper, has produced few outright starters in Xabi Alonso's current squad. But the business model has become one of the most lucrative in European football: Madrid rarely sells outright, instead retaining sell-on percentages and buyback clauses that keep generating income long after a player has left Valdebebas.

Spanish outlets have reported broadly similar figures for the summer haul, with some outfits, including VAVEL and El Español, putting the cumulative academy income closer to €186–200 million once every minor deal and add-on is counted — a reminder that even the precise total is a moving target as clauses are triggered through August.

Real Madrid's academy has now generated close to €600 million in transfer income over the past two decades, a sum the club's hierarchy points to as proof that La Fábrica pays for itself even in years when none of its graduates make the breakthrough into Florentino Pérez's star-studded first team.

title: Leonid Kaufman lays out his plan to turn Gorbenko into an Olympic medal contender by 2028
dek: Israel's veteran swimming coach, back in charge after Paris, says a fully focused four-year cycle could carry Anastasia Gorbenko into multiple finals — and perhaps a medal — in Los Angeles

verificationSources.label: Wikipedia - Swimming at the 2012 Summer Olympics, Men's 200m backstroke

body: Leonid Kaufman is 67 years old, has already taken Israeli swimmers to five Olympic Games, and is now back in the pool deck chair with one target in mind: Los Angeles 2028. About a year and a half after Paris, the national team coach has laid out, in detail, how he intends to get Anastasia Gorbenko from a world and European medallist to a genuine Olympic finals contender — and, he believes, a possible medallist.

"If she dedicates herself to swimming as her primary focus for a full Olympic cycle, she could reach finals in multiple events and dream of an Olympic medal," Kaufman said, according to ONE. It is a bold framing from a coach who does not hand out such assessments lightly — his own Olympic benchmark for Israeli swimming is the seventh-place finish Yakov Toumarkin produced in the 200m backstroke final at London 2012, still the best Olympic result an Israeli swimmer has ever posted.

Kaufman coached Toumarkin to that result and led the national team through five Olympiads before Rio 2016 ended in disappointment. His return to the job, roughly 18 months after Gorbenko and the rest of the squad competed in Paris, was built specifically around one four-year project: preparing the team, and Gorbenko above all, for 2028.

Gorbenko has already made her own history for Israeli swimming, collecting medals at world and European championship level and setting national records across the medley and backstroke disciplines. Her best event remains the 200m individual medley, according to Kaufman, though he expects her programme in Los Angeles could also stretch to the 400m medley, the 100m backstroke or the 100m breaststroke.

The strategy for getting there, as Kaufman describes it, marks a deliberate break from the approach of previous cycles. Gorbenko will skip the European Championships entirely in the Olympic year itself, freeing the calendar for a block of three consecutive altitude training camps built purely around peaking for the Games. She will be 25 in Los Angeles — the same age she was, effectively at her competitive peak, when she swam in Paris in 2024.

Kaufman's optimism comes against a backdrop of real attrition on the national team. Three swimmers who carried the squad through recent cycles — Gal Cohen Grumi, 23, Tomer Frankel, 24, and Ron Polonsky — have retired in the past period. The coach attributes the departures to burnout after years of gruelling training combined with the financial reality of the sport: swimmers in Israel earn far less support than athletes in more heavily funded disciplines, making it hard to justify staying in the pool into their mid-20s without a clear payoff.

There is also a structural challenge Kaufman is candid about: roughly 90 percent of the current national team trains through American college programmes rather than under his day-to-day supervision in Israel. He calls it "a compromise" — one that gives swimmers scholarships, competition and high-level facilities, but limits how much direct influence he has over their training in the years between major championships.

Beyond the Gorbenko project, Kaufman set out benchmarks for the team as a whole heading into the next European Championships: 10 to 12 semi-final appearances, five finals, and at least one medal. He also named a specific target for the men's 4x200m freestyle relay — a time of 7:06, which would represent a significant step forward for a squad still rebuilding after this year's retirements.

None of it is guaranteed, and Kaufman's own language — "could reach," "dream of a medal" — reflects a plan rather than a promise. But for a federation short on funding and now short on senior swimmers too, a coach with an Olympic finalist already on his résumé setting out a specific, altitude-camp-by-altitude-camp route to Los Angeles is itself the news: after Rio's disappointment and Paris's mixed results, Israeli swimming again has a stated destination for its biggest star.

title: Hapoel Rishon LeZion demand NIS 1.134 million for Zrihan's release
dek: The Institute for Player Status must weigh the National League club's training-compensation claim against the departing defender's bid for a nominal fee, after WhatsApp messages surfaced showing he had offers from abroad under review.

verificationSources.label: ONE report on the Institute for Player Status filing and the NIS 1,134,000 claim
ONE player profile confirming Roei Zrihan's identity and Hapoel Rishon LeZion affiliation

body: Hapoel Rishon LeZion have taken their pursuit of training compensation for departing defender Roei Zrihan to Israeli football's Institute for Player Status, demanding NIS 1,134,000 for a player they raised from the youth ranks into a fixture of their first team, ONE reports.

Zrihan, 24, is a product of Rishon LeZion's academy who worked his way up through the under-19 side and went on to make roughly 220 official appearances over five seasons in the National League, the country's second tier. As he now moves on from the club, the size of that contribution sits at the heart of the dispute.

Under Israeli football's status rules, a club that develops a young player through its youth system can seek development and training compensation when he leaves, particularly when no transfer fee changes hands directly. It is that mechanism Rishon LeZion have now invoked, and the figure they are seeking is a substantial one for a club at National League level.

The club's submission to the panel is blunt. "All the player's efforts to evade payment of fair and proper compensation are based on false factual claims," Rishon LeZion said, according to ONE, casting Zrihan's resistance to the demand as an attempt to dodge money the club believes it is owed after five years of development.

Zrihan and his attorney see it very differently. They are asking the Institute to grant a full exemption or, failing that, to cap any payment at a symbolic NIS 40,000 — a fraction of the club's claim. Central to their argument is a complaint about how his exit was handled: "the club chose not to offer any new contract and did not conduct genuine negotiations," the attorney told ONE.

That argument has been complicated by evidence that has emerged during the proceedings. WhatsApp messages from June 2026, cited by ONE, show Zrihan telling the club at the time: "I have several offers from abroad that we're examining." The messages cut against any suggestion that he lacked market interest, a point that could work in the club's favour when the panel weighs the size of the award.

For a National League side like Rishon LeZion, training compensation rulings of this kind are not a peripheral matter. Academy graduates who move on for little or no fee are one of the few revenue streams available to clubs outside the top flight, and a six-figure award would be a meaningful sum for a club competing below Ligat HaAl.

No ruling has yet been issued. The Institute for Player Status will now have to weigh the club's account of a player it developed for half a decade against Zrihan's case that he was allowed to leave without a genuine effort to keep him — with the WhatsApp evidence likely to loom large over wherever the panel eventually lands.

title: Monaco basketball excluded from French league after financial collapse
dek: The reigning French champions are barred from both major domestic divisions and next season's EuroLeague after owner Alexey Fedorychev's frozen assets triggered a debt crisis a last-ditch takeover could not resolve in time.
body: AS Monaco Basket, the reigning champions of France, have been formally shut out of both professional divisions of French basketball for the 2026-27 season, ONE reports, after a rescue plan aimed at saving the club collapsed in the final hours before a federation deadline.

The French Basketball Federation's Appeals Chamber confirmed the exclusion after Monaco failed to submit the financial guarantees and documentation it had been given until July 31 to produce, ending a month-long fight to keep Europe's most star-studded club roster intact for another season.

The saga began on July 3, when the DNCCG, French basketball's financial oversight body, refused to admit Monaco into either the Betclic Élite, the country's top flight, or the second-tier Élite 2, citing insufficient guarantees over the club's economic viability and the slow progress of an ownership takeover.

At the heart of the crisis is Alexey Fedorychev, Monaco's majority owner and principal sponsor since 2022, whose assets were frozen amid international legal proceedings, including a reported seizure of roughly 41 million euros in Italy. The fallout left the club unable to pay wages on time and drew repeated financial penalties from the EuroLeague over the past season.

Monaco's obligations were put at around 24 million euros, including some 8 million euros in liabilities recorded at the end of June, on top of 16 million euros the Principality of Monaco had already advanced as guarantor simply to let the club finish last season and its EuroLeague playoff run.

Given a hearing before the Appeals Chamber on July 20, the club won a further ten days to finalize a takeover and hand over a bank guarantee. That lifeline centred on former NBA All-Star Jamal Mashburn, whose investment vehicle, Helen Holdings, was negotiating to take over from Fedorychev and had proposed slashing the budget to somewhere between 10 and 12.5 million euros for next season.

For a moment it looked as though the deal might land: French outlets reported the Appeals Chamber was expected to validate the takeover once a roughly 7 million euro bank guarantee was lodged. It never arrived in time, and the federation confirmed Monaco simply "was not able to produce the requested documents within the allotted timeframe."

The consequence is stark. Monaco, French champions for the third time in four seasons, are barred not only from the Betclic Élite and Élite 2 but also lose their place in next season's EuroLeague as a direct result of the domestic ban.

The club retains a theoretical route to challenge the decision, first before the National Olympic Committee and then, if needed, the Administrative Court, but neither avenue is likely to restore Monaco's place before the new season's rosters and schedules are locked in.

For a club that built one of the EuroLeague's most competitive rosters in recent years around captain Mike James, the ruling effectively dissolves the team as constructed, with players and staff now expected to seek new clubs before the season begins elsewhere.

The club can still appeal to the CNOSF and then the Administrative Court, though this is unlikely to restore its league place before the new season.

title: Solomon sets up Tonali as Tottenham beat Chelsea 2-1, but Spurs 'don't use him enough'
dek: The Israeli winger's assist for Sandro Tonali's first Spurs goal drew praise from English media in Sydney, even as his long-term future at Tottenham remains unresolved.
body: Manor Solomon spent the winter shuttled between two loan clubs and out of Tottenham's plans. On Saturday, in front of a sell-out 80,363 crowd at Sydney's Accor Stadium, he gave English football writers reason to ask why Spurs keep leaving him out.

The Israeli winger set up Sandro Tonali's first goal in Tottenham colours as Spurs beat Chelsea 2-1 in the Sydney Super Cup, a feisty pre-season friendly that also produced a Kevin Danso red card three minutes into the second half and a stoppage-time winner from Richarlison.

Solomon's pass found Tonali arriving late into the box; the Italian's side-footed effort took a deflection off Levi Colwill and wrong-footed the goalkeeper. Chelsea levelled four minutes later through Estevao, before Danso's dismissal for scything down Joao Pedro left Tottenham to see out the win with ten men.

According to ONE, the assist and Solomon's overall display drew pointed praise from the English press covering the match. Football London gave him a 7 out of 10 rating and wrote that he "looked lively," adding that Tottenham "doesn't use him enough" and that he was one of the few Spurs players to repeatedly exploit the team's quick transitions.

The BBC's coverage singled him out too, describing "a wonderful assist with a precise cross from the Israeli" that put Tottenham back in front, while a Tottenham supporters' site credited him with "a smart assist" for Tonali's opener.

The reviews land at an awkward moment. Solomon only returned to north London for pre-season after a loan at Villarreal was cut short in January and he was immediately sent out again, to Fiorentina in Serie A, where he made 16 appearances and scored twice.

Spurs Web reported this week that manager Roberto De Zerbi has already told the 26-year-old he is not part of his plans for the season, with the club open to letting him leave permanently rather than out on another loan. "I also know he really appreciates me, but the situation at Tottenham is different," Solomon said of his relationship with the Italian coach, who previously worked with him at Shakhtar Donetsk.
Fiorentina are reported to retain interest in a permanent deal but want Tottenham to significantly lower their asking price, leaving the two clubs some way apart with the transfer window still open.

Solomon has been down this road before. Since joining Tottenham from Shakhtar Donetsk in 2023, he has rarely settled, with injuries and squad competition pushing him out on loan for three of his four seasons at the club, including a productive spell at Leeds United during their Championship-winning 2024-25 campaign.

Saturday's assist changes little about his immediate prospects at Tottenham. But if pre-season notices from the English press are any guide, there are already voices in London wondering whether letting him go would be a mistake.

title: US Open final tickets top $20,000 as tournament's money machine hits new highs
dek: Resale seats for the men's singles final at Flushing Meadows have climbed past $20,900, ONE reports, as the USTA's soaring revenues collide with an $800 million redevelopment of the site.

verificationSources.label: Sportico - USTA Enters U.S. Open With $624M In Revenue
Tennis365 - US Open ticket prices revealed

body: Less than a month before the year's last Grand Slam gets under way at Flushing Meadows, ticket prices for the US Open have reached levels that even seasoned observers of the sport's economics are calling startling, according to a report by ONE.

Resale seats for the men's singles final on September 13 are changing hands for more than $20,900 apiece, the outlet reports, with the tournament's American Express presale window drawing enormous demand from fans chasing a seat inside Arthur Ashe Stadium for the sport's biggest American night.

It is not only the showpiece finals driving the market. A resale ticket for a Roger Federer exhibition appearance sold for nearly $12,000, ONE reports, while even first-round seats at Arthur Ashe are listed above $400. A basic grounds-pass ticket starts at $65 - the cheapest route in, though hardly cheap by the standards of American sport.

This year's tournament runs from August 31 to September 13, and the prize fund on offer has grown alongside the ticket prices: total prize money stands at $90 million, up 20 percent on last year, with the singles champions - men's and women's - each collecting $5 million.

The numbers reflect just how lucrative the US Open has become for its governing body. The United States Tennis Association reported $623.8 million in overall revenue, with $559.6 million of that - the vast majority - generated by the championship itself.

That translated into an operating profit of more than $277 million for the event, underlining why the USTA has both the appetite and the resources to keep pushing prices upward even as it invests heavily elsewhere on site.

Much of that investment is going into an $800 million redevelopment of the Flushing Meadows complex, a project ONE frames as central to understanding the tournament's pricing strategy: the USTA is leaning on record ticket revenue and hospitality demand to help fund the upgrade.

For the ordinary fan hoping to walk through the gates for a session of first-week tennis, the arithmetic is becoming steadily less forgiving - a trend ONE notes is fuelling wider debate in the tennis world about who, increasingly, a Grand Slam is actually for.

title: Israel's women beat Haudenosaunee 7-4 to win first-ever lacrosse world championship medal
dek: A perfect group stage, an upset of Australia and a bronze-medal statement in Tokyo — Israeli women's lacrosse has never had a week like this one.

verificationSources.label: USA Lacrosse — Haudenosaunee, Israel make historic statements
USA Lacrosse — USA downs Israel, headed to world championship game
World Lacrosse — day six quarterfinal recap

body: Israel's women's lacrosse team made history in Tokyo on Sunday, beating the Haudenosaunee Nationals 7-4 in the bronze-medal match to claim the country's first-ever medal at a World Lacrosse Women's Championship.

Israel controlled the contest from the opening whistle at the Prince Chichibu Memorial Rugby Ground, leading 3-0 after the first quarter and pulling clear to 6-1 by halftime. Haudenosaunee, the Iroquois Confederacy's national side, cut into the deficit after the break but could not find a way back into the game, ONE reported.

The bronze caps an extraordinary run through the sixteen-team tournament for a program that had never previously reached a semifinal, let alone a medal match. Israel went 4-0 in the group stage, beating the Philippines, the Czech Republic and host nation Japan.

The signature result came in the quarterfinals, where Israel stunned fourth-ranked Australia 12-11 — snapping the Australians' run of never having missed the tournament's top four since the championship began in 1982. Hanna Hilcoff scored four goals in that win.

That victory sent Israel into a first-ever semifinal, where the United States proved too strong, winning 19-7 on July 31 to advance to the gold-medal game against Canada, which had beaten Haudenosaunee 18-5 in the other semifinal.

The defeat to the Americans set up Sunday's bronze-medal meeting with Haudenosaunee, a fixture billed beforehand as a historic first for whichever side won it — neither nation had ever medalled at a women's world championship.

Jordyn Lipkin was named Player of the Match after the bronze-medal win and finished as the tournament's leading scorer overall, with 19 goals and six assists for 25 points across the championship, according to ONE.
"It's a tremendous honour to represent something far greater than us," Lipkin said after the final whistle, calling the achievement one of the best feelings in the world.

Ian Kadish, chief executive of the Israel Lacrosse Association, said the squad "made history and brought Israel its first world championship medal," while Arik Kaplan — president and chief executive of Ayelet, Israel's federation for non-Olympic sports — said the team "proved today that it belongs among the world's elite."

The medal lands at a symbolic moment for the sport in Israel: lacrosse returns to the Olympic programme at Los Angeles 2028 for the first time in more than a century, giving a fast-growing but still niche Israeli program a marquee reason to build on Tokyo's breakthrough.

title: Itamar Chizhik blasts players' committee reform as 'shame and disgrace'
dek: The former Maccabi Haifa chief executive, who quit as chairman of the Israeli Football Association's player status body over the shake-up, says clubs and young players are being treated 'like an Excel spreadsheet' — and predicts Haifa itself won't challenge for the title this season.

verificationSources.label: Sport1/Maariv — Player Status Institute heads resign over reform
Sport5 — Worko signs for Beitar, compensation to be decided
Walla Sport — Daniel Worko signs for Beitar Jerusalem
ONE — Refaelov appointed Maccabi Haifa's professional director

body: Itamar Chizhik does not do half-measures when he is angry, and on Israeli sports channel ONE this week he let go with both barrels at the reform that just swept through Israeli football's player status system. "Players are not an Excel spreadsheet — it's a shame and a disgrace, what's being done," he said, in an interview that doubled as a farewell shot at the body he used to lead.

Chizhik, for close to fifteen years the chief executive of Maccabi Haifa before stepping down in 2016, later returned to the game as chairman of the Israeli Football Association's Player Status Institute — the panel that rules on compensation disputes when young players move between clubs. He has just resigned that post, after the association pushed through changes that folded the institute's powers into a new arbitration body staffed largely by legal arbitrators rather than football people.

His central complaint is process. "Not only did nobody speak to me, nobody spoke to the committee," Chizhik said, arguing the shake-up rides roughshod over the association's own bylaws, which he says spell out exactly how such decisions must be reached. Among the practical changes he singled out: the panel of arbitrators has been cut from three to one, a reduction he says removes the checks and balances that used to shape rulings on sensitive transfer disputes.

To illustrate what he means by clubs being reduced to numbers on a spreadsheet, Chizhik pointed to the case of Daniel Worko, the young Israel youth international who left Hapoel Ramat Gan for Beitar Jerusalem this year. Hapoel Ramat Gan, who developed him, had sought roughly 1.2 million shekels in development compensation; the panel settled on just 240,000 shekels. "That's simply a shame and a disgrace," Chizhik said, framing it as a case study in how the new mechanism undervalues the clubs that actually raise talent.

The wider worry he raised is structural: if compensation caps are set too low, academies and lower-division clubs lose the financial incentive to keep developing players, since they will rarely see a meaningful return once those players move on to bigger clubs.

Chizhik then turned to the club he ran for the best part of two decades. Maccabi Haifa, he said flatly, will not be competing for the championship this season. His reasoning centred on a squad he considers short at the back and thin up front — he described the team as having only one genuine senior striking option, with alternatives fit mainly to be introduced from the bench late in matches rather than to start and carry a title challenge.

He also took aim at the club's off-field restructuring, questioning the decision to install Lior Refaelov — the former Belgian-league star only recently retired from playing — as Maccabi Haifa's professional director. Chizhik suggested Refaelov, appointed to the role in late May, would be better used as a coaching consultant close to the pitch than as the executive shaping the club's broader football strategy, and argued Haifa would be better served trusting its academy graduates than chasing further outside recruitment.

Asked about the supporter unrest that has trailed Maccabi Haifa into the new season — the Green Apes ultras group has staged stand walkouts and banner protests targeting owner Yaakov "Yankele" Shachar — Chizhik sided with the club's ownership. He said the fans had "crossed a line of good taste" with their demonstrations, adding that Shachar's contribution to the club over the years deserved more credit than the protests were giving him.

Taken together, it was a rare public airing of grievances from one of the more respected administrative figures in Israeli football — aimed as much at the corridors of the association as at his old club's boardroom.

title: About 2,000 Hapoel Tel Aviv fans secure tickets for Katowice clash in Miskolc
dek: The club is expecting roughly 3,500 supporters to turn Hungary into a home fixture for the Conference League qualifier, even as it awaits a UEFA ruling over pyrotechnics

verificationSources.label: boon.hu - Hapoel Tel Aviv creates home ground in Miskolc
Sky Sports - Hapoel Tel Aviv vs GKS Katowice

body: Hapoel Tel Aviv's supporters are once again making the trip across Europe in force: around 2,000 fans have already bought tickets for the club's Conference League third qualifying round first leg against GKS Katowice, ONE reports, with the club anticipating a final crowd of roughly 3,500.

The match, scheduled for August 6, will again be played in Miskolc, Hungary, where Hapoel have based their European "home" fixtures because of the security situation in Israel. It is a routine now for the club and its fan base — pack flights and buses east, and turn a rented Hungarian stadium into as close to Bloomfield Stadium as circumstances allow.

Reaching this stage already represents a landmark European run for Hapoel, who won through their second qualifying round tie against Ludogorets of Bulgaria to set up the meeting with the Polish side. Katowice arrive off the back of their own qualification exploits domestically.

But the ticket-sale news comes with a disciplinary shadow hanging over the club. According to ONE, UEFA has yet to rule on an incident involving flares set off by Hapoel supporters during the away leg in Bulgaria against Ludogorets, with a decision still pending.

That case follows an existing sanction: Hapoel were fined €25,000 by UEFA over pyrotechnics set off during the first leg against Ludogorets in Miskolc. The club is also carrying a suspended partial stadium closure — a conditional 10 percent shutdown of the crowd at its next home European fixture, valid for a two-year period — should further incidents occur.

None of that appears to be denting appetite among the fan base. Hapoel's ultras have built a reputation as some of the most vocal travelling support in Israeli football, and the away-from-home European campaign has, if anything, sharpened that identity — with Miskolc functioning as an adopted home end for successive rounds.

For now the disciplinary matters remain a background concern rather than an active threat to this fixture; the pending Ludogorets ruling and the standing fine do not affect Hapoel's eligibility to play the Katowice tie as scheduled.
The second leg is due in Poland, with Hapoel looking to build on home advantage — in spirit, if not literally on Israeli soil — before travelling for the return.

title: Shtilman raises bid for Maccabi Tel Aviv's Recanati stake to $120 million
dek: Rapyd chief executive Arik Shtilman has gone back to Udi and Shai Recanati with a sweetened, non-binding offer for their 58% of the basketball club, up from $100 million, alongside a pledge to inject a further $30 million with no strings attached.
body: Arik Shtilman, the Rapyd chief executive who has bankrolled Maccabi Tel Aviv's basketball team as principal sponsor, has come back to the club's controlling family with a bigger number. ONE reports that Shtilman has submitted a fresh, non-binding offer to buy the Recanati family's 58% stake in the club for $120 million — a $20 million jump on the $100 million bid he tabled only weeks earlier.

The new proposal is not just about the headline price. According to the report, Shtilman has also committed to injecting a further $30 million directly into Maccabi's accounts immediately upon completion, with no strings attached — meaning the club's other shareholders would not need to stump up matching capital or see their holdings diluted to unlock the cash.

It is the latest twist in a messy ownership saga that has played out over the Israeli summer. Shtilman, whose company Rapyd lends its name to the team as Maccabi Rapyd Tel Aviv, signed on as principal sponsor under a seven-year deal worth $3 million a year, or $21 million in total.

He later moved to deepen his involvement by buying into Dani Felderman's Padanco Sport, acquiring 14.5% of Felderman's 29% holding in the club as part of a wider plan — alongside other investors — to pump $30 million into Maccabi and take a seat on its board.

That plan was upended when the Recanati family exercised its right of first refusal under the club's shareholders' agreement, buying out Padanco's entire 29% stake for a reported $50 million. The move lifted Udi and Shai Recanati's combined holding to 58%, handing them clear control and effectively shutting Shtilman out of the ownership structure he had been trying to enter.

Shtilman's response has been to go over the top of that deal with an outright buyout offer for the family's stake — first at $100 million, and now at $120 million plus the additional $30 million cash injection. Whether the Recanatis, who have only just consolidated control, have any appetite to sell is unclear; ONE's report characterises the offer as non-binding, and there has been no public response from the family confirming or rejecting it.

The saga underlines how unsettled the ownership picture remains at Israel's most decorated basketball club, even as it prepares for another EuroLeague campaign. For now, the figures are Shtilman's alone — the next move belongs to the Recanatis.

title: World Cup sensation Vozinha lands in Chile to a hero's welcome from Colo Colo fans
dek: Hundreds of supporters packed Santiago's airport in the middle of the night to greet the 40-year-old Cape Verde goalkeeper, whose heroics at the 2026 World Cup turned him from journeyman into a global phenomenon with almost 30 million new followers.
body: Around 600 Colo Colo supporters, some with children in tow on a winter Sunday night, packed the international arrivals hall at Santiago's Arturo Merino Benítez Airport to greet a 40-year-old goalkeeper from an island nation of half a million people most of them had never heard of two months earlier.

Vozinha, the Cape Verde shot-stopper whose real name is Josimar José Évora Dias, touched down close to 20:30 local time between Sunday and Monday, stepping off an Airbus A350 into a wall of chants of "¡Vozinha es de Chile!", white flags and, in an unusual touch, the blue-and-white colours of Cape Verde waved by fans who had adopted him as their own before he had even signed.

He emerged roughly half an hour later alongside sports manager Daniel Morón into what one Chilean outlet described as a cauldron of noise, and thanked the crowd in Spanish for their patience through a signing process delayed by several days of migration paperwork and personal matters.

The scenes capped an extraordinary rise. Two months ago Vozinha was a veteran net-minder plying his trade for Chaves in Portugal's second tier, largely unknown outside the small football world of Cape Verde, which was appearing at its first ever World Cup.

He became the story of the tournament almost by accident, keeping a scoreless draw against Spain — the side that would go on to lift the trophy — with seven saves in that match alone and 18 across Cape Verde's run to the last 32, making him the oldest goalkeeper on record to keep a clean sheet on his World Cup debut.

FIFA later named him to its official Team of the Tournament, a squad that also featured Lionel Messi, Kylian Mbappé, Erling Haaland and Michael Olise — remarkable company for a player who had spent his career bouncing between clubs in Cape Verde, Angola, Moldova, Portugal, Cyprus and Slovakia.

The football briefly became a secondary story. His Instagram following exploded from around 50,000 before the tournament to close to 30 million, a rate of growth that turned him into one of the most talked-about athletes on the planet during the World Cup's closing weeks.

Colo Colo moved to capitalise, with club president Aníbal Mosa confirming an agreement for the free agent before his travel to Chile for a medical and formal unveiling. Chile's most decorated club — 34-time domestic champions — currently top the Primera División table with 39 points from 13 wins and three defeats, 13 clear of second-placed Universidad Católica.

For a club already running away with the league, the addition of the World Cup's most viral goalkeeper is as much a marketing coup as a football one — though after his display against Spain, few in Chile are treating it as a gimmick.

title: UEFA threatens legal action against Infantino and FIFA over collapsed investment plan
dek: European football's governing body says it is weighing litigation, arbitration and regulatory complaints over the abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise scheme, and has warned Infantino against destroying evidence.
body: UEFA has told FIFA president Gianni Infantino it is actively weighing legal action against him personally and against world football's governing body, in a dramatic escalation of the fallout from FIFA's abandoned plan to sell a stake in its own commercial rights to outside investors.

A letter sent by UEFA to Infantino, disclosed by The Telegraph and reported in Israel by ONE, states that European football's governing body is "actively considering legal steps, arbitration procedures and/or filing regulatory complaints" over the collapsed venture known as FIFA Forward Enterprise, or FFE.

FFE was unveiled by FIFA on July 28 as a new commercial subsidiary that would take over the sale of marketing and broadcast rights for FIFA's flagship events, including the World Cup and the Club World Cup. The plan envisaged selling roughly a fifth of the new entity to private investors, with FIFA reportedly pitching a valuation of around $20 billion and seeking to raise as much as $4.2 billion.

The proposed lead investor was Thrive Eternal, a firm launched earlier this year by businessman Joshua Kushner, brother of Jared Kushner, with JPMorgan Chase working alongside FIFA to structure the deal.

The scheme triggered an almost immediate revolt. UEFA, CONCACAF and Asian football's governing body all voiced fierce opposition, and a wave of national federations effectively threatened to boycott the project, arguing FIFA was moving to privatize control over the sport's biggest prize without proper consultation.

Facing that backlash, Infantino reversed course and shelved the plan over the weekend, just a day before UEFA's letter became public. But the retreat has not repaired the damage to FIFA's relationship with its European counterpart.

UEFA's letter goes further than simply objecting to the now-scrapped scheme: it explicitly instructs FIFA and Infantino to preserve every document and piece of electronic correspondence relating to FFE, a standard pre-litigation step aimed at guarding against the destruction of evidence that could be used in future proceedings.

UEFA did not stop at Infantino. According to the reporting, it sent similarly worded warning letters to some of the people and institutions involved in the deal on the investment side, naming Joshua Kushner, TripAdvisor chairman Greg Maffei and JPMorgan directly, along with the firm Open Economics.

The episode marks one of the most serious public ruptures between FIFA and UEFA in years, with Aleksander Čeferin's organization signalling it no longer trusts Infantino's leadership even after he abandoned the privatization plan. ONE's report, sourced to The Telegraph, frames it as a story still unfolding, with UEFA's next formal steps yet to be announced.
facts: UEFA sent FIFA president Gianni Infantino a letter warning it is considering litigation, arbitration or regulatory complaints over the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) project.
FFE, unveiled by FIFA on July 28, 2026, proposed selling roughly 20% of a new commercial subsidiary controlling World Cup and Club World Cup rights to private investors.
The plan reportedly valued the entity at around $20 billion and aimed to raise up to $4.2 billion.
Thrive Eternal, a firm launched by businessman Joshua Kushner, was the proposed lead investor, with JPMorgan Chase also involved.
UEFA, CONCACAF and Asian football bodies, plus numerous national federations, opposed the plan, prompting FIFA to abandon it days before UEFA's letter was revealed.
UEFA's letter demanded FIFA and Infantino preserve all documents and electronic records related to FFE, and similar letters were sent to Joshua Kushner, Greg Maffei, JPMorgan and Open Economics.

title: Barcelona waiting on Álvarez, but relaxed about the striker position
dek: Hansi Flick's side still have no formal answer from Atlético Madrid on their €100m bid for Julián Álvarez, but ONE reports Barcelona feel well covered up front after signing Anthony Gordon and Karim Adeyemi.
body: Barcelona are still waiting. More than two months after tabling an offer for Julián Álvarez, the club has yet to receive a formal response from Atlético Madrid, and ONE reports that despite the silence, the Camp Nou hierarchy is in no hurry to panic over its centre-forward options.

The €100 million bid for the Argentine World Cup winner went in with Hansi Flick's explicit backing, part of a summer in which Barcelona have made rebuilding their attack after Robert Lewandowski's exit a stated priority. Club officials still regard the offer as fair value, according to the report.

Atlético have shown no willingness to negotiate. The Madrid club has pushed back publicly and lodged complaints with both the Spanish football federation and FIFA, alleging Barcelona approached Álvarez without going through proper channels — a claim Barcelona reject.

Álvarez himself has not hidden his position. Speaking during the World Cup, the striker said he wanted his club to sit down and negotiate a sale, arguing it was the right outcome for everyone involved, though he stopped short of naming Barcelona directly.

August 10 looms as a potential flashpoint: that is the date Diego Simeone's squad expects Álvarez back at training, and how the player and club handle his return will be watched closely for signs of where the saga heads next.

Barcelona's calm, per ONE, stems largely from business already done elsewhere. The club has added Anthony Gordon from Newcastle United and Karim Adeyemi from Borussia Dortmund this summer, both signed to 2031 deals, giving Flick fresh pace and directness across the front line.

With Lamine Yamal, Raphinha and Ferran Torres already in the squad, and Dani Olmo able to fill in as a false nine when required, Barcelona believe they are not short of attacking options even without a recognised out-and-out replacement for Lewandowski.

President Joan Laporta has previously stressed that Barcelona's patience — and its offer — is not open-ended, and the club is said to be tracking alternatives in case the pursuit of Álvarez ultimately breaks down.
For now, the two clubs remain at an impasse: Atlético holding firm on a player under contract until 2030, and Barcelona betting that time, and their own squad depth, are on their side.
facts: Barcelona have offered Atlético Madrid roughly €100 million for Julián Álvarez, with no formal response yet, per ONE.

Barcelona's forward options also include Lamine Yamal, Raphinha, Ferran Torres and Dani Olmo, who can play as a false nine.

title: Leeds come back from 2-0 down to beat Liverpool 4-2 in Chicago
dek: Dominic Calvert-Lewin scored twice as Leeds overturned a two-goal deficit to hand Andoni Iraola his first defeat as Liverpool manager in a pre-season friendly at Soldier Field.
body: Liverpool's final pre-season workout before the new Premier League campaign ended in an ugly collapse, as Leeds United came from 2-0 down at Soldier Field in Chicago to win 4-2 and hand Andoni Iraola his first defeat since taking charge at Anfield.

It had looked routine for the Reds inside the first 40 minutes. Young defender Luke Chambers headed in unmarked from a flicked-on Dominik Szoboszlai corner in the seventh minute, and Florian Wirtz doubled the lead just before the break, arriving first to a Jeremie Frimpong cross to turn the ball home.

Leeds, promoted back to the Premier League last season and preparing under Daniel Farke for their top-flight return, made wholesale changes at the interval that transformed the game. Dominic Calvert-Lewin and Harry Wilson were among those introduced, and within 20 minutes of the restart the contest had flipped completely.

Brenden Aaronson pulled one back in the 60th minute to spark the fightback. Calvert-Lewin, the former Everton striker who joined Leeds on a free transfer, headed in a long throw from Ethan Ampadu to level in the 71st, and Sean Longstaff put Leeds ahead for the first time two minutes later.

Calvert-Lewin completed his brace in the closing stages, again converting from an Ampadu long throw, to seal a 4-2 win that exposed exactly the kind of defensive fragility that dogged Liverpool for long stretches of last season.

According to ONE, Szoboszlai was blunt in his post-match assessment, saying the team had conceded twice from set pieces and "must address this," adding that "each player must fulfil their role correctly."

There were individual positives for Iraola to take. Wirtz, back with the squad after featuring for Germany at this summer's World Cup, scored a composed goal, while academy prospect Trey Nyoni again caught the eye. Alexander Isak and Ryan Gravenberch also featured after returning from international duty.

It was the first loss of Iraola's short Liverpool tenure, following the Bournemouth-bound Spaniard's summer move to Anfield to replace Arne Slot, with the club having beaten Sunderland 4-2 and Wrexham 1-0 earlier on their United States tour.

For Leeds, the result is a timely confidence boost as Farke's side prepare for a first Premier League season back among the elite, having shown they can absorb a rocky start against top-flight opposition and still find a way to win.

title: Israel's U20 women fall 17-12 to Italy at European water polo championship
dek: Mia Tirosh scored four and Tava Dorfman three as Israel slipped to a second straight defeat in Oeiras, with defending champions Spain up next.

verificationSources.label: European Aquatics - day one report, Women's U20 European Championship

body: Israel's U20 women's water polo team lost for the second time in as many days at the European Championship in Oeiras, Portugal, going down 17-12 to Italy, ONE reports.
The Israelis started slowly, trailing 4-1 after the first quarter and 6-2 at halftime, before improving markedly after the break to make the scoreline respectable against a strong Italian side.

Mia Tirosh led the Israeli attack with four goals, with Tava Dorfman adding three. Carmel Racham scored twice, while Maya Katzir, Yuval Raz and Shir Weisman each found the net once, according to ONE's report.
"I am very proud of my team, because it showed heart, passion and a strong desire to win until the last moment," coach Orestis Salachas said afterwards, per ONE.

It was Israel's second defeat of the tournament. The team had opened the championship a day earlier with an 18-13 loss to Greece, a result independently confirmed by European Aquatics, which reported Israel trailing 4-4, 8-4, 12-7 and eventually 18-13 across the four quarters.
The Women's U20 European Water Polo Championship, running from August 3 to 9 in Oeiras, gathers 20 of the continent's national teams and doubles as the age-group's flagship event this summer.
Italy themselves have had a difficult start to the tournament, having been beaten 16-8 by Spain on the opening day, underlining the strength of Israel's group.
Israel's next assignment is against Spain, the reigning European champions, who have won every match so far in the group stage.

title: Hapoel Hadera drawn against Hapoel Marmorek in Liga Alef South opener
dek: The Israel Football Association's fixture release for the 2026/27 third-tier season pairs two clubs with a single, brief taste each of Israeli football's top flight in round one, ONE reports.
body: The Israel Football Association has published the fixture list for the 2026/27 Liga Alef season, and the pairing opening the campaign in the South division brings together two clubs who each spent exactly one season in Israeli football's top flight: Hapoel Marmorek and Hapoel Hadera meet in round one, ONE reported.

It reads as a modest fixture on paper - both sides play in the third tier of the Israeli pyramid - but each carries more history than its current level suggests. Marmorek, based in the Rehovot area, won promotion to the old National League for the only time in the club's history at the end of the 1971-72 season, beating Maccabi Shaarayim 2-1 in a playoff final settled by two goals from Tony Sharabi. The club came straight back down after that single 1972-73 top-flight campaign and has spent the decades since in the lower divisions.

Hadera's history runs deeper still. Photographs of the club's earliest players date back to 1939, when, according to accounts held with the club's archive, its founders travelled to away matches by horse and cart. Hapoel Hadera have remained a fixture of the Israeli game since, even as the club has drifted through the divisions.
Elsewhere in the Liga Alef South round-one draw, ONE reported that Shimshon Tel Aviv host Beitar Yavne, while Maccabi Kiryat Malakhi take on Hapoel Mahane Yehuda.
In the parallel North division, the opening round pits Maccabi Ata Bialik against Hapoel Migdal HaEmek, with Hapoel Beersheba facing Beitar Neria among the other headline pairings, the report said.

Both Liga Alef sections field 18 clubs apiece for the new season, which the Israel Football Association has scheduled to open on September 4, 2026, a week after the State Cup's fifth round begins on August 28.
The calendar includes a mid-season break from October 13-17 - timed around the Sportiad - with no league fixtures played, followed by a longer winter break running from November 14-21.

The regular season is due to finish on April 16, 2027, with playoff finals following from April 23-26, divisional finals on May 6-7, and the promotion play-off between the two divisions' contenders scheduled for May 13-14.
Round one itself is still more than a month away, but Marmorek and Hadera at least now have a date and an opponent to build their pre-season toward.

title: Berman and Skorka appointed to officiate Women's Champions League qualifiers
dek: The Israeli pair will take charge of matches in a four-team mini-tournament in Slovenia as clubs from Austria, Croatia, Romania and the hosts chase a place in the next qualifying round.

verificationSources.label: UEFA.com - Women's Champions League second qualifying round ties

body: Two Israeli match officials have been handed a plum European assignment: referee Sapir Berman and assistant referee Nofar Skorka have been appointed by UEFA to work matches in the second qualifying round of the Women's Champions League, ONE reported.

The pair will operate at a four-team mini-tournament being staged in Slovenia, one of several such groups UEFA uses to whittle down the competition's Champions Path before the group stage. The bracket brings together Austria Wien, Hajduk Split, hosts NŠ Mura and Farul Constanța.

Under the format, the four sides split into two semi-finals, with the winners meeting in a final and the losers playing off for third. Only the overall winner advances, into the third qualifying round. According to ONE, the games run between August 5 and August 8.

The Israel Football Referees Association congratulated Berman and Skorka on social media following the appointment, a rare moment in the spotlight for officials rather than players in an Israeli football week usually dominated by transfer and results news.

Berman's rise has already made headlines well beyond Israel. In March 2025 she became the first transgender woman to referee an international match, taking charge of a Women's Under-17 European Championship qualifier between Northern Ireland and Montenegro in Belfast. She has refereed in Israel's men's Premier League for over a decade and holds a UEFA international badge.

Skorka, from Rishon LeZion, brings her own playing background to the assignment. A former forward for Hapoel Ironi Rishon LeZion, Maccabi Holon and Ramat HaSharon in the Israeli women's top flight, she has run the line as an assistant referee in the national league since the 2016/17 season and now carries an international assistant's badge of her own.

For Israeli football, appointments like this have taken on added significance in recent years, with UEFA and FIFA continuing to hand officiating posts to Israeli referees at continental and global tournaments even as the men's national team's own path through Europe remains fraught. Berman and Skorka's assignment in Slovenia is the latest example.

title: Maccabi Tel Aviv drawn against OFI Crete in Europa League play-off round
dek: The Israeli State Cup holders will meet the Greek side for a place in the league phase — but only if they first get past CSKA Sofia in the third qualifying round.
body: Maccabi Tel Aviv now know their possible route into the Europa League's league phase: the club has been drawn against Greek side OFI Crete in the competition's play-off round, ONE reported on Monday, though the pairing only comes into effect if the Israeli champions first see off CSKA Sofia.

The reigning Israeli State Cup holders — Maccabi lifted their 25th title, and first since 2021, by beating Hapoel Beer Sheva at Teddy Stadium in Jerusalem in May — must clear the Bulgarian side in the third qualifying round before the OFI Crete tie becomes real.

That CSKA Sofia assignment comes first: the opening leg is set for August 6, hosted, as all of Maccabi's continental fixtures are this season, in Batumi, Georgia, because of the security situation at home. The return leg follows on August 13 at the Vasil Levski National Stadium in Sofia.

Should Maccabi get through, the play-off against OFI Crete would be played over August 20 (away in Greece) and August 27 (the home leg, again in Batumi). Victory there would send the club into the Europa League's league phase and secure a fourth straight winter of European football for the Yellow-and-Blue.

Maccabi arrive at this point off the back of a comfortable dispatch of Sheriff Tiraspol in the second qualifying round, winning 5-0 at home before closing out the tie with a 1-0 second leg, a 6-0 aggregate that carried them into the third round without much drama.

A defeat to CSKA Sofia would not end the European adventure outright — Maccabi would instead drop into the Conference League play-off round, contested on the same August 20 and 27 dates, against an opponent from a separate bracket to be confirmed once that stage of the draw is finalised.

OFI Crete, formally founded in 1925 and based in Heraklion, are one of Greek football's more storied provincial clubs and play their home matches at the 26,240-capacity Pankritio Stadium. They compete in the Super League Greece, the country's top flight.

For now the immediate task is domestic in scope but continental in stakes: beat CSKA Sofia over two legs, and the road to OFI Crete — and a shot at extending Maccabi's run of winter European nights to a fourth consecutive year — opens up in three weeks' time.

title: Referees chief Ziv Adler details Israeli football's expanded VAR powers and new rules
dek: The Israel Football Association's referees committee chairman explains the new season's VAR overhaul, tougher substitution timing and a crackdown on time-wasting.

verificationSources.label: ONE - השינויים בחוקה וסמכויות ה-VAR: זיו אדלר בראיון
Sky Sports - IFAB confirms new VAR powers, 10-second substitutions and tactical timeout ban

body: Israeli referees are heading into the new season with a noticeably fatter rulebook, and the man in charge of enforcing it has now laid out exactly what players, coaches and fans should expect to see on the pitch.

Ziv Adler, chairman of the Israel Football Association's referees committee, spoke to ONE about a package of new officiating rules adopted for Israeli football this season, most of them mirroring changes IFAB has approved globally ahead of the 2026 World Cup.

The headline change is an expansion of VAR's authority. The video assistant will now be able to intervene to overturn a yellow card shown in error, and can correct a wrongly awarded corner or goal kick via the referee's headset before play restarts. VAR still cannot step in to add a yellow card that was not shown on the pitch in the first place.

Substitutions are also getting stricter. A player must leave the field within ten seconds of the fourth official raising the board, and if he does not, his side plays on with ten men until the ball next goes out of play rather than being allowed to bring the substitute straight on. Adler called the sanction "more serious" than a yellow card and said it is designed specifically to stop players from stretching out substitution stoppages.

Injuries are being treated the same way. A player receiving treatment must now wait a full minute off the pitch before he is allowed back on, closing off what had become a familiar way for teams to run down the clock late in matches.

Goalkeepers face a tighter clock too. They now have just five seconds to release the ball from a throw-in or a goal kick, and a breach is punished with a corner or an indirect free-kick rather than a yellow card, a change intended to keep the ball moving rather than simply punishing keepers after the fact.

On player conduct, Adler noted a specific gap between Israeli practice and the World Cup: covering the mouth during a confrontation with an opponent is carded yellow in Israel, where it would be a straight red at the World Cup. He added that referees only act on abusive language when they hear it directly themselves.

Adler does not oversee this alone. He described working alongside senior officials Alon Yefet, who handles referee scheduling, Erez Papir, and Moshe Buhbot, while Idan Layba has moved from on-field refereeing into VAR duty.

He also pointed to numbers to back the system's track record: last season saw 141 critical errors corrected across 240 matches, a rate Adler said comfortably beats the roughly 50 percent correction rate typically cited for the Champions League.

The Israeli changes track closely with IFAB's 2026/27 Laws of the Game, which take effect from July 1, 2026 and were built with the World Cup in mind - extended VAR review of cards and corners, the 10-second substitution rule and a broader push against time-wasting. Adler's comments confirm Israeli football is adopting that global framework in full rather than a scaled-down local version.

title: Israel Under-18 handball team beat Switzerland 44-38 for first win at European Championship
dek: Goalkeeper Ruben Unanuno's 22 saves and 14 goals from Jonathan Pelach carried Israel's youth side to victory in Belgrade, keeping alive their hopes of reaching the World Championship.

verificationSources.label: Wikipedia — 2026 European Men's U-18 Handball Championship

body: Israel's youth national handball team picked up its first win of the European Men's U-18 Championship on Monday, beating Switzerland 44-38 in Belgrade to keep alive its hopes of qualifying for the World Championship, ONE reported.

The result mattered more than most group-stage wins. Israel had opened the tournament with a 33-29 loss to Croatia, followed by a 30-30 draw with the Czech Republic and a 30-22 defeat to Portugal, leaving the team fourth in its group and moving on to the intermediate round rather than the top bracket. The win over Switzerland now puts Israel back in contention for places 9-16, the bracket that leads to next year's World Championship.

According to ONE, the match itself was not straightforward. Israel fell behind 8-5 early on before clawing back to level at 10-10, then took control to lead 21-16 at halftime. Switzerland rallied in the second half and cut the gap sharply, but Israel steadied to close out the game 44-38.
Goalkeeper Ruben Unanuno was singled out by ONE as the standout performer, making 22 saves to keep Switzerland at arm's length through the tense closing stretch.

Jonathan Pelach led the scoring with 14 goals and also set up several of his teammates, continuing a tournament in which he has been Israel's most productive attacker — he scored 14 against Croatia as well.

Gav Dagani and Navo Masika each added seven goals, Tomer Michlis scored five, and the rest of the tally was shared around: Rom Tobis and Itay Gorbitz with three apiece, Uri Bochnik and Ido Malul with two each, and Noam Levi with one, per ONE's report.

Dor Rosso's squad now turns to Montenegro on Tuesday at 13:00 local time in a match that could effectively decide qualification — a win would confirm Israel's place among the teams heading to the World Championship qualifying bracket.

The championship, hosted across Serbia from July 29 to August 9, doubles as a qualifier for the 2027 IHF Men's U19 World Championship, giving the group stage and intermediate round extra weight for teams like Israel chasing a spot on the global stage.

title: Israel finish seventh in team free routine final at European Aquatics Championships
dek: France and Ukraine overtook Israel in the medal round in Paris, dropping the squad from fifth after prelims to seventh in the final standings, ONE reports.

verificationSources.label: ONE - מקום שביעי לישראל בגמר החופשי בשחייה אומנותית

body: Israel's artistic swimming team finished seventh in the team free routine final at the European Aquatics Championships in Paris on Monday, ONE reports, a step back after the squad had briefly looked on course for a higher finish.

The team scored 214.2970 points in the final, a clear improvement on the 206.4693 it posted in the preliminary round, according to ONE. That earlier score had been enough to send Israel through to the final in fifth place.

Finals night reshuffled the standings further down the field. France and Ukraine both raised their scores in the medal round and passed Israel, dropping the Israeli squad two places to seventh by the close of competition, ONE reported.

The eight swimmers who carried the routine were Yogev Dagan, Katy Konin, Alexandra Lerman, Noga Levi, Lior Mekamel, Leah Mekamel, Aya Mazor and Noya Tzarfati, a mixed group of established internationals and newer faces in the national programme.

There was little time to dwell on the placing. ONE reported that the same squad was already scheduled to return to the pool the following evening for the team technical routine final, offering an immediate chance to improve on its standing at these championships.

The result caps a mixed few days in the French capital for Israel's artistic swimming programme, which has expanded in recent years but is still working to close the gap on the sport's traditional European powers in team events.

title: Modric 2.0? The role Mourinho has in mind for Bernardo Silva at Real Madrid
dek: Free from Manchester City after nine seasons, the Portuguese midfielder has signed a two-year deal as Mourinho looks for a Modric-style presence to control tempo at the Bernabeu.
body: Bernardo Silva's free-transfer arrival at Real Madrid has been framed by returning manager Jose Mourinho as far more than squad depth. ONE reports that Mourinho wants the Portuguese midfielder to become the closest thing the club has had to a Luka Modric replacement since the Croatian's departure.

Silva, 31, completed the move after nine seasons at Manchester City, where his contract expired at the end of last season. He has signed a two-year deal, according to Ynet, running through 2028, with Sport5 reporting the club also holds an option for a third season.

It is a free transfer, but hardly a lesser one. Real Madrid saw off interest from both Barcelona and Atletico Madrid to land Silva's signature, after a campaign in which he made 55 appearances for City and started all 38 of their Premier League matches.

According to ONE, Mourinho is not expecting Silva to replicate Modric's game so much as replace the function he once served in midfield: supplying experience, footballing intelligence and control of tempo, even as the outlet stresses they are "two players with different characteristics."

The comparison carries extra weight given Mourinho's own history with Modric. It was Mourinho, during his first spell in charge at the Bernabeu, who pushed the club to sign the Croatian from Tottenham back in 2012, a deal that preceded more than a decade of Champions League and domestic success.

Positionally, ONE reports, Silva's versatility is central to the plan. He can play on the right wing, as a right-sided midfielder, in the number 10 role, or drop deeper to help build attacks from the back, giving Mourinho several ways to deploy him across a long season.

The move also reunites Silva with Kylian Mbappe, with whom he won the French title at Monaco in 2016-17, and Sport5 notes he is Real Madrid's second summer signing of the Mourinho era, following the arrival of defender Marc Cucurella.

ONE frames the signing as part of a broader shift in Real Madrid's recruitment strategy: after several transfer windows geared toward developing young talent, the club is again prioritizing ready-made experience alongside its emerging core.

title: Serbian coach warns Red Star: Ganah is a handful, Ventura is Be'er Sheva's key man
dek: Dušan Matović, who spent nearly a decade coaching in Israel, breaks down Hapoel Be'er Sheva's threat for Serbian media ahead of Tuesday's Champions League qualifier against his native Red Star Belgrade.

verificationSources.label: Jerusalem Post - Hapoel Beersheba advances to face Red Star Belgrade

body: On the eve of one of the biggest nights in the club's recent history, it is a voice from within Serbian football itself sounding the alarm about Hapoel Be'er Sheva's attacking threat.

Israeli champions Be'er Sheva host Red Star Belgrade on Tuesday (20:30 Israel time) in the first leg of the Champions League third qualifying round, a tie that will be played, as is now standard for Israeli clubs in Europe, at a neutral venue in Szombathely, Hungary. It is the first-ever meeting between the two clubs, with the winner advancing to the playoff round.

Ahead of the game, Dušan Matović — a Serbian coach who spent close to a decade working in Israeli football, including spells with Maccabi Haifa and Hapoel Tel Aviv — was called on by Serbian media to scout Be'er Sheva's squad, according to ONE.

Matović singled out winger Amir Ganah as the player who should worry Red Star's back line most. He is "dynamic, plays from the wing but loves to cut inside with his right foot," the coach said, describing him as a player who reads game situations well and is particularly difficult to defend against one-on-one.

Ganah, a 21-year-old academy product of the club, has been in prime form in this European run — he was on the scoresheet in Be'er Sheva's 2-0 win over Vikingur Reykjavik last week that sent them through 3-2 on aggregate, alongside a goal from Zahi Ahmad.

On the other side of the pitch, Matović pointed to Brazilian midfielder Lucas Ventura as the man who controls the team's identity. Ventura, he said, is "responsible for game management and applying pressure," acting as the hub of Be'er Sheva's aggressive, high-pressing style.

The coach did identify a potential route in for Red Star, however: breaking Be'er Sheva's initial press line, he suggested, is where the team can be hurt. He also flagged that right back Guy Mizrahi occasionally leaves space in behind — though he was careful to stress that, overall, Be'er Sheva are a well-organised, well-coordinated side.
Be'er Sheva arrive at this stage having needed a response after a 2-1 first-leg defeat away to Icelandic champions Vikingur Reykjavik, before winning the return 2-0 to progress on aggregate.
Red Star, by contrast, have barely broken sweat, thrashing Northern Ireland's Larne 9-0 across two legs of the previous round to book their place in the third qualifying round as Serbian champions.

For Be'er Sheva, a result over the two legs would represent a landmark European run for the club and open the door to the Champions League playoff round — with Ganah's directness and Ventura's control, by the assessment of a coach who knows Israeli football intimately, central to any chance of pulling it off.

title: Maccabi Tel Aviv fined and ordered to play Europa League tie without fans
dek: UEFA hits the Israeli champions with a €40,000 fine and a closed-doors order for the visit of CSKA Sofia, after pyrotechnics were set off during the win over Sheriff Tiraspol.

verificationSources.label: Maccabi Tel Aviv FC - Club Statement
Ynet - UEFA orders Maccabi to freeze ticket sales for European match

body: UEFA has fined Maccabi Tel Aviv €40,000 and ordered the club to play its next European home match without spectators, ONE reports, after supporters set off pyrotechnics during the Europa League qualifier against Sheriff Tiraspol.

The punishment lands directly on Maccabi's next fixture: the Europa League third qualifying round first leg against CSKA Sofia at Bloomfield Stadium on August 9, kick-off 19:00, which will now be played in an empty stadium.

The disciplinary case was opened after flares and other pyrotechnic devices were ignited by fans during Maccabi's home leg against the Moldovan side Sheriff Tiraspol. UEFA had already moved to freeze ticket sales for the CSKA Sofia fixture while the process ran its course, with the club stressing at the time that the sales freeze did not necessarily mean the match would be closed to fans.

That caveat no longer applies. With the disciplinary process now concluded, UEFA's ruling means Kenny Miller's side will have to try to build a first-leg advantage in near silence, before travelling to Bulgaria for the return fixture.

Miller, the Scottish head coach who took interim charge of Maccabi during last season's play-offs and led the club to State Cup glory over Hapoel Be'er Sheva, was subsequently handed the job on a permanent basis. The closed-doors order against CSKA Sofia is an early setback in his first full campaign, robbing his team of home advantage at a stadium UEFA competition matches usually pack out.

It is not the first time Maccabi's fans have drawn UEFA's attention this year. The club was previously fined €20,000 and given a suspended one-match ban on away ticket sales over alleged racist or discriminatory chanting by supporters during a Europa League trip to Stuttgart, with that punishment held in abeyance for a probationary period.

CSKA Sofia arrive in Tel Aviv with their own disciplinary baggage. UEFA fined the Bulgarian club separately and imposed a one-match travelling ticket ban after crowd trouble, including an alleged racist salute, object-throwing and fans breaching security barriers, marred their own qualifying tie against Ireland's Derry City.

For Maccabi, the immediate consequence is sporting as much as financial: a European home tie stripped of its crowd just as the club looks to build momentum through the qualifying rounds and toward the group stage.
